167:
## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Peṭakopadesa Pāḷi
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One.
## 1. The First Stage: Proclamation of the Noble Truths
## Homage to the Fully Enlightened Ones, who see the ultimate meaning and have reached the perfection of virtues such as morality.

There are two causes and two conditions for the arising of right view (sammādiṭṭhi) in a disciple: the voice from another (paratoghosa) in connection with the Truths, and internal wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). Among these two, what is the voice from another? It is the teaching, advice, instruction, talk on truth, and that which is in conformity with the Truths coming from another. There are four Truths: suffering (dukkha), the origin (samudaya), cessation (nirodha), and the path (magga). The teaching, showing, opening, analyzing, making clear, and first-hand proclamation of these four Truths is called the voice in conformity with the Truths (paratoghosa).

Among these two, what is internal wise attention (yoniso manasikāra)?

Internal wise attention is the wise attention that occurs without directing the mind toward external objects in the Dhamma as it has been taught. This is called wise attention.

The mode of that wise attention is the proper door, the method, and the means. For example, just as a man who places dry wood, devoid of sap, on a dry fire-drill and rubs it on the ground is capable of obtaining fire. Why is that? Because it is the proper method for obtaining fire. In the same way, there is the attention to the undistorted teaching of the Dhamma concerning suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. All this is called wise attention (yoniso manasikāra).
168:
Just as three similes, unheard of before and with no prior precedent, become clear—such as 'whatever person is not yet free from lust for sensual pleasures...' (and so on)—two similes are mentioned regarding improper attention in the latter causes. Among those two causes, there are the voice from another (paratoghosa) and internal wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). The wisdom that arises from the voice from another is called wisdom consisting in what is heard (sutamayi-paññā). The wisdom that arises from internal wise attention is called wisdom consisting in reflection (cintāmayi-paññā). These two types of wisdom should be understood, as well as the two previously mentioned causes. These two causes and two conditions are for the arising of right view in a disciple.

Among those causes, it is impossible that one who does not understand the meaning of the voice from another taught in connection with the Truths will become one who experiences the meaning. It is not that one who experiences the meaning will not attend wisely; rather, he will. It is possible that one who understands the meaning of the voice from another taught in connection with the Truths will become one who experiences the meaning. And it is possible that one who experiences the meaning will attend wisely. This alone is the cause, the object, and the means for the disciple's liberation; there is no other. If that cause is not joined with the understanding of the meaning of the Sutta or with the application of the teaching, it is impossible for one who does not understand the meaning of the voice from another to attain the superhuman state (uttari-manussadhamma), the noble knowledge and vision capable of destroying defilements. Therefore, one who desires Nibbāna should seek the meanings through wisdom consisting in what is heard. In seeking that meaning, the sequence is as follows: the sixteen hāras (modes of conveyance), the five nayas (methods), and the eighteen mūlapadas (root terms).

## Regarding the search for meaning, this is the Summary Verse (Uddāna-gāthā):

The Netti text with sixteen hāras, the five methods for seeking the meaning of the Dispensation,
And the eighteen root terms were shown by the Elder of the Kaccāyana lineage.

Among them, what are the sixteen hāras?

Desanā-hāra (Mode of Teaching), Vicaya-hāra (Mode of Investigation), Yutti-hāra (Mode of Reasoning), Padaṭṭhāna-hāra (Mode of Proximate Cause), Lakkhaṇa-hāra (Mode of Characteristic), Catubyūha-hāra (Mode of Fourfold Array), Āvaṭṭa-hāra (Mode of Cycling), Vibhatti-hāra (Mode of Analysis), Parivattana-hāra (Mode of Reversal), Vevacana-hāra (Mode of Synonyms), Paññatti-hāra (Mode of Description), Otaraṇa-hāra (Mode of Landing), Sodhana-hāra (Mode of Cleansing), Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra (Mode of Formulation), Parikkhāra-hāra (Mode of Requisite), and Samāropana-hāra (Mode of Co-ordination). These are the sixteen hāras.
170:
## In this regard, these are the summary verses (Uddānagāthā):

Craving (taṇhā), ignorance (avijjā), greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), and likewise delusion (moha), and the four perversions (vipallāsa)—these nine are the ground of defilements (kilesabhūmi). The foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), tranquility (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the wholesome roots (kusalamūla)—all these wholesome states are the nine terms of the ground of faculties (indriyabhūmi). All wholesome states are associated with these nine terms, and likewise, all unwholesome states are associated with nine terms. Each has nine root terms, making eighteen root terms in both categories.

Among these eighteen root terms, those nine terms that are unwholesome constitute the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (dukkhasamudayasacca). Those nine terms that are wholesome constitute the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodhagāminīpaṭipadā, i.e., the Path). Thus, the fruit of the origin (samudaya) is suffering (dukkha), and the fruit of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering is cessation (nirodha). These Four Noble Truths were taught by the Blessed One in the city of Vārāṇasī.

Among these four truths, the Blessed One taught the Noble Truth of Suffering through infinite letters, words, phrasing, modes, language, and descriptions, for the purpose of clarifying, revealing, disclosing, analyzing, making plain, and making known its meaning. This is the same for all the truths. Thus, each truth should be sought through infinite letters, words, phrasing, modes, language, and descriptions. Those phrasings should be sought both through the diversity of meaning and the diversity of phrasing.

If any ascetic or brahmin were to say, "I will reject this suffering and point out another suffering," it would be a mere matter of words, and if questioned, he would not be able to explain it. Such are the truths. Whatever the Blessed One spoke between the night he attained supreme enlightenment and the night he attained final Nibbāna without residue—whether Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, or Vedalla—all of it is the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka). There is nothing of the Buddhas...
171:
In the teaching of the Buddhas, there is nothing outside the Wheel of Dhamma; all those discourses (suttas) should be sought within the Noble Truths. For the purpose of such discernment, these four Noble Truths are the permanent realities that serve as light.

Among those four, what is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth (jāti), aging (jarā), sickness (byādhi), death (maraṇa), and in brief, the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) are suffering. To describe their characteristics: birth has the characteristic of manifestation; aging has the characteristic of ripening; sickness has the characteristic of affliction; death has the characteristic of falling away. Sorrow (soka) has the characteristic of separation from the loved, of change, and of burning; lamentation (parideva) has the characteristic of wailing; pain (dukkha) has the characteristic of bodily oppression; displeasure (domanassa) has the characteristic of mental oppression; despair (upāyāsa) has the characteristic of being burnt by defilements. Association with the unloved (appiyasampayoga) has the characteristic of meeting with those who are disliked; separation from the loved (piyavippayoga) has the characteristic of being parted from those who are liked; non-gain (alābha) has the characteristic of the frustration of desire when not obtaining what is wanted. The five aggregates of clinging have the characteristic of being incomprehensible. Aging and death have the characteristics of ripening and falling away. Passing away and rebirth have the characteristics of manifestation and falling away. The origin (samudaya) has the characteristic of producing rebirth. Cessation (nirodha) has the characteristic of abandoning the origin. The path (magga) has the characteristic of eradicating the latent tendencies (anusaya). Suffering has the characteristic of being an affliction; the origin has the characteristic of making known the cause of the round of rebirth; the path has the characteristic of leading out of the round; cessation has the characteristic of peace. The Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa nibbānadhātu) has the characteristic of non-rebirth and cessation. There are combinations of suffering and origin, suffering and cessation, suffering and path; origin and suffering, origin and cessation, origin and path; cessation and origin, cessation and suffering, cessation and path; path and cessation, path and origin, and path and suffering.

In this regard, there are these discourses:
"From the first night a person dwells in the womb, he proceeds as if the sun has risen; as he goes, there is no turning back."

Ānanda, these eight types of rebirth due to giving (dānupapatti) are in the Ekuttarika Nikaya. This is birth (jāti).

Among those sufferings, what is aging (jarā)?
"Those who have not lived the holy life, nor gained wealth in their youth, pine away like old herons in a dried-up pond without fish."

There are also the five omens among the devas. This is aging (jarā).
172:
## Among those sufferings, what is sickness (byādhi)?

"O King, was that aging not made by yourself? You too say that you are aging. The world is the fruit of kamma; indeed, one cannot abandon kamma."

There are three types of sick persons (gilāna). This is sickness (byādhi).

## Among those sufferings, what is death (maraṇa)?

Just as all clay vessels made by a potter—whether small or large, whether baked or unbaked—all end in breaking, so too is the life of mortals ended by death.

Look at these beings trembling over what they cherish as 'mine,' like fish in a pond with little water and a drying stream. Seeing this, one should live without 'mine-making,' not forming attachment to existences.

The Udakkappana Sutta; this is death (maraṇa).

## Among those sufferings, what is sorrow (soka)?

An evil-doer sorrows in this world, he sorrows in the next; he sorrows in both places. He sorrows and is vexed, seeing his own defiled kamma.

There are the three types of misconduct (duccarita). This is sorrow (soka).

## Among those sufferings, what is lamentation (parideva)?

Those who are greedy for sense pleasures, obsessed, deluded, of unspeakable nature, and established in the uneven [sense objects], when brought to suffering, they lament: "What will we become after passing away from here?"

There are the three types of failure (vipatti). This is lamentation (parideva).
173:
Among those sufferings, what is suffering (dukkha)?

Like hundreds of iron spikes are all the various feelings;
they are crowded and disturbed by a mass of flames, like a blazing forest fire.

That burning is indeed very intense. As stated in the Sutta of the Sacca Saṃyutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya—this is dukkha.

Among those sufferings, what is displeasure (domanassa)?

Oppressed by wrong thoughts, he broods like a poor man;
hearing the (reproachful) voices of others, such a person becomes dejected.

These two are the things that cause remorse—this is domanassa.

Among those sufferings, what is despair (upāyāsa)?

Just as a smith's furnace burns within and not without,
so my heart burns upon hearing what has arisen (unpleasantness).

The fires are three—this is upāyāsa.

Among those sufferings, what is association with the unloved (appiyasampayoga)?

Just as rust arising from iron eats away that very iron,
so his own deeds lead the one of transgressive conduct to a miserable destination.

These two persons slander the Tathāgata, as stated in the Sutta of the Book of Twos in the Ekuttara Nikāya—this is appiyasampayoga.

Among those sufferings, what is separation from the loved (piyavippayoga)?

Just as a man who has awakened does not see the meeting he had in a dream,
even so, one does not see the beloved person who has passed away and died.

Those devas, knowing the sign of passing away, exhort with three words. This is piyavippayoga.
174:
The three daughters of Māra do not obtain what they desire.
If those sensual pleasures of a being who is filled with desire and longing
should fail, he suffers and is distressed like one pierced by an arrow.

In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering (dukkha).

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind
are the terrible baits (āmisa) of the world.
In these sense bases, worldlings are attached.

Monks, these five aggregates are called dukkha (suffering).

Among those sufferings, what are aging and death (jarā and maraṇa)?
Short indeed is this life; one dies within a hundred years.
Or even if one lives longer, one surely dies of old age.
The Sutta in the Pasenadi Saṃyutta of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, "My grandmother has passed away"—this is jarā and maraṇa.

Among those sufferings, what are passing away and rebirth (cuti and upapatti)?
"All beings will die, for life ends in death;
they will go according to their kamma, undergoing the results of their own deeds."
This is cuti and upapatti.

By these suttas and other similar ones, nine kinds of suttas are shown. Entering into them in order and knowing dukkha by its characteristics, the common (sādhāraṇa) and uncommon (asādhāraṇa) Noble Truth of Dukkha should be pointed out. Verse should be inferred by verse, and exposition (vyākaraṇa) by exposition—this is the Truth of Dukkha.

In that context, what is the origin of suffering (dukkhasamudaya)?
Beings attached to sensual pleasures, clinging to the fetters of sensuality, not seeing the danger in the fetters,
can never cross the vast and great flood (ogha).
The Sutta on the Four Taints (āsava) is dukkhasamudaya.
175:
Among those four truths, what is the cessation of suffering (dukkha-nirodha)?

In whom deceit (māyā) does not dwell and conceit (māna) does not exist,
who is free from greed, without possessiveness, and without longing,
who has discarded anger and has a calmed mind—
he is called a Brahmin, he is a Samana, he is a Bhikkhu.

These two types of liberation—liberation of mind (cetovimutti) through the fading of lust, and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) through the fading of ignorance—are called the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca).

Among those four truths, what is the Truth of the Path (maggasacca)?

This is the only path; there is no other for the purification of vision.
This is the Noble Eightfold Path; it is the bewilderment of Māra.

Monks, these seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are called the Truth of the Path.

In that teaching, what are the Four Noble Truths?

"Of those things that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has told the cause,
and also their cessation; this is the doctrine of the Great Samana."

Things arising from a cause are the Truth of Dukkha; the cause is the Truth of Samudaya; that Dhamma of Nibbāna taught by the Blessed One is the Truth of Nirodha. For those who dwell contemplating gratification in things that are fetters, the craving of defilements increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises... thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. Therein, whatever fetter exists—this is the Truth of Samudaya. The things that are fetters and the sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair that arise—this is the Truth of Dukkha. The repeated contemplation of the danger in things that are fetters—this is the Truth of the Path. Liberation from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and lamentation, up to despair—this is Nibbāna. These are the Four Truths.

In that teaching of the truths, what is the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa nibbānadhātu)?

For one who has reached the end (ceased), there is no measure; there is no means by which one could describe him.
When all things (attachments) are completely removed, all paths of speech are also removed for the wise one who knows all.

## The Godhika Saṃyutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
176:
These are the uncommon discourses (asādhāraṇa suttas). In whichever discourses the truths are pointed out, one should investigate that meaning through the characteristics of the truths and through immeasurable phrasing. In such investigation, one should seek the following of the meaning by the phrasing, and the following of the phrasing by the meaning. With these discourses as they are laid down, the immeasurable phrasing of each of those truths and the Four Noble Truths (Ariyasaccāni) should be pointed out. Verses should be compared with verses included in the five Nikāyas, and exposition (byākaraṇa) with exposition. These are the uncommon discourses.

## These are the summary verses (uddāna gāthā) for them

First staying (in the womb) for one night, the eight rebirths through giving,
The five portents, and like a pond with dried-up fish.
The discourse "Where is there danger for King Sāma?", the three sick deities,
Like the potter's jar, like the river without water.
He sorrows here, he sorrows hereafter, and the three misconducts,
Lustful and obsessed with sensual pleasures, as far as the three failures.
Living for a hundred years, feeling like a glowing iron spike, great burning,
He is oppressed by wrong thoughts and by torments.
Like the smith's forge, the three fires are shown,
Like rust arising from iron, false accusations against the Tathāgata.
The deities admonish with three words, like meeting in a dream,
The three daughters of Māra, and the affliction like one pierced by an arrow.
The eye, ear, nose, and the five aggregates are shown,
The discourse "This life is indeed short, my grandmother is old."
All beings shall die, the collection of birth and death,
Beings obsessed with sensual pleasures, and the four taints (āsavas).
In whom no deceit (māyā) dwells, the two kinds of liberation of mind,
This alone is the path, there is no other, and the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgas) are well-taught.
177:
For one who has reached the end (of suffering), there is no measure; the Elder Godhika has attained Parinibbāna. Those who repeatedly contemplate the fetters and the phenomena arising from causes.

## These are the ten summary verses (uddāna gāthā) for them.

Among those summary verses, there are common discourses (sādhāraṇa suttas) in which the common truths are taught in direct order (anuloma), reverse order (paṭiloma), or mixed order (vomissaka). Here is the beginning:

"The world is obstructed by ignorance;
It is not manifest due to confusion and negligence.
I call craving the smearing;
Suffering is its great fear."

In that teaching, ignorance and confusion are the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The great fear is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). These are the two truths: suffering and origin. In the Citta Saṃyutta of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, there is an exposition: "The fetter and the things that are objects of the fetter." There, the fetter is the Truth of the Origin. The things that are objects of the fetter are the Truth of Suffering. These are the two truths: suffering and origin.

Among them, what are suffering and the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca)?

"For the monk who has cut off craving for existence,
Who has cut the cord (of fetters),
The cycle of birth is exhausted;
Now there is no more renewed existence."

Whatever mind there is, this mind is the Truth of Suffering. The cutting off of craving for existence is the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. "The cycle of birth is exhausted, there is no more renewed existence" is the description. These are the two truths: suffering and cessation. Monks, there are these two liberations: liberation of mind through the fading away of lust (rāga-virāga), and liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance (avijjā-virāga). Whatever mind there is, this mind is the Truth of Suffering. Whatever liberation there is, this liberation is the Truth of Cessation. These are the two truths: suffering and cessation.

Among them, what are suffering and the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca)?

"Knowing this body to be like a jar,
Establishing this mind like a city,
One should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom;
One should protect what has been won and be unattached to defilements."
178:
Among those truths, the body which is like a pot and the mind which is like a city are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The practice that one should fight Māra, the defilements, with the weapon of wisdom is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). These are the two truths. O monks, that which is not yours should be abandoned. The fetter is the Truth of the Path. The things from form up to consciousness, which are to be abandoned as they are not-self, are the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Path.

Among those truths, what are the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin, and the Truth of Cessation?

In the world, there are many forms of sorrow and lamentation.
These sorrows and so forth arise depending on a dear object.
If there is no dear object, these sorrows and so forth do not arise.

That sorrow, lamentation, and the manifold suffering born of affection (pema) are the Truth of Suffering. That affection is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The removal of desire and lust (chandarāga) for that dear object is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). These are the three truths. Timbaruka the wanderer wanders with the view: "Suffering is self-created, suffering is created by others." Such investigation is the Truth of Suffering. Not approaching these two extremes, the Middle Way—from the arising of volitional formations caused by ignorance up to the arising of aging and death caused by birth—is also the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Origin. Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, becoming, birth, aging and death are the Truth of Suffering. Ignorance, volitional formations, craving, and clinging are the Truth of the Origin. Thus, in investigating this Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) as self-created, the suffering involved in Dependent Origination is pointed out as the Truth of the Origin. The cessation of volitional formations due to the cessation of ignorance, up to the cessation of aging and death, is the Truth of Cessation. These are the three truths: Suffering, Origin, and Cessation.

Among those truths, what are the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin, and the Truth of the Path?

"When one has seen suffering and the source from which it arises, how could that person incline towards sensual pleasures?
Knowing that sensual pleasures are a bond (fetter) in the world, a mindful person should train to remove those sensual pleasures" (thus He taught).
179:
He who sees suffering, this is the Truth of Suffering. The cause from which it arises, this is the Truth of the Origin. The result that occurs in the present is due to a cause; the training to remove that craving is the Truth of the Path. These are the three truths.

## The Gopālakopama Sutta in the Ekādasakanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

In that teaching, the six sense bases associated with form, and the mind that covers like a wound, and the noble joy and rapture (pīti-pāmojja) of four kinds which has the physical body as its basis and is associated with jhāna—this is the Truth of Suffering. The physical body (rūpakāya) which is a collection of longings and so forth—this is the Truth of the Origin. Knowing the various ways of covering the wound which is pleasant in the longing associated with form, and being skilled in the pasture (objects of meditation)—this is the Truth of the Path. The remaining states exist; the cause exists; the supporting conditions (upanissaya) exist; the consequence which is beneficial, the consequence due to much offerings, the state of having good friends (kalyāṇamitta), and the state of knowing the ultimate reality (paramattha-dhamma) are called the cause—these are the three truths.

Among those truths, what are Suffering, the Path, and Cessation?

Mindfulness of the body is established,
There is restraint in the six sense bases,
The monk who is always concentrated,
Should know his own Nibbāna.

In those teachings, the mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) and the six sense bases that exist in a person—all that is called the Truth of Suffering. The mindfulness of the body, the restraint of virtue (sīla), the concentration (samadhī), and the mindfulness that exists—this is the aggregate of wisdom (paññā-kkhandha). All the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) are called the aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration—this is the Truth of the Path. One who dwells in this way should know Nibbāna—this is the Truth of Cessation. These are the three truths. Established in virtue, one should develop the two states: serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). In that teaching, the states that arise together with the mind exist due to a cause—this is the Truth of Suffering. The serenity and the insight that exist—this is the Truth of the Path. Due to the fading away of lust, there is liberation of mind (cetovimutti, the fruit of Non-returning); due to the fading away of delusion, there is liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti, the fruit of Arahantship)—this is the Truth of Cessation. These are the three truths.
180:
Among those truths, which are the Truth of Origin and the Truth of Cessation?

Longing, desire, and delight are established in many elements. Those [desires] rooted in ignorance, I have completely eliminated along with their roots.

By the phrase 'rooted in ignorance', the previously mentioned Truth of Origin is shown. By the phrase 'I have completely eliminated along with their roots', the Truth of Cessation is shown. These are the two truths. The non-understanding and non-penetration of the four qualities should be elaborated. In terms of noble virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation, the non-understanding and non-penetration of these four qualities is the Truth of Origin. The penetration of the 'lead to becoming' (bhavanetti) is the Truth of Cessation. This is the Truth of Origin and the Truth of Cessation.

Among those truths, which are the Truth of Origin and the Truth of the Path?

Whatever streams [of craving] there are in the world, mindfulness is their restraint. I call it the restraint of the streams; they are closed by wisdom.

This teaching, 'Whatever streams there are', is the Truth of Origin. That wisdom and that mindfulness which are the restraint and the closing [of the streams] is the Truth of the Path. These are the two truths. In the Sañcetanīya Sutta, the manner of King Daḷhanemi is pointed out through six months. Therein, whatever bodily action occurs with crookedness, with fault, and with the stain of defilements—that crookedness, faultiness, and stain is the Truth of Origin. Similarly, in verbal and mental actions, whatever occurs without crookedness, without fault, and without the stain of defilements—that lack of crookedness, faultiness, and stain is the Truth of the Path. The same applies to verbal and mental actions. These are the two truths: the Truth of Origin and the Truth of the Path.

Among those truths, which are the Truth of Origin, the Truth of Cessation, and the Truth of the Path?

'For one who is dependent, there is wavering; for one who is independent, there is no wavering. When there is no wavering, there is tranquility; when there is tranquility, there is no inclination. When there is no inclination, there is no coming and going; when there is no coming and going, there is no passing away and reappearing. When there is no passing away and reappearing, there is neither this world, nor the world beyond, nor anything between the two. This itself is the end of suffering.' (Thus He taught).
181:
In that teaching, there are two dependencies; this is the Truth of Origin. Non-dependency on the three rounds of existence and non-inclination is the Truth of the Path. The state where there is no going towards the noble path [in the sense of worldly movement] and no knowledge of passing away and reappearing, which is the end of suffering—this is the Truth of Cessation. These are the three truths. From unestablished mindfulness of the body etc., whatever reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) there is, this is the Truth of Origin. The eleven fruits of Arahantship with their supporting conditions arise for one who dwells with established mindfulness of the body until the fulfillment of the supporting conditions. Restraint through virtue and whatever reviewing knowledge and vision there is, is the Truth of the Path. Whatever the fruit of Arahantship is, is the Truth of Cessation. These are the three truths: the Truth of Origin, the Truth of Cessation, and the Truth of the Path.

Among those truths, which are the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path?

By that Noble Truth realized by oneself, having reached Nibbāna by direct realization and crossed over doubt,
Knowing the end of existence in the world, that monk who has first exhausted rebirth (reaches Cessation and the Path).

Attaining through the Truth is the Truth of the Path. The exhaustion of rebirth is the Truth of Cessation. These are the two truths. The five bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana) should be elaborated: 'The Teacher or a certain wise fellow-monk teaches the Dhamma.' For one who penetrates the meaning, joy arises; for one who is joyful, rapture arises; this teaching, which leads up to disenchantment and dispassion, is the Truth of the Path. Whatever the fruit of Arahantship is, is the Truth of Cessation. Thus the five bases of liberation should be understood in detail. These are the two truths: the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path.

These suttas are generally common (sādhāraṇa). A person who does not decline should point out other suttas by incorporating them through penetration and through characteristics using these common suttas as they are laid down. Verses should be compared with verses, and explanations (vyākaraṇa) with explanations. These ten expanding (parivaḍḍhaka) suttas and the one explanation of the groups of four (catukka-niddesa) are called common suttas. This is the miscellaneous explanation (pakiṇṇaka-niddesa). All those miscellaneous explanations that point out parts consist of one, five, or six. Excluding these two—the common and the miscellaneous—the ten previously mentioned and these twelve expanding suttas are the truths. By this much sequence of words, all suttas are not limited; they are like explanations or verses. A heedful person should point them out by seeking to enter into them through these twelve expanding suttas.

In that context, the summary is as follows: All suffering converges into seven terms. Which seven? Association with the unloved and separation from the loved. These...
182:
All suffering should be indicated by two terms. Its bases are two: the body and the mind. Therefore, it is said, "bodily suffering and mental suffering." There is no suffering that is neither bodily nor mental. All suffering should be indicated by these two types of suffering: bodily suffering (kāyika-dukkha) and mental suffering (cetasika-dukkha). It is comprised of three modes of suffering: the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkhatā), the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā), and the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā). Thus, all suffering is comprised of these three modes of suffering. Thus, this suffering is of three kinds. Suffering is of two kinds: bodily and mental. It is also of two kinds: association with the unloved (appiyasampayoga) and separation from the loved (piyavippayoga). This is suffering in seven ways.

In that teaching, the origin (samudaya), which is neither a fourth nor a fifth, is of three kinds. What are the three kinds? Craving (taṇhā), view (diṭṭhi), and kamma. Among those, craving and kamma are the origin of existence (bhava-samudaya). Likewise, the state of being low or exalted of one who has arisen is also called the truth of origin. Thus, whatever is low or exalted in the realms of existence, whatever is comprised of the three modes of suffering, and whatever body with consciousness arises through the two roots for one who is obstructed by ignorance (avijjā) and fettered by craving for existence—that body is also comprised of the three modes of suffering.

Furthermore, wrong view (diṭṭhi) should be understood through perversion (vipallāsa). That view should be indicated in seven ways. One perversion, three perversions, and four objects of perversion are indicated. Therein, what is the one perversion? It is that which is a distorted grasp; it is indicated by rejection, an entry, such as taking what is impermanent as "permanent," thus grasping distortedly. Thus, there are four perversions. This one perversion exists as perversion of perception (saññā), mind (citta), and view (diṭṭhi). What are the four objects of perversion? Body (kāya), feeling (vedanā), mind (citta), and phenomena (dhammā). For one who has thus reached perversion, it increases the unwholesome. Therein, the perversion of perception increases the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa). The perversion of mind increases the unwholesome root of greed (lobha). The perversion of view increases the unwholesome root of delusion (moha). Therein, the fruits of the unwholesome root of hatred are three wrong states that occur as a consequence: wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood. The fruits of the unwholesome root of greed are three wrong states that occur as a consequence: wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration. The fruits of the unwholesome root of delusion are two wrong states that occur as a consequence: wrong view and wrong mindfulness. Thus, the unwholesome occurs with its cause (hetu) and with its condition (paccaya); the perversions are also causes. The unwholesome roots have causes. These very unwholesome states, neither less nor more, should be indicated by two conditions through their opposites. In the truth of cessation (nirodha) and the truth of the path (magga), based on perversion, the four truths are indicated subsequently through their opposites.
183:
## In this (First Stage of the Proclamation of the Noble Truths), there are these summary verses:

The world is obstructed by ignorance; the mind also has fetters. That (bhikkhunī) has cut off craving for existence; these liberations are only two.

(Regard) this body as like a jar; abandon the form that is not yours. Indefinite sorrow and lamentation arise because of one's own performed kamma; the deity Timbruka also (suffers because of his own performed kamma).

Arisen suffering and view are like a cowherd. Mindfulness directed to the body is called tranquillity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).

There are longing, love, and delight, and those currents (sota) such as craving in the world. Because of not knowing the four things, (one is fixed in saṃsāra) just as a rim makes a vehicle firm.

For one who relies, there is trembling; one who does not manifest mindfulness of the body makes himself free (from trembling) through the truth he has performed and through the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana).

The First Stage, which is the Proclamation of the Noble Truths, spoken by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana in the Peṭakopadesa in accordance with the teaching of the living, well-proclaiming Tathāgata Buddha, who is like me, is finished.

## 2. The Second Stage: The Setting Forth of the Dispensation (Sāsanapaṭṭhāna)

Among those settings forth of the dispensation, what is the setting forth of the dispensation? Suttas dealing with defilement (saṃkilesa), suttas dealing with habitual tendencies (vāsanā), suttas dealing with penetration (nibbedha), suttas dealing with the one beyond training (asekha); suttas dealing with both defilement and habitual tendencies; suttas dealing with both defilement and penetration; suttas dealing with defilement, penetration, and the one beyond training; suttas dealing with both habitual tendencies and penetration. Suttas on instruction (āṇatti), suttas on fruit (phala), suttas on means (upāya); suttas on instruction and fruit; suttas on fruit and means; suttas on instruction, fruit, and means. Suttas on gratification (assāda), suttas on danger (ādīnava), suttas on escape (nissaraṇa); suttas on gratification and danger; suttas on gratification and escape; suttas on danger and escape; suttas on gratification, danger, and escape. Mundane suttas, supramundane suttas, suttas on both mundane and supramundane. Suttas on kamma, suttas on result (vipāka), suttas on kamma and result. Suttas that are specified (niddiṭṭha), suttas that are unspecified (aniddiṭṭha), suttas on both specified and unspecified. Suttas on knowledge (ñāṇa), suttas on the knowable (ñeyya), suttas on knowledge and the knowable. Suttas on vision (dassana), suttas on development (bhāvana), suttas on vision and development. Suttas on kamma as result (vipākakamma), suttas on kamma that is not result (navipākakamma), (and so forth).
184:
Discourses that are neither result (vipāka) nor result-producing kamma, discourses of one's own words, discourses of others' words, discourses of both one's own and others' words, discourses based on beings, discourses based on dhammas, discourses based on both beings and dhammas, causal discourses, discourses based on one's own words, discourses based on others' words, discourses based on both one's own and others' words, functional (kiriya) discourses, fruition (phala) discourses, discourses of both function and fruition, permitted discourses, prohibited discourses, and discourses that are both permitted and prohibited. These six types are called rejected (paṭikkhitta) discourses.

Among those discourses, what is a discourse leading to defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya)?

Blinded by sensual lust, covered by the net of craving,
shrouded by the roof of craving,
bound by Māra like fish in the mouth of a trap,
beings follow aging and death,
just as a suckling calf follows its mother.

## Monks, these are the five hindrances (nīvaraṇas).

Among those discourses, what is a discourse leading to habit (vāsanābhāgiya)?

Mind precedes all mental states, mind is their chief, they are mind-made.
If with a pure mind one speaks or acts,
happiness follows him as a consequence,
even as a shadow that never leaves.

## A discourse taught in the Saṃyutta.

The Blessed One taught this discourse, which develops faith and virtue, in detail for the Sakyan Prince Mahānāma in the city of Kapilavatthu. That discourse should be developed through perception; such development will occur in the future.

Among those discourses, what is a discourse leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya)?

Freed from lust above [in the fine-material and immaterial realms], below [in the sense realm], and everywhere,
the Arahant who does not perceive 'this body is I',
being thus liberated, has crossed the flood
never crossed before, for the sake of non-becoming again.

"What is the purpose of virtues (sīlas)?" Venerable Ānanda asked the Teacher.
185: Among these, which is the sutta partaking of the adept (asekkhabhāgiya)? "The mind of an Arahant is steady like a solid rock, unshaken by worldly conditions. Being detached from objects of lust, he does not get angry at objects of anger. How can suffering come to such a person whose mind is thus developed? (It cannot)." The Blessed One said: "A certain elder named Sāriputta, having offended me, has departed on a journey without asking for forgiveness; an explanation should be made for Sāriputta. If mindfulness of the body is not developed and not practiced frequently by someone," this should be explained in detail. Among these, which is the sutta partaking of both defilement and habit? "Rain seeps into the covered, but not into the open. Therefore, one should open what is covered; thus, the rain will no longer wet him." "Rain seeps into the covered" refers to defilement. "Not into the open" refers to habit. This is explained in detail starting with "One who is in darkness and bound for darkness." In that teaching, the person who is in darkness and the person who is bound for darkness represent defilement. The person who is bound for light and the person who has light as his destination represent habit. Among these, which is the sutta partaking of both defilement and penetration? "The wise do not say that a bond made of iron, wood, or hemp is a strong bond. But the intense attachment and longing for jeweled earrings, sons, and wives—this is a strong bond." "The longing for sons and wives" refers to defilement. "The wise cut even this bond and renounce, without longing, abandoning all sensual pleasures"—this refers to penetration. The unwholesome volition, unwholesome thought, and the descent into name-and-form—these four terms show defilement. The latter four terms show penetration. Among these, which is the sutta partaking of defilement, penetration, and the adept?
186:
This world is afflicted by burning (with sorrow and distress), oppressed by contact, it speaks of (suffering) as 'self'. In whatever way they conceive it (to remedy their suffering), for that reason, that suffering becomes otherwise (than what was conceived). This world, being attached to existence and prone to becoming otherwise, delights only in existence. What it delights in is fear; what it fears is suffering. Indeed, this holy life is lived for the abandoning of existence.

Whatever recluses or brahmins say that liberation from existence is by means of existence, I say all of them are 'not liberated from existence'. Or whatever recluses or brahmins say that escape from existence is by means of non-existence (annihilationism), I say all of them have 'not escaped from existence'. Dependent on acquisitions such as the aggregates, this suffering arises; with the destruction of all clinging, there is no more arising of suffering. Look at this world: various beings, overcome by ignorance, delighting in the collection of the five aggregates, are unable to be liberated from existence. Whatever existences there are, in every way and everywhere, all these existences are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.

'When one sees this as it really is with right wisdom, craving for existence is abandoned, and one no longer delights in non-existence (annihilationism). With the total destruction of cravings, the remainderless fading away and cessation is called Nibbāna. For that bhikkhu whose defilements are quenched, there is no further becoming in a new existence because of non-clinging. That bhikkhu has crushed the five Māras, won the battle, and being such a one, has transcended all existences,' so He taught.

The teaching from 'Ayaṃ loko santāpajāto' to 'dukkha' is the defilement of craving (taṇhā-saṅkilesa). Again, the teaching from 'Ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā bhavena bhavassa vippamokkhamāhaṃsu' to 'anissaṭā bhavasmāti vadāmi' is the defilement of views (diṭṭhi-saṅkilesa). Both of these are called defilements (saṅkilesa). Again, from 'Bhavavippahānāya brahmacariyaṃ vussati' to 'sabbupādānakkhayā natthi dukkhassa sambhavo' is called leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). From 'Tassa nibbutassa bhikkhuno' to 'upaccagā sabbabhavāni tādīti' is called belonging to the adept (asekhabhāgiya).

The four types of persons who go with the stream (anusotagāmī) are defilements (saṅkilesa). The person who goes against the stream (paṭisotagāmī) and the one of steady soul (ṭhitatto), etc., are leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). 'Standing on the dry land' (thale tiṭṭhati) (standing on the dry land of Nibbāna), etc., is called the stage of the adept (asekhabhūmi/asekhabhāgiya). Among those discourses, which discourse is both leading to habitual tendency (vāsanābhāgiya) and leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya)? It is the discourse starting with 'Dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḑhati', which He taught as: 'Merit increases for the giver; for the one who guards the body, speech, and mind, enmity does not accumulate; the merit of the Noble Path abandons evil; with the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, defilements are quenched.'
187:
Both the discourse on the defilement of views and the discourse on the defilement of craving are called defiling (saṅkilesa) discourses. Again, this discourse on living the holy life under the Buddha for the sake of abandoning existence with clinging, up to the arising of the destruction of all clinging (Nibbāna), is called a discourse leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). This discourse, 'Tassa nibbutassa bhikkhuno... upaccagā sabbabhavāni tādī', is called a discourse belonging to the adept (asekhabhāgiya). This discourse on the four types of blind worldlings who go with the stream (anusotagāmī) is called a defiling (saṅkilesa) discourse. This discourse starting with the person of steady soul (ṭhitatto) and the noble worldling who goes against the stream (paṭisotagāmī) is called a discourse leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). This discourse starting with 'Standing on the dry land' (thale tiṭṭhati) (standing on the dry land of Nibbāna) is called a discourse belonging to the adept (asekhabhāgiya).

Among those discourses, which discourse is also leading to habitual tendency (vāsanābhāgiya) and leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya)?
'Merit increases for the giver; for the one who is self-controlled in body, speech, and mind, enmity does not accumulate; the one with the merit of the Noble Path abandons evil; with the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, there is the quenching of defilements,' so He taught.

The discourse 'Dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḑhati, saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyati' is called a discourse leading to habitual tendency (vāsanābhāgiya). The discourse 'Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakaṃ, rāgadosamohakkhayā sanibbuto' is called a discourse leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya).

When the six sense objects, which follow the stream of craving and so on, are mastered by speech, reflected upon repeatedly by the mind, and penetrated and known by path-knowledge, five benefits can be obtained. In this Dispensation, for some persons, the teachings are retained, mastered by speech without forgetfulness, reflected upon repeatedly by the mind, and penetrated and known by path-knowledge, thus they become very learned. If that person strives, exerts, and makes an effort, they reach the extraordinary Dhamma in this very life. If they do not reach it in this very life, they reach it at the time of illness. If they do not reach it at the time of illness, they reach it at the time of death. If they do not reach it at the time of death, they reach it when they become a deva. If they do not reach it when they become a deva, through the longing and delight in that Dhamma, they reach the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha.

Among those, this discourse on reaching [attainment] in this very life is called a discourse leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). This discourse on reaching the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha in a future life is called a discourse leading to habitual tendency (vāsanābhāgiya). These sixteen discourses stand encompassing the entire Dispensation. By these sixteen discourses, the ninefold sutta is analyzed. That analysis is for the wise, not for the unwise; for the committed, not for the uncommitted. For one who lives without the work of meditation, by nature in the world...
188:
Corruption (saṃkilesa) wanders and moves through the cycle of birth and death. That corruption is of three kinds: corruption of craving (taṇhā-saṃkilesa), corruption of view (diṭṭhi-saṃkilesa), and corruption of misconduct (duccarita-saṃkilesa). The corruption arising from these three types of corruption dwells in unwholesome states and in worldly states. Among them, if a person with the eye of wisdom and skill should misapprehend that virtue or that view, for him, corruption of craving arises. If, however, a person holds a wrong view such as, "By this virtue, or by this practice, or by this holy life, I shall become a god or some superior Brahma among the gods," for him, corruption of wrong view arises.

If a person established in virtue does not misapprehend it, for that virtuous one, that right view, when taken up with wise attention, generates freedom from remorse up to the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana). That knowledge occurs for him in this very life, or at the time of death, or in other lives. As it is heard regarding other aggregates, "Well-practiced kamma leads to the formation of habitual tendencies (vāsanā)," this discourse is called the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

Among those discourses, the mind of one established in virtue is free from hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Because of that freedom from hindrances, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi). Such a person reaches Nibbāna, which is clearly seen through the path-knowledge. If he does not reach Nibbāna within the Dispensation, he attains the six higher powers (abhiññā) in a single sitting.

If he cannot reach it thus, two types of persons, the faith-follower (saddhānusārī) and the Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī), attain the Noble Dhamma. Between these two, the Dhamma-follower is one of quick understanding (ugghaṭitannū), and the faith-follower is one who needs guidance (neyya). That ugghaṭitannū is of two kinds: one with sharp faculties and one with dull faculties. Likewise, the neyya person is of two kinds: one with sharp faculties and one with dull faculties. Among them, the ugghaṭitannū with dull faculties and the neyya person with sharp faculties are those with unequal faculties. Among those persons, those with equal faculties decline from being an ugghaṭitannū or from being a neyya; such a person established in the middle ground is one who understands through elaboration (vipañcitannū). These are the three types of persons.

Among those persons, the fourth and fifth are the ugghaṭitannū, vipañcitannū, and neyya. Among them, the ugghaṭitannū person, having acquired the faculties and being established in the stage of vision (dassana-bhūmi), attains the fruit of stream-entry; he is the first type of stream-enterer called 'one-seeder' (ekabījī). The vipañcitannū person, having acquired the faculties and being established in the stage of vision, attains the fruit of stream-entry; he is the second type of stream-enterer called 'family-to-family' (kolaṃkola). The neyya person, having acquired the faculties and being established in the stage of vision, attains the fruit of stream-entry; he is called 'seven-times-at-most' (sattakkhattuparama).
189:
This third type of stream-enterer is the 'seven-times-at-most' (sattakkhattuparama). These three persons are established in the fruit of stream-entry due to the difference in their faculties.

The ugghaṭitannū person is an ekabījī stream-enterer; the vipañcitannū person is a kolaṃkola stream-enterer; the neyya person is a sattakkhattuparama person. This discourse is called the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta. If one strives further than that, one reaches Nibbāna, which is clearly seen through the path-knowledge.

Among those persons, that ugghaṭitannū person with sharp faculties reaches the fruit of non-returning and becomes either an attainer of Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī) or an attainer of Nibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī); thus there are these two persons. Among those persons, that vipañcitannū person with sharp faculties, upon reaching the fruit of non-returning, becomes either an attainer of Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī) or an attainer of Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī); thus there are these two persons. Among those persons, the neyya person, upon reaching the fruit of non-returning, becomes one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī).

Through the distinction of faculties, if the ugghaṭitannū person has sharp faculties, he is an antarāparinibbāyī; if the ugghaṭitannū person has dull faculties, he is an uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī. Through the distinction of faculties, if the ugghaṭitannū person has sharp faculties, he is a sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī; if he has sharp faculties, he is an antarāparinibbāyī; if the ugghaṭitannū person has dull faculties, he is an upahaccaparinibbāyī. If the vipañcitannū person has sharp faculties, he is an asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī; if the vipañcitannū person has dull faculties, he is a sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī; the neyya person is an upahaccaparinibbāyī. If the vipañcitannū person has sharp faculties, he is an asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. If the vipañcitannū person has dull faculties, he is a sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī; the neyya person is an uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī. Thus, there are five types of non-returners (anāgāmī); with the sixth being the once-returner (sakadāgāmī), and three types of stream-enterers (sotāpanna), these nine persons are called learners (sekha).

Among those noble ones, if the ugghaṭitannū person has sharp faculties, upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, there are two types: the both-ways liberated person (ubhatobhāgavimutta) and the wisdom-liberated person (paññāvimutta). Among those persons, if the ugghaṭitannū person has dull faculties, upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, there are two types: the ṭhitakappī and the paṭivedhanabhāva person. If that vipañcitannū person with sharp faculties reaches the fruit of Arahantship, there are two types: the cetanābhabba person and the rakkhaṇābhabba person. Among those persons, if the vipañcitannū person has dull faculties, upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, there are two types: "if he intends, he does not attain Nibbāna; if he does not intend, he attains Nibbāna," and "if he repeatedly protects, he does not attain Nibbāna; if he does not protect, he attains Nibbāna." Among those persons, the neyya person, being devoted to the practice of meditation...
190: A person to be led (neyya) is one who, through exertion in meditation, possesses qualities that do not decline. Regarding these nine types of Arahants, whether they are those whose actions are fixed (kammaniyata) or those who attain the end of life and the end of defilements simultaneously (samasīsī), this fourfold discourse is called both 'partaking of defilement' (saṅkilesabhāgiya) and 'partaking of the beyond-training' (asekhabhāgiya). In these individuals, the ten powers (bala) of the Tathāgata operate. What are the ten? In this Dispensation, before the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion by the Blessed Buddhas, high-ranking deities (mahesakkha devaputta) came forward to request: 'Venerable Sir, may the Sugata teach the Dhamma.' While surveying with the peerless Buddha-eye, the Buddha saw the three groups of beings: the group fixed in rightness (sammatta-niyata), the group fixed in wrongness (micchatta-niyata), and the unfixed group (aniyata). Among these three, for the group fixed in rightness, it is impossible that they would fall into wrong mindfulness; it is impossible that they would attain final Nibbāna without a teacher; but it is possible that they would enter meditative attainments. Among those beings, for the group fixed in wrongness, it is impossible that they would practice and enter noble attainments; but it is possible that they would practice ignoble wrong conduct. Among those individuals, for the unfixed group, it is possible that by practicing rightly, they will reach the group fixed in rightness; it is impossible that by practicing wrongly, they will reach the group fixed in rightness. It is possible that by practicing rightly, they will reach the group fixed in rightness; it is possible that by practicing wrongly, they will reach the group fixed in wrongness. For me, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveying with the peerless Buddha-eye, it is impossible that anyone could justly reproach me, saying, 'These things are not fully understood by you.' For you, who claim to be free from lust, it is impossible that anyone could justly reproach you on the grounds of not being an Arahant. Because of this, it is impossible that the Dhamma taught to this unfixed group who tend toward wrong views would not be evident for the total destruction of suffering; it is impossible that a disciple in the unfixed group, thus exhorted by me, would not realize the distinction between before and after. It is impossible that the Sage, having tamed devas, nāgas, and yakkhas with various methods and various languages by defining the Dhamma, would not reach the other shore, which is the fruit of Arahantship, through that cause. This is the analytical insight into the Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā). It is impossible that these analytical insights into the Dhamma would not depend on the seven types of sounds. This is the analytical insight into language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā). It is impossible that the analytical insight into language would not make the meaning known to disciples who delight in harmony. This is the analytical insight into meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā). High-ranking deities approach and ask questions. It is impossible that the meaning could not be analyzed for those oppressed by physical or mental pain, those with deformed hands, the lame, or the dull-witted. This is the analytical insight into perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). If that wisdom exists in someone, it exists for them; it is impossible for it not to be manifest in that person. If someone has impaired wisdom, it does not exist for them; it is impossible that it would exist for one with impaired wisdom. Likewise, for the cessation of lust, it is impossible that the ten unwholesome paths of action would arise. It is impossible that Māra, Sakka, Brahmā, a Tathāgata, or a Cakkavatti would certainly be a woman.
191: (The deities) ask questions. It is impossible that the meaning could not be analyzed for one who is oppressed by physical or mental pain, one with deformed hands, the lame, or the dull-witted. The analytical insight into perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) exists. If that wisdom exists in someone, it exists for them; it is impossible that it would not be manifest in that person. If someone does not have impaired wisdom, it does not occur to them; it is impossible that impaired wisdom would arise in them. In this way, for the cessation of the origin (samudaya), the ten unwholesome paths of action arise. It is impossible that one who is a Māra, Sakka, Brahmā, Tathāgata, or Cakkavatti would certainly be a woman. It is possible that only a man would be a Cakkavatti or Sakka, the ruler of devas. Thus, the Blessed Buddha possesses such power and such knowledge. This knowledge is called the knowledge of the possible and the impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna-ñāṇa), which is indicated as the first power of the Tathāgata. Based on the three groups, the four grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja), and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the occurrence, cessation, and portions of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) are also indicated. Wholesome states arise in wholesome results, and such is the nature of women and men. The Buddha knows this first power in this way. For those who belong to the group fixed in rightness (sammatta-niyata), this is not a practice leading everywhere; it is only a practice leading to Nibbāna. Between those two, if there is a group fixed in wrongness (micchatta-niyata), this too is not a practice leading everywhere. Let it be only a practice leading to the origin of the self-view (sakkāya-samudaya). This person, established in various practices, goes to Nibbāna, goes to the woeful states, or goes to the worlds of devas and humans. Whatever practice one follows, one goes to all destinations; this is called the practice leading to all destinations (sabbatthagāminī-paṭipadā). The knowledge that knows this as it really is, is called the knowledge of the practice leading to all destinations (sabbatthagāminī-paṭipadā-ñāṇa), which is the second power of the Tathāgata. That practice leading to all destinations involves various dispositions (adhimutta). Some are intent on sensual pleasures, some on difficult practices, some on the practice of self-mortification, some believe in purification through saṃsāra, and some reach the development of non-perception (anajjā-bhāvanā). The Buddha knows as it really is the knowledge of beings bound by various temperaments, and the various knowledges concerning the many dispositions of the world. This is the third power of the Tathāgata. In that knowledge, beings have dispositions; they frequent, develop, and cultivate them. For those beings who rely on kamma and are inclined toward that kamma, that element (dhātu) of disposition itself carries them along. What is that element? The element of renunciation (nekkhamma-dhātu), the element of power (bala-dhātu), certain elements of success (sampatti), and elements of wrongness (micchatta) become their dispositions. They do not see beyond other dispositions. They only [remain] in the sphere of that element of disposition...
192:
I reflect on aging and death and say, 'Only this view of mine is true, other views are vain.' There is knowledge in that teaching according to reality, in the manner spoken by the Blessed One to Sakka, the Lord of Devas. This is called the fourth Tathāgata Power.

Among those powers, the knowledge that knows the elements of disposition (āsayadhātu) is supreme. Therefore, one exerts effort through body, through speech, and through mental energy regarding those various elements. Volitional kamma is exerted. Effort made by body and speech is exerted. Because of being mental, the Tathāgata, who knows the distinction of kamma, understands thus: 'This being, with such a disposition, has performed such a kamma in the past because of this cause; he experiences such a result in the present life, or will experience it in the future.' Likewise, He understands the present: 'This person with such a disposition performs this action.' Because of this cause, which is both craving and wrong view, the result will not arise for him in this very life, nor at the moment of rebirth in the second life, nor in subsequent successive lives—thus He understands. 'This person will perform such a kamma in the future; because of this cause, such a result will arise for him; because of this cause, there are four bases of practice (kammaṭṭhāna) up to the four truths; this basis of practice is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future,' and so on. Thus, He understands the diversity of results of the undertaking of kamma in the past, future, and present, by way of cause and by way of occasion. Thus, there is the state of being low or exalted, inferior or superior. This is called the knowledge of the result of kamma (kammavipākañāṇa), the fifth Tathāgata Power.

In that manner, beings undertake whatever kamma they undertake. In that undertaking, He understands: 'For this person who is intent on kamma and has a temperament of lust, the elements of renunciation (nekkhammadhātu) reach fulfillment.' For that person who is empty of meditation due to following lust, the first jhana will be defiled by the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). If, through further great effort, with a mind that has reached purification of jhana, the practice leading to distinction is undertaken. For that yogi established in the first jhana, which has the part of abandoning the hindrances, the second jhana reaches purification. For the yogi wishing to attain the third jhana, the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) stands having completely exhausted the mind. That rapture (pīti) of his stands facing the third jhana which has the part of non-distinction. If he knows the escape for that person according to reality, for such a yogi, the fourth jhana indeed reaches purification. There are hindrances which are the part of decline of the fourth jhana. Those states also arise in whomsoever they arise, and through which meditations the purification of the fourth jhana is seen. Thus, for the person who attains the attainment with noble intention, there are the four attainments, the three doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha), and the eight liberations of jhana (vimokkhajhāna)—thus the four jhanas are called liberations. There are also the eight liberations and the three doors to liberation. As for concentration (samādhi)...
193: The four concentrations are: concentration of intention (chanda-samādhi), concentration of energy (viriya-samādhi), concentration of consciousness (citta-samādhi), and concentration of investigation (vīmaṃsā-samādhi). The four attainments are attainments according to intention. Thus, such defilement (saṅkilesa) of the liberations and attainments of these jhanas occurs for a person of lustful temperament. Likewise for a person of hateful temperament and a person of deluded temperament. For a person of lustful temperament, such purification (vodāna) occurs. Thus, in this teaching, the knowledge that knows according to reality, which is not shared with all beings, is called the sixth Tathāgata Power. In those teachings, the Blessed One understands thus: Mundane states and supramundane states, based on their predominance in the part of development (bhāvanā), receive the name 'faculties' (indriya). Based on that faculty of mind (manindriya) which is a consciousness that has reached strength, they receive the name 'powers' (bala). Based on the element of endeavor (ārambhadhātu), they receive the name 'energy' (viriya). Thus, such knowledge arises for that Blessed One. He also gave the Dhamma teaching: 'These persons are endowed with these states.' He taught by way of mode, by way of mixture, to those persons who have intention (āsayajhāsaya) and are endowed with resolution (adhimutti). Thus, the knowledge of the diversity of the faculties, powers, and energy of other beings and other persons is called the seventh Tathāgata Power. Among those powers, the Blessed One understands the destination (gati) of the fetters (saṃyojana) and of the trainees (sekha) in the four planes by means of two powers. Through the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsanussatiñāṇa), He knows the past saṃsāra, and in the present, through the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), He knows the passing away and rebirth of beings. Thus, these two powers are brought forth from the divine eye. That divine eye is the range (gocara) of the divine eye in the past. That divine eye is now the range of mindfulness. Thus, these two which know one's own and others' manifold recollection of past lives and the present time through the divine eye are called Tathāgata Powers. The eighth is the knowledge of recollection of past lives, and the ninth is the knowledge of the divine eye. Furthermore, the Blessed One understands the pure jhana belonging to the part of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya) of the noble persons (ariya). He understands: 'This person, by this path and this practice, through the destruction of the taints (āsava), realizes for himself in this very life the taintless liberation of mind (cetovimutti) and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti), and having attained them, he dwells in them.' Thus, He understands the knowledge of the destruction of one's own taints, and based on the four planes, He understands the destruction of taints of the trainees (sekha) which is partial (limited) and the destruction of taints of the Arahants which is total (without limit), up to the nine types of Arahants. In that teaching, liberation of mind is free from the two taints: the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the taint of existence (bhavāsava). Liberation by wisdom is free from the two taints: the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). The knowledge that knows these two liberations according to reality is called the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa). This is the tenth Tathāgata Power.
194:
Established in these ten powers, the Blessed One teaches the fivefold Dispensation: that which pertains to defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), that which pertains to habit-tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya), that which pertains to vision (dassanabhāgiya), that which pertains to mental development (bhāvanābhāgiya), and that which pertains to the adept (asekkhabhāgiya). Among those teachings, the escape from the defilement caused by craving is non-greed (alobha). The escape from the defilement caused by wrong view is non-delusion (amoha). The escape from the defilement caused by misconduct is the three wholesome states. For what reason? It is because of these three mental misconducts: covetousness (abhijjhā), ill-will (vyāpāda), and wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi).

Among these three, the mental misconduct of covetousness gives rise to bodily action; it gives rise to taking what is not given (adinnādāna) and all verbal actions connected with it. All instances of deviation, lack of truth, ingratitude, and frivolous false speech (musāvāda) have their unwholesome root in covetousness. In terms of good conduct, the volition of abstaining from false speech, taking what is not given, and covetousness is right conduct. Therein, ill-will gives rise to bodily action which is mental misconduct; it gives rise to killing living beings (pāṇātipāta) and verbal actions connected with pulling, dragging, and constant interference. It also gives rise to slanderous speech (pisuṇavācā) and harsh speech (pharusavācā). Wrong view causes the mental misconducts of covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view to be associated. For such a person, the relinquishing of wrong view arising from all forms of wrong view, whether born of lust or born of hatred, gives rise to wrong view for this reason. It gives rise to verbal actions such as sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra) and idle chatter (samphappalāpa). These three types of misconduct have unwholesome roots.

Covetousness is greed (lobha). Ill-will is hatred (dosa). Wrong view is delusion (moha). These give rise to the eightfold wrongness (micchatta). When these three unwholesome roots are suppressed, the tenfold mass of unwholesome states reaches completion. The escape from these three types of defilement of misconduct is the Sutta pertaining to habit-tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya). Therein, where greed, hatred, and delusion are pointed out in many Suttas, greed is spoken of; for that reason, greed is designated in those states. Therein, this delusion is unwholesome delusion; this is ignorance (avijjā). That ignorance, being wrongly obsessed with form (rūpa), regards form as self. One possessed of ignorance regards self as having form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form.

Therein, which word speaks of the view of annihilation (uccheda) in the personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)? The statement 'the soul is the same as the body' constitutes the nihilistic view (natthika-diṭṭhi), the view of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppanna-diṭṭhi), and the view that 'one performs the action and another experiences the result.' Among the last sixty aeons, three words fall into the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) of personality belief. The statement 'the soul is one thing, the body is another,' the view of non-action (akiriya-diṭṭhi), and for one who desires suffering, the view of non-causality (ahetuka-diṭṭhi) occur. The non-existence of kamma (anajjhābhāva) and all forms of conceit (māna) are also included. Among those views, 'This alone is the truth, all else is empty'...
195:
The eighty-six types of Ājīvakas prescribe purification through the round of rebirth (saṃsāra). Just as there are four bases in the personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) of such a nature, likewise, through the personality belief with twenty bases regarding the five aggregates, one clings to the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). Other Ājīvakas also cling to the eternalist doctrine and the clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa), wrongly assuming: 'By this practice, I shall become a god or one among the great powerful gods.' This is called clinging to rites and rituals. Among those views, through personality belief, that person regards form as self. Regarding the view 'the soul is the same as the body,' he doubts, is uncertain, cannot resolve, and cannot gain confidence, doubting about the past, the future, and both the past and future... Thus, for one established in the Suttas pertaining to habit-tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya), this is the corruption (upakkilesa).

Among those corruptions, through the faculty of faith (saddhiddriya), he abandons all doubt; through the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), he sees the arising and passing away; through the faculty of concentration (samādhiddriya), he makes the mind one-pointed; through the faculty of energy (vīriyiddriya), he makes an effort. Through these five faculties, becoming a faith-follower (saddhānusārī) and constantly delighting in unwavering confidence, he produces the immediate concentration (anantarika-samādhi). With purified faculties, the Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī), being without conditions, produces the immediate concentration. He knows as it really is: 'This is suffering.' This Sutta is the Sutta pertaining to vision (dassanabhāgiya) which shows the Truths. For him, among the five lower fetters (saṃyojana), the three fetters to be abandoned by vision (the path of stream-entry) are abandoned entirely; the unwholesome states are abandoned by two types of persons. Among those abandoned states, when the three unwholesome roots to be abandoned by the higher paths are cast upwards, they give rise to six existences. Among them, when covetousness and ill-will are attenuated, those six existences reach their limit due to exhaustion; only two existences remain. For him, covetousness and ill-will are entirely exhausted. Only one existence remains. That person also brings about existence through the power of conceit (māna). Although the other four defilements—lust for form (rūparāga), lust for existence (bhāvarāga), ignorance (avijjā), and restlessness (uddhacca)—are conceits like a pinnacle, they are not able to uproot the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna); however, all of them strive to abandon the conceit 'I am.' When those defilements are exhausted, they no longer occur beyond this stage of vision. Among the five trainees (sekkha), this Sutta occurring for the three who stand in the paths and the two who stand in the fruits is the Sutta pertaining to mental development (bhāvanābhāgiya). Beyond that is the Sutta pertaining to the adept (asekkhabhāgiya); in some places, the ground (bhūmi) is suppressed. This is the fifth Sutta. It is taught for three types of persons: the worldling (puthujjana), the trainee (sekkha), and the adept (asekkha). The Sutta pertaining to defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya) is taught for the worldling, while the Sutta pertaining to habit-tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya) is for the trainee and the adept. The Sutta pertaining to vision (dassanabhāgiya) is for the worldling, and the Sutta pertaining to mental development (bhāvanābhāgiya) is for the five trainees. The Sutta pertaining to the adept (asekkhabhāgiya) mentioned first is for all Arahants. That Sutta should be sought in twenty-seven modes within the fivefold division. Among those modes, the occurrences of that Sutta pertaining to the adept are superior to that. That adept-sutta also falls into fifty modes in brief.
196:
In brief, it falls into fifty modes. If the fifty modes described in the Dispensation (Sāsana) are condensed, they fall into ten modes. Because the Noble Truths (Ariyasacca) are established in a condensed form, they fall into eight modes when condensed. If the grounds for the confluence of modes (hārasampāta) in the four common Suttas are condensed, they fall into five types of Suttas: those leading to defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), those leading to habitual tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya), those leading to development (bhāvanābhāgiya), those leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), and those leading to the state of one beyond training (asekkhabhāgiya).

If those modes are condensed, they fall into four types of Suttas: saṃkilesabhāgiya, vāsanābhāgiya, nibbedhabhāgiya, and asekkhabhāgiya. If those modes are condensed, they fall into three types of Suttas: those leading to worldlings (puthujjanabhāgiya), those leading to those in training (sekkhabhāgiya), and those leading to those beyond training (asekkhabhāgiya). If those modes are condensed, they fall into two types of Suttas: nibbedhabhāgiya and those leading to previous application (pubbayogabhāgiya).

As spoken by the Blessed One, the Tathāgatas, Arahants, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, seeing two special benefits, teach the Dhamma in the form of Sutta, Geyya, and so on. The Teacher, without causing fatigue to those endowed with previous merit, observes them with proper reflection. It is for the purpose of bringing about proper reflection, thinking that previous merits will arise in the continuities of those to be guided (veneyya). In that teaching, by clearly seeing one's own distinction in wisdom, one should apply it to whichever of the eight condensed Suttas one is able. Having applied it there, the meaning of the Sutta should be pointed out. For, while feeling (vedanā) exists, it is not possible for anyone to demonstrate the meaning of a Sutta as it really is by merely holding the mind in some random way.

## Among those teachings, these are the summary verses (uddāna-gāthā) of the preceding Suttas:

Those blinded by sensual desire, covered by the net (of craving), and the five hindrances,
Phenomena preceded by the mind, and Mahānāma the Sakyan.
The Sutta on being released above and below, the Sīla Sutta on 'what is the purpose?',
The one whose mind is like a rock, the Sutta beginning with Upatissa's question.
The Kāyagatāsati Sutta, the one covered by defilements and following darkness,
That bond is not firm, the Cetasika Sutta, the Sutta beginning with 'This world'.
The four types of persons, the increase of merit for the giver,
In the Suttas on the Dhamma followed by the ear, these are the summary verses for them.

Among those, what is the Injunction (āṇatti)?

If you are afraid of suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you,
Do not perform evil deeds, whether in the open or in secret.
197:
"Rādha, be one who is without longing for the form that is past"—this should be expanded. "Ānanda, a virtuous person should always act in such a way that there is no remorse (avippaṭisāra)"—this teaching is called the Injunction (āṇatti).

Among those, what is the Fruit (phala)?

Just as a great umbrella protects (the one who carries it) in the rainy season,
So the Dhamma truly protects the one who practices the Dhamma.
This is the benefit of the Dhamma well-practiced;
The Dhamma-practitioner does not go to a state of misery.

## This is the Fruit (phala).

Among those, what is the Means (upāya)?

"All phenomena are non-self"—when one sees this with insight wisdom,
Then one grows weary of suffering; this is the path to purity.

"A bhikkhu endowed with seven factors could move even the Himavant, the king of mountains; what then to say of destroying the low ignorance with the small knives of the Path of Arahantship?"—thus it is taught. This is the Means (upāya).

Among those, what are the Injunction and the Fruit (phala)?
