If you are afraid of suffering, if suffering is unloved by you,
Do not perform evil deeds, whether in the open or in secret.
If you have done or will do an evil deed,
There is no escape from suffering for you, even if you flee into (another) life.

By the first verse, it is the Injunction; by the second verse, it is the Fruit. Established in virtue, two things should be developed: the development of the mind (citta-bhāvanā) and the development of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā); this is the Injunction. The fading of lust (virāga) alone is the Fruit.

Among those, what are the Fruit and the Means (upāya)?

Established in virtue, the man of wisdom, developing the mind and wisdom,
The ardent and sagacious bhikkhu, he would disentangle this tangle.

By the first half-verse, it is the Means; by the second half-verse, it is the Fruit. Sakka, the king of gods, rejoices. The hermit who desires a retinue, starting from the Sutta taught to a single ogre...
198:
...as long as effort is made in the six dhammas. Beyond that, whatever effort is made in the five dhammas is the Means (upāya). The mind of one who is not associated with defilements is also released from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava)—in all the six and three, this is both the Means and the Fruit.

Among those teachings, what are the Injunction (āṇatti), the Fruit (phala), and the Means (upāya)?

"Mogharāja, always mindful, look upon the world as void (of self).
Having utterly removed the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), one would thus be one who has crossed over death."

"Look upon the world as void, Mogharāja" is the Injunction. "Always mindful" is the Means. "Having utterly removed the view of self, one would thus be one who has crossed over death" is the Fruit. "Bhikkhus, develop concentration; a bhikkhu who is concentrated knows form as impermanent. A noble disciple seeing thus is released from birth... etc... and from despairs"—in this Sutta, all three (Injunction, Means, Fruit) are included.

Among those teachings, what is Gratification (assāda)?

If for one who desires objective sensuality, that sensuality is fulfilled—this is Gratification.

"Brahmin, because of the reasons of practicing the Dhamma, practicing with equanimity, and practicing what is wholesome, some beings here, after the breakup of the body, reach a good destination, the heavenly world." This is Gratification.

Among those teachings, what is the Danger (ādīnava)?

Truly, one is harmed because of sensual pleasures, one suffers excessively—this is the Danger. The Sutta in the Pasenadi Saṃyutta with the simile of the mountain—this is also the Danger.

Among those teachings, what is the Escape (nissaraṇa)?

"He who avoids sensual pleasures as one would (avoid stepping on) the head of a snake with one's foot, that mindful person safely overcomes the craving that clings to the world."

The Sutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya which is like the falling of old yellow leaves of the Pāricchattaka tree is the Escape.
199:
Among those Suttas, what are gratification (assāda) and danger (ādīnava)?

Whatever deeds a man performs, those he sees in himself. The doer of good sees good results; the doer of evil sees evil results.

Between these two types of persons, that which the doer of evil experiences as the result of evil is called gratification (assāda). Regarding the explanation of the eight worldly conditions such as gain and loss—among them, loss, obscurity, blame, and suffering are called danger (ādīnava). Gain, fame, happiness, and praise are called gratification (assāda).

Among those Suttas, what are gratification (assāda) and escape (nissaraṇa)?

"The result of merit is happiness, and one's aspirations are fulfilled. Swiftly, one attains Nibbāna, the supreme peace."

That which is the result of merit and that which is the fulfillment of aspirations is called gratification (assāda). Attaining Nibbāna, the supreme peace, swiftly is called escape (nissaraṇa).

For the Great Man endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, there are only two destinies. If he lives the household life, he becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) after conquering [the world]; this is called gratification (assāda). If he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he escapes from saṃsāra through the medicine [of the path of Arahatship]; this is called both gratification (assāda) and escape (nissaraṇa).

Among those Suttas, what are danger (ādīnava) and escape (nissaraṇa)?

Knowing the occurrence of birth and death as a danger for the person who does not give, he exists for the sake of not giving due to the destruction of birth and death.

By the first half-verse, the occurrence of birth and death is called danger (ādīnava). The teaching "he exists for the sake of not giving due to the destruction of birth and death" is called escape (nissaraṇa).

This world has indeed fallen into distress, in that it is born and it dies. In this teaching, the contemplation, "When will there be an end to this suffering, or will it be in the future?" is called danger (ādīnava). Knowing the greed for the old royal city and renouncing it to go into the forest is called escape (nissaraṇa). This is danger (ādīnava) and escape (nissaraṇa).
200:
Among those teachings, what are gratification (assāda), danger (ādīnava), and escape (nissaraṇa)?

Sensual pleasures are variegated, diverse, and delightful. Through their various forms, they agitate and entangle the mind. O King, therefore I have gone forth; the state of a monk is indeed superior.

The teaching, 'Sensual pleasures are variegated, diverse, and delightful' is called gratification (assāda). The teaching, 'Through their various forms, they agitate and entangle the mind' is called danger (ādīnava). The teaching, 'O King, I have gone forth from the household life; the state of a monk is indeed superior' is called escape (nissaraṇa).

In the powerful Bālopama Sutta, one clings to kamma that is to be experienced through craving. According to that clinging, whatever evil kamma one experiences, therein, as long as there is kamma with painful feeling, an undeveloped body, and a limited mind, it shows the danger (ādīnava). Through kamma with pleasant feeling, one finds gratification (assāda). The one who is like before [is in danger]. This state of King Mahānāma, who has a developed mind, a developed body, developed wisdom, and an expansive mind, is called escape (nissaraṇa).

Among those Suttas, what is a mundane (lokiya) Sutta?

An evil deed committed does not curdle at once like fresh milk. Smoldering like fire covered with ashes, it follows the fool, burning him.

Going to the four wrong paths (agati); this is a mundane Sutta.

Among those Suttas, what is a supramundane (lokuttara) Sutta?

'Whose faculties have gone to tranquility, like horses well-tamed by a charioteer; such a one, with pride abandoned and free from taints (āsavas), even the gods envy.'

'Bhikkhus, I will teach you the noble Right Concentration (Sammāsamādhi)'; this teaching is a supramundane Sutta.
201:
Among those Suttas, what is a Sutta that is both mundane and supramundane?

As if pierced by a spear, or as if one's head were on fire,
A mindful bhikkhu should live striving for the abandonment of sensual lust.

The teaching, "As if pierced by a spear, or as if one's head were on fire" is called mundane (lokiya). The teaching, "A mindful bhikkhu should live striving for the abandonment of sensual lust" is called supramundane (lokuttara). The teaching that there is desire for edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) is a mundane Sutta. The teaching that there is no desire is a supramundane Sutta.

Among those Suttas, what is kamma?

One who destroys life, and speaks what is not true,
Who takes in the world what is not given, and goes to another's wife.
One who is devoted to drinking fermented and distilled liquors,
Without abandoning these five enmities, such a person of poor virtue is called immoral (dussīla).

Bhikkhus, these are the three types of misconduct (duccarita). This is called kamma.

Among those teachings, what is the result (vipāka)?

For sixty thousand years, he undergoes experience accordingly.

"Bhikkhus, I have seen the hells named the six spheres of contact (phassāyatana). Bhikkhus, I have seen the heavens named the six spheres of contact." This is called the result (vipāka).

Among those Suttas, what are both kamma and result (vipāka)?

Just as rust arising from iron, having sprung from it, eats that very iron,
So too, their own deeds lead those of excessive conduct in the use of requisites to a miserable state (duggati).

The teaching from "Ayasāva malaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ" to "sāni kammāni" is called kamma. The teaching "nayanti duggatiṃ" is called the result (vipāka).

When one practices rightly towards these four persons—mother, father, the Tathāgata, and the disciples of the Tathāgata—whatever right practice there is, this is called kamma. Arising in the heavenly realms because of that merit is called the result (vipāka). This is both kamma and result.
202:
Among those, what is the discourse with explicitly stated meaning (niddiṭṭha)?

There is a chariot with faultless parts, covered with a white cloth, and having a single axle. See the monk coming without distress, whose stream of craving is cut, and who is without bonds. Just as the householder Citta sees the mind in ascetics, (see that monk).

Thus, the meaning is explicitly stated by this verse.

In the Gopālaka Sutta, there are eleven factors. By the words, "Thus, monks, a monk is one who knows form" and "He is one who honors with excessive offerings," the meaning of those eleven factors is explicitly stated as they were spoken.

Among those, what is the discourse with meaning not yet explicitly stated (aniddiṭṭha)?

Seclusion is happiness for one who is contented, who has heard the Dhamma, and who sees. In the world, restraint and non-violence toward living beings is happiness.

Dispassion in the world and the overcoming of sensual desires is happiness. The removal of the conceit "I am" is indeed the highest happiness.

This is aniddiṭṭha (the part where the meaning is not yet explicitly stated). The eight thoughts of a great man (mahāpurisavitakka) are also aniddiṭṭha.

Among those, what is the discourse that is both niddiṭṭha and aniddiṭṭha?

With clear eyes, a beautiful face, a tall and straight body, and majestic power, You shine like the sun in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks.

The teaching from "With clear eyes" to "You shine like the sun" is niddiṭṭha (the meaning is clearly shown). The part to be questioned, such as "How are the eyes of the Blessed One clear?", "How is the face beautiful?", "How is the body tall?", "How is it straight?", "How is there majestic power?", and "How is there radiance?", is aniddiṭṭha. In the discourse explained by the foam simile, the presentation of the five aggregates through five similes—form like a lump of foam, feeling like a bubble, consciousness like a magic trick, and so on—is niddiṭṭha. The part to be analyzed, such as "For what reason is form like a lump of foam?", "How is it that all forms cognizable by the eye or those cognizable by the other four bases are so?", "How is feeling like a bubble?", and "Which feeling is it: pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful?", is aniddiṭṭha. Thus, it is both niddiṭṭha and aniddiṭṭha.
203:
Among those (discourses), what is knowledge (ñāṇa)?
Wisdom alone is supreme in the world; it is the penetrative wisdom (nibbedhagāminī).
Through that wisdom, one rightly knows the destruction of birth and death (Nibbāna).
These three faculties—the faculty of "I shall know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya), the faculty of knowledge (aññindriya), and the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya)—are called knowledge.

Among those, what is the state to be known (neyya)?
Beings are attached to sensual pleasures with sensual lust, not seeing the danger in fetters.
Beings who are attached and clinging to fetters can never truly cross the vast and great flood of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Those endowed with four factors are reborn among the devas after the breaking up of the body. The Kapiya Sutta and the Apaṇṇaka-pasādanīya Sutta in the Udāna—these are called neyya.

Among those, what is both knowledge (ñāṇa) and that to be known (neyya)?
When one sees with insight-wisdom that "all phenomena are non-self" (sabbe dhammā anattā),
Then one becomes weary of the suffering of the round of rebirths. This weariness is the path to the purity of Nibbāna.
"Yadā passati" (When one sees) is called knowledge. Establishing all phenomena in the aspect of non-self is called neyya.
Among the Four Noble Truths, the (first) three truths are called neyya. The Truth of the Path (magga-sacca), which consists of the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha), is called both knowledge and neyya.

Among those, what is vision (dassana)?
This (Eightfold) Path alone exists for the purity of vision; there is no other path besides the Path of Stream-entry.
You should practice this path; it is the one that confuses Mara by uprooting the defilements.
A noble disciple endowed with four factors may declare of himself: "I am finished with hell; I am one who is no longer subject to rebirth in lower worlds, I am fixed in destiny, and I am bound for enlightenment (a Stream-enterer)." This is called vision.
204:
Among those discourses, what is the discourse on development (bhāvanā)? To whomsoever the faculties are well-developed internally, externally, and in the whole world. That person, though possessing wisdom, is one who perceives form and, having reached delusion, does not know. These four states—non-covetousness, non-ill will, right mindfulness, and right concentration—are the factors of Dhamma (dhammapada). This is development.

Among those discourses, what is the discourse on vision (dassana) and development (bhāvanā)? One who is not conflicting in speech, mind, or bodily action, having known the Dhamma well and aspiring toward the state of Nibbāna, should live well in the world. When asked what states should be attended to by one desiring to realize the fruit of Stream-entry, the Blessed One taught the five aggregates of clinging. This is vision and development.

Among those discourses, what are the states that have results as their nature (vipākadhamma-dhamma)? The details should be known starting with "A man performs those actions." Monks, these are the three types of good conduct (sucarita). These are the states that have results as their nature.

Among those discourses, what are the states that do not have results as their nature (navipākadhamma-dhamma)? There are form, feeling, perception, consciousness, and volition. One who sees thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self," becomes dispassionate. Monks, the five aggregates are these states that do not have results as their nature.

Among those discourses, what is that which is neither a result nor a state having results as its nature (nevavipāka-navipākadhamma)? It is said: "Those who practice in this way, according to the method taught by the Buddha, following the Teacher's instruction, will make an end of suffering." Thus, whatever is right practice (sammā-paṭipatti) and whatever is cessation (nirodha), both of these are neither results nor states having results as their nature. Monks, I will teach you the holy life (brahmacariya) and the fruits of the holy life. The Noble Eightfold Path is the holy life. The fruits from the fruit of Stream-entry up to the fruit of Arahantship are the fruits of the holy life.
205:
Among those discourses, what is the Sakavacana (the Buddha's own words)?

Not to do any evil, to cultivate the good, to purify one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Monks, these three are the doors to liberation (vimokkhamukhāni). This is called Sakavacana.

Among those discourses, what is the Paravacana (others' words)?

There is no love like that for a son, there is no wealth like cattle, there is no light like the sun, and the ocean is the greatest of lakes.

"Friend Kosiya, victory in battle comes through well-spoken words," and "Monks, that Sakka, Lord of the Devas, also enjoys the fruit of his own deeds," and so on, should be expanded. This is called Paravacana.

Among those discourses, what is the discourse that is both Sakavacana and Paravacana?

"Both the benefit already attained and the benefit yet to be attained are covered with the dust of defilement; those who hold such a view do not exist, for them there is fault in sensual pleasures." This statement is called Paravacana. For those who practice without approaching those two extremes, there is no cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa) to be designated. This is called Sakavacana.

"One with sons rejoices in sons; likewise, one with cattle rejoices in cattle. For acquisitions (upadhi) are a man's joy; one without acquisitions does not rejoice." This statement is Paravacana.

"One with sons sorrows because of sons; likewise, one with cattle sorrows because of cattle. For acquisitions (upadhi) are a man's sorrow; one without acquisitions does not sorrow." This statement is Sakavacana.

## This is the discourse that is both Sakavacana and Paravacana.
206:
Among those discourses, what is the Sattādhiṭṭhāna (person-based discourse)?

Whatever beings will come to be, all of them will go, abandoning the body.
Having understood this total loss, the wise one, 
Standing firm in the Dhamma, should lead the holy life.

Monks, there are these three teachers: the Buddha (Tathāgata), the Arahant, and the trainee (sekha). This is Sattādhiṭṭhāna.

Among those discourses, what is the Dhammādhiṭṭhāna (teaching-based discourse)?

Whatever sensual happiness there is in the world, and whatever divine happiness there is,
These are not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of the destruction of craving.

Monks, there are these seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgā). This is Dhammādhiṭṭhāna.

Among those discourses, what is both Sattādhiṭṭhāna and Dhammādhiṭṭhāna? Just as the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) is difficult for fools to see, so too the truth of the path (magga-sacca) is difficult to see; I say that for one who knows and sees, there is no craving. The teaching "The truth of cessation is difficult for fools to see, as is the truth of the path" is Dhammādhiṭṭhāna. The teaching "For one who knows and sees, there is no craving" is Sattādhiṭṭhāna. In the simile of the log in the Ganges river, not being stranded on this bank or the far bank, not staying on the dry land, not becoming rotten at the core, not sinking in the middle, and not being caught by humans or non-humans—this is Dhammādhiṭṭhāna. The teaching "In this way, the monk will be inclined towards Nibbāna, leaning towards Nibbāna" is Sattādhiṭṭhāna. This is both Sattādhiṭṭhāna and Dhammādhiṭṭhāna.

Among those discourses, what is Thava (praise)?

Among paths, the Eightfold Path is the best; among truths, the four statements (truths) are the best.
Among things, detachment (virāga) is the best; and among bipeds, the One with Vision (the Buddha) is the best.

Monks, there are these three supreme things: the Buddha is supreme among beings, detachment is supreme among dhammas, and the Saṅgha is supreme among groups. This is Thava.
207:
Among those discourses, which is the Anuññāta (prescribed/allowed) discourse?

Restraint in body is good, restraint in speech is good.
Restraint in mind is good, restraint in everything is good.
The monk restrained in everything is liberated from all suffering.

## This practice is prescribed by the Blessed One.

Monks, there are these three things to be done: good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind. This teaching is called the Anuññāta discourse.

Among those discourses, which is the Paṭikkhitta (prohibited/rejected) discourse?

"There is no love like that for a son." The expansion of this teaching should be understood. This teaching is called the Paṭikkhitta discourse.

Monks, there are these three things not to be done, which I have taught having known them with direct knowledge. What three? Bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. This teaching is also called the Paṭikkhitta discourse.

Among those discourses, which is both Anuññāta and Paṭikkhitta?

One should perform merit with the body, and be restrained in body.
Having abandoned bad conduct of body, one should practice good conduct of body.

With the first two lines and the fourth line, He prescribes (merit and restraint). With the third line, "Having abandoned bad conduct of body," He prohibits (misconduct). The Mahāvibhaṅga and Aciratapāsāda etc. should be understood in this way.

## These are the summary (Uddāna) verses for those teachings:

If you fear suffering, do not delight in the future.
Like an umbrella in the rainy season, one should practice wholesome deeds in succession.

One should investigate the assembly of all things as non-self (anatta).
There is no release from suffering for you other than through tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).

One who, being attached to sensual desire, is consumed by thoughts,
Should clear this jungle of craving through the well-developed factors of enlightenment.

Look upon the world as empty (suññata), and develop concentration (samādhi).
For one who desires sensual pleasure, lead him to a good destination by the practice of Dhamma.

Though oppressed by dangers from the four quarters, one may be liberated,
If one avoids sensual pleasures like the celestial coral tree (pārichattaka).
208:
Whatever actions a man performs, the worldly conditions (lokadhamma) are revealed. The fruit of merit is happiness; there is no other (third) fruit besides the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala) and the fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala).

Knowing the danger of hoarding (not giving), birth and aging occur. Sensual pleasures (kāma) are manifold and diverse; furthermore, the similes of salt and the arrow were taught.

An evil deed committed leads to the four wrong paths (agati). For a monk whose faculties (indriya) have reached tranquility, likewise, the five Pañcañāṇika Suttas were taught.

It was taught as if being pierced by a spear, and regarding the establishment of consciousness (viññāṇa). Whoever quickly kills living beings, those three types of misconduct (duccarita) [bring results].

Having obtained the rare moment (khana) of a Buddha's arising, [it brings results] for sixty thousand years. The simile of rust arising from iron was taught, as well as the conduct in the four types of persons.

The Sutta of the white covering with good limbs (Nelaṅga) was taught, as well as the simile of the cowherd. For the contented, the seclusion of viveka is happiness; thoughts (vitakka) were also well-taught.

Form (rūpa) is like a lump of foam; the state of having a body like that of the Great Brahma was taught. Wisdom is indeed supreme in the world; the three faculties (indriya) such as anaññātaññassāmītindriya were also taught.

Beings who are attached to sensual pleasures by way of sensual lust, and also that which is worthy of praise, were taught. All phenomena are non-self (anattā), and the Noble Truths (ariya-sacca) were taught.

This alone is the path, there is no other; one should declare [him] a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). For a monk whose faculties are well-developed, it was also taught through the Dhammapada verses.

By speech and by mind, the five aggregates (khandha) should be viewed as impermanent (anicca). Whatever actions a man performs, the three types of good conduct (sucarita) are also performed.

The five aggregates—form, feeling, and perception—were revealed. Whoever practices thus is said to practice the sublime life (brahmacariya), and it is called the fruit of the sublime life.

The non-doing of all evil and the liberations (vimokkha) were taught. There is no love equal to [that for] a son, neither among gods nor asuras.

Because of the benefit attained and the benefit to be attained, one always rejoices or sorrows. Whatever beings will come to be, the teachers were also revealed.
209:
Whatever sensual happiness there is in the world, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) were also well-taught.
Among paths, the Eightfold Path is the most excellent; there are also the three attainments of the highest (Arahatta-phala).
Restraint by body is good; the duty to be performed was also taught.
There is no love equal to self-love; the three Noble [Truths/Persons] were also taught.
One who delights in merit by body removes sensual happiness in the world.
The factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) were well-taught; the hard-to-see Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) and the flood of Saṃsāra were also taught.

## The Second Ground called Sāsanappaṭṭhāna in the Peṭakopadesa is completed.

## 3. Suttādhiṭṭhāna Tatiya Bhūmi

Therein, what is Suttādhiṭṭhāna?
It is the basis of greed (lobha), the basis of hatred (dosa), the basis of delusion (moha), the basis of non-greed (alobha), the basis of non-hatred (adosa), the basis of non-delusion (amoha), the basis of bodily action, the basis of verbal action, the basis of mental action, the basis of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), the basis of the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya), the basis of the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), the basis of the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), and the basis of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya).

Therein, what is the basis of greed (lobha)?
"For a being crushed by his own thoughts (kāma-vitakka), possessing intense lust, and habitually looking for beauty (subha),
Craving increases even more; he makes the bond firm."

'Crushed by thoughts' (vitakkamanthitassa) refers to sensual lust (kāma-ragā). 'Looking for beauty' (subhānupassino) refers to the objective basis of sensual lust. 'Craving increases even more' (bhiyyo taṇhā pavaḍḍhati) refers to sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā). 'He makes the bond firm' (esa gāḷhaṃ karoti bandhanaṃ) refers to lust (rāga). Thus, whatever dhamma is laid down as the root, that very dhamma is to be extracted and shown here. The Blessed One does not teach one dhamma based on another. To whom sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) arises, that very thought is pointed out as sensual thought. By the words 'of intense lust' (tibbarāgassa), the objective basis of that thought is pointed out. By the words 'for one looking for beauty, craving increases even more', that very lust is pointed out as sensual craving. By the words 'he makes the bond firm', that very fetter of craving is pointed out. Thus, it should be understood by comparison in the verses. In the explanatory discourses (veyyākaraṇa), it should be understood in this same way.
210:
In that teaching, the Blessed One points out one Dhamma in three ways: by way of consequence (nissanda), by way of cause (hetu), and by way of fruit (phala).

One who gives is dear; many associate with him.
He attains fame, and his reputation grows.
Without being crestfallen, he enters an assembly;
That man, free from stinginess, is confident.

"Giving" (dadaṃ) refers to whatever gift they give; this gift is a meritorious action consisting in giving (dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu). Among those meritorious actions, it is the cause (hetu). "Many associate with him, and fame..." refers to the good sound of reputation that spreads in the world, being dear and pleasing to many people, and dying without remorse; this is the consequence (nissanda). Being reborn among the devas after the breaking up of the body is the fruit (phala). This is the domain based on greed (lobhādhiṭṭhāna).

Among those, what is the domain based on hatred (dosādhiṭṭhāna)?

He who kills living beings and speaks falsehood,
Who takes in the world what is not given, and goes to another's wife,
And the man who is addicted to drinking fermented and distilled intoxicants.
Without abandoning these five enmities, he is called immoral (dussīla).
That unwise man, after the breaking up of the body, is reborn in hell.

"He who kills living beings" (yo pāṇamatipāteti) means an angry person kills living beings. "And speaks falsehood" (musāvādañca bhāsati) means speaking falsehood to conceal or eliminate one's own faults. "And the man who is addicted to drinking fermented and distilled intoxicants" (surāmerayapānañca yo naro anuyuñjati) means hatred is the root cause. One who is addicted to drinking intoxicants, like one who habitually consorts with another's wife, creates enemies.

"Without abandoning the five enmities" (pañca verāni appahāya) means that transgressing the five precepts is the transgression of all things born of hatred; such transgression is merely a designation. Because of that very kamma produced by hatred, he is called immoral (dussīla). That Dhamma should also be pointed out by way of cause, consequence, and fruit.

There are three characteristics of a fool: he is a speaker of bad speech (dubbhāsitabhāsī), a thinker of bad thoughts (duccintitacintī), and a doer of bad deeds (dukkaṭakammakārī). Among these three, whatever he strives to do with body and speech is called being a doer of bad deeds (dukkaṭakammakārī). Just as he speaks falsehood...
211:
As previously explained, speaking badly is the bad speech of that fool. Thinking of ill-will (byāpāda), which is mental misconduct, is the bad thought of that fool. Because that fool is possessed of these three characteristics of a fool, he experiences three kinds of corresponding suffering and grief. When he goes to a gathering or an assembly, others speak words that are appropriate to him. When the ten courses of unwholesome action, such as killing living beings, occur to him, he experiences suffering and grief rooted in those unwholesome courses of action.

Furthermore, when he sees a thief, a royal offender, caught by the king and deprived of life, it occurs to that fool: "If the king were to know about me too, he would have me caught and deprived of life." Because of that reason, he experiences suffering and grief.

Furthermore, while the fool is sitting in his seat (or rising from his seat), he thinks: "After passing away from this life, what will be my destination (gati)?" Because of that reason, he experiences suffering and grief. This is the cause (hetu) known as the characteristic of a fool. The three corresponding sufferings are the consequence (nissanda). Being reborn in hell after the breaking up of the body is the fruit (phala). This is the domain based on hatred (dosādhiṭṭhāna).

Among those, what is the domain based on delusion (mohādhīṭṭhāna)?

For hundreds and thousands of aeons,
They will wander in Saṃsāra,
Or even much longer than that,
They will go from womb to womb.
Without clinging to the Buddha's words,
But clinging to formations as self,
That they will make an end of suffering—
This is an impossibility.

One who has entered the beginningless Saṃsāra is born and dies; this is caused by ignorance (avijjāhetuka). Whatever the purposes of formations are, they too are conditioned by ignorance (avijjāpaccaya). Not seeing the Buddha's words is called ignorance; this is pointed out in the Avijjā Sutta itself. One who takes formations as self falls into five views regarding the five aggregates. "This is mine, this I am, this is my self"—this sutta is placed in ignorance; it is deposited in ignorance. Thus, the Teacher points out the Dhamma in the sutta by way of method. In that sutta, only the unique (asādhāraṇa) Dhamma should be pointed out, and no other.

Monks, some recluses and brahmins do not understand in detail the Four Noble Truths as "This is suffering." That lack of understanding is suffering; this is the cause (hetu). One who does not understand performs various formations; this is the consequence (nissanda). Clinging to views such as "This alone is the truth, all else is false" is also the consequence (nissanda).
212:
Because it brings about a new existence, this is called the result (phala). This dhamma is also well-explained in terms of cause (hetu), result (phala), and consequence (nissanda).

In this teaching, however, some dhammas are common (to other suttas). Indeed, the cause will be placed at the very beginning in the sutta. How is that, monks? In existence, there are these four wrong courses (agati). Among those four, there is taking the wrong course through desire (chandāgati) and taking the wrong course through fear (bhayāgati); this is called the unwholesome root of greed (lobha). That which is through hatred is the root of hatred (dosa) itself. That which is through delusion is the root of delusion (moha) itself. Thus, these three unwholesome roots should be investigated from the very beginning. In a sutta where one should be pointed out, one is pointed out. Just as three are pointed out, so too are two. Where they are not laid down at the beginning, the cause, consequence, or result should not be pointed out.

## In this sutta, there is this verse:

Through desire, hatred, fear, or delusion, whoever transgresses the Dhamma,
His fame diminishes like the moon in the waning fortnight.

In that sutta, there is desire (chanda), and this desire is called greed (lobha) as previously pointed out. This is a dhamma based on delusion (moha).

Among those, what is the dhamma based on non-greed (alobha)?

"One who dwells contemplating the foul, well-restrained in the senses,
Moderate in eating, faithful, and with energy aroused,
Māra certainly cannot overcome him, just as the wind cannot move a rocky mountain."

In that teaching, there is investigation through the foul; this is called renunciation (pariccāga) by seeing the danger in sensual pleasures. Being well-restrained in the senses has the benefit of non-attachment to the dhamma acquired through my sense bases for the sake of the fulfillment of that non-greed. By the teaching "moderate in eating," there is the benefit of abandoning craving for tastes. Thus, this non-greed is maintained by the object through the contemplation of the foul; that non-greed is the cause (hetu). It is maintained by the sphere of activity because of having guarded doors in the senses; it is maintained as being safe because of moderation in eating; this is called the consequence (nissanda). This teaching, "Māra certainly cannot overcome him, just as the wind cannot move a rocky mountain," is called the result (phala). Thus, whatever dhamma is placed at the beginning, that same dhamma is placed in the middle and at the end.

Monks, I do not see even a single other dhamma for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire (kāmacchanda) or for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire, other than this sign of the foul (asubhanimitta). In that teaching...
213:
For one who attends to the sign of the foul, unarisen sensual desire does not arise, and arisen sensual desire is abandoned. This is the cause (vatthu) of non-greed. Furthermore, the taking up of unarisen lust for the sensual realm, lust for the form realm, and lust for the formless realm—this is the result (phala). Thus, this dhamma is also pointed out in terms of cause, consequence, and result. This is the foundation of non-greed (alobhādhiṣṭhāna).

## Tattha katamaṃ adosādhiṭṭhānaṃ?

If one develops loving-kindness with a mind free from ill-will towards even a single being, he becomes one who has merit through that loving-kindness.
Compassionate in mind towards all beings, the noble one (ariya) performs much merit.

This teaching, "develops loving-kindness with a mind free from ill-will towards even a single being," is called non-hatred (adosa). There is gratification (assāda) through the suppression (of hatred). "He becomes one who has merit through that loving-kindness" means that being associated with that wholesome dhamma, he arrives at the designation of Dhamma. One who has merit (kusala) is like one who is called wise (pañño) because of having wisdom (paññā), or called a sage (paṇḍita) because of sagacity (paṇḍicca). "The noble one performs much merit" is only the ripening (vipāka) of that mundane wholesome deed, not of the supramundane. In that teaching, the development of loving-kindness is the cause (hetu). Becoming wholesome is the consequence (nissanda). The production of much merit in the realm of non-affliction is the result (phala). Thus, non-hatred is pointed out in terms of cause, consequence, and result.

There are eleven benefits of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti). Among those, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness which is the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust for noble dhammas is called (the fruit of non-returning/anāgāmiphala). The mundane level is the cause (hetu). The happiness that becomes pleasant to humans in the future—these eleven dhammas are the consequence (nissanda). Rebirth in the Brahma realm without having done anything else is the result (phala). This is the foundation of non-hatred (adosādhiṣṭhāna).

## Tattha katamaṃ amohādhiṭṭhānaṃ?

Wisdom is indeed supreme in the world, that which leads to penetration,
By which one rightly understands the destruction of birth and death (Nibbāna).
214:
The statement "Wisdom alone is supreme" is the subject matter. "Penetrating" means realizing things as they really are in the Dhamma that leads to Nibbāna. "He rightly knows the end of birth and death (Nibbāna)" refers to non-delusion (amoha). Wisdom is the cause (hetu). The knowing that exists is the natural result (nissanda). The end of birth and death that exists is the fruit (phala). Thus, non-delusion is explained by way of cause, natural result, and fruit.

Monks, there are these three faculties. They are: the faculty of "I shall know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya), the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya), and the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya). Among these three, what is the faculty of "I shall know the unknown"? Here, monks, a monk arouses desire, makes an effort, stirs up energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the realization of the Noble Truth of Suffering that has not yet been realized. The same is done for all four Noble Truths. Among these three, what is the faculty of final knowledge? Here, monks, a monk knows as it really is: "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering." That which is the Path is the faculty of final knowledge. Through the destruction of the taints, he becomes taintless; this is called the faculty of one who has known.

In the same way, this wisdom is the cause (hetu). The arousing of desire, the effort, and the specific knowing are the natural results (nissanda). That by which the destruction of all taints is caused, and the knowledge that arises regarding destruction and non-arising, is the natural result (nissanda). Arahantship is the fruit (phala). Among those, the teaching "Birth is exhausted for me, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done" is the knowledge of destruction (khaye ñāṇa). The teaching "He knows there is no further work for this state" is the knowledge of non-arising (anuppāde ñāṇa). Thus, these faculties are explained as non-delusion by way of cause, natural result, and fruit. These are the explanations of the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) states.

Among those, what are the common (sādhāraṇa) wholesome roots? Monks, I will teach you the wholesome and the wholesome roots. Therein, what are the wholesome roots? They are non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha). Therein, what is the wholesome? They are the eight right states (sammattāni) from Right View to Right Concentration. Therein, the wholesome roots that exist are the cause (hetu). Non-greed originates three actions: Right Intention, Right Effort, and Right Concentration; this is the natural result (nissanda) of non-greed. Therein, non-hatred is the cause (hetu). It establishes three states: Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood; this is the natural result (nissanda). Therein, non-delusion is the cause (hetu). It brings forward two states: undistorted vision (aviparitadassana) and non-expression (anabhilāpana); this is the natural result (nissanda). The fruit of this holy life consists of the two liberations: liberation of mind (cetovimutti) through the fading of lust, and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) through the fading of ignorance; this is the fruit (phala). Thus, these three wholesome roots are explained.
215:
(They are explained) by way of cause, natural result, and fruit. Thus, the common wholesome states should be penetrated.

In some suttas by way of two, in some suttas by way of three (they are common). In this regard, there is this verse:

"The Sage abandoned the measurable and the immeasurable origin, the formations of existence.
Delighting in the internal, well-concentrated, he broke his own existence like a coat of mail."

"The measurable and the immeasurable origin" (tula-atulañca sambhavaṃ) refers to the measurable conditioned (saṅkhata) and the immeasurable unconditioned (asaṅkhata). Among those two, conditioned states are called "measurable" (tula). Those measurable states are twofold: gratification (assāda) and danger (ādīnava). They are weighed (as permanent, impermanent, etc.). He knows Nibbāna specifically as: "Gratification in the sense pleasures is to this extent; the danger of this sense pleasure is to this extent; this is the escape (nissaraṇa)." Nibbāna cannot be measured due to two reasons. It is called "immeasurable" (atula) because it is known that there is no state more excellent than this Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is called "immeasurable" because of its marvelous nature, like a precious jewel cherished by those who reach Nibbāna.

In that teaching, the knowing and seeing of the arising of the wholesome is non-delusion (amoha). Therein, knowing and abandoning the formations of existence is non-greed (alobha). According to the teaching "delighting in the internal, well-concentrated," the removal of distraction is non-hatred (adosa). Thus, these three are called wholesome roots. The teaching "the measurable and immeasurable origin" is non-delusion. Greed, which is the gathering of the formations of existence, is the gratification (assāda) of right concentrations and is the cause (hetu). The breaking of the eggshell of ignorance by one who delights in the internal is the natural result (nissanda). That process (pavaṭṭi) and these three wholesome roots are explained by way of cause, natural result, and fruit.

By this much, this process (pavaṭṭi) and this cessation (nivaṭṭi) occur because of unwholesome roots and cease because of wholesome roots. Through these three, all unwholesome roots reach a convergence. That unwholesome root is indicated in the Dhamma or by the spoken word through various terms such as: craving (taṇhā), anger (kodha), lack of clear comprehension (asampajañña), underlying tendency (anusaya), disparaging (makkha), domineering (paḷāsa), lack of mindfulness (assati), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), and ignorance (aññāṇa). These two words of gratification (assāda) are indicated as Dhammapadas. That defilement (gratification) does not exist (for the Sage). That gratification which reaches convergence in these nine terms is defilement; it is neither greed, nor hatred, nor delusion.

Just as the unwholesome roots were indicated, so too the wholesome portions should be indicated by way of their opposites.

## This is the Heading of Non-delusion (Amoha-adhiṭṭhāna).
216:
Among those suttas, what is the establishment of bodily action (kāyakammādhiṭṭhāna)? One should perform wholesome deeds with the body; one should be restrained in body. Having abandoned bodily misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the body. Monks, these are the three types of good conduct: abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. This is called the establishment of bodily action.

Among those suttas, what is the establishment of verbal action (vācākammādhiṭṭhāna)? The virtuous say that well-spoken speech is best. One should speak the Dhamma, not what is not Dhamma; that is the second excellence. One should speak what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant; that is the third excellence. One should speak the truth, not what is false; that is the fourth excellence. These four types of verbal good conduct are called the establishment of verbal action.

Among those suttas, what is the establishment of mental action (manokammādhiṭṭhāna)? One should perform wholesome actions with the mind; one should be restrained in mind. Having abandoned mental misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the mind. Monks, the three types of mental good conduct—non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), non-ill will (abyāpāda), and right view (sammādiṭṭhi)—are called the establishment of mental action. These are the unshared (asādhāraṇa) suttas.

Among those suttas, what are the shared (sādhāraṇa) suttas? One who is a guardian of speech, well-restrained in mind, should also not perform unwholesome deeds with the body. One should purify these three pathways of action (kammapatha) and strive to attain the Path declared by the Seer (the Buddha). Monks, these purifications (pārisuddhi) are three: purification of bodily action, purification of verbal action, and purification of mental action. Among those three, what is the purification of bodily action? Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. Among those three, what is the purification of verbal action? Abstaining from false speech... [and so on until] abstaining from frivolous speech. Among those three, what is the purification of mental action? Non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view. This is called a shared sutta.

Among those suttas, what is the establishment of the faculty of faith (saddhindriyādhiṭṭhāna)? For one whose faith in the Buddha...
217:
In this way, shared suttas and unshared suttas should be penetrated. Having penetrated them, the meaning of the sutta should be pointed out by way of speech and body.

Among those suttas, what is the establishment of the faculty of faith (saddhindriyādhiṭṭhāna)?
For one whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable and well-established,
Whose virtue (sīla) is excellent, dear to the Noble Ones, and praised,
Who has confidence in the Saṅgha, and whose vision is straight,
They say that person is not poor; their life is not in vain.
One should indeed delight in a person of faith; one should not [merely] delight in their faith. Thus all should be; such clear confidence in the Dhamma is called confidence in the Buddha.

## This is the establishment of the faculty of faith.

Among those suttas, what is the establishment of energy (vīriyādhiṭṭhāna)?
Exert yourselves! Strive! Devote yourselves to the Buddha's Teaching!
Destroy the army of Death, as an elephant destroys a hut of reeds.
Monks, these four right efforts (sammappadhāna) are called the establishment of energy.

Among those suttas, what is the establishment of the faculty of mindfulness (satindriyādhiṭṭhāna)?
For the mindful one, there is always auspiciousness; may there be auspiciousness for the mindful one.
For the mindful one, it is always better; the mindful one attains happiness.
The four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) should be practiced in detail; this is called the establishment of the faculty of mindfulness.

Among those suttas, what is the establishment of the faculty of concentration (samādhindriyādhiṭṭhāna)?
O Charioteer of men to be tamed, the devas and humans who long for You have reflected with their minds.
All beings, even those of the totality (kasiṇa), would know one who cultivates the peaceful, harmless concentration.
Monks, there are these three kinds of concentration: concentration with thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), concentration without thought but with examination only, and concentration without both thought and examination. This is called the establishment of the faculty of concentration.
219:
One should perform wholesome deeds with the body, and [abandon] mental misconduct. The guarding of the body at all times and the three purities [were also taught].

The Sutta which teaches that one's faith is in the Tathāgata and in the arising [of the Dhamma]. "Exert yourselves, go forth from laziness"—thus he taught in sequence up to Right Effort (Sammappadhāna).

It is always good for one who is mindful; he also taught the development of the foundations of mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna). The Buddha who is desired, the faculty of "I shall know the unknown" (Anaññātaññassāmītindriya), and the three kinds of concentration [were also taught].

Wisdom alone is supreme in the world; the three kinds of wisdom are revealed. The Sutta which teaches that there is lust not yet free from the objects of sensual desire; likewise, he taught the faculty of wisdom (Paññindriya).

## Thus ends the chapter called Suttādhiṭṭhāna (The Establishment of Suttas),
## in the Peṭakopadesa of the Elder Mahākaccāyana,
## a resident of Jambuvana.
## 4. Suttavicaya-catuttha-bhūmi

Among those modes of conveying the teaching (hāra-naya-sāsanapaṭṭhāna), what is the investigation of Suttas (Suttavicaya)?

In that investigation, one should thoroughly examine [the Sutta] in terms of wholesome states and unwholesome states, in their preceding and succeeding order. Should this Sutta be undertaken... (p)... should it be combined with those Suttas and their perspectives, or should it not be combined? (Thus one should reflect).

In whatever manner the Buddha taught the defilements (kilesa) at the beginning of that Sutta, one should investigate whether he taught the abandonment of those defilements or not. If the Buddha did not teach the abandonment of those defilements, then the wholesome states that lead to the abandonment of those unwholesome states should be sought. If, upon seeking, they are not found, then the unwholesome states in that Sutta should be extracted; if the defilements are extracted, one should investigate the Sutta dealing with defilements (Saṃkilesabhāgiya-sutta). If [those Suttas] do not provide [the answer], then the states of the Noble Path (Ariya-magga) should be investigated in that Sutta; one should reflect whether the defilements reach abandonment in those stages (bhūmi) [of vision and development] or not.

To whatever extent the defilements are taught, the states of the Noble Path are not taught to that same extent. In a Sutta where defilements reach abandonment, those defilements which are not consistent with the opposition of the Noble Path states should be extracted; if they are extracted, [one should see] if it provides a connection. In that teaching, one should investigate thus: "Two, three, or more defilements reach abandonment by a single Noble Path." If, upon such investigation, it provides a connection, then it should be examined in that Sutta. One should investigate the meaning of the Sutta (the six aspects of meaning) through the lineage of oral tradition or through the completeness of the Piṭaka. If it is not possible to point out those aspects of meaning or the Sutta itself, one should not have doubt in the Pāḷi text. Thus, at the beginning, wholesome states occur. Which...
220: "Those defilements should be abandoned"—thus those defilements should be examined. One should learn the preceding wholesome state or the preceding teaching as an opposite, without deficiency or excess. Like the first Uttila, one should investigate: "For which defilements are which states of the Noble Path now taught? Are these defilements abandoned by these states of the Noble Path, or are they not?" If, upon examination, they fit, they should be accepted. If they do not fit, those defilements that are not opposites should not be examined. Those states of the Noble Path that are opposites should be extracted. For the Noble state of the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga) does not reach the abandonment of [certain] defilements (such as lust for form and formless realms), nor do the states of the Noble Path lead to the abandonment of all defilements [simultaneously]. For example, between wholesome loving-kindness (mettā) and unwholesome lust (rāga), having decided that wholesome loving-kindness is not called lust, ill-will (byāpāda) does not lead to the abandonment of unwholesome lust; only ill-will reaches abandonment through loving-kindness. Therefore, both types of defilements should be examined. Whatever state is indicated, whether wholesome or unwholesome, that state should be extracted. If those states fit, then once extracted, there is nothing further to examine. One should investigate whether two defilements are abandoned by one Noble state, or whether one defilement is abandoned by two Noble states. ## Furthermore, when examined in this way, it should be made to fit. In that teaching, if a discourse that is being investigated cannot be pointed out as to how it fits, there is no room for doubt in the discourse. When the states of the Noble Path are taught, the defilement should be examined by me through the two parts of vision (dassana) and development (bhāvanā). One should inquire: "These defilements that were taught by way of verse (gāthā) or exposition (vyākaraṇa)—are these defilements abandoned by these Noble states, or are they not? Do these Noble states lead to the abandonment of these defilements?" Although unwholesome states reach abandonment through wholesome states, not all unwholesome states reach abandonment through all Noble states. For example, loving-kindness is called wholesome, and lust is called unwholesome. Having decided that wholesome loving-kindness is not lust, and the unwholesome is lust, lust does not reach abandonment through loving-kindness; only ill-will reaches abandonment through loving-kindness. Thus, it reaches abandonment by being decided through the Noble Path as taught in the Pāḷi text as a defilement. Deciding the Pāḷi text as the Noble Path does not lead to the abandonment of all defilements. But the Noble state of the discourse which is the opposite of a corruption—that corruption reaches abandonment through that [Noble state]. ## In that discourse or exposition, if the corruptions do not fit when wholesome states are being taught, those states of the Noble Path should be pointed out in part within the Great Authorities (mahāpadesa).
221:
(These states) should be removed. In that teaching, among the defilements (kilesas) and the Noble Paths (ariya-magga) taught, if those defilements are abandoned by that Noble Path, one should investigate further in that teaching. One should reflect: "For what reason are these defilements to be abandoned? For what reason are the Noble Paths taught?" In whatever way the Noble Paths are taught, in that same way this defilement persists. Indeed, there is a certain defilement that is to be abandoned either by that Noble Path or in another way. It is like wrong view (diṭṭhi), lust (rāga), and ignorance (avijjā) being abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (dassana). If that ignorance or those states are within the scope of cultivation (bhāvanā) and are to be abandoned by cultivation, then only the higher path is called 'higher' (uddhambhāgiya). Due to seeing Nibbāna, it is abandoned by the signless (animitta) concentration of mind (ceto-samādhi) through non-attention (amanasikāra) [to signs]. Thus, one should investigate both the meaning (attha) and the phrasing (byañjana). For defilements to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry, the Noble Path is taught in the manner of vision (dassana). For defilements to be abandoned by the three higher paths, the Noble Path is taught in the manner of cultivation (bhāvanā). If they are to be abandoned by frequenting, the Noble Path is taught in the manner of frequenting (patisevanā). Thus, the defilements to be dispelled and abandoned should be treated up to the seven taints (āsavas) or in other ways. If this unwholesome state is abandoned in one way, but the Noble Path is taught in another way, then that Noble Path should be sought in another way. If the teacher teaches in whatever way to the one seeking this Noble Path, that Noble Path should be sought; by that way, the defilement is abandoned. That Noble Path should be investigated in that teaching. If it does not fit, then the Sutta established by that Pali text should be examined. It should be accepted as it fits. If it does not fit, it should not be accepted, [concluding] "Certainly, this was not spoken by the Blessed One," or "It was wrongly grasped by the Venerable Kaccāna," as indicated in the Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa). The Blessed One taught according to reality. The cause (paccaya) of the taught wholesome and unwholesome states should be sought. Without a cause, an effect cannot arise causelessly. In such a search, what is the method?

In that teaching, this Sutta should be examined [to see] if that state occurs according to its respective causes, having a productive cause (janaka) and a decisive support cause (upanissaya). That cause is threefold: soft (mudu), medium (majjha), and intense (adhimatta). Therein, for a soft cause, a soft state (effect) should be taken. In this way, the cause is twofold: the remote cause (paramparā-paccaya) and the immediate cause (samanantara-paccaya). Through a soft cause, an intense cause should be sought. Why? Because any single cause reaches maturity or fulfillment through other causes. In that teaching, whatever Noble Path is taught, of that Noble Path...
222:
The root cause (hetu) of the state should be sought by this reason or that reason. Just as the decisive support cause (paccaya) is sought through the productive cause (hetu), and the productive cause through the decisive support cause, the natural result (nissanda) of that state should also be sought. As indicated in the search for prominence in the foundation (adhiṭṭhāna), that cause should be sought. Indeed, the result of a soft (mudu) state cannot be an intense (adhimatta) result, nor can the cause of an intense result be a soft state. Rather, a soft result for a soft cause, a medium result for a medium cause, and an intense result for an intense cause is consistent. If there is such consistency, it should be accepted; if there is no consistency, it should not be accepted.

Whatever Dhamma the Blessed One endeavors to teach, He teaches that same Dhamma through the beginning, middle, and end. Just as states are indicated at the beginning in the foundation of the Sutta (suttādhiṭṭhāna), that same state is extensively present until the end of that Sutta. By the power of that Dhamma, that Sutta arises as a verse (gāthā), an exposition (byākaraṇa), a short discourse (khuddaka), or a long discourse (mahanta). Just as there are two kinds, namely, appropriate establishment (anurūpa-thapanā) and teaching establishment (desanā-thapanā), the nature (rūpa) of the state should also be sought. Just as the Blessed One taught the restraint of the five faculties (pañca-indriya) to suppress craving (taṇhā), it is only the desire (icchā). As the Blessed One spoke in the Gopālaka-upama Sutta and other Suttas, it is only the desire. In the Majjhima Nikāya, that state which is called a thought (vitakka) consistent with the Blessed One's teaching should also be sought in other exposition (veyyākaraṇa) Suttas. One should not look at only one Sutta. Only what is consistent should be accepted.

Among those, what is an authorized (anuññāta) Sutta? Even if not spoken by the Blessed One Himself, whatever Sutta is evident in the Suttas themselves should be upheld in this way (as the Buddha's word). If it is said that a certain person spoke it, that Sutta should be examined. Is this Sutta suitable and authorized by the Blessed One, or is it not authorized? Some forms of Suttas are suitable and authorized by the Blessed One, while some are not. If the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) teaches the range (gocara) without it entering one's own knowledge entirely, all those Suttas are not suitable as authorized by the Blessed One. There is a disciple who knows the range of the Ten-Powered Ones either partially or without limit. However, he cannot know that power (ñāṇa-bala) entirely, but only through hearing from others.

Just as the Venerable Sāriputta instructed a Brahmin, that Venerable did not possess the knowledge of the variation in the power of faculties (indriya-bala-vematta-ñāṇa). Therefore, not knowing the high or low nature of individuals, he caused [the Brahmin] to attain [a lower state] while there was still a higher task to be done, and thus he was rebuked by the Blessed One. Just as the Venerable Mahākassapa instructed his nephew, the Venerable Mahākassapa was endowed with the Noble attainment (ariya-samāpatti) that occurs immediately after [the mundane attainment] (anantariya). Without showing his fingers through psychic power, he possessed the knowledge that truly knows the root cause and condition of those who undertake karma based on the entire nature. With that knowledge, he instructed that nephew. That instruction is said to be made by the Blessed One. "Kassapa, even if you could bring ten colors, if that person lacks the sensitivity of the eye (cakkhu-pasāda), he will not be able to see forms," He said. Indeed, just as a messenger instructs the citizens with the king's words, the rest of the assembly was made to know according to the maturity of their faculties. He teaches the Dhamma to others. The Sutta that is consistent with authorization should be taken; the inconsistent one should not be taken. Among those, what is the confusion of Suttas (sutta-saṅkara)? There are five kinds of Suttas: those dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), those dealing with impressions (vāsanābhāgiya), those dealing with vision (dassana-bhāgiya), those dealing with cultivation (bhāvanā-bhāgiya), and those dealing with the beyond-training (asekkha-bhāgiya). If one delights in the other, the fruit of Arahantship...
223:
Venerable Mahākassapa, without pointing his fingers, possesses the knowledge that knows according to reality the root causes and the originating conditions of all phenomena and the undertaking of kamma. With that knowledge, he admonishes him; such admonishment is said to be done by the Blessed One.

"Kassapa, even if you were to carry ten lamps, he would not see forms, for he has no eye-sensitivity."

Indeed, just as a messenger instructs the people of a country by the king's word, so too, having made the rest of the assembly understand according to their faculties, he teaches the Dhamma to others. A Sutta that is suitable for acceptance should be taken. A Sutta that is not suitable for acceptance should not be taken.

Therein, what is the mixing of Suttas (Sutta-saṅkara)? Suttas are of five kinds: those dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), those dealing with impressions (vāsanābhāgiya), those dealing with vision (dassanabhāgiya), those dealing with mental development (bhāvanābhāgiya), and those dealing with the beyond-training (asekhabhāgiya). Desiring to satisfy one kind of Dhamma (the fruit of Arahantship), he teaches another kind of Dhamma; he points out the meaning of one Sutta in another Sutta. He also points out the meaning of a Sutta in its various aspects. In explaining the meaning for the realization of the Noble Path, he points out the meaning of a Sutta dealing with impressions in Suttas dealing with vision. He points out the meaning of the lower fetters in the higher fetters. He points out the meaning of dull and medium faculties in Suttas meant for sharp faculties.

Thus, the mixing of these Suttas by way of cause, by way of natural result, by way of fruit, by way of pointing out, by way of being dull, medium, or sharp, and by way of meaning and phrasing—this mixing is called Sutta-saṅkara. That which is not mixed is called Sutta-vicaya.

## Therein, this is the Summary Verse:
The Sutta taught continuously from the previous ones, the Sutta taught as the cause of reality, the Sutta taught as the natural result, the five Suttas including those dealing with impressions, the accepted Sutta, and the Sutta taught as the mixing of Suttas.

## Of the Elder Mahākaccāyana
## The Fourth Stage named Sutta-vicaya.
## 5. The Fifth Stage: Hāravibhaṅga
Therein, what is the Analysis of Modes (Hāravibhaṅga)? It is where the sixteen modes (hāras) reach distinction by way of phrasing. Among them, at the beginning, is the Mode of Teaching (Desanā-hāra). Therein, the investigation in a Sutta as to "Whether wholesome states or unwholesome states, or the Truths, or a portion of the Truths—how are they taught?" is called the Mode of Teaching. The laying down (nikkhepa) of the four Noble Truths is...
224:
The Truths are of two kinds: shared (sādhāraṇa) and unshared (asādhāraṇa). Among the eighteen terms of suffering, there are seven in brief. They are: bodily suffering, mental suffering, suffering from association with the disliked, suffering from separation from the liked, and the three conditioned states. Among those sufferings, there are three characteristics of the conditioned and three kinds of suffering. Arising (uppāda) is a characteristic of the conditioned. Suffering in the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā) is also a characteristic of the conditioned. Suffering in the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā), which is alteration (aññathatta), is also a characteristic of the conditioned. There is also suffering in the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkhatā). Among these three characteristics of the conditioned, in the three planes of feeling, the arising of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is a characteristic of the conditioned. In the suffering of formations, the three characteristics of the conditioned are known as suffering. In pleasant feeling, the suffering of change and the state of suffering as alteration is a characteristic of the conditioned. Painful feeling is the suffering of pain, and in this context, it is called suffering. In these nine terms, in the first seven terms, and in the sixteen terms, suffering should be sought. The characteristics of the eleven kinds of suffering are explained in the Exposition (Niddesa). Birth (jāti) has the characteristic of manifestation. Death (cuti) has the characteristic of falling away from manifestation. Thus, fifteen terms should be made in detail. Thus, this Sutta is taught in terms of shared and unshared Suttas in the seven and ten terms, in the Dispensation's foundation consisting of mindfulness and awareness, in the eighteen foundations of Suttas, in the ten Sutta-regulations, in the sixteen modes (hāras), and in the twenty-one kinds of investigation and scrutiny (pavicaya-vīmaṃsā). This Sutta, taught according to reality, is called the Mode of Teaching (Desanā-hāra).

Therein, what is the Mode of Investigation (Vicaya-hāra)?

The term, the problem, and the question,
What is before and what is after,
The subsequent singing (anugīti)—the investigation of these is the Vicaya-hāra;
The Mode of Investigation is thus pointed out.

"Term" (pada) means the first term. What is its meaning? The meaning asked of the Blessed One by the Venerable Ajita should be taken. In the verse, "By what is the world enveloped?", how many terms are asked? These four terms are the question (pucchā) for the answer. There is the connection of terms (saṅkāsanā) in the question with the terms answered by the Blessed One. This is called "Term" (pada).

"Problem" (pañhā) refers to these four terms. How many problems are there? There may be one, two, or more. These four terms constitute one problem. The phrasing (byañjana) follows the meaning. Even many terms may ask about only one meaning. These four terms follow each other in phrasing. That question is only one problem in terms of phrasing. "By what is the world enveloped?"...
225:
## 
"The world" refers to the world of sentient beings (satta-loka) in this question. "By what is the world enveloped?", "Why does it not shine?", and "What is its smear?"—all these questions refer to that same world of beings. "What is its great fear?" also refers to that same world of beings. Thus, the phrasing that follows the meaning constitutes a single question. That question is of four types: those to be answered categorically (ekāṃsa-vyākaraṇīya), those to be answered analytically (vibhajja-vyākaraṇīya), those to be answered with a counter-question (paṭipucchā-vyākaraṇīya), and those to be set aside (ṭhapanīya).

Among these four, the question "Is the eye impermanent?" is one to be answered categorically. The question "Is that which is impermanent, suffering?" is one to be answered analytically. Apart from the eye, some other things are impermanent, but the eye itself is not [the only impermanent thing]. When asked whether other existing bases (āyatana) which are not the eye are also impermanent, the answer "They are simply not the eye" is an analytical answer. The question "Does that nature of seeing constitute the eye-faculty?" is one to be answered with a counter-question. The question "Is that nature of seeing a being (tathāgata)?" is one to be set aside, because a being does not exist in the ultimate sense. Since the question is asked excluding the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), it is a question to be set aside.

How was this question put to the Blessed One? It was asked regarding the defilement (saṃkilesa) of the world of beings. Why? Because defilement is threefold: the defilement of craving, the defilement of views, and the defilement of misconduct. Among these three, the phrase "enveloped by ignorance" (avijjāya nivuto) indicates ignorance; the word "desire" (jappā) indicates craving; and "great fear" (mahabhayaṃ) indicates the result of unwholesome kamma. The Blessed One explained that for the 'stream' (sota) of craving, there is no possibility that the result of kamma which produces pleasant feeling would instead be painful feeling. He taught this through the four phrases beginning with "The world is enveloped by ignorance..."

Beyond that, he asks further with the verse "The streams flow everywhere" (savanti sabbadhi sotā). He asks four phrases, and the Blessed One answers with two phrases:

Whatever streams there are in the world, mindfulness is their obstruction;
I speak of the restraint of the streams, by wisdom they are shut off.

These four phrases [of the question] are answered with two phrases. How was this phrase asked? It was asked regarding the purification (vodāna) of that defiled world of beings. The six 'streams' are designated by many names according to the six groups of craving through all the bases. By asking "By what are those streams obstructed?", he asks about the abandonment of the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna). By asking "By what are the streams shut off?", he asks about the uprooting of the underlying tendencies (anusaya). Therein, the Blessed One teaches mindfulness regarding the six doors. For one who dwells clearly comprehending and has mindfulness as a gatekeeper, his faculties become guarded. In those guarded faculties, whatever insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) exists, that insight-wisdom leads to the final abandonment of those respective streams and of that ignorance by which the world is enveloped. Thus, the streams are shut off. Beyond that, he asks again.
226:
## 
Regarding the question asked to the Blessed One, "Where do wisdom, mindfulness, and name-and-form cease?", the Blessed One answers these four phrases with a single statement.

Ajita, as to the question you have asked, I shall tell you—
With the cessation of consciousness, herein this [name-and-form] ceases.

What is asked by this question? It asks about the Nirvana element without residue remaining (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). The Blessed One also answers in terms of the Nirvana element without residue remaining. Among these questions, the first question asks about the cause of defilement (saṃkilesa). The second question asks about purification (vodāna). The third question asks about the Nirvana element with residue remaining (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). The fourth question asks again about the Nirvana element without residue remaining, and beyond that, he asks further.

Those who have fully comprehended the Dhamma (saṅkhātadhamma), and the many learners (sekha) here;
O Wise One, being asked, please tell me their conduct (iriyā).

These four phrases are what he asks. How many are those questions? They concern the Arahants who have fully comprehended the Dhamma and the learners. The meaning is: who is first and who is last? Among them, whom does he ask about first, and whom later? He asks about the Arahant first. Therein, by the term 'saṅkhātadhamma', the Arahants are taken; by the term 'phuthū' (the many), the learners are taken. The phrase "O Wise One, [tell] me of them" is a general (sādhāraṇa) phrase addressed to the Blessed One. In those questions, both general and specific points should be asked. The Blessed One answers that.

He does not answer in the order asked; he answers what was asked first later, and what was asked later first. What was asked? He asked, "What is the conduct of the purified Arahants and the learners who are being purified?" To that question, with the verse "One should not be greedy for sense pleasures, and the mind should not be turbid," the Blessed One restrains the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) through thought (vitakka). As explained regarding the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), it is the restraint of the two obsessions through the non-turbidity of thought. With the words "They are skilled in all dhammas," he answers regarding the Arahant.

In the verse "By what does one cross the flood (ogha)?", these four phrases are indeed four questions. Why? Because in this teaching, the phrasing that follows the meaning is not like the first questions of Ajita. For that person, the answer is not just one; indeed, the answers are many. The questions are also many. It is not a single question and answer; when he asks everything, it was already answered previously, as in the fourth question of Ajita.
227:
In these teachings, in the fourth, the Ajita's Question, the answers are given through the connection of terms sought according to reality; likewise, one seeks the questions and answers according to reality. Again, in this teaching, whoever asks a question in this way, this is the manner of questioning in that teaching. There is the verse: "A tangle within, a tangle without" [SN 1.23]. This verse should be sought through question and answer. When the Blessed One was asked, "Where is the answer?", the Blessed One answered with the verse: "A man established in virtue, endowed with wisdom..." [SN 1.23]. In that verse, Samatha is the development of the mind (concentration), and Vipassanā is the repeated development of wisdom. In that teaching, it should be understood thus: those states which are abandoned by Samatha and Vipassanā are these "tangles within and tangles without." In that teaching, the answer is: through Samatha, lust (rāga) is abandoned; through Vipassanā, ignorance (avijjā) is abandoned. Lust based on one's own internal basis is the "tangle within"; lust based on an external basis is the "tangle without." Identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) based on the internal is the "tangle within." The sixty-one types of views based on external bases are the "tangles without." Whatever entanglement or knot occurs through the group of views based on the internal, that is called a "tangle" (jaṭā). Likewise, in brief, whatever craving (taṇhā) and view (diṭṭhi) based on the internal, that is the "tangle within." Whatever craving and view based on the external, that is the "tangle without."

Just as a deity asked the Blessed One with the verse: "Four wheels, nine doors..." [SN 1.2]. In that questioning, the Blessed One answered with the verse: "Having cut the thong and the strap..." The Blessed One answered with this Truth of the Path, which is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. By this answer, the Blessed One should be understood as comparing the defilements (kilesas) mentioned in the previous verse. That is true: "four wheels" refers to the four limbs (two hands, two feet). "Nine doors" refers to the nine openings of wounds. Another way: "four wheels" refers to the four types of clinging (upādāna). Because of clinging, existence (bhava) arises. Because of the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence occurs. "Nine doors" refers to the nine varieties of conceit (māna). For one who has the nature of conceit, suffering arises through the conceit of superiority over others; the three triads (tika) are complete. Lust (rāga) associated with the five cords of sensual pleasure is joined with the triads. In that teaching, "thong" (naddhī) is explained as craving (taṇhā). "Strap" (varatta) is explained as conceit (māna). "Evil desire and greed" refers to lust (rāga) associated with the five cords of sensual pleasure. In that verse, unbalanced greed is indicated as "evil" (pāpaka) and "craving with its root" (samūla-taṇhā). "Craving rooted in ignorance" (aññāṇamūlakā taṇhā) means craving that does not know the Noble Path; it is the abandoning of craving and view. Again, however many other persons are associated with the Wheel of Dhamma that teaches the Four Truths and with that cause, all states leading to Saṃsāra should be indicated. In that teaching, this verse of answer also accords with the question and the answer. If a verse accords with the preceding and following sequence, then it accords with the exposition (veyyākaraṇa) and the subsequent song (anugīti). In the teaching called "Investigation" (vicaya), however many terms the Blessed One sets down, He repeats the previous teaching with that many terms.
228:
"Monks, a monk endowed with eight qualities is fit to go on a mission as a messenger." These eight terms are set down. The Blessed One repeats them with six terms:

"He who does not tremble when reaching an assembly that speaks highly,
Who does not lose his words, nor hides the message.
He speaks without hesitation, and when questioned, he does not get angry;
Such a monk is indeed fit to go on a mission as a messenger."

In that teaching, however many terms the Blessed One sets down, He repeats with that many terms. "Monks, a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta) endowed with seven qualities is dear, respected, and worthy of development"—this teaching is made in detail. The Blessed One repeats this teaching with seven terms. Thus, one of great learning repeats; He sets down in the minds of those to be taught either a brief word or term, or He sets down a long teaching or nine terms; He repeats a short teaching or repeats a long teaching. Therefore, this teaching is called "Subsequent Song" (anugīti) and "Investigation" (vicaya). This is called the Mode of Investigation (vicaya-hāra).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Construing (yukti-hāra)?

"The examination of the fitness and unfitness of the ground and the range of all the modes is indicated as the Mode of Construing."

The teaching that is indicated according to the exposition and according to the investigation of the sixteen modes is called Specification (niddesa). The inquiry therein, "This question does not fit with the Suttas," is called Construing (yukti).

Just as beings who have a generative cause (janaka) and a supporting condition (upanissaya) are defiled—there is a generative cause and a supporting condition for the defilement of beings—so beings who have a generative cause and a supporting condition are purified; there is a generative cause and a supporting condition for the purification of beings.
