"Ānanda, a virtuous person should not ask with an unanswered question, 'Why should remorse arise in me?' ... (pe) ... he should only remain without answering; this is the cause of purification." What is the generative cause and what is the supporting condition for that? For the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), there are four generative causes and four supporting conditions. There is the association with good people and living in a suitable locality; this is called having a supporting condition because of the nature of the condition for clinging. Whatever old kamma is the result of that generative kamma is the supporting condition; because of that supporting condition, there is the right directing of oneself.
230:
The acquisition (pariggaha) of external objects is the proximate cause of the conceit of "mine" (mamaṃkāra). Attachment to the body is the proximate cause of wrong view (diṭṭhi). Bodily suffering (kāyika-dukkha) is the proximate cause of anger (dosa). Bodily stain of defilement (kāyika-kāsāva) is the proximate cause of greed (lobha). Whatever state (dhamma) arises by means of whatever object, or by the determination of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna), or by the determination of the Dhamma (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), or by an underlying tendency (anusaya), that state is the proximate cause of that object, etc. That state arises together with that object.

For example, if a person does not find a footing (padaṭṭhāna) for the first step, he raises the second step; then he brings forward the following step. If he does not find a footing for the second step, he raises another step. That becomes his condition (paccaya). In the same way, a state—whether wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), or indeterminate (abyākata)—cannot arise without finding a proximate cause. Just as there is wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) for a state that is applied, this explanation is called the Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra).

## Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇa-hāra)?

When one state is mentioned, all states that have the same characteristic are considered to have been mentioned by it; this mode is named the Mode of Conveying Characteristics.

When it is taught by the verse, "Those for whom mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) is always well-undertaken," all four foundations of mindfulness—mindfulness of feelings, mindfulness of the mind, and mindfulness of phenomena—are taught by means of that one foundation of mindfulness. Indeed, the mind does not stay in a single station of consciousness (viññāṇatṭhiti) but arises in various destinations (gati). Therefore, when mindfulness of the body is taught, mindfulness directed towards feelings, mind, and phenomena is also taught. Indeed, when mindfulness of the body is developed, the four foundations of mindfulness do not fail to reach the fulfillment of development (they reach it). Thus, when states similar to that foundation of mindfulness are taught, all states are taught.

In the verse, "Purifying one's own mind, this is the teaching of the Buddhas," mental factors (cetasika) are taught; when the mind is taught, matter (rūpa) is also taught. This mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) is the Noble Truth of Suffering (dukkha-ariyasacca). Furthermore, whatever insight (vipassanā) purifies one's own mind, that meditative mind that purifies is the Truth of Suffering. That by which one purifies is the Path (magga), which is the Truth of the Path (maggasacca). That because of which there is purification from defilements (Nibbāna), that Nibbāna is the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca). Eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye-sensitivity and forms; in that occurrence, these states—feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—which arise together, have the same characteristic in terms of the characteristic of arising (uppāda). He who is weary of form is also weary of feeling; he is also weary of perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
231:
Thus, when one phenomenon among phenomena of the same characteristic is pointed out, all those phenomena are considered pointed out. This is called the Mode of Characteristic (Lakkhaṇa-hāra).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of the Fourfold Array (Catubyūha-hāra)?

Etymology (Nirutti), Intention (Adhippāya), the [six] aspects of Phrasing (Byañjana), and Teaching (Desanā); the meaning of the Sutta (Suttattha) and the sequence of what precedes and follows (Pubbāparasanidhi)—this is the Mode of the Fourfold Array.

Among those four, what is Etymology? How should it be regarded? Just as the Blessed One said: "A bhikkhu endowed with eleven factors quickly attains greatness in the Dhamma." [That bhikkhu] is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in etymology (Nirutti), skilled in feminine designations, skilled in masculine designations, skilled in neuter designations, skilled in designations of the past, skilled in designations of the future, and skilled in designations of the present. He is skilled in a single intention and skilled in various intentions. How are the past, future, and present taught? All Suttas are pointed out through feminine, masculine, and neuter designations. One who reflects on the good or bad etymology of a Sutta through phrasing and etymological skill [thinks]: "This Sutta should be established in this way; this should not be established." This is called proficiency in etymology (Nirutti-kosalla).

Among those, what is proficiency in intention (Adhippāya-kosalla)? When the turn of an entire taught Sutta arrives, it should be understood as: "The Blessed One taught this to these [people]." For example, the verse: "Heedfulness (Appamāda) is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness (Pamāda) is the path to death." What is the Blessed One's intention here? Those who wish to live for eighty years will live heedfully. This is called Intention (Adhippāya).

'The time for yoga does not return,
And he does not arise there among the evil ones;
The Sage has declared the path of feeling,
One who has shaken off the dust of taints is released from suffering.'

What is the Blessed One's intention here? Those who are weary of suffering will strive for the destruction of suffering. This is the Blessed One's intention (Adhippāya) in that teaching. Thus, whether taught by a verse or an explanation, when the evidence is taught through this Sutta, the disciple who practices the way in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma is desired. This is called the Intention of the Teaching (Desanādhippāya). Among those modes, what is the sequence of what precedes and follows (Pubbāparasanidhi)? In a verse or in Suttas, there are eighty words. These words are as taught. Of that verse or Sutta...
232:
The disciple who thus practices the way in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma is desired. This which has been stated is called the Intention of the Teaching (Desanādhippāya).

Among those modes, what is the sequence of what precedes and follows (Pubbāparasanidhi)? In a verse or in Suttas, there are eighty words. The preceding words and the following words of that verse or Sutta should be combined. Thus, that combination is known as the sequence of what precedes and follows (Pubbāparasanidhi). There are one, two, or three verses well-undertaken. For the words taught in one part of that verse, there is a meaning not pointed out by the untaught verses; that meaning should be compared. The specific knowledge of that person who searches for the Sutta in its entirety should be sought in other Suttas. This is called the sequence of what precedes and follows (Pubbāparasanidhi). Proficiency (Kosalla) means: proficiency in the origin (Nidāna-kosalla) by way of the subject matter, proficiency in etymology (Nirutti-kosalla) by way of phrasing, proficiency in the intention of the teaching (Desanādhippāya-kosalla), and proficiency in the sequence of what precedes and follows (Pubbāparasanidhi-kosalla). In that search, when the verses of that Sutta are sought, whether the origin (Nidāna) is found or not, the meaning should be pointed out. Proficiency in the origin and proficiency in the meaning (Attha-kosalla) are shown by way of the subject matter. When the meaning is sought through these four factors, it is sought according to reality. Alternatively, everything is sought by way of the subject matter or the origin. Whatever intention, phrasing, etymology, and sequence are superior, this connection should be explained and joined by the meaning of the Sutta. This is the Mode of the Fourfold Array (Catubyūha-hāra).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Reversal (Āvaṭṭa-hāra)?

'In one proximate cause (Padaṭṭhāna),
He searches for the remaining proximate causes;
It turns through opposites,
That mode is named Reversal (Āvaṭṭa).'

For example, the verses beginning with 'Unnaḷānaṃ pamattānaṃ' (Of the haughty and heedless). That which is heedlessness (Pamāda)—of what is this the proximate cause? It is the proximate cause for the decline of wholesome states. Of what is the decline of wholesome states the proximate cause? It is the proximate cause for the practice of unwholesome states. Of what is the practice of unwholesome states the proximate cause? It is the proximate cause for the practice of wholesome states. Of what is the practice of unwholesome states the proximate cause? It is the proximate cause for the practice of the objects of defilement (Kilesavatthu). Thus, due to heedlessness, wrong view (Diṭṭhi) which belongs to the side of delusion (Moha), and ignorance (Avijjā) which belongs to the side of desire and lust (Chanda-rāga), become proximate causes. In that context, due to craving (Taṇhā) and wrong view, the four taints (Āsava) arise: the taint of sensual desire (Kāmāsava), the taint of existence (Bhavāsava), the taint of wrong view (Diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (Avijjāsava). Among those four, wrong view is the taking of 'it exists in the mind' and among mental factors, the taking of 'it is permanent'; Kāmāsava is by way of bringing the flavor of the objects in the five cords of sensual pleasure; Bhavāsava is by way of attachment to rebirths. Between those two, the material body (Rūpa-kāya) is the proximate cause for Kāmāsava and Bhavāsava. The mental body (Nāma-kāya) is the proximate cause for Diṭṭhāsava and Avijjāsava. Among those four taints, bringing [objects] to the internal by way of attachment is the characteristic of Kāmāsava. It is also the characteristic of longing, obsession, conditioning, and bodily formations (Kāya-saṅkhāra). Unwise attention and wrong grasping are the characteristics of Diṭṭhāsava. Non-penetration of phenomena and lack of reflection are the characteristics of Avijjāsava. These four taints are the four clingings (Upādāna): Kāmāsava is clinging to sensual pleasure (Kāmupādāna), Bhavāsava is clinging to existence (Bhavupādāna), Diṭṭhāsava is clinging to wrong views (Diṭṭhုပါဒါန်), and Avijjāsava is clinging to the doctrine of self (Attavādupādāna). Due to these four clingings, the five aggregates arise. Among those five aggregates, Avijjāsava is abandoned in the mind. That Avijjāsava in the mind...
233:
The physical body (rūpakāya) is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the taint of existence (bhavāsava). The mental body (nāmakāya) is the proximate cause of the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava).

Among those four taints, the characteristic of the taint of sensual desire is the bringing into the internal through clinging. The characteristics of the taint of existence are longing, binding, volitional formations, and bodily formations. The characteristics of the taint of views are misapprehension and misinterpretation. The characteristics of the taint of ignorance are non-penetration of dhammas and lack of clear comprehension. These four taints are indeed the four graspings (upādāna). The taint of sensual desire is the grasping of sensual pleasure (kāmupādāna); the taint of existence is the grasping of existence (bhavupādāna); the taint of views is the grasping of views (diṭṭhupādāna); the taint of ignorance is the grasping of the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). Because of these four graspings, the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha) arise.

Among those five aggregates, the taint of ignorance should be abandoned in the mind; that taint of ignorance is abandoned for one who develops the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā) in the mind. The taint of views should be abandoned in the contemplation of dhammas; that taint of views is abandoned for one who develops the contemplation of dhammas (dhammānupassanā) in dhammas. The taint of existence should be abandoned in the attachment to existence; that taint of existence is abandoned for one who develops the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā) in feelings. The taint of sensual desire should be abandoned in the five cords of sensual pleasure; that taint of sensual desire is abandoned for one who develops the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) in the body.

Among those four, the contemplation of the body resorts to the Noble Truth of Suffering (dukkha-ariyasacca). The contemplation of feelings, while being beneficial to the five faculties—the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity—is the objective field where the defilements of beings roam; therefore, it resorts to the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The contemplation of the mind in the mind resorts to the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). The contemplation of dhammas in dhammas resorts to the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Therefore, for that person, through seeing with the four paths, all defilements are abandoned. For those who delight in the cycle of existence and are negligent, as previously shown, the taints increase. Indeed, for one who knows and sees the Four Noble Truths, the destruction of the taints occurs. Unwholesome states such as suffering, origin, cessation, and the path should be sought in this way. As far as the destination (gati) of that unwholesome state extends, one searches for unwholesome states by way of their opposites and turns back by conveying those defilements. This method is called the Mode of Conveying a Rotation (Āvaṭṭa-hāra). In the same way, wholesome (sukka) states should also be sought. The arrival at unwholesome states should occur [by way of contrast].

The ground (bhūmi) of that Mode of Conveying a Rotation consists of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the perversions (vipallāsa), the four knowledges, the practice leading to the arising of the existing body (sakkāya), and the practice leading to the cessation of the existing body.

## Tattha katamo vibhatti hāro?

A mode that answers by analyzing and classifying any particular dhamma is called the Mode of Conveying a Formulation (Vibhatti-hāra). For example, it is said to one who asks: "Does a person come back again, or does he not?" Such asking and speaking is not an answer based merely on someone's personal wish. Such analysis is called the Mode of Conveying a Formulation.
234:
...whether he comes or does not come. When a question is asked, speaking not according to someone's personal wish but answering by such analysis is called the Mode of Conveying a Formulation (Vibhatti-hāra).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Reversal (Parivattana-hāra)? Pointing out by way of the opposite is called the Mode of Conveying a Reversal. It is as the Blessed One said: "For a person of right view, wrong view is worn away," and so on in detail for all the path factors. This way of conveying by the opposite is called the Mode of Conveying a Reversal.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacana-hāra)?

When a single dhamma is explained by many synonyms,
One who knows this in the Suttas is a 'knower of Suttas' (suttavidū);
That mode is called the Mode of Conveying Synonyms.

It is as the Venerable Sāriputta was praised by the Blessed One regarding a single matter with various synonyms: "Sāriputta is of great wisdom (mahāpañño), of joyous wisdom (hāsapañño), of swift wisdom (javanapañño)." These are synonyms for wisdom (paññā). And just as in the Analysis of the Path (Magga-vibhaṅga), the meaning of leading out (niyyāna) and each path factor are shown by synonyms; and just as the synonyms of ignorance (avijjā) are shown. Although the unwholesome root is only one, it is known by various terms in various regions. People only know the synonyms they are accustomed to using; there is no other way of naming for them. In the phrase "for the bhikkhu who has abandoned all sensual desires (kāma)," it is called by the name 'sensual desire'. In the phrase "one who has crossed over doubt," that same sensual desire is called 'doubt' (saṅkā). In the phrase "they are first infatuated," that same sensual desire is called 'infatuation' (rajjana). Thus, one should search for the dhamma taught in a Sutta, asking: "What dhamma is this name for? What dhamma is this synonym for?" Since the All-Knowing Buddhas teach according to the linguistic usage found in various regions, the synonyms of that dhamma should be sought. This is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying Designations (Paññatti-hāra)? Pointing out the Sutta as "The Four Noble Truths" is the designation of placement (nikkhepa-paññatti). There is also the designation of origin (samudaya-paññatti). In the case of physical nutriment (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra), there is desire, there is lust, up to the point where consciousness is established. In that context, consciousness is designated as the designation of source (pabhava-paññatti). "In physical nutriment there is no desire..." (and so on) is the designation of eradication (samugghāti-paññatti).

It makes known the designation of abandoning (pahāna-paññatti) by saying: "The mind of that person is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of existence, and liberated from the taint of ignorance." For one who is preceded by craving...
235:
The verse "For whom craving is in the forefront, wisdom revolves" (taṇhā yassa purakkhatā paññā parivattati) makes known the pleasing designation (manāpapannatti). With the passage "Thus, the pleasing designation," the Blessed One makes known a single phenomenon. Indeed, without deciding that craving is the origin of suffering, craving is pointed out as the origin (samudaya) in all instances. In the case of not tolerating, removing, and making an effort to abandon the arisen sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka), it is called the designation of rejection (paṭikkhepapannatti).

In this way, among all phenomena, whether wholesome or unwholesome, the field of phenomena (dhammakhetta) of that person arises; only that wholesome or other phenomenon arises in that existence, and the remaining phenomena follow in the wake of that phenomenon. That designation is of two kinds: dependent designation (parādhīnapannatti) and independent designation (sādhīnapannatti). What is independent designation? "Monks, develop concentration; a monk who is concentrated knows according to reality. He knows according to reality that 'form is impermanent'." This designation is called independent designation. What is dependent designation? That designation is the designation of wisdom and virtue. For example, when it is said, "Develop the four jhānas," that person has the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya); the four remaining weak faculties are dependent (parādhīna) in relation to the Four Noble Truths. Through unwavering confidence in the Three Jewels, the faculty of concentration is dependent. The four faculties are dependent in relation to the Four Noble Truths. The faculty of wisdom is called independent (aparādhīna). In the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and the right efforts (sammappadhāna), the faculty of energy is called independent. Thus, in its own proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), like a person who is a master of his own field, that phenomenon is independent (sādhīna); that very phenomenon should be designated in that place. The total suppression and destruction of the opposites of that phenomenon should also be pointed out. In this context, the mode (hāra) concerning the reason why this designation with many aspects is designated for this phenomenon is called the Mode of Designation (Pannatti-hāra).

## Among those modes, what is the Mode of Entry (Otaraṇa-hāra)?
It should be made to enter into six phenomena. Into which six? It should be made to enter into the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), faculties (indriya), truths (sacca), and dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). There is no discourse (sutta), verse (gāthā), or exposition (vyākaraṇa) that is not included in one of these six phenomena. To this extent, the aggregates, elements, bases, truths, or dependent origination alone constitute the entire teaching. In that teaching, among the five aggregates, the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for lust, hatred, and delusion. In that teaching, feelings are of three kinds. Among those three feelings, in pleasant feeling, joy (somanassa) occurs together with sustained thought (vicāra); in painful feeling, grief (domanassa) occurs together with sustained thought; in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, equanimity (upekkhā) occurs together with sustained thought. Furthermore, whatever experiencing there is among those feelings, this experiencing is called the Noble Truth of Suffering. Among the aggregates, it is called the aggregate of volitional formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). In that teaching, the body (kāya) arises in one who is negligent. When that body reaches the state of volitional formation, it is caused by kamma that enters the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in two ways, and by the three types of formations: meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra). These occur in all those with lust, but not in those free from lust. There are also the constructions (abhisaṅkhāra) of hatred. One who is not free from lust performs volition (cetanā) and performs planning (pakappa).
236:
One who is free from lust, however, performs volition but does not perform volitional construction (abhisaṅkhāra). Just as a hot thunderbolt (vajira) falling on firewood, a tree, or any other place both breaks and burns it, so too, the volition of one with lust both wills and constructs. Just as a cold thunderbolt does not break or burn, so too, the volition of one free from lust wills but does not construct. In that teaching, among the five aggregates, the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) is a single body not connected with the faculties (anindriya-sarīra).

In that teaching, the elements (dhātu) are eighteen. Among those elements, when the ten material elements are taught, they are pointed out as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha); that is the Noble Truth of Suffering. The six groups of consciousness and the seventh, the mind-element (manodhātu), are also pointed out as the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha); that too is the Noble Truth of Suffering. The element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) is the meeting place of phenomena. That element of phenomena is pointed out by whatever aspect it is obtained: by cause (hetu), by consequence (nissanda), by fruit (phala), by function (kicca), or by synonym (vevacana). Whether it be wholesome, unwholesome, indeterminate (avyākata), or unconditioned (asaṅkhata). Among the twelve bases (āyatana), ten bases are material; those material bases should be pointed out as the Noble Truth of Suffering. The aggregate of form and the mind-base (manāyatana) should be pointed out by the aggregate of consciousness; that is the Noble Truth of Suffering. The base of phenomena (dhammāyatana) is the meeting place of various phenomena. Among those phenomena, those that are faculties should be pointed out among the faculties; those that are not faculties should be pointed out among the non-faculties. They should also be made to enter according to the sequence of the teaching. Just as the element of phenomena is sought, so too the base of phenomena should be sought. Whatever is the element of phenomena, that itself is the base of phenomena, without deficiency or excess.

In that teaching, dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is of three kinds, four kinds, and two kinds. Therein, the three-fold dependent origination consists of cause (hetu), fruit (phala), and consequence (nissanda). Ignorance, formations, craving, and clinging are the cause (hetu). Consciousness, mind-and-form, the sixfold base, contact, and feeling are the condition (paccaya). Existence (bhava) is the fruit (vipāka). Birth and death are the consequence (nissanda).

How is it four-fold: cause (hetu), condition (paccaya), fruit (vipāka), and consequence (nissanda)? Ignorance, craving, formations, and clinging are the cause (hetu). Consciousness is the condition (paccaya) for mind-and-form. Mind-and-form arises; for the mind-and-form thus arisen, the sixfold base, contact, and feeling are the conditions (paccaya). This is called the condition (paccaya). Existence is the fruit (vipāka). Birth and aging-and-death are the consequence (nissanda).

How is dependent origination two-fold? Ignorance, formations, craving, and clinging are the Noble Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca). Consciousness, mind-and-form, the sixfold base, contact, feeling, existence, and birth...
237:
Death is also this: it is the Truth of Suffering. That which is the cessation of formations due to the cessation of ignorance—these cessations are the two truths by way of their opposites. Therefore, Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) should be pointed out in whatever manner it is indicated, and it should be explained in those various ways.

Likewise, there are the twenty-two faculties (indriya). Among the twelve faculties, there is the eye-faculty. Because there is the faculty of grief (domanassindriya), this is the Truth of Suffering. The male faculty (purisindriya) is the proximate cause for views and craving. For whatever reason a man exists, there is the state of being a man. At that time, he delights in his own internal nature. This delight is called 'I-making' (ahaṃkāra), the intoxication with the pride of being male. Being thus possessed of 'I-making' and lusting after fame, he seeks externally; this is called 'Mine-making' (mamaṃkāra), the intoxication with the pride of being male. In this same way, a woman also has attachment. Among those faculties, the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) and the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) are followers of the male faculty. The states of greed that fulfill that man's desires increase the unwholesome roots. If this desire of that man does not reach fulfillment, the faculty of pain (dukkhindriya) and the faculty of grief (domanassindriya) arise for him. Hatred (dosa) also increases the unwholesome root. If, however, he develops equanimity, he desires to follow the faculty of equanimity (upekkhindriya). Non-delusion (amoha) then increases the wholesome root.

Thus, these seven faculties arise based on the basis of defilements. For all beings who are neither inferior nor superior, they arise based on feeling (vedanā). There are the female faculty and the male faculty. Among those faculties, there are the eight faculties starting from the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) up to the faculty of one who has final knowledge (aññātāvindriya). These eight faculties are called the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (Magga-sacca). Among the ten faculties, the wisdom faculties (paññindriya) are the proximate cause (padaṭṭāna) of sensual lust (kāmarāga). The mind-faculty (manindriya) is the proximate cause of lust for existence (bhavarāga). The wisdom faculties are the proximate cause of lust for fine-material existence (rūparāga). The female faculty and the male faculty are the proximate cause of the seven designations. In that teaching, whatever faculty it is associated with, or whatever can be made to enter into a verse, it should be pointed out by that respective faculty. Thus, it is pointed out in terms of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), truths (sacca), and dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). This is called the Method of Entry (Otarana-hāra).

## Among those methods, what is the Method of Clearing (Sodhana-hāra)?

That which the Blessed One will preach, having undertaken a verse in one part. In that verse, when one teaching is preached, the meaning is not yet pointed out in the remaining teachings to be preached. Why is that? Because that meaning has not been preached first. It is not possible to point out that meaning which has not been preached. For example, like the verse: 'Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless' (Appamādo amataṃ padaṃ). This one verse should be pointed out. Why? Because there is a part of this undertaken teaching that has not yet been preached.

Knowing this distinction, the wise delight in heedfulness (appamāda),
Rejoicing in the domain of the Noble Ones (ariya).
238:
This teaching is one that has not yet been fully spoken. In the preaching of this verse, the meaning should also be pointed out. Why? Because there is still a remainder in that teaching. When verses such as 'Those who are meditative, persevering, and always of strong effort' (Te jāyino sātatikā, niccaṃ daḷhaparakkamā) are cited, then the meaning should be pointed out. Thus, in Suttas or Expositions (Vyākaraṇa) that have not been heard before, a teaching with a single indication is preached. Whatever investigation (vīmaṃsā) and weighing (tulanā) there is, this is the task: whether this Sutta is preached, and whether its synonym (vevacana) is pointed out or not. Whatever investigation is there, that is called the Method of Clearing (Sodhana-hāra).

Among those methods, what is the Method of Terms of Expression (Adhiṭṭāna-hāra)? It is Unity (ekattatā) and Diversity (vemattatā). Therein, there are designations of information (kita-paññatti) and designations of function (kicca-paññatti). That designation of function is called wisdom (paññā) because it knows diversity through a single synonym according to the designation. That wisdom is also a designation by way of its sense of predominance (adhipateyya). Wisdom designated by way of its non-deficient sense is called the power of wisdom (paññā-bala) by that same non-deficient sense. Practice until reaching Nibbāna, which is the object, is called mindfulness (sati) because it occurs in accordance with that object. By way of repeated non-perverted recollection of the Three Jewels, there are: recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānuṣṣati), recollection of the Dhamma (Dhammānuṣṣati), and recollection of the Saṃgha (Saṃghānuṣṣati). Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) is called the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṃga) by way of selecting and examining states. It is called direct knowledge (abhiññā) by way of its leading forward. In brief, the paths are called Unity (ekatta) by way of the non-divergence of their individual essences. For example, cold water mixed with hot water becomes hot water; hot water mixed with cold water becomes cold water; just as there are salty water and sweet water. This is Unity and Diversity.

Furthermore, there is a single nature derived from a collection of various states. As appropriate, the four elements are excluded; because that very nature is called 'matter' (rūpa), it is called Unity (ekattatā). To speak of the earth element, water element, fire element, and air element is called Diversity (vemattatā). Thus, calling all four elements 'matter' is Unity, while distinguishing them as earth, water, fire, and air is Diversity. The earth element is Unity by way of its characteristic, but it is Diversity by way of its mixed substances. Whatever has the characteristic of hardness is all the earth element, which is Unity. To speak of hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, and hide is Diversity. Thus, calling all four elements 'matter' is Unity, while speaking of sound, smell, taste, and touch is Diversity.

Furthermore, there is a state that receives another name due to its diversity. In the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), nine perceptions such as the perception of a livid corpse (vinī laka-saññā) and the perception of a bloated corpse (uddhuma-taka-saññā) are obtained. This is called the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā). Whatever Unity there is from the diversity of objects, that Unity is also called the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) for one who contemplates the danger in perception and feeling. That very concentration in states...
239: In those very phenomena, the cultivation of the perception of non-self is the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya); it is the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) among phenomena. For one who abandons the perception of self (attasaññā) in the mind, it is the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya); it is the contemplation of mind (cittānupassanā) in the mind. Whatever range of knowledge is without limit, being the object of wisdom, is called wisdom (paññā). This is called diversity (vemattatā). Just as there is diversity in craving, such as craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for views. Thus, the knowledge, investigation, and weighing in terms of unity (ekattatā) and diversity (vemattatā) is the Mode of Conveying a Formulation (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra). Among these, what is the Mode of Conveying Requisites (parikkhāra-hāra)? The search for both purification (vodāna) and defilement (saṅkilesa) together with their causes (hetu) and conditions (paccaya) is the Mode of Conveying Requisites. Thus, the cause (hetu) of phenomena that have causes should be sought, and the condition (paccaya) of phenomena that have conditions should be sought. What is the difference between cause (hetu) and condition (paccaya)? One's own nature is the cause; another's nature is the condition. The support of another's nature can also be a cause; for a cause that is one's own nature, the support of some other nature is called a condition, not a cause. What is internal is the cause; what is external is the condition. One's own nature is the cause; another's nature is the condition. That which brings about arising is the cause; that which receives (or causes again) is the condition. That which is resident is the cause; that which comes as a guest is the condition. That which is uncommon (asādhāraṇa) is the cause; that which is common (sādhāraṇa) is the condition. A single thing is the cause; successive things are the condition. The support of the cause should be brought forth. That is the originating cause (samudāna-hetu). Therein, the cause is of two kinds, and the condition is also of two kinds: the immediate condition (samanantara-paccaya) and the successive condition (parampara-paccaya); the immediate cause (samanantara-hetu) and the successive cause (parampara-hetu). Therein, what is the successive condition? Ignorance (avijjā) is the successive condition for name-and-form (nāmarūpa); consciousness (viññāṇa) is the condition by way of being an immediate condition. If ignorance ceases at the beginning, name-and-form also ceases. Therein, what is the immediate reason? The successive condition is brought forth as the immediate condition; this is by way of condition. Therein, what is the successive cause? For one who knows, it is the cause by way of being a successive cause; another mode is the cause by way of being an immediate cause. For whomsoever the immediate result arises, that is the cause for him. Because of the cessation of birth, the external appearance (ākāra) ceases; because of the cessation of appearance, the stick (daṇḍa) ceases; because of the cessation of the stick, the piece (khaṇḍa) ceases. Thus, that cause should also be seen in two ways.
240: In dependent origination, just as ignorance is a condition, what is the condition for that ignorance? Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) is the condition. For what is that unwise attention a condition? It is the condition for formations (saṅkhāra). Thus, what is the root cause of those formations, which are both the condition and that which has arisen from conditions? It is ignorance itself. For that reason, the preceding point (the beginning) is not evident. In that teaching, the latent tendency of ignorance (avijjā-nusaya) is the root cause (productive cause) of the obsession of ignorance (avijjā-pariyuṭṭhāna). The preceding cause is the subsequent condition (upanissaya). That ignorance is also the condition for formations through four reasons: by way of conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), immediate condition (samanantara-paccaya), overflowing condition (abhisandana-paccaya), and establishing condition (patiṭṭhāna-paccaya). How is ignorance a condition for formations by way of conascence condition? Whatever mind is obsessed by lust, therein, by the obsession of ignorance, the entire range of wisdom is destroyed. In that teaching, because of standing in three conditions and the greatness of the extent of the planes, when these formations arisen together with ignorance reach growth, increase, and abundance, wisdom is abandoned through four reasons. What are the four reasons? Latent tendency (anusaya), obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), fetter (saṃyojana), and clinging (upādāna). Among those four, the latent tendency becomes obsession; the obsession that by its nature destroys the wholesome is associated; because of association, one clings; because of the condition of clinging, existence (bhava) comes to be. Thus, those formations that have arisen and reached the planes are of three kinds. They do not exist elsewhere. When these formations are analyzed by the Path, they reach a state of strength and are no longer to be disciplined; therefore, those things are called formations (saṅkhāra). Thus, because of the sense of arising with causes, the productive cause (janaka-hetu) certainly exists. There is also the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) that benefits the formations. Removing the wholesome and unwholesome that have been shown, one should insert the wholesome person and the unwholesome person. Removing the resultant phenomena (vipāka-dhamma), one should insert the expressible (vacanīya) and the inexpressible (avacanīya). Until the cessation of existence, the entire Sutta should be contemplated. The ten Powers of a Tathāgata and the four Intrepidities are of the pure side; they are not made by another cause. Ignorance is the condition for formations by way of immediate condition. The mind that arises immediately after the mind with which ignorance arose, arises. For that subsequent mind that arises immediately, the preceding mind is the condition by way of root-cause condition (hetu-paccaya). Therefore, ignorance is called the productive cause (janaka-hetu). Because of that mind, clinging makes the state of no-opportunity, and thus knowledge does not arise. Whatever element of heedfulness (appamāda-dhātu) of that person is moistened by greed (abhijjhā), in that element of heedfulness, the perversions (vipallāsa) arise, such as 'beauty in the foul' and 'pleasure in suffering'. In such perversion, because of the obsession of lust, the obsession of ill-will, and the obsession of ignorance, the heart is ruined, and because of the original volition (cetanā), formations arise. The perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa) is shown in the description of the basis (vatthu-niddesa).
241:
The distortion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa) is pointed out in the exposition of the subject matter. Because one knows with a perverted mind, this knowing is called the distortion of mind (citta-vipallāsa). Because one firmly grasps with a perverted perception, this grasping is called the distortion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa). Because one attends with a perverted view, this attending is called the distortion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa). The eight wrongnesses (micchatta) increase. The three unwholesome states produce consciousness and knowledge [cognition] in unwise attention. Thus, in the preceding and succeeding states, the formations (saṅkhāra) that cannot be surpassed by the unwholesome reach growth and abundance. These formations, being mostly unpenetrated, become formations leading to renewed existence (ponobbhavikā saṅkhārā). Thus, ignorance (avijjā) is a condition for formations by way of conascence-condition (sahajāta-paccaya) and contiguity-condition (samanantara-paccaya).

How is ignorance a condition for formations in the sense of moistening? That ignorance moistens and pervades those formations. For example, a blue lotus or a red lotus might grow in water. When it is sprinkled and poured over with cool water, it reaches growth, development, and abundance. Similarly, ignorance is a condition for formations in the sense of moistening.

How is ignorance a condition for formations in the sense of being a foundation? Those formations, depending on ignorance, reach growth, development, and abundance. For example, a blue lotus or a red lotus, depending on the earth and standing on the earth, reaches growth, development, and abundance. Similarly, these formations, standing on ignorance and depending on ignorance, reach growth, development, and abundance. Thus, ignorance is a condition for formations in the sense of being a foundation.

Furthermore, through the result of the karma of desire (kāma) accompanied by lust (rāga), existence (bhava) is produced in rebirth. All that is produced in that new existence through the power of ignorance is called 'formations leading to renewed existence' (ponobbhavikā saṅkhārā). In this way too, there are formations with ignorance as condition. Furthermore, among the five types of persons, those who are trainees (sekha), those who have entered the attainment of non-perception (asaññī-samāpatti), those who have reached the peak of existence (bhavagga), those who are moisture-born (saṃsedaja) within, and some others who are non-returners (anāgāmī) do not intend or wish. By what condition do formations arise for these persons? Furthermore, they still have lust (rāga). Their formations, clingings (upādāna), and minds are indeed repeatedly recollected. Because the mass of results (vipāka) that have not yet ripened has not been uprooted and the conditions have not been cut off, they go to existence again. Thus, there are formations having ignorance as condition. Furthermore, for them, there are no clingings or formations [at certain times], yet because the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya) have not been uprooted or cut off, there is an underlying tendency having those formations as object. For the sake of the standing of consciousness, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) arises with consciousness as condition. In this way too, there are formations with ignorance as condition. Furthermore, whatever karma leads to accumulation, all that is through the power of ignorance...
242:
...is conditioned by the power of ignorance, is clung to by the power of craving (taṇhā), and through the power of not knowing, one does not know the danger in those formations. That consciousness itself is the seed; that craving itself is the moisture (sap); that ignorance itself is the delusion. In this way too, it should be said that formations arise because of ignorance. Thus, by these modes, ignorance is the cause of formations.

The root cause (hetu) of that ignorance is unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). There is the cutting off of that round [of rebirth]; it brings about the third power in that Nibbāna; this is rebirth [cessation]. In that teaching, because it has not yet been uprooted by the Path, there is the non-interruption called 'arising in a new existence'; this non-interruption is called an underlying tendency (anusaya).

For example, when two people squeeze a cloth or a garment, even if they squeeze with strength a cloth soaked in water, it cannot dry. The water-element (āpo-dhātu), which is like moisture in that cloth, must be matured and dried. If, depending on the heat-element (tejo-dhātu), one places that cloth outside, it would become even more moist because of dewdrops. Without obtaining the heat-element, it cannot reach absolute dryness.

In the same way, even the attainment (samāpatti) that is the peak of existence (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) is not capable of uprooting and abandoning the corresponding lust. Those born in that realm cling and misapprehend; they do not reach the abandoning of craving through craving. In that case, there is the non-uprooting.

The underlying tendency (anusaya) of ignorance disturbs the mind; this disturbance is called obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna). The non-penetration of consciousness according to reality is called the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). Ignorance is the seed of consciousness. As long as the cause, which is the seed, is not cut off, one undergoes rebirth. One who undergoes rebirth cannot reach the uprooting [of suffering]. Defilements overwhelm the mind that is not uprooted. One with an overwhelmed mind does not know according to reality. Thus, there are the sense of being with taints (sāsava), the sense of ignorance, the sense of cause (hetu), the sense of cutting off (avaccheda), the sense of non-turning back (anivatti), the sense of fruit (phala), the sense of rebirth (paṭisandhi), the sense of renewed existence (punabbhava), the sense of non-uprooting (asamugghāta), the sense of underlying tendency (anusaya), the sense of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), and the sense of non-penetration (appaṭivedha) of perception.

By this much, the field of ignorance has been pointed out. This is called the Mode of Conveying: Equipment (Parikkhāra-hāra).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying: Siting (Samāropana-hāra)? When the Dhamma that is evident is spoken in detail to a person of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), he would know the mind in detail; this is the Mode of Conveying: Siting. In that mode, there are the pointing out of names, the pointing out of the basis of destruction (upaghātaka-vatthu), and the detailed exposition of synonyms and bases. For example, 'it should be abandoned by the monks through practice' is called the destruction (upaghaṭanā).
243:
In this context, what is Samāropana (Application)? There is nothing to be said; one should abandon lust for form (rūparāga) or the extremity of name (nāma). These should be performed in detail up to consciousness (viññāṇa). The state of ignorance (avijjā) should be made known through a simile; this is Samāropana.

For a mind dependent on ignorance, the limited phenomena, craving (taṇhā), and wrong view (diṭṭhi) are the supports (nissaya). Among these phenomena, wrong view, ignorance, craving, and volitional formations (saṅkhāra) are included. Among these four, craving arises with wrong view as a condition; volitional formations arise with ignorance as a condition. In that teaching, consciousness dependent on ignorance and this consciousness conditioned by volitional formations occur up to aging and death (jarāmaraṇa). Thus, when dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is taught in brief, the remaining parts of dependent origination are applied.

For one who is independent of ignorance, there is no agitation (calita) of the mental disposition; therefore, for such a person, there is the abandoning of wrong view and craving. In that context, consciousness arising from the cessation of wrong view and ignorance, in phenomena that are the basis for lust, runs from one phenomenon to another like the simile of a monkey, without sticking to them. However, for that person, there is no desire and lust (chandarāga) for the sensual phenomena that are the basis for lust; for that reason, how could there be agitation of the mental disposition? He establishes the mind in superior beings; that unestablished consciousness, being without cause, ceases. With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease, and so on up to the cessation of aging and death. This is Samāropana.

In that context, the agitation of consciousness through the power of lust is accompanied by possessiveness; when that agitation is absent, the three fires, which are called the occurrence of defilements, are extinguished. Therefore, He said: "When there is no agitation, there is tranquility." In that context, this application means that one with a tranquil body experiences pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā); the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. Up to liberation (vimutti), the knowledge and vision "I am" arises. That person, through the destruction of the taints (āsava), exists in liberation. For one who has reached that Nibbāna as an object, because there is no coming or going (āgati-gati), he does not arise here, nor hereafter, nor in between the two. This is the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa nibbānadhātu), which is the end of suffering.

This Nibbāna element without remainder is called the applied (samāropita) in the middle of this Sutta. There should be application in both dependent origination and liberation. They do not analyze the meaning of that Sutta, which was taught in brief, in detail. Such an application is called the Samāropana-hāra (The Mode of Application). One should not apply phenomena belonging to defilement by means of a Sutta belonging to defilement (saṅkilesabhāgiya), nor should other phenomena be applied. Likewise, they are not applied in Suttas belonging to the habit-stack (vāsanābhāgiya) or Suttas belonging to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). This is the Samāropana-hāra. These are the sixteen modes (hāras).

The Fifth Ground in the Peṭakopadesa of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, the great hero who dwelt in the Jambu grove, is finished.

## Suttatthasamuccayabhūmi

The Dispensation of the Buddhas is classified into three categories: aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana). Among these three, there are the five aggregates from the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) to the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha).
244: ## 6. The Ground of the Collection of Sutta Meanings The Dispensation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is classified into three divisions: aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana). Among these three, there are five aggregates from the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) to the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). The ten material bases from the eye and forms to the body and tangibles are called the aggregate of form. Among those aggregates, the group of six classes of feeling from feeling born of eye-contact to feeling born of mind-contact is called the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). Therein, the group of six classes of perception from perception of forms to perception of mental objects is called the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha). Therein, the group of six classes of volition from volition regarding forms to volition regarding mental objects is called the aggregate of volitional formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Therein, the group of six classes of consciousness from eye-consciousness to mind-consciousness is called the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). These are the five aggregates. What is the full understanding (pariññā) of those aggregates? The full understanding of those aggregates is the full understanding as impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), perception (saññā), and non-self (anattā). In that context, what is the meaning of 'aggregate' (khandha)? The meaning of 'aggregate' is the meaning of 'group', the meaning of 'heap', and the meaning of 'mass'. Just as there is a mass of substance, a mass of forest, a mass of wood, a mass of fire, a mass of water, or a mass of air, so too, the inclusion of everything within the aggregates is the meaning of 'aggregate'. Therein, there are eighteen elements (dhātu), starting from the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and so on, up to the mind-element, the mental-object-element, and the mind-consciousness-element. These are the eighteen elements. The full understanding of those elements as impermanence, suffering, perception, and non-self is the full understanding of those elements. In that context, what is the meaning of 'element' (dhātu)? The meaning of 'component' (avayava) is said to be the meaning of 'element'. By 'component' is meant the sensitivity (pasāda) of the eye is the eye-element. Thus it is for the five elements. Furthermore, the meaning of 'cutting off' lust (rāga) is the meaning of 'element'. Indeed, the eye-element cuts off lust. Thus it is said for the five elements. Furthermore, the meaning of 'element' is said by way of 'nature' (pakati). For example, just as it is said that by nature this man is of a bilious nature, a phlegmatic nature, a windy nature, or a nature of combined humors, so too the natural eye-element is among the ten faculties out of all the faculties... the meaning of 'dissimilar' (visabhāga) is the meaning of 'element'. Therein, what are the twelve bases (āyatana)? They are the six internal bases and the six external bases. From the eye-base to the mind-base are the internal bases; from the form-base to the mental-object-base are the external bases. These are the twelve bases. What is the full understanding of those bases? The full understanding of those bases is the full understanding as impermanence, suffering, perception, and non-self.
245:
In another way, full understanding (pariññā) is of two kinds: full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā) and full understanding as abandonment (pahānapariññā). Among these two, full understanding by noting as impermanent, suffering, and non-self is called full understanding of the known. The abandonment of desire and lust (chandarāga) is called full understanding as abandonment.

In that teaching, what is the meaning of 'āyatana' (base/sphere)? It is said that the meaning of 'āyatana' is 'place' (ākara). Just as a gold mine is the place of gold, or a place of poor color, and just as various cattle stay in those two kinds of places; in the same way, the 'cattle' of consciousness and mental factors, as well as kamma-defilements and states of suffering, stay in these bases. Again, it is said that the meaning of 'āyatana' is 'source of income' (āyadāna). Just as a king's income arises from sources of income, in the same way, the meaning of 'āyatana' is 'source of income'.

The Noble Truths are four: suffering (dukkha), origin (samudaya), cessation (nirodha), and the path (magga). Briefly, righteous conduct (dhammacariya) and the mind are called the truth of suffering. Briefly, ignorance and craving are called the truth of origin. Briefly, knowledge (vijjā) and liberation (vimutti) are called the truth of cessation. Briefly, serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are called the truth of the path.

In that truth of the path, what are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma)? From the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) up to the Noble Eightfold Path, these are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The states that lead to the Nibbāna of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the past, future, and present are called the truth of the path. The foundations of mindfulness are four. What are the four? Here, a monk dwells contemplating the body (kāya) in the body. He also dwells contemplating the right efforts (sammappadhāna), the bases of power (iddhipāda), the faculties (indriya), and the powers (bala).

In that context, what is the meaning of 'faculty' (indriya)? The meaning of faculty is the meaning of lordship (inda), the meaning of predominance (ādhipateyya), the meaning of clarity (pasāda), and the meaning of performing an action without association with others (kiriya). The meaning of power (bala) is the meaning of non-wavering (anavapariya), the meaning of strength (thāma), the meaning of steadfastness (upādāya), and the meaning of support (upatthambhana).

Among those factors of enlightenment, what are the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)? They are from the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga) up to the enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhāsambojjhaṅga). Therein, what is the Eightfold Path? It is from Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) up to Right Concentration (sammāsamādhi). That Eightfold Path is divided into three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), and the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). Among these three, Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood are called the aggregate of virtue. Right Mindfulness, Right Effort, and Right Concentration are called the aggregate of concentration. Right Thought and Right View are called the aggregate of wisdom. Thus, these three aggregates are called the three trainings (sikkhā). In this way, by three modes, the ten terms arise.

Among those ten, the practitioner established in the aggregate of virtue does not grasp the unwholesome state of anger (dosa), uproots the underlying tendency of anger (dosānusaya), removes the dart of anger (dosasalla), fully understands painful feeling (dukkhavedanā), and transcends the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu). The person established in the aggregate of concentration does not grasp the unwholesome state of greed (lobha), uproots the underlying tendency of lust (rāgānusaya), removes the dart of greed (lobhasalla), fully understands pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā), and transcends the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu). The person established in the aggregate of wisdom does not grasp the unwholesome state of delusion (moha), uproots the underlying tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya), removes the dart of delusion and the dart of views (diṭṭhisalla), fully understands neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukhavedanā), and transcends the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu). Thus, through the three aggregates, one does not grasp the three unwholesome roots, removes the four darts, fully understands the three feelings, and transcends the three realms (tedhātuka).
246:
Among those ten, the practitioner established in the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) does not grasp the unwholesome state of anger, uproots the underlying tendency of anger, removes the dart of anger, fully understands painful feeling, and transcends the sense-sphere. The person established in the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha) does not grasp the unwholesome state of greed, uproots the underlying tendency of lust, removes the dart of greed, fully understands pleasant feeling, and transcends the fine-material sphere. The person established in the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) does not grasp the unwholesome state of delusion, uproots the underlying tendency of ignorance, removes the dart of delusion and the dart of views, fully understands neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and transcends the immaterial sphere. Thus, through the three aggregates, one does not grasp the three unwholesome roots, removes the four darts, fully understands the three feelings, and transcends the three realms.

Among those three unwholesome roots, what is ignorance (avijjā)? It is the lack of knowledge regarding the Four Noble Truths, etc., which is explained in detail; it is like the doubt and pondering that occurs when constructing a structure (pāṇasajja). In explaining those Four Noble Truths, what is consciousness (viññāṇa)? The six classes of consciousness, feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—this group of states starting with consciousness is called 'name' (nāma). Among name and form, what is form (rūpa)? It is the designation of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements. Thus, the 'name' mentioned previously and this 'form' together are called 'name-and-form' (nāmarūpa). Among those, the 'six bases' (saḷāyatana) are the six internal bases: the eye-base is an internal base, up to the mind-base which is an internal base. 'Contact' (phassa) refers to the six classes of contact: from eye-contact up to mind-contact. The six classes of feeling are 'feeling' (vedanā). 'Craving' (taṇhā) refers to the six classes of craving. 'Clinging' (upādāna) refers to the four types of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self. 'Existence' (bhava) refers to the three types of existence: sense-sphere existence, fine-material existence, and immaterial existence.

In that discourse, what is birth (jāti)? It is the first arising of the aggregates, the first arising of the elements, the first arising of the bases, the conception, the production, the descent into the womb, the generation, and the manifestation of the aggregates; this is called birth. In that discourse, what is aging (jarā)? Aging is broken teeth, graying hair, wrinkled skin, decline, the disfigurement of the four great elements, and brokenness. That state is called aging. It is the waning, the waning away, the loss of life-span, the total loss, the breaking of the faculties, the oppression, and the ripening; all this is called aging. In that discourse, what is death (maraṇa)? Death is the passing away, the state of passing away, the dying, the making of an end, the breaking up of the body of bloated beings, and the cutting off of the life-faculty among various classes of beings; all this is called death. Thus, the aging mentioned previously and this death together are called 'aging-and-death' (jarāmaraṇa).
247:
In that Dependent Origination, ignorance (avijjā) has the characteristic of not knowing according to reality due to extreme darkness; it is the proximate cause of volitional formations (saṅkhāra). Volitional formations have the characteristic of constructing; they have the manifestation of accumulating and establishing in a new existence. These volitional formations are the proximate cause of consciousness (viññāṇa). Consciousness has the characteristic of knowing based on a physical base; that consciousness is the proximate cause of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Name-and-form has the characteristic of multiple supports; that name-and-form is the proximate cause of the six sense bases (saḷāyatana). The six sense bases have the characteristic of defining the faculties; those six sense bases are the proximate cause of contact (phassa). Contact has the characteristic of conjunction (of object, base, and consciousness); that contact is the proximate cause of feeling (vedanā). Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing the taste of the object; that feeling is the proximate cause of craving (taṇhā). Craving has the characteristic of attachment and delight; that craving is the proximate cause of clinging (upādāna). Clinging has the characteristic of grasping and surrounding oppression; that clinging is the proximate cause of existence (bhava). Existence has the characteristic of casting into various destinies (gati); that existence is the proximate cause of birth (jāti). Birth has the characteristic of the manifestation of the aggregates (khandha); that birth is the proximate cause of aging (jarā). Aging has the characteristic of leading [towards death] and maturation; that aging is the proximate cause of death (maraṇa). Death has the characteristic of the end of the life-span and the cessation of the life faculty; that death is the proximate cause of suffering (dukkha). Suffering has the characteristic of oppressing the body; that suffering is the proximate cause of displeasure (domanassa). Displeasure has the characteristic of oppressing the mind; that displeasure is the proximate cause of sorrow (soka). Sorrow has the characteristic of sorrowing; that sorrow is the proximate cause of lamentation (parideva). Lamentation has the characteristic of crying out verbally; that lamentation is the proximate cause of despair (upāyāsa). Whatever weariness there is, that is called despair (upāyāsa).

There are nine factors where the entire unwholesome side is gathered and converged. What are these nine factors? They are: two root defilements, three unwholesome roots, and four perversions (vipallāsa). Among those nine, the two root defilements are ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). The three unwholesome roots are greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha). The four perversions are: the perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa), the perversion of mind (citta-vipallāsa), and the perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa) regarding the permanent in the impermanent; the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding pleasure in suffering; the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding self in non-self; and the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding the beautiful in the ugly.

Among those, ignorance (avijjā) is the not knowing according to reality regarding the four Noble Truths; this is called ignorance. Craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) is whatever lust, intense lust, desire, infatuation, longing, delight, attachment, and non-relinquishment there is regarding existences; this is called craving for existence.

Among those unwholesome roots, what is the unwholesome root of greed? Greed is [the lust] for various objects belonging to others, possessions of others, places of others, and the essential wealth of others...
248:
...lust, the state of lusting, desire, infatuation, longing, delight, attachment, and non-relinquishment regarding things possessed by others. This greed is an unwholesome root. Of what is this the root? Greed is the root of unwholesome bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions born of greed, as well as of the mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) associated with them.

Among those unwholesome roots, what is the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa)?

It is the malice, intolerance, lack of support, anger, intense anger, desire for harm, and the irritation and repulsion of the mind towards beings. This hatred is an unwholesome root.

Of what is this the root?

It is the root of bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions born of hatred, as well as of the mental states and mental factors associated with those actions.

Among those unwholesome roots, what is the unwholesome root of delusion (moha)?

It is the non-realization of the four Noble Truths, the incomplete grasping, the non-penetration, delusion, the state of being deluded, intense delusion, the state of intense delusion, ignorance (avijjā), darkness, the mass of darkness, obstruction, hindrance, the covering of defilements, the base covering, and the state of being excluded from wholesome states. This delusion is an unwholesome root.

Of what is this the root?

It is the root of unwholesome bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions born of delusion, as well as of the mental states and mental factors associated with them.

In that teaching, the perversions (vipallāsa) should be known. The objects (vatthu) of the perversions should be known. Whatever state is a perversion, that state should be known. Among those perversions, there is one perversion, three perversions, and four objects of perversion. What is the one perversion by which one wrongly grasps through opposition?

Taking 'the permanent in the impermanent,' 'pleasure in suffering,' 'self in non-self,' and 'the beautiful in the ugly'—this is the one perversion.

What are the four objects of perversion?

They are the body (kāya), feeling (vedanā), mind (citta), and mental objects (dhamma). These four are called the objects of perversion.

What are the three perversions?

They are perception (saññā), mind (citta), and view (diṭṭhi). These three are called the three perversions.

Among those three, the grasping of a sign in a pleasant object, in the sphere of the faculties, or in the base of colors is called the perversion of perception. Among those perversions, for one with a distorted mind, the intimation (viññatti) when an object is present is called the perversion of mind. Among those perversions, for one with a distorted mind, the acceptance, preference, inclination, decision, wrong view, seeing, and investigation of 'the beautiful in the ugly' regarding that form is called the perversion of view. Among those perversions, by way of the division of objects, there are twelve perversions regarding the body and so forth.
249:
There are three perversions in the body, three in feeling, three in the mind, and three in phenomena. There are four perversions of perception, four perversions of mind, and four perversions of view. By way of the accumulation of the bases (āyatanūpacayato), there are twelve perversions in forms for one endowed with the perception of eye-consciousness. Up to one endowed with the perception of mind, there are twelve perversions in phenomena. Thus, these six groups of twelve are the four perversions. Due to the diversity of objects and due to the states of being inferior, superior, or middling, there are immeasurable and incalculable perversions for immeasurable and incalculable beings.

Among those, the five aggregates are the four bases of selfhood (attabhāva-vatthu). The body, which is the aggregate of form, is a base of selfhood. Feeling, which is the aggregate of feeling, is a base of selfhood. The phenomena, which are the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of mental formations, are a base of selfhood. The mind, which is the aggregate of consciousness, is a base of selfhood. Thus, the five aggregates are the four bases of selfhood. Among those bases of selfhood, in the body, there occurs the perversion of 'the beautiful in the foul.' Similarly, in feelings... [pe]... in the mind... [pe]... and in phenomena, there occurs the perversion of self. To eradicate these four perversions, the Blessed One taught and established the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). For one who dwells contemplating the body in the body, he eradicates the perversion of 'the beautiful in the foul.' The same should be applied to feelings, mind, and phenomena.

Among those, ignorance (avijjā) has the nature of covering like a mass of darkness and the characteristic of non-penetration; perversion is its proximate cause. Craving (taṇhā) has the characteristic of swallowing the object; the nature of the dear and the nature of the pleasant are its proximate causes. Greed (lobha) has the characteristic of deceiving with one's desired object; taking what is not given (adinnādāna) is its proximate cause. In this world, hatred (dosa) has the characteristic of quarreling; taking life (pāṇātipāta) is its proximate cause. Delusion (moha) has the characteristic of error regarding the object; wrong practice is its proximate cause. The perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) has the characteristic of taking conditioned phenomena as non-perishing; all formations are its proximate cause. The perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā) has the characteristic of approaching contact accompanied by taints (āsava); the sense of 'mine' (mammaṅkāra) is its proximate cause. The perception of self (atta-saññā) has the characteristic of approaching phenomena; the sense of 'I' (ahaṅkāra) is its proximate cause. The perception of beauty (subha-saññā) has the characteristic of grasping the outward appearance; non-restraint of the faculties is its proximate cause. By these nine pointed-out terms, the entire unwholesome side is explained. And that can be known only by one of great learning, not by one of little learning; by the wise, not by the foolish; by one endowed with wisdom, not by one devoid of wisdom.
250:
In the nine wholesome terms, all wholesome factors are included and converge. What are these nine terms? They are tranquility (samatha), insight (vipassanā), non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), non-delusion (amoha), the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā), the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā), and the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā).

Among those nine, what is tranquility? It is the steadiness of mind, its good steadiness, its firm steadiness, staying, established staying, presence, concentration (samādhi), composure, non-distraction, freedom from remorse, peace, and one-pointedness of mind. This is called tranquility.

Among those nine, what is insight? Whether in the aggregates, elements, bases, mentality-materiality, dependent origination, or phenomena arisen through dependent origination; whether in the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, or the truth of the path; whether in wholesome or unwholesome phenomena, blameworthy or blameless phenomena, dark or bright phenomena, or phenomena to be cultivated or not to be cultivated—it is the investigation of things as they really are, analytical investigation, scrutiny, supreme scrutiny, grasping with wisdom, wisdom that is uplifted, wisdom that is collected, selection by the mind, weighing, examining, knowledge, clear vision, the eye of wisdom, understanding, sagacity, wisdom, the brilliance of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the illumination of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the iron arrow of wisdom, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga), and the path factor of right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). This is called insight. Therefore, this wisdom is called insight. Alternatively, it is called insight because it sees in various ways. This insight is called insight because it has the distinctions of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Indeed, this insight is called insight into phenomena (dhamma-vipassanā). By this insight, one sees pairs of phenomena such as the beautiful and the foul, the dark and the bright, what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, kamma and its result, bondage and liberation, the cause of accumulation (rebirth) and the cause of diminution (Nibbāna), arising and ceasing, and defilement and purification. Thus it is called insight. Or else, the prefix 'vi' means 'various' and 'passanā' means 'seeing'; therefore it is called insight. This is insight.

Among those phenomena, there are two diseases in beings: ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). To eradicate these two diseases, the Blessed One taught two medicines: tranquility and insight. One who makes use of these two medicines realizes two states of health: the deliverance of mind (ceto-vimutti) through the fading away of lust, and the deliverance by wisdom (paññā-vimutti) through the fading away of ignorance. Therein, for the disease of craving, tranquility is the medicine, and the deliverance of mind through the fading away of lust is the state of health. For the disease of ignorance, insight is the medicine, and the deliverance by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the state of health. Thus the Blessed One said: 'Two things are to be fully understood: mentality and materiality. Two things are to be abandoned: ignorance and craving for existence. Two things are to be developed: tranquility and...'
251:
Vipassanā as well; the two states to be realized are knowledge (vijjā) and liberation (vimutti). Among those states, one who develops calm (samatha) fully understands form (rūpa); by fully understanding form, one abandons craving (taṇhā); by abandoning craving, due to the fading away of lust, one realizes the liberation of mind (ceto-vimutti) [the fruit of non-returning]. One who develops insight (vipassanā) fully understands mind (nāma); by fully understanding mind, one abandons ignorance (avijjā); by abandoning ignorance, due to the fading away of ignorance, one realizes the liberation by wisdom (paññā-vimutti) [the fruit of arahantship]. When the two states, mind and form, are fully understood by a bhikkhu, then for him, the two states, ignorance and craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), are abandoned. The two states, calm and insight, are developed; the two states, knowledge and liberation, are realized. To this extent, the bhikkhu has completed what was to be done. This is the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (sopādisesa-nibbānadhātu). With the exhaustion of his life and the cessation of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), this present suffering ceases, and no other future suffering arises. In that state, the cessation and stilling of these aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana), and the non-rebirth and non-manifestation of other aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, is the Nibbāna element without residue remaining (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

Therein, what is the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha)? It is the absence of greed, the manner of not being greedy, the state of not being greedy, the absence of desire, the absence of longing, the absence of liking, and the absence of attachment to objects. This is called the wholesome root of non-greed. Of what is this the root? It is the root of wholesome bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions born of non-greed, and of the states of mind and mental factors associated with them. Alternatively, the Noble Eightfold Path is called wholesome; that non-greed is the root of three path factors. Which three? It is the root of Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa), Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma), and Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi); therefore, it is called a wholesome root.

Therein, what is the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa)? It is the absence of ill-will, the absence of resentment, the absence of trouble, the absence of malice, the absence of hate, the presence of loving-kindness (mettā), the manner of loving-kindness, the desire for welfare, the desire for benefit, and the clarity of mind toward beings or formations. This is called the wholesome root of non-hatred. Of what is this the root? It is the root of wholesome bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions born of non-hatred, and of the states of mind and mental factors associated with them. Alternatively, it is the root of three path factors. Which three? It is the root of Right Speech (sammā-vācā), Right Action (sammā-kammanta), and Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva); therefore, it is called a wholesome root.

Therein, what is the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha)? It is the knowledge and vision of the four Noble Truths as they really are, the penetration, the non-perverted vision, the realization, the absence of confusion, the manner of non-confusion, the absence of bewilderment, the manifestation of knowledge, and the light...
252:
...the unobstructed (anāvaraṇa) state for the wholesome qualities of those in higher training (sekhas); this non-delusion (amoha) is called the wholesome root. Of what is this the root? It is the root of wholesome bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions born of non-delusion, and of the states of mind and mental factors associated with them. Alternatively, this is the root of two path factors. Which two? It is the root of Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) and Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati). Because it is the root of these two path factors, it is called a wholesome root. Thus, the Noble Eightfold Path should be joined with these three wholesome roots.

Therein, among those states on the side of purification (vodānapakkhadhamma), what is the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā)?
