The perception, the perceiving, the defining, and the grasping that 'all formations (saṅkhāra) are subject to arising and passing away' is called the perception of impermanence. What is its result (nissanda)? When the perception of impermanence is developed and cultivated, the mind does not cling, does not associate, and does not settle in the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma); instead, equanimity or revulsion is established. This is its result.

What is the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā)? The perception, the perceiving, the defining, and the grasping that 'all formations are suffering' is called the perception of suffering. What is its result? When the perception of suffering is developed and cultivated, the mind does not cling, does not associate, and does not settle in laziness, negligence, and amazement (vimhaya); instead, equanimity or revulsion is established. This is its result.

What is the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā)? The perception, the perceiving, the defining, and the grasping that 'all states (dhamma) are non-self' is called the perception of non-self. What is its result? When the perception of non-self is developed and cultivated, the mind does not cling to I-making (ahaṅkāra), does not associate with it, and my-making (mamaṅkāra) does not settle; instead, equanimity or revulsion is established. This is its result.

What is the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā)? The perception, the perceiving, the defining, and the grasping that 'beings and formations are foul' is called the perception of foulness. What is its result? When the perception of foulness is developed and cultivated, the mind does not cling, does not associate, and does not settle in the sign of beauty (subha-nimitta); instead, equanimity or revulsion is established. This is its result.

In that teaching, the Blessed One taught the full understanding (pariññā) of the five aggregates. Among those five aggregates, the perception of foulness is the full understanding of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha); the perception of suffering is the full understanding of the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha); the perception of non-self is the full understanding of the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha); the perception of impermanence is the full understanding of the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). Therein, through calm, one eradicates craving; through insight...
253:
One completely eradicates ignorance; one completely eradicates hatred with non-hatred; one completely eradicates delusion with non-delusion; one completely eradicates the perception of permanence with the perception of impermanence; one completely eradicates the perception of pleasure with the perception of suffering; one completely eradicates the perception of self with the perception of non-self; one completely eradicates the perception of beauty with the perception of foulness.

For serenity (samatha), which has the characteristic of stilling mental distraction, the jhānas are the proximate cause. For insight (vipassanā), which has the characteristic of penetrating all phenomena as they really are, all knowable things are the proximate cause. For non-greed (alobha), which has the characteristic of not being drawn towards desire, abstinence from taking what is not given is the proximate cause. For non-hatred (adosa), which has the characteristic of non-anger, abstinence from taking life is the proximate cause. For non-delusion (amoha), which has the characteristic of non-obstruction regarding the object (knowing according to its nature), right practice is the proximate cause. For the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), which has the characteristic of grasping the destruction of conditioned phenomena, arising and passing away is the proximate cause. For the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā), which has the characteristic of knowing contact accompanied by taints (sāsava-phassa), feeling (vedanā) is the proximate cause. For the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā), which has the characteristic of not adhering to all phenomena as self, the perception of conditioned phenomena (dhamma-saññā) is the proximate cause. For the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā), which has the characteristic of grasping the livid corpse, the festering corpse, and the bloated corpse as unattractive objects, disenchantment (nibbidā) is the proximate cause. When these nine terms are shown, the entire wholesome side is shown. Such a presentation can be understood only by one of great learning (bahussuta), not by one of little learning; by the wise, not by the foolish; by one endowed with wisdom, not by one devoid of it.

Among those nine terms, for one resolved on the perception of permanence, who inclines the mind here and there and does not reflect with mindfulness, the perception of impermanence does not appear. For one resolved on the enjoyment of pleasure in the five cords of sensual pleasure, who does not reflect on the change of postures (agati), the perception of suffering does not appear. For one resolved on self in the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, who does not reflect on the analysis of various elements and manifold elements, the perception of non-self does not appear. For one who delights in the appearance and shape of the body and is resolved on beauty, the perception of foulness does not appear because it is concealed.

Faith (saddhā) has the characteristic of clarity (absence of dissatisfaction); its manifestation is belief. The four factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyanga) are the proximate cause of that faith. Thus it was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, where is the faculty of faith to be seen? It is to be seen in the four wholesome factors of stream-entry.'

The faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) has the characteristic of not abandoning courage; its manifestation is the arousal of energy. The four past right efforts (sammappadhāna) are the proximate cause of that energy. It is as the Blessed One said: 'Monks, where is the faculty of energy to be seen? It is to be seen in the four right efforts.'
254:
Mindfulness (sati) has the characteristic of remembering; its manifestation is non-confusion. The four past foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are the proximate cause of that mindfulness. It is as the Blessed One said: 'Monks, where is the faculty of mindfulness to be seen? It is to be seen in the four foundations of mindfulness.' Concentration (samādhi) has the characteristic of stability; its manifestation is non-distraction. The four knowledges are the proximate cause of that concentration. It is as the Blessed One said: 'Monks, where is the faculty of concentration to be seen? It is to be seen in the four jhānas.' Wisdom (paññā) has the characteristic of understanding; its manifestation is the investigation of the true meaning. The four Noble Truths are the proximate cause of that wisdom. It is as the Blessed One said: 'Monks, where is the faculty of wisdom to be seen? It is to be seen in the four Noble Truths.'

The four wheels (cakka) are: the wheel of living in a suitable locality (patirūpadesavāsa), the wheel of associating with superior persons (sappurisūpanissaya), the wheel of right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi), and the wheel of having performed merit in the past (pubbekatapuññatā). Among these four, the wheel of living in a suitable locality has the characteristic of reliance on the Noble Ones; that wheel is the proximate cause of associating with superior persons. Associating with superior persons has the characteristic of reliance on the Noble Ones; that wheel is the proximate cause of right self-direction. Right self-direction has the characteristic of right practice; that wheel is the proximate cause of meritorious deeds. Merit has the characteristic of accumulating wholesome states; that merit is the proximate cause of all attainments and prosperity.

There are eleven states rooted in virtue (sīla). For one who is virtuous, freedom from remorse (avippaṭisāra) arises... that person understands through the knowledge and vision of liberation: 'After performing these sixteen functions of the path, there is no further task to be done.' In that teaching, the characteristic of abstinence is called virtue; that virtue is the proximate cause of freedom from remorse. Freedom from remorse has the characteristic of absence of self-reproach; that freedom from remorse is the proximate cause of gladness (pāmojja). Gladness has the characteristic of exultation; that gladness is the proximate cause of rapture (pīti). Rapture has the characteristic of delighting the mind; that rapture is the proximate cause of tranquillity (passaddhi). Tranquillity has the characteristic of wieldiness; that tranquillity is the proximate cause of happiness (sukha). Happiness has the characteristic of freedom from anxiety; that happiness is the proximate cause of concentration (samādhi). Concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction; that concentration is the proximate cause of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana). Wisdom has the characteristic of non-perverted investigation; that wisdom is the proximate cause of disenchantment (nibbidā). Disenchantment has the characteristic of non-attachment; that disenchantment is the proximate cause of dispassion (virāga). Dispassion has the characteristic of non-defilement; that dispassion is the proximate cause of liberation (vimutti). Liberation has the characteristic of seclusion from unwholesome states; that liberation is the proximate cause of purification (vodāna).

The four Noble Planes (ariya-bhūmi) are the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). Among these four, whoever understands according to reality, this understanding is called the plane of vision (dassana-bhūmi). That person also [attains] the fruit of stream-entry...
255:
Knowing as it really is, one becomes disenchanted. This disenchantment is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the attenuation of sensual lust and ill-will. The fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmiphala) is also the fading away of subtle lust. This fading away of lust is called liberation of mind (cetovimutti). The fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala) is liberation from defilements due to the fading away of ignorance. This liberation is called the stage of completion (katabhūmi). The fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta) and the fruits of asceticism (sāmaññaphala)—what is the meaning of the term? The Noble Eightfold Path is called asceticism (sāmañña). Its fruits are called the fruits of asceticism (sāmaññaphala). Why are they called the fruits of the holy life (brahmaññaphala)? The Noble Eightfold Path is called the holy life (brahmañña). Its fruits are called the fruits of the holy life (brahmaññaphala).

In that regard, how does one become a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna)? Simultaneously with the realization of the Truths, three fetters (saṃyojana) are abandoned by the noble disciple: personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), and clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa). Through the abandoning and destruction of these three fetters, the noble disciple becomes a Stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in lower worlds, and certain of reaching the end of suffering.

Among those fetters, what is personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)? An uninstructed, foolish worldling, unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, regards form as self... up to regarding consciousness as self. That worldling clings to these five aggregates as 'this is I' or 'this is mine'. He runs and wanders about with an attitude of being uncontrolled, associated with them, supported by them, latent in them, and as major or minor parts. Whatever acceptance (khanti), preference (ruci), consideration (pekkhanā), reflection on appearances (ākārapari-vitakka), pondering over views (diṭṭhinijjhāyanā), or extreme devotion (abhippasannā) such a person has—all this is called personality belief.

In that personality belief, five views resort to annihilationism (uccheda). Which five? Regarding form as self... up to regarding consciousness as self; these five resort to annihilationism. The remaining fifteen views resort to eternalism (sassata). Thus, by abandoning personality belief, the sixty-two types of wrong views are abandoned. By abandoning it, one does not resort to annihilationism or eternalism. Thus, by abandoning annihilationism and eternalism, the noble disciple has no wrong views whatsoever, other than the supramundane right view (lokuttara sammādiṭṭhi). How, then, does personality belief not arise? Here, the noble disciple is well-instructed. He performs all that belongs to the side of light (sukkapakkha). Being skilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, he regards form as non-self... up to regarding consciousness as non-self. For one who regards them thus, personality belief does not arise.
256:
How does doubt (vicikicchā) not arise? Here, the noble disciple does not hesitate or doubt regarding the Buddha, but has extreme confidence, knowing all the Buddha's qualities such as 'For this reason, the Blessed One is worthy of offerings...' and so on. He does not hesitate or doubt regarding the Dhamma, knowing all the Dhamma's qualities such as 'The Dhamma is the destruction of craving, the fading of lust, cessation, and Nibbāna.' He is endowed with this second desirable quality. He does not hesitate regarding the Saṅgha... up to 'worthy of offerings from gods and humans.' He is endowed with this third desirable quality.

He does not hesitate or doubt when it is taught that 'All conditioned things are suffering,' but applies his mind and has extreme confidence. He does not hesitate or doubt when it is taught that 'Craving is the origin (samudaya) of suffering.' He does not hesitate or doubt when it is taught that 'With the cessation of craving comes the cessation (nirodha) of suffering.' He does not hesitate or doubt when it is taught that 'The Noble Eightfold Path is the practice (paṭipada) leading to the cessation of suffering,' but applies his mind and has extreme confidence. Whatever hesitation, doubt, indecision, agitation, instability, failure to reach a conclusion, or lack of certainty there may be regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path—all those states are abandoned, pulled out, uprooted, made like a palm-tree stump, rendered non-existent, and made not to arise again in the future by that noble disciple.

Among those fetters, clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa) is of two kinds: clinging regarding virtue (sīla) and clinging regarding purification (suddha). Therein, clinging to rites and rituals regarding virtue is the thought: 'By this virtue, or this vow, or this penance, or this holy life, I shall become a god or one among the gods. When I become so, I shall play, delight, and enjoy myself with goddesses who have complexions like the feet of pigeons.' Preference, liberation, lust, views influenced by lust, and the viewing of mind and matter, which are called the vision of things as they are, constitute the clinging to rites and rituals of one who is not content. Therein, what is clinging to rites and rituals regarding purification (suddha)? Here, someone wrongly adheres to virtue, thinking: 'By virtue one is purified, by virtue one is led to Nibbāna, by virtue one is liberated, by virtue one transcends pleasure, transcends pain, transcends both pleasure and pain, and by higher virtue one gradually reaches Nibbāna.' He wrongly adheres to both virtue and vows, thinking: 'By both virtue and vows they are purified, liberated, led to Nibbāna, transcend pleasure, transcend pain, transcend both pleasure and pain, and gradually reach Nibbāna.' For one who again takes up a practice that does not purify and does not lead to liberation from defilements as a practice that purifies and leads to liberation, whatever preference, desire, liberation, viewing, reflection on appearances, view, or observation arises—this is called clinging to rites and rituals regarding purification. Both these kinds of clinging are [abandoned] by the noble disciple.
257:
These (misapprehensions/parāmāsa) are abandoned to the point of not arising again in the future. That noble disciple is one possessed of virtue, endowed with virtues loved by the noble ones, which are unbroken and lead to peace (Nibbāna). Due to the abandonment of these three fetters, the well-taught noble disciple becomes a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), not subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, [assured of the final goal]. (Everything is fully known.)

What is the meaning of 'simultaneous realization of the truths' (sahasaccābhisamaya)? There are four types of realization (abhisamaya): realization by full understanding (pariññābhisamaya), realization by abandonment (pahānābhisamaya), realization by personal experience (sacchikiriyābhisamaya), and realization by development (bhāvanābhisamaya).

Among these four, the noble disciple realizes the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) through the realization by full understanding; realizes the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) through the realization by abandonment; realizes the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) through the realization by personal experience; and realizes the truth of the path (magga-sacca) through the realization by development. Why is that? Because there is full understanding of suffering, abandonment of the origin, personal experience of cessation, and development of the path.

How does one realize through tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā)? By firmly binding the mind to the object (restraining the hindrances), one views the five aggregates as suffering. Therein, that which is the binding (restraining the hindrances) is tranquility. That which is the penetrating investigation (into wholesome states) is insight. For one who views the five aggregates as 'suffering,' the attachment (ālaya), longing (nikanti), approach (upagamana), adherence (ajjhosāna), desire (icchā), infatuation (mucchā), aspiration (paṇidhi), and yearning (patthanā) toward the five aggregates are abandoned.

In that teaching, the five aggregates are called the truth of suffering. The attachment, longing, approach, adherence, desire, infatuation, and yearning toward those five aggregates are called the truth of the origin. The abandonment of that origin is the truth of cessation. Tranquility and insight are the truth of the path. Thus, the realization (abhisamaya) of these four noble truths occurs at one time, in one moment, in one single mind-state, neither before nor after (simultaneously). Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Through the simultaneous realization of the truths, the three fetters of the noble disciple are abandoned.'

In that teaching, when the pair of tranquility and insight occurs, they perform four functions at one time, in one moment, in one single mind-state. One realizes the truth of suffering through the realization by full understanding, up to realizing the truth of the path through the realization by development. Why is that? Because the truth of suffering is the realization by full understanding, up to the truth of the path being the realization by development. For example, as a boat traveling on water performs four functions: it reaches the far shore, it leaves the near shore, it carries the load, and it cuts the current. In the same way, when the pair of tranquility and insight occurs, they perform four functions at one time, in one moment, in one single mind-state. One realizes the truth of suffering through the realization by full understanding, up to realizing the truth of the path through the realization by development.

Another example: when the sun rises, it performs four functions simultaneously, neither before nor after: it dispels darkness, it manifests light, it reveals forms, and it removes cold. In the same way, when the pair of tranquility and insight occurs, at one time (it performs the four functions). When a lamp burns, it performs four functions simultaneously, neither before nor after: it dispels darkness, it manifests light, it reveals forms, and it consumes the fuel. Just as these four functions are performed, in the same way, when the pair of tranquility and insight occurs, at one time (it performs the four functions). At the time when the noble disciple becomes a Stream-enterer, at that time he is not subject to rebirth in the lower worlds and is certain to make an end of suffering. This is called the Ground of Vision (dassanabhūmi).
258:
(The pair of tranquility and insight) performs (the functions). One realizes the truth of suffering through the realization by full understanding, up to realizing the truth of the path through the realization by development. For example, when the sun rises, it performs four functions at the same time, neither before nor after: it dispels darkness, it manifests light, it reveals forms, and it removes cold. In the same way, when the pair of tranquility and insight occurs, in a single moment (it performs the four functions). When a lamp burns, it performs four functions at the same time, neither before nor after: it dispels darkness, it manifests light, it reveals forms, and it consumes the fuel. In the same way, when the pair of tranquility and insight occurs, in a single moment (it performs the four functions).

When the noble disciple becomes a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), he is not subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, is fixed in destiny, and will make an end of suffering. This is called the Ground of Vision (dassanabhūmi). A Stream-enterer established in the fruit of stream-entry, while further developing tranquility and insight, through the occurrence of the pair of tranquility and insight, becomes a noble disciple (Once-returner) due to the abandonment of the majority of sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill-will (byāpāda). Because the Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī) has completed the practice, he comes to this sensual world only once more and makes an end of suffering. This is called the Ground of Thinning Out (tanubhūmi).

That person established in the fruit of once-returning, while developing insight, completely abandons sensual lust and ill-will along with their underlying tendencies (anusaya). When sensual lust and ill-will are abandoned without remainder, the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana)—namely, self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), attachment to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa), doubt (vicikicchā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda), and ill-will (byāpāda)—are abandoned. Due to the abandonment of these five lower fetters, the noble disciple becomes a Non-returner (Anāgāmī). He attains Parinibbāna in that very Brahma world and is of a nature not to return from that world. This is called the Ground of Freedom from Lust (vītarāgabhūmi).

One established in the fruit of non-returning, while further developing tranquility and insight, abandons the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana): lust for form (rūparāga), lust for the formless (arūparāga), conceit (māna), restlessness (uddhacca), and ignorance (avijjā). Due to the abandonment of these five higher fetters, the noble disciple becomes an Arahant. He is one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), who has lived the holy life (vusitavā), who is liberated through right knowledge (sammadanya-vimutta), whose fetters of existence are exhausted, and who has attained his own goal (arahatta-phala). This is called the Ground of Completion (katabhūmi).

Becoming an Arahant is itself the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). With the exhaustion of that Arahant's life and the cessation of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), this (present) suffering ceases, and no other suffering arises. This cessation of suffering, this peace, and the non-manifestation of further suffering is called the Nibbāna element without residue remaining (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Thus, these are the two Nibbāna elements. In this way, the truths have been taught; the knowledge of the truths, the discrimination of defilements, abandonment, the grounds (bhūmi), the powers (bala), and the Nibbāna elements have been taught. When these truths and so forth are taught, the knowledge of everything is taught. Effort should be made in this teaching of the truths.
259:
This is the Nibbāna element without residue of the results of kamma and matter (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). These are the two Nibbāna elements. Thus, the Truths have been taught. The realization of the Truths (saccābhisamaya) has been taught, the definition of defilements has been taught, the abandonment has been taught, the planes have been taught, the fruits have been taught, and the Nibbāna elements have been taught. When these Truths and so forth are taught, it is called the teaching of Universal Enlightenment (sabbabodhi). In these Truths and other such dhammas, effort should be made.

Among those dhammas, what are the nine successive attainments (anupubba-samāpatti)? They are the four jhānas, the four formless attainments (arūpa-samāpatti), and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Among those attainments, what are the four jhānas? Here, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures... and so forth (as found in the Dīgha Nikāya), should be understood in detail. Among those jhānas, what are the four formless attainments? Indeed, it is spoken for one who is free from lust for form; it should be performed in detail up to the attainment of cessation. These are called the nine successive attainments.

Among those jhānas, what is the first jhāna? It is the jhāna dissociated from five factors and possessed of five factors. From which five factors is it dissociated? It is dissociated from the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). What are those five hindrances? Sensual desire (kāmacchanda)... and so forth, should be expanded in detail. Among those hindrances, what is sensual desire? It is whatever excessive lust, affection, longing, being captivated by and completing the enjoyment, desire, infatuation, craving, non-relinquishment, underlying tendency, and obsession there is regarding the five cords of sensual pleasure; this is called the hindrance of sensual desire.

Among those hindrances, what is the hindrance of ill-will (byāpāda)? It is whatever resentment towards beings and formations... and so forth, just as in hatred, there is close oppression; this is called the hindrance of ill-will. Among those hindrances, what is torpor (middha)? It is the dullness of mind, heaviness of mind, unreadiness of mind, dropping of the mind, drowsiness, nodding, sleepiness, and slumbering; this is called torpor. Among those hindrances, what is sloth (thina)? It is the unreadiness of the body, dullness, heaviness, and lack of tranquility of the body; this is called sloth. Thus, both this sloth and the previously mentioned torpor together are called the hindrance of sloth and torpor (thina-middha-nīvaraṇa). Among those hindrances, what is restlessness (uddhacca)? It is the lack of tranquility of the mind; this is called restlessness. Among those hindrances, what is remorse (kukkucca)? It is the scratching of the mind, non-marking, special non-marking, the scratching of the heart, and the regret of the heart; this is called remorse. Thus, both this remorse and the previously mentioned restlessness together are called the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca-nīvaraṇa). Among those hindrances, what is the hindrance of doubt (vicikicchā)? It is whatever doubt there is regarding the Buddha, or the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha... and so forth; this is called doubt. Indeed, there are five kinds of doubt: doubt that is an obstacle to the cessation of defilements, doubt that is an obstacle to the region, doubt that is an obstacle to attainment, doubt that is an obstacle to the Path, and doubt that is an obstacle to heaven. These are the five...
260:
...kinds of doubt. However, in this context, doubt that is an obstacle to attainment is intended. These are the five hindrances.

Among those hindrances, what is the meaning of 'hindrance' (nīvaraṇa), and from what do they obstruct? They obstruct from all wholesome parts. How do they obstruct? Sensual desire obstructs from the perception of foulness (asubha); ill-will obstructs from loving-kindness (mettā); sloth obstructs from tranquility (passaddhi); torpor obstructs from the arousal of energy (vīriyārambha); restlessness obstructs from serenity (samatha); remorse obstructs from freedom from remorse (avippaṭisāra); doubt obstructs from wisdom (paññā) and from dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).

In another way: Sensual desire obstructs from the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha); ill-will obstructs from non-hatred (adosa); sloth and torpor obstruct from concentration (samādhi); restlessness and remorse obstruct from the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna); doubt obstructs from the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha).

In another way: There are three abidings: the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra), the sublime abiding (brahma-vihāra), and the noble abiding (ariya-vihāra). The divine abiding refers to the four jhānas; the sublime abiding refers to the four immeasurables (appamaññā); the noble abiding refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma). Among those three, sensual desire, restlessness, and remorse obstruct the divine abiding; ill-will obstructs the sublime abiding; sloth, torpor, and doubt obstruct the noble abiding.

In another way: Sensual desire, ill-will, restlessness, and remorse obstruct serenity (samatha); sloth, torpor, and doubt obstruct insight (vipassanā). Therefore, they are called hindrances (nīvaraṇa). The first jhāna is that which is dissociated from these five factors.

By which five factors is the first jhāna possessed? It is possessed of initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). The arising, acquisition, possession, and realization of these five factors is called 'having attained the first jhāna.' One abides having produced these five factors; therefore, it is said that one abides having entered upon the first jhāna by way of the divine abiding.

Among those jhānas, the second jhāna is possessed of these four factors: rapture, happiness, one-pointedness of mind, and internal confidence (ajjhatta-sampasādana). One abides having produced and perfected these four factors; therefore, it is said that one abides having entered upon the second jhāna.
261:
Among those jhanas, one dwells having produced and perfected the third jhana, which is endowed with five factors: mindfulness (sati), clear comprehension (sampajañña), happiness (sukha), one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā), and equanimity (upekkhā). Therefore, it is said that "one dwells having attained the third jhana."

Among those jhanas, the fourth jhana is endowed with four factors: equanimity, purity of mindfulness (satipārisuddhi), neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha vedanā), and one-pointedness of mind. Thus, the arising, acquisition, perfection, and realization of these four factors is called "having acquired the fourth jhana." One dwells having produced, perfected, and attained these four jhanas; therefore, it is said that "one dwells in the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra)."

Among those (truths), what is the meaning of impermanence (anicca)? The meaning of oppression is the meaning of impermanence; the meaning of being subject to destruction, the meaning of reaching (the end), and the meaning of seclusion are the meanings of impermanence. This is the meaning of impermanence.

Among those, what is the meaning of suffering (dukkha)? The meaning of oppression is the meaning of suffering; the meaning of intense oppression, the meaning of terror, and the meaning of pain are the meanings of suffering. This is the meaning of suffering.

Among those, what is the meaning of emptiness (suñña)? The meaning of being unstained (by defilements) is the meaning of emptiness; the meaning of non-production, the meaning of burning (appaṭṭha), and the meaning of being detached are the meanings of emptiness. This is the meaning of emptiness.

Among those, what is the meaning of non-self (anatta)? The meaning of lack of mastery is the meaning of non-self; the meaning of not following one's will, the meaning of inability to act as one desires, and the meaning of parivida are the meanings of non-self. This is the meaning of non-self.

## The Peṭakabhūmi called Saṃvattisantika, known as Suttatthasamuccaya, is completed.

## 7. Hārasampātabhūmi

Jhana is dispassion (virāga). The four jhanas should be treated in detail. They are of two kinds: those dissociated from the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and those associated with the factors of enlightenment. Among them, those dissociated from the factors of enlightenment belong to outsiders (bāhiraka); those associated with the factors of enlightenment belong to noble persons (ariya-puggala). Among them, setting aside the roots of the six types of persons, there are those of lustful temperament, hateful temperament, deluded temperament, lustful-hateful temperament, lustful-deluded temperament, hateful-deluded temperament, and balanced temperament. For these persons who enter into jhana, the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are the opposites; being unable to suppress those hindrances, the three...
262:
...unwholesome roots (akusalamūla) are suppressed. Covetousness (abhijjhā), restlessness (uddhacca), and mental distraction arising from the unwholesome root of greed (lobha) are suppressed by the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha). Remorse (kukkucca) and doubt (vicikicchā), which are on the side of delusion (moha), are suppressed by non-delusion (amoha). Hatred (dosa) and sloth-and-torpor (thina-middha), which are on the side of hatred, are suppressed by non-hatred (adosa).

Among those three roots, one thinks of the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) to fulfill non-greed. One thinks of the thought of non-ill will (abyāpāda-vitakka) to fulfill non-hatred. One thinks of the thought of non-harming (avihiṃsā-vitakka) to fulfill non-delusion. Due to the fulfillment of non-greed, one is secluded from sensual pleasures. Due to the fulfillment of non-hatred and non-delusion, being secluded from evil, unwholesome states, one dwells having attained the first jhana, which is accompanied by initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra), and filled with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion.

There are three kinds of thoughts (vitakka): the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-harming. Among them, the first falling upon the object is called initial application (vitakka). The examining and pondering of the acquired object is called sustained application (vicāra). For example, a man sees someone coming from afar but cannot immediately know whether it is a woman or a man. When he gains the correct knowledge that "this is a woman" or "this is a man," having such a color or such a shape, while thinking about those features, the further investigation as to whether "Is this person virtuous or immoral?" or "Is this person wealthy or poor?" is sustained application (vicāra). Thus, sustained application enters into initial application and follows along, examining in accordance with it.

For example, a bird first makes an effort (to fly up) and later stops making effort (while gliding); the effort is like initial application, and the spreading of the wings is like sustained application. Sustained application protects and examines initial application. The opposite of the perception of sensual desire (kāmasaññā) is initial application, and the opposite of the perception of ill will (byāpādasaññā) and the perception of harming (vihiṃsāsaññā) is sustained application. The function of initial application is the non-attention to the unwholesome, and the function of sustained application is the restraint of the chief states.

Initial application should be understood as an energetic person performing recitation in silence. Sustained application should be understood as the repeated contemplation of that very same subject. Non-differentiation is initial application; differentiation is sustained application. Initial application occurs in the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā). Sustained application occurs in the analytical knowledge of principles (dhammapaṭisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā). The proficiency and skill of the mind is initial application, and the skill in directing the mind toward the object is sustained application.

"This is wholesome, this is unwholesome, this is to be developed, this is to be abandoned, this is to be realized"—thinking in this way is called initial application. Acting so that abandonment, development, and realization occur is called sustained application. For one established in these initial and sustained applications, the two kinds of suffering—bodily and mental—do not arise, and only the two kinds of happiness arise.
263:
Physical pain and mental pain do not occur. Physical pleasure and mental pleasure occur. Thus, the mental pleasure and rapture born of thought (vitakka), and physical pleasure, occur only in the body. The one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā) in that jhāna is called concentration (samādhi). Thus, the first jhāna abandons five factors and is possessed of five factors.

Because of the frequent cultivation of those very same thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), the mind is inclined towards those thought and examination in that first jhāna. To him, thought and examination appear coarse. Rapture, pleasure, and renunciation (nekkhamma) also become coarse. Alternatively, rapture and delight (rati) born of concentration arise. That jhāna has examination as its object. With the subsiding of those thought and examination, the mind becomes serene within. One respectfully bears the two factors of thought and examination which should be recollected, and the present sign (nimitta). With the subsiding of those thought and examination, there is unification of mind (ekodibhāva), which is the state of excellence. That jhāna reaches the fulfillment of rapture because of that state of excellence. Whatever rapture there is, that is called the faculty of joy (somanassindriya). Whatever pleasure there is, that is called the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya). Whatever one-pointedness of mind there is, this is called concentration (samādhi). That second jhāna is possessed of four factors. That person, through the fading away of rapture, proceeds while abandoning the inferior hindrance accompanied by the attachment of craving.

In that second jhāna, there is attachment to the joyful mind; thus, that yogi, investigating that jhāna, attends only to equanimity. That yogi, through the abandoning of rapture, dwells equanimous. Just as one experiences the feeling of pleasure through rapture, he dwells experiencing that pleasure with the body and endowed with clear comprehension. By which mindfulness and clear comprehension, one reaches the fulfillment of equanimity. This third jhāna is possessed of four factors.

Likewise, due to the abandoning of physical pleasure, the faculty of joy ceases in the first jhāna. In the second jhāna, the faculty of pain (dukkhindriya) ceases. That yogi, due to the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and because of the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. In that fourth jhāna, equanimity is serene through the four faculties: the faculty of pain (dukkhindriya), the faculty of grief (domanassindriya), the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya), and the faculty of joy (somanassindriya). Due to the cessation of those feelings, equanimity and clear comprehension occur. In that jhāna, because of the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy, lack of mindfulness might occur; due to the cessation of that pleasure and joy, he becomes mindful. Because of the faculty of pain and the faculty of grief, lack of clear comprehension might occur; due to the cessation of that pain and grief, he becomes one with clear comprehension. Thus, due to the perception of equanimity, there is one-pointedness of mind that is mindful and clearly comprehending. This is called the fourth jhāna.

Among those who have attained jhāna, for a person of lustful temperament, the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy occur. For a person of hateful temperament, the faculty of pain and the faculty of grief occur. For a person of deluded temperament, lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension occur.
265:
There are these four jhānas; these states (such as initial thought, etc.) are called their factors (jhānaṅga). The collection of these factors is called the factor. This is the distinction in terms of the plane of jhāna (jhānabhūmi). Such a distinction should exist. These distinct states are called requisites (sambhāra). Through these requisites, this jhāna (the collection of factors like initial thought, etc.) arises. This arising has this as its proximate cause (upanisā). Through that proximate cause, this cultivation (bhāvanā) occurs. Because of that cultivation, this danger (ādīnava) arises. Therefore, this is called decline (parihāni). Of whom is the decline? It is the decline of the person who enters that jhāna. To one who reflects on that example as stated, this is the distinction. Because of that distinction, this gratification (assāda) occurs. Of whom is the gratification? It is the gratification of the person who meditates without [actual] jhāna. For that person who meditates without jhāna, this jhāna is called imposing. The jhāna established in skillfulness reaches the unshakable strength of jhāna (jhānabala). For one established in the strength of jhāna and having reached the pinnacle, these jhāna factors consist of non-turbid thoughts, and in the first jhāna, the jhāna factors become manifest. Because that person follows after rapture (pīti), the jhāna factors in the first jhāna arise depending on that first jhāna, and thus the qualities of the factors of that jhāna occur.

Rapture (pīti) is a jhāna factor in the second jhāna because of its nature as a jhāna factor; for one who proceeds in such a manner, the co-arisen jhāna factor is a jhāna factor because it possesses happiness (sukha), is serene within oneself, and because it clarifies the mind in the second jhāna, and because it arises depending on that clarity. Rapture is a jhāna factor in the second jhāna, being serene within oneself, and steady rapture is called a jhāna factor in the second jhāna. Unification of mind (ekodibhāva) is a jhāna factor in the second jhāna. Equanimity (upekkhā) is a jhāna factor in the third jhāna, being associated with contact. Happiness (sukha) is a factor of that jhāna. Unification of mind is a jhāna factor in the fourth jhāna. Equanimity, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, is a jhāna factor in the fourth jhāna. The purity of mindfulness (sati-pārisuddhi) caused by equanimity, which is the supporting plane, is a jhāna factor in the fourth jhāna. Purity of mindfulness is also associated with jhāna factors in many planes of jhāna; thus, rapture and unification of mind are called jhāna factors in the fourth jhāna.

Among those jhānas, what is the plane of jhāna (jhānabhūmi)? Following after the seclusion of states accompanied by initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) is the plane of jhāna in the first jhāna. Following after rapture (pīti), which produces internal serenity in states without initial thought and sustained thought, is the plane of jhāna in the second jhāna. States accompanied by rapture, combined with the enjoyment of the feeling of happiness (sukha), are the plane of jhāna in the third jhāna. The state of that rapture accompanied by pleasure and pain, and accompanied by resolution (abhinīhāra), is the plane of jhāna in the fourth jhāna. Being accompanied by the immeasurable (appamāṇa) and taking beings as an object is the plane of jhāna in the first jhāna. States accompanied by the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) and having the perception of form are the plane of jhāna in the second jhāna. For states accompanied by liberation (vimokkha), having freedom from the hindrances is the plane of jhāna in the third jhāna. The bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) accompanied by contemplation (anupassanā) is well-established as the plane of the fourth jhāna.
266:
Among those jhānas, what are the distinctions of jhāna? Being secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from evil unwholesome states, there is the transcendence of the sense-sphere element accompanied by consciousness and mental factors; this is a distinction of jhāna. Without applied thought and without sustained thought, due to the presence of rapture and mindfulness, perceptions and mental activities accompanied by rapture arise; this is a distinction of jhāna. In the plane without applied thought and without sustained thought, mental activities accompanied by equanimity and following mindfulness arise. Mindfulness, which occurs in accordance with that state, remains firm. One enters and dwells in that plane; this is a distinction of jhāna. Perceptions and mental activities accompanied by the purity of mindfulness arise, and one enters and dwells in that plane; this is a distinction of jhāna. In the plane accompanied by the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana), perceptions and mental activities accompanied by the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) arise, and one enters and dwells in that plane; this is a distinction of jhāna.

The requisites (sambhāra) of jhāna are as follows: The requisite of the thought of renunciation (nekkhammavitakka) is the desire to dispel the thought of sensual desire. The requisite of the thought of non-ill will (abyāpādavitakka) is the desire to dispel the thought of ill will. The requisite of the thought of non-harming (avihiṃsāvitakka) is the desire to dispel the thought of harming. Guarding the doors of the sense faculties and fewness of wishes are requisites; pure livelihood and the requisites for the four attainments (samāpatti) are the state of dwelling without being unworkable. The requisite of the path (magga) is the state of reaching the attainments. The requisite of fruition (phala) is the arrival at jhāna because of the production of jhāna. Due to wholesome causes, jhānas reach arising. Some do not reach arising from any cause other than reaching renunciation. Concentration, which is the cessation of the object, being manifest, they reach arising. Having reached the path and fruition of jhāna without transgression, they reach arising. By abandoning the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy, they reach arising through the state of non-affliction. They reach arising with the intention of that very abandonment. They reach arising for the sake of non-burning. This is called the arrival of knowledge (ñāṇasamudāgama).

In that context, what is the proximate cause (upanisā)? Good friendship is the proximate cause of jhāna. Devotion to good friends is the proximate cause of jhāna. Guarding the doors of the sense faculties is the proximate cause of jhāna. Dissatisfaction with wholesome states is the proximate cause of jhāna. Hearing the true Dhamma is the proximate cause of jhāna. For one who is stirred at a place of urgency, there is wise attention; this is the proximate cause of jhāna.
267:
Among those insights, what is development (bhāvanā)? Cultivating loving-kindness (mettā) is the development of thoughts of non-ill will (avyāpāda-vitakka). Cultivating compassion (karuṇā) is the development of thoughts of non-harming (avihiṃsā-vitakka). The development of appreciative joy (muditā-bhāvanā) brings about rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and clear comprehension (sampajañña). The development of equanimity (upekkhā-bhāvanā) consists of equanimity with observation, equanimity without observation, equanimity (upekkhā), and indifferent equanimity (ajjhupekkhā). The development of the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā-bhāvanā) involves painful practice, slow direct knowledge, direct knowledge that connects to existence, and the connection to existence. These six types of development are to be developed, frequently practiced, repeatedly cultivated, made a basis, made a vehicle, mastered, and well-undertaken. This is development.

For one who develops thus, there is this disadvantage. In the first jhāna, this state associated with formations (saṅkhāra) belongs to the unlearned and is accompanied by taints (āsava). If this state occurs, this virtue (sīla) associated with concentration is merely an immediate opposite. This state involves longing, sustained thought (paticāra), and further sustained thought (pativicāra). It is also the total coarseness of the attainments. This state consists of applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra). In that state, they agitate the mind. Here, the body becomes fatigued. When the body is fatigued, the mind is distressed. It is simply unfit for being directed towards direct knowledge (abhiññā). These are the disadvantages in the first jhāna.

In the second jhāna, these are the disadvantages: this state is accompanied by the pervading of rapture (pīti). The mind will not be active. If one approaches without purification, this state is an enemy of the substrate (upagami-parissaya). This state is an enemy of displeasure (domanassa). For those states associated with various jhānas, this state is difficult because it is an enemy of rapture. Excluding the state of non-arisen terror, in the four types of suffering, this state—due to the faith that leads successively to Nibbāna—consists of the nature of suffering, the nature of suffering as an impediment (palibodha), the nature of suffering in direct knowledge, and the nature of suffering as a disease. These are the disadvantages in the second jhāna.

What are the disadvantages in the third jhāna? In being accompanied by the happiness of equanimity, among the five feelings that find delight in that happiness of equanimity, the happiness of equanimity is subject to reversal. Therefore, it occurs even to those with the perception of permanence for certain reasons. Happiness that approaches suffering, based on the agitation of the mind, flows into pleasure and pain. Based on following pleasure and pain, the mind becomes unfit for being directed towards direct knowledge. Among the states realized through direct knowledge, all these states in the three jhāna attainments, for those who are successively pierced by the four types of suffering, consist of the nature of suffering, the nature of suffering as an impediment, and the nature of suffering in direct knowledge. These are the disadvantages in the third jhāna.
268:
In that fourth jhāna, what are the disadvantages? For those who have the attainment of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) and those states occurring in accordance with that attainment, many types of wrong views arise for foolish worldlings who find delight in the plane of the sphere of nothingness. These jhānas, which occur appropriately with coarse and subtle perceptions of form (rūpa-saññā), are always common to the successive parts of the lineage of jhāna and loving-kindness (anudaya-mettā) for beings. All four great requisites (sambhāra) are difficult. These jhānas that have come into being also arise in dependence on one another. In that case, these states that have come into being are not completed. These states, whose signs (nimitta) are not well-grasped, also decline. These states cease, are not clung to, and are factors of cessation. For these states, the jhānas are called causes; the perception of the cause of jhāna is not confused. It occurs because it was not previously attained and by the power of entering jhāna. Due to these disadvantages, this decline of jhāna occurs.

Due to not reflecting on the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), for one who has the remaining perceptions, the perception and attention associated with the sphere of nothingness arise; that person falls away from the attainment of cessation. For one who has the perception of the imperturbable (āneñja) or for one who enters the sphere of non-perception (asaññāyatana), the attentions associated with the sphere of nothingness arise, and they do not know that plane of existence; that person falls away from that plane. For one who enters the sphere of nothingness, the perception and attention of the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) arise, and they do not know that state; that person falls away from that plane. For one who enters the sphere of infinite consciousness, [the states] associated with the perception of form [arise]. In detail... up to the first jhāna, [the states] associated with the perception of sensuality (kāma-saññā) should be applied. One falls away from one's own jhāna; one enters into a fragmented jhāna, enters while investigating all around, enters while destroying hindrances (nīvaraṇa), enters without attachment, enters while making an effort, and enters while constantly practicing some state. One enters while running excessively, enters while perceiving excessively, enters into what is not a requisite in the bodily formation (kāya-saṅkhāra), enters without knowing the escape from obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), and enters being overcome by hindrances. Giving attention to the arrival at that jhāna is called the gratification (assāda) of jhāna; abandoning the obsession with sensual lust (kāmarāga) is called the gratification of jhāna. States that have sensual lust as their cause arise; the jhānas that have the factors of cessation of those states, as well as the higher subtle equanimity, and the abandoning of the defilements of sensual actions are called gratification. Thus, again, what is called the gratification of jhāna is that in the world-habitation (loka-sannivāsa) which is not oppressed by great association, one will be free from the place of ignorance; this is called the abandoning of jhāna. This is called the seeking in the world-habitation that is without disturbance. This jhāna is the benefit called the abandoning of saṃsāra for beings who are involved in the beginningless saṃsāra; this is the benefit.
269:
The abandoning of lust is called the gratification (assāda) of meditative absorption (jhāna). States that have sensual lust as their cause arise. The jhānas whose factors have ceased, the higher pleasure and equanimity, and the abandoning of the defilements of sensual actions are also called gratification. Thus, the gratification of jhāna will disappear from the unknown in the world-dwelling that is not oppressed by great association; this is called the abandoning of jhāna (jhānappahāna). This is called seeking in the world-dwelling that is without disturbance. This jhāna is the consequence of abandoning the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) for beings who are immersed in the beginningless saṃsāra. The fruit of this jhāna is called the gratification of jhāna. For one who has an unknown jhāna, it occurs through the body. Those who have jhānas that are not attained, attain them without reflection. Whatever steps there are for one who attains fragmented jhāna, those steps occur accordingly in opposition.

Therein, what is skillfulness in jhāna (jhāna-kosalla)? Skill in attainment is jhāna-kosalla; skill in distinction of jhāna is jhāna-kosalla; skill in the interval (cause) of jhāna is jhāna-kosalla; skill in emergence from attainment is jhāna-kosalla; skill in knowing the nature (sabhāva) of jhāna is jhāna-kosalla; skill in seeing the danger in jhāna is jhāna-kosalla; skill in the means of escape from jhāna is jhāna-kosalla. Skillfulness based on the fruit of jhāna, and by playing through the attainment of jhāna that has arisen with the nature of non-decline in the fruit reflected upon by the fruit of jhāna, one also obtains jhāna partaking of distinction (visesabhāgiya-jhāna). This jhāna may be the state of excessively leading to existence and the grasping of the sign of the object. It is not the power of non-exertion (anabhinīhāra-bala). One-pointedness of mind occurs together with the proper grasping of the sign of the object. It is also obtained through the non-sinking by the power of serenity (samatha), and when serenity called Path and Fruit occurs in jhāna, the power of mindfulness which is uplifting and the locus of the preceding and succeeding signs, disturbed by the equanimity of one in concentration, and in the common power of insights (vipassanā) that bring about that power of mindfulness.

Therein, what is the perfection of jhāna (jhāna-pāramitā)? It is loving-kindness (mettā) which is a good perfection. In whichever Sutta the two truths of suffering (dukkha) and the origin (samudaya) are shown by the conventional usage of the teaching: "Beings attached to sensual pleasures are attached by the bond of sensuality." By the mode of investigation (vicaya-hāra), it is impossible that those who do not see the fault in states that are objects of the fetters will cross the flood (ogha). There is this logic (yutti) and investigation (vicaya) that they will not be able to cross. What is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for this failure to cross the flood? "Attached to sensual pleasures" refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure; those five cords of sensual pleasure are the proximate cause of sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā). Not seeing the fault in the fetters is the proximate cause of ignorance (avijjā). Indeed, the fact that they cannot cross the vast and great flood because of attachment to the fetters is the proximate cause of clinging (upādāna). In this teaching, "attached to sensual pleasures," there are two kinds of sensuality: sensuality as objective basis (vatthu-kāma) and sensuality as defilement (kilesa-kāma). Between those two, the sensual craving called sensuality as defilement is associated with sensual craving. Craving for form (rūpa-taṇhā) and craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) occur by the mode of characteristic (lakkhaṇa-hāra). In the phrase "not seeing the fault in the fetters," it means not seeing the fault of the fetters. In that teaching, whatever desire and lust (chanda-rāga) exists, what is its proximate cause? It is pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) and the two faculties: the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) and the faculty of joy (somanassindriya). Thus, when pleasant feeling is taken, all three feelings are taken. When the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) is taken, all five aggregates are taken. Visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles are taken. When objective sensuality is taken, all six external sense bases (bāhira-āyatana) are taken. Whatever mindfulness exists regarding the internal and external sense bases, this mindfulness is called the mode of characteristic (lakkhaṇa-hāra). In that mode of characteristic, there is the overcoming of gross defilements and the overcoming (disposition/inclination - ajjhāsaya) of all defilements. Therefore, one cannot be one whose lust is gone in very subtle matters. In such a case, there is wrong attention (micchā-manasikāra) as "mine" regarding external fetters and as "I" regarding internal fetters. In that teaching, what is the Exalted One's intention? Those who wish to cross the flood will dwell frequently contemplating the fault in states that are objects of the fetters. This is the Exalted One's intention in this matter. "Attached to sensual pleasures" means there is attachment in those two kinds of sensuality, with those two kinds of sensuality, and for those two kinds of sensuality. This mode of attachment (satta) is of four kinds and is called the portion of the mode (hāra-bhāgiya) that conveys the notion of "I" to all beings.
270:
When objective sensuality (vatthukāma) is taken, all six external sense bases (bāhira āyatana) are said to be taken. Whatever mindfulness exists regarding internal and external sense bases, this mindfulness is called the Lakkhaṇa Hāra (Mode of Conveying Characteristics). In that [mode], there is the state of being overwhelmed by gross defilements and being overwhelmed by all defilements. Because of that, one cannot be one whose lust is faded away (vītarāga) in matters more subtle than those defilements. In such a case, one considers the external fetter as "mine" and the internal fetter as "I". What is the Blessed One's intention in this teaching? The Blessed One's intention here is that those who wish to cross the flood (ogha) will dwell contemplating the disadvantage (ādīnava) in those things that are objects of the fetters. "Those attached to sensual pleasures" means they are attached to which sensual pleasures, by which sensual pleasures, and for which sensual pleasures. Attachment in these four ways is called Hārabhāgiya (sharing in the mode) for all.

In that text, what are the three perversions (vipallāsa) and their proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna)? The three perversions—perversion of mind (citta-vipallāsa), perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa), and perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa)—are the proximate causes of the three unwholesome roots (akusalamūla). The three unwholesome roots are the proximate causes of the performed kamma that is low or exalted. Among the four types of clinging (upādāna), the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa) is evident. It is the proximate cause of the performed kamma that is low or exalted. For example, one gives safety to a mother, a father, or another person, or again to a noble monk. In that giving, another person might act wrongly by body or by speech. Then, that person, based on ill-will (byāpāda), gives safety to those noble ones while constantly guarding them by protecting those noble ones. When safety is given to them, whoever acts wrongly in that giving, then that person, based on ill-will, performs kamma born of hatred. In that kamma, the bad faculties are whichever hindrance (nīvaraṇa); one provides safety to them in an exalted way. I [take] this mark as "the exalted cause." Again, in that situation, there is wrong practice. This wrong practice is called ill-will; kamma leading to a low destination is performed. These hindrances, greed (lobha) and delusion (moha), are taught. Those hindrances are called the four types of clinging. Through those four types of clinging, there is attachment as "woman" or "man"; that very attachment to those five aggregates is called the origin (samudaya). This suffering (dukkha) and origin (samudaya) occur. That very truth is called the Desanā Hāra (Mode of Conveying a Teaching).

In that mode, those who do not practice in sensual pleasures practice in the contemplation of disadvantage. Therefore, there is the state of wishing to depart from that sensual element (kāmadhātu); this state of wishing to depart is called the desire for renunciation (nekkhamma-chanda). In that teaching, whoever purifies something among the non-conditioned (anabhisaṅkhāra), that person has constant effort; this constant effort is called the desire for non-ill-will (abyāpāda-chanda). [If one] harms something, this harming is called the desire for cruelty (vihiṃsā-chanda). Thus, the desires that lead towards renunciation are three: the desire for renunciation, the desire for non-ill-will, and the desire for non-cruelty (avihiṃsā-chanda).
271:
In that teaching, the desire for renunciation is called non-greed (alobha), the desire for non-ill-will is called non-hatred (adosa), and the desire for non-cruelty is called non-delusion (amoha). These three wholesome roots are beneficial to others in the eight types of attainment (sampatti); they lead only to the cessation of those four types of clinging. Again, if one performs dark kamma (unwholesome) or bright kamma (wholesome), they lead to the abandoning of the results of that kamma. This kamma that is neither dark nor bright leads to the destruction of kamma. Among those wholesome roots, whatever cessation of the three unwholesome roots exists, this cessation is called the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca). That very practice is called the truth of the path (magga-sacca); therein, these practices are two truths; these four truths are called the Āvaṭṭa Hāra (Mode of Conveying a Reversal).

"Attached to sensual pleasures" means there are those who are trainees (sekha); they are attached in only one way. There are those who are worldlings (puthujjana); they are attached in two ways; regarding them, this question should be answered by making a distinction. Although a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) is attached in the use [of sensual pleasures], he is not attached through insistence (abhinivesa) on the object; the reason is that a trainee strives for the reduction [of existence], not for its accumulation. A trainee uses sensual pleasures by the power of defilements. A worldling, however, uses sensual pleasures for the sake of giving rise to defilements. Therein, the analytical explanation that "beings attached to sensual pleasures will cross the four floods" is called the Vibhatti Hāra (Mode of Conveying a Classification).

## Parivattana means: those who are attached only by defilement in sensual pleasures and are not conjoined with the fetters will cross the extensive and great flood. This is the opposite (paṭipakkha) of the sutta.

## Vevecana means: whatever attachment to sensual pleasures exists, and whatever quality (guṇa) of sensual pleasures exists therein, there is attachment to those sensual qualities like poison. There is also attachment like poison to the things that bring about sensual pleasures. Therein, the synonyms (vevacana) for sensual pleasures are: ripening (pāka), dust (raja), dart (salla), boil (gaṇḍa), calamity (īti), and misfortune (upaddava). Or among other synonyms, the synonym "poisonous attachment" (viso satto) is also included. They are: attached (satta), bound (bandha), infatuated (mucchita), greedy (gadhita), cleared (ajjhosita), transgressing in sensual pleasures (ajjhāpanna), released (parimutta), and dwelling much in that (tabbahulavihārī). Or there are other synonyms; this is called the Vevacana Hāra (Mode of Conveying Synonyms). The designation of the mind by the designation of the range of sensual pleasures and the designation of the object of defilements is called Vevacana. "Attached, dwelling much in that" means there are also other designations. These things are designated by the designation of the range of sensual pleasures and the designation of the object of defilements; they are designated by the designation of seed (bīja); formations (saṅkhāra) are designated by the designation of fetters (saṃyojana); clinging (upādāna) is designated by the designation of cause (hetu); the person (puggala) is designated by the designation of many (puthu).

## Otaraṇa means: by this [mode], there is dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and suffering and origin. Whatever defilements, whatever formations, and whatever fetters exist; among the five aggregates, the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) ...
272:
Among the bases of mental objects (dhammāyatana), there are unwholesome bases of mental objects; among the faculties (indriya), there are the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) and the faculty of joy (somanassindriya). This is the entry into faculties (indriyotaraṇa). Cleansing (sodhana) is of this extent. This very undertaking should be pointed out as the meaning of the Sutta.

Establishment (adhiṭṭhāna) means: these dhammas are designated by way of unity (ekattatā) and some are designated by way of diversity (vemattatā). Those perceptions (saññā) that are external to sensual pleasures are designated by way of diversity. Beings attached to the five strands of sensual pleasure—these are designated by way of diversity as obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) and perversions (vipallāsa). They should cross the flood (ogha). In the phrase 'vast and great' (vipulaṃ mahantaṃ), ignorance (avijjā) is designated by way of unity.

Requisite (parikkhāra) means: what is its root cause (hetu), what is its supporting condition (paccaya)? It assists by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) assists as a condition for the support of the object-condition. Ignorance assists by way of the proximity-condition (samanantara-paccaya). The underlying tendency to lust (rāgānusaya) assists by way of the root-condition (hetu-paccaya). This is the root cause, this is the supporting condition.

Attribution of condition (samāropana-paccaya) means: the view of beings attached to sensual pleasures that 'they have a good destination, they have a beautiful form' is the desire and lust (chanda-rāga) in the sensual realm (kāmadhātu). Those desires and lusts are demeritorious formations (apuññamaya saṅkhāra). By what condition do those formations arise? They have ignorance as their condition. Of what are those formations the condition? They are the condition for consciousness (viññāṇa). Thus, with ignorance as condition, formations arise; with formations as condition, consciousness arises, and so on up to aging and death (jarāmaraṇa). In this way, there is the origin of this whole mass of great suffering. Thus, one Sutta is completed. A Sutta connected with the five hindrances should be made.

Therein, what is the mode of teaching (desanāhāra)? That which is covetousness (abhijjhā), ill-will (byāpāda), and restlessness (uddhacca)—this is craving (taṇhā). That which is sloth and torpor (thina-middha), remorse (kukkucca), and doubt (vicikicchā)—this is wrong view (diṭṭhi). However, the unworkability of the body (akammaniyatā), even if it is torpor (middha), is not called a defilement because it is not a natural defilement (sabhāva-kilesa). Thus, the shrinking of the mind (sallīyanā) and the unworkability of the body are called associated defilements (pakkhopa-kilesa), but not natural defilements. Among those, the mind attached to the perception of self, when weary, and the mind associated with remorse, is called sloth (thina); it is the shrinking of the mind. Thus, among these five hindrances, four hindrances are not called natural defilements; sloth and torpor is a defilement that is an associate of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa-pakkhopa-kilesa). Just as the four taints (āsava) are taints by their nature as taints, but not taints by way of being taints of the mind. They are taints by nature. They are taints by way of association. Furthermore, it is said in the Sutta that those dhammas, whether associated with or dissociated from those taints, are to be called 'with taints' (sāsava) or 'without taints' (anāsava).
274:
Thus, up to doubt (vicikicchā), these hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are ten. Internal and external defilements are these two fetters (saṃyojana): the internal fetter and the external fetter. Among those two fetters, the notion of 'I' is called internal; the notion of 'mine' is called external. Personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is internal; the sixty-one types of wrong view are external. Whatever lust and desire (chandarāga) exists internally toward forms, where one is not free from lust and not free from desire—thus up to consciousness—this is called internal craving (ajjhatta-taṇhā). The consumption of the flavor of objects in the six external bases and in the three realms of existence is called external craving (bahiddhā-taṇhā). These are the two truths, the fetters, and the things that are objects of the fetters. Among those things that are fetters, whatever contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā) exists, this is called the Path (magga). Whatever abandonment of the fetters exists, this is called Cessation (nirodha). This is the Āvaṭṭa-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Round).

## Among those modes, what is the Vibhatti-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Combined Terminology)?
The term 'fetter' (saṃyojana) is not categorical (ekāṃsa). When it is said that the fetter of conceit (māna-saṃyojana) belongs to the side of wrong view (diṭṭhi), that conceit is not categorical; it does not abandon the conceit that arises depending on conceit that is not wrong view. Whatever five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya) of conceit exist, although that conceit may be on the side of wrong view, it does not lead to the abandonment of the lower fetters (orambhāgiya). For one who has not yet penetrated and known the conceit of 'I' (ahaṃkāra), such a thought occurs: 'When will I realize and dwell in that peaceful base, Nibbāna, which the noble ones realize and dwell in?' This is greed (abhijjhā), but it is not a hindrance (nīvaraṇa). Even for an Arahant, there is the occurrence of bodily fatigue (kāya-kilesamiddha), but that impurity is not a hindrance. It cannot be categorically said that the sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha) of that Arahant is a hindrance. This is the Vibhatti-hāra.

The Parivattana-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Reversal) is that the five hindrances are abandoned by the five-factored jhāna. This [jhāna] is the opposite of those hindrances. One should not infer another's state by saying, 'The hindrances of such a person have been abandoned'; it has a noble meaning (paramattha) within the internal continuity. This is the Parivattana-hāra.

## Among those modes, what is the Vevacana-hāra (The Mode of Conveying Synonyms)?
Sensual desire (kāmacchanda), lust and desire (chandarāga), affection (pema), and attachment (nikanti) are synonyms (vevacana). Hindrance (nīvaraṇa), covering (chadana), defilement (upakkilesa), and obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) are synonyms.

The Paññatti-hāra (The Mode of Conveying Designations) is the designation of function (kicca-paññatti) caused by ignorance (avijjā); ill-will (byāpāda) is a designation in the designation of distraction (vikkhepa-paññatti); sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha) is a designation in the designation of non-uprooting (asamugghāta-paññatti). Thus, in this Sutta, all these five hindrances are designated in the designation of distraction.

## Among those modes, what is the Otaraṇa-hāra (The Mode of Conveying an Entry)?
There are these five hindrances, ignorance (avijjā), and craving (taṇhā). Among them, the hindrances have ignorance as their root. Whatever craving and mental formations (saṅkhāra) exist, they have ignorance as their cause.
275:
These two things are included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) among the five aggregates. Among the bases, they are the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana); among the elements, they are the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu). Among the faculties, the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of these things is the proximate cause of the pleasure faculty (sukhindriya), the joy faculty (somanassindriya), the female faculty (itthindriya), and the male faculty (purisindriya).

Among those modes, what is the Sodhana-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Cleansing)? The purpose for which this Sutta was undertaken and laid down is taught by these five terms.

In that teaching, sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill-will (byāpāda), and doubt (vicikicchā) are not designated as a single entity. 'Sensuality' (kāma) is also not designated as a single entity; rather, they are designated by way of various distinctions. This is the Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Manifestation).

Among those modes, what is the Parikkhāra-hāra (The Mode of Conveying Requisites)? For sensual desire, unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) has a beautiful object as its condition (paccaya), and the sign of beauty (subhanimitta) is the productive cause (hetu). For ill-will, unwise attention and grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu) are the conditions, and the underlying tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) is the productive cause. For sloth and torpor, withdrawal (paṭisaṃhāra) is the condition, and fatigue and sluggishness during occurrence are the productive cause. For restlessness and remorse (uddhaccakukkucca), the condition is incomplete knowledge of an attractive and pleasurable object, and the productive cause is the perception of sensuality (kāmasaññā) and the underlying tendency of views (diṭṭhi-anusaya). For doubt, the nine types of conceit as an object is called the underlying tendency of conceit (mānānusaya); that underlying tendency of conceit itself is the condition, and the underlying tendency of doubt (vicikicchānusaya) is the productive cause. These five things arise with causes and conditions.

Among those modes, what is the Samāropana-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Coordination)? These five hindrances, the four taints (āsava), the boils (gaṇḍa), the darts (salla), and the clingings (upādāna) [are not external]. Only in those things does it reach the designation of 'Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta' (The Discourse on the Side of Defilement). This is the Samāropana-hāra.

## The Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta has been pointed out.

There is the verse: 'Mind is the forerunner of all things' (Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā).

In that verse, what is the Desanā-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Teaching)? What is the meaning in this Sutta? By defining the aggregates, the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) is taught; by defining the elements, the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) is taught; by defining the bases, the mind base (manāyatana) is taught; by defining the faculties, the mind faculty (manindriya) is taught. What are the things that act as forerunners of that verse? Briefly, the six things—the wholesome roots and unwholesome roots—are called the things that act as forerunners. In this Sutta, the wholesome root is taught. In that Sutta, what are the things that have mind as their forerunner? Among those mental aggregates, the aggregate of consciousness is the forerunner. Just as the king is the forerunner among the troops.
276:
In this very way, mental states have mind as their forerunner. This being a forerunner is of three kinds: the desire for renunciation (nekkhamma-chanda), the desire for non-ill will (abyāpāda-chanda), and the desire for non-harming (avihiṃsā-chanda). Non-greed has the desire for renunciation as its forerunner. Non-hatred has the desire for non-ill will as its forerunner. Non-delusion has the desire for non-harming as its forerunner.

In that verse, 'manoseṭṭhā' means these states are abundant through the mind, or they are created by the mind. Because the mind alone is the most noble among these states, the mind alone is greater than these states, and the mind alone exercises lordship over these states, they are called 'manoseṭṭhā'. 'Manojavā' means that to whichever object the mind goes, these states also follow to that object; thus they are called 'manojavā'. Or, just as the wind moves swiftly, or as any other swift mover is called 'swift as the wind' or 'swift as a bird', in this same way, these states, arising well because of the mind, rush towards the object. Because these states tend to rush to that object, they are called 'manojavā'. These states are of three kinds: being produced by desire, being undisturbed, and thought (saṅkappa). There are also seven: the three types of bodily good conduct and the four types of verbal good conduct. These constitute the ten courses of wholesome action (kusala-kammapatha).

In that verse, 'with a clear mind' refers to mental action (manokamma). 'Whether one speaks' refers to verbal action (vacīkamma). 'Or acts' refers to bodily action (kāyakamma).
