In this sutta, although the ten courses of wholesome action through these three actions are very noble, the state of being virtuous is the most noble. That state of being virtuous occurs in vivaṭṭa (the round of existence). This is a vāsanābhāgiya sutta, not for the purpose of escaping from the world. This is the Desanā-hāra (Mode of Conveying a Teaching).

Among those modes, what is the Vicaya-hāra (Mode of Investigation)? 'Mental states have mind as their forerunner' refers to the wholesome roots and the states of perfection (sammatta) endowed with the eight factors. This is the Vicaya-hāra sutta.

The Yutti-hāra (Mode of Construing) is: whatever result of the ten wholesome courses of action there is, that result has non-ill will (abyāpāda) as its forerunner and has the nature of experiencing happiness. 'Like a shadow that never leaves' means it follows along; this is the Yutti-hāra.

The Padaṭṭhāna-hāra (Mode of Proximate Cause) is: it is the proximate cause of the eighteen mental explorations (manopavicāra). 'Mental states have mind as their forerunner' means these states are the proximate cause of the entire wholesome side. 'With a clear mind' refers to whatever clarity of mind there is; this is the proximate cause of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). 'Whether one speaks' is the proximate cause of right speech (sammā-vācā). 'Or acts' is the proximate cause of right action (sammā-kammanta) and right effort (sammā-vāyāma).

The Lakkhaṇa-hāra (Mode of Characteristic) is: when it is said 'states that have a forerunner', these states also have feeling (vedanā) as their forerunner, perception (saññā) as their forerunner, and mental formations (saṅkhāra) as their forerunner. All conascent (sahajāta) states are the forerunners of these states. In the phrase 'because of such action, happiness follows him', joy (somanassa) also follows him; whatever shadow of great happiness there is, that happiness also follows him.
277:
Among those modes, what is the Catubyūha-hāra (Mode of Fourfold Array)? This phrase 'manopubbaṅgamā' is not of a single kind. Why? Among all these six groups of consciousness, what is the Blessed One's intention? "Let those who desire happiness clarify their minds"—this is the Blessed One's intention in this sutta. The meaning has already been explained before.

Whatever wholesome roots there are, those wholesome roots are the cause (hetu) equivalent to the eight benefits; this is the Eightfold Path itself. The ten causes are the causes of the teaching (desanā), and because of the cause of the teaching, there is the detailed explanation (niddesanā). In that teaching, by the factor of the truth of consciousness, the wholesome roots abandon the mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) that is accompanied by suffering; thus, arising in a plane where [defilements] are not yet abandoned is the Truth of Origination (samudaya-sacca). The abandoning of those states is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). These are the Four Noble Truths. This is the Āvaṭṭa-hāra (Mode of Revolving).

Vibhatti (Analysis) is:
Mental states have mind as their forerunner, mind as their chief, and are mind-made.
If one speaks or acts with a clear mind,
Then happiness follows him like a shadow that never leaves.

That teaching does not apply absolutely to a recluse or a brahmin. If a person of wrong view were to have confidence in his own view, and with that confident mind were to speak or explain, happiness would not follow him, nor would it be like a shadow following him; only suffering would follow him. It is like the wheel following the hoofprint of the ox that draws the cart. This is a matter to be explained analytically (vibhajja-byākaraṇīya). When it is said that performing bodily and verbal actions with a clear mind leads to the experience of happiness, happiness is experienced in a rightly directed (samaggata) action, while suffering is experienced in a wrongly directed (micchaggata) action. This is the Vibhatti-hāra.

Therein, what is the Parivattana-hāra (Mode of Reversal)? 'Mental states have mind as their forerunner' refers to the two suttas taught: that if one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, suffering follows him; this is the very opposite (paṭipakkha). Vevecana (Synonyms) refers to these states: mano, citta, viññāṇa, manindriya, and manoviññāṇadhātu.

Paññatti (Description) is: in the phrase 'mental states have mind as their forerunner', this 'mind' (mano) is described by a certain description. 'States' (dhammā) is described by the description of the wholesome courses of action. 'Manoseṭṭhā' is described by a distinguished (visiṭṭha) description. 'Manojavā' is described by a conascent (saha) description. 'Citta' is described by the description of renunciation (nekkhamma). 'With a clear mind' is described by the description of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). 'With a clear mind' is also described by the description of the second jhāna which has undisturbed thought. With a clear mind...
278:
“Manasā ce pasannena” (With a mind that is pure) refers to the designation of the opposite of those who lack faith. “Bhāsati vā” (Or speaks) refers to the designation of Right Speech (sammā-vācā). “Karoti vā” (Or acts) refers to the designation of Right Action (sammā-kammanta). “Tato naṃ sukhamanveti” (Then happiness follows him) refers to the designation of the attainment of Jhana. Among the faculties (indriya), it is the mind faculty (manindriya). In Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), it is consciousness (viññāṇa). “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā” (Mind precedes all mental states) refers to the second and third Jhanas among loving-kindness (mettā), gentleness (mudutā), and the Jhanas. Among the aggregates (khandha), it is included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhāra-kkhandha). Among the elements (dhātu), it is the mind-object element (dhamma-dhātu); among the bases (āyatana), it is the mind-object base (dhamma-āyatana). Whichever wholesome state among the faculties is the pleasure faculty (sukhindriya) and the joy faculty (somanassindriya) is called the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). Among these dependently arisen states, due to the condition of contact (phassa), there is contact to be felt as pleasant (sukhavedanīya-phassa) and pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). Among the mental explorations (manopavicāra), it is exploration accompanied by joy (somanassa-vicāra); among the thirty-six initial terms, six terms are based on renunciation accompanied by joy (somanassa-nekkhammassita). This is the Otaraṇa-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Landing).

## Among those modes, what is Sodhana-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Clearing)?
The meaning for which this Sutta was spoken is examined; the Sutta was spoken based on that meaning. This is Sodhana-hāra.

## Among those modes, what is Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra (The Mode of Conveying a Formulation)?
“Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā” is a designation by synonym (vevacana-paññatti), not a designation by unity (ekatta-paññatti). “Dhammā” is a designation by unity, not a synonym. “Manasā ce pasannena”: that purity is of two kinds—internal (ajjhatta) and external (bahiddha) through conviction (okappana) by removing ill-will (abyāpāda-vikkham-bhana). That internal confidence (ajjhatta-pasāda) is of two kinds: confidence through eradication (samugghāta-pasāda) which completely abandons the obsession of ill-will (byāpāda-pariyuṭṭhāna), and confidence through suppression (vikkham-bhana-pasāda). The destroyed root confidence does not have an arisen root. Confidence is the purity through the destruction of states accompanied by ill-will. “Tato naṃ sukhamanveti”: there is bodily happiness (kāyika-sukha), mental happiness (cetasika-sukha), separation from the unloved, union with the loved, the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamm-asukha), the happiness of worldlings (puthujjana-sukha), the joy enlightenment factor (pīti-sambojjhaṅga), and mental happiness. The happiness felt by one with a tranquil body is bodily happiness, and the enlightenment factors are mental happiness. Both the happiness felt by one with a tranquil body and that tranquil body itself have happiness as their proximate cause. As stated in the designation, that ungrasped (aparāmaṭṭha) meaning belongs to wholesome states. “Anveti” (Follows): absorption (appanā) is evident; having reached this absorption, it does not [merely] follow. This Sutta should be formulated in two ways: by cause, which is having a pure mind, and by result, which is the experience of suffering.

Parikkhāra-hāra (The Mode of Conveying Requisites) means: The Blessed One entered the city of Rājagaha with a Saṅgha of five hundred monks. At that time, a person served the Blessed One; confidence arose in him who had previous practice of wholesome roots (kusala-mūla-pubba-yoga). He told others, “How fortunate for me! Those in whose house the Blessed One enters [are blessed], and if He were to enter our house, we too would gain confidence in the Blessed One.” He stood in a suitable place with a mind free from anger, saluting with joined palms, saying, “Homage to the Blessed One, homage to the Blessed One.” After He entered, the Blessed One spoke this Sutta: “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā...” All speech spoken to others is verbal action (vaci-kamma). Saluting with joined palms is bodily action (kāya-kamma). Confidence of mind is mental action (mano-kamma). Among these three actions, showing the Buddha's qualities to others, preaching, and the reason for having a mind of loving-kindness towards the Blessed One...
279:
The Blessed One entered the city of Rājagaha together with five hundred monks. At that time, a certain man, seeing and serving the Blessed One, felt a sense of devotion. Having the basis of past merit, he said to others: "How fortunate are those householders into whose homes the Blessed One enters! If he were to enter our home as well, we too would have the opportunity to show devotion to the Blessed One." Then, raising his hands in anjali towards where the Blessed One was, he stood respectfully to one side with a mind free from ill-will, saying, "Homage to the Blessed One, homage to the Blessed One." After he had entered, the Blessed One taught this sutta beginning with "Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā."

The speech spoken to others is verbal action (vaci-kamma). Raising the hands in anjali is bodily action (kāya-kamma). The devotion of the mind is mental action (mano-kamma). Among these three actions, expressing the Buddha's virtues to others and praising the benefit of the householders where the Blessed One visits are his root of merit of non-greed (alobha). Having a mind of loving-kindness towards the Blessed One is the root of merit of non-hatred (adosa). In raising the hands in anjali and subduing pride, the root of merit of non-delusion (amoha) becomes manifest. Obtaining noble wisdom is the abandoning of the perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa). Such restraint is the abandoning of the perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa). The clarity of mind is the abandoning of the perversion of thought (citta-vipallāsa). Thus, it is the cause for the displacement and abandoning of the unwholesome perversions.

The three roots of merit and the unclouded thought (anāvila-cittasaṅkappa) are called his wise attention (manasikāra). The displacement of defilements, the perversions being a cause through the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), the roots of merit being a cause through their manifestation—this wise attention causes the mind to arise through the generative cause (janaka-hetu) and the strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Therein, the mind that occurs by taking its own meaning as an object is the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati). Reflecting on the virtues of the Blessed One is the recollection of the Dhamma (dhammānussati). Therein, mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) are the generative cause, and this is also the strong dependence condition. Verbal wisdom is the generative cause, and initial and sustained thoughts (vitakka-vicāra) are the strong dependence condition. Bodily formations (kāya-saṅkhāra) and the formation of kamma (kamma-abhisaṅkhāra) are the generative cause or non-condition (apaccaya). The accumulation (upacaya) of kamma to be experienced as happiness is the generative cause, and the accumulation of bodily kamma is the strong dependence condition.

## Tattha katamo samāropano hāro?

Among these modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Combined Teaching (samāropana-hāra)? One has devotion in these Triple Gems only with a clear mind and only while being mindful. Alternatively, through the purification of the mind, beings are liberated from defilements. Therefore, beings have the mind as their forerunner. With a clear mind, the volition (cetanā) also becomes one with the mind in that regard. Therefore, due to the clarity of volitions, this body is also clear. He makes an effort with devotion. His perceptions (saññā) are also undistorted and correct. The fivefold displacement (vikkhambhana) is only the tranquility of the body (kāya-passaddhi). Although devotion (pasāda) arises depending on the mind, the mind has already become clear beforehand. This is the Mode of Conveying a Combined Teaching. Thus, the fivefold clarity is stated.

By the words "Tato naṃ sukhamanveti" (Then happiness follows him), what does the Blessed One refer to? He refers to the truth of the self (atta-sacca). The result (vipāka) of that kamma follows. The means (upāya) of that kamma follows. When joy (somanassa) arises due to the cause of a smile, the gladness of heart also follows. This is the Mode of Conveying a Combined Teaching. There is a sutta concerning Mahānāma the Sakyan. In that sutta, it is said: "If one were to die without mindfulness and without wise reflection, one would be reborn in the sensual realm." It is stated in detail: "Mahānāma, do not fear. For a long time, your mind has been infused with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom." What is shown by generosity and wisdom? The existing faith is the clarity of the mind. The unclouded thought is faith. Why? Because faith has the characteristic of being unclouded (anāvila). Other teachers say it has the characteristic of reaching the end of virtues. Some say faith has the characteristic of accepting words with trust.
280:
When joy (somanassa) arises due to the cause of smiling, non-remorse (avippaṭisāra) also follows. This is called the Sammāropana-hāra (The Mode of Application).

There is the Sutta of Mahānāma the Sakyan. In that Sutta, it is said that if one were to pass away at that time without mindfulness and without clear comprehension, one would be reborn in the sensual realm. There is one who is led forth without mindfulness. It is stated in detail: "Mahānāma, do not fear; that mind which has for a long time been fortified by faith, fortified by virtue, and fortified by learning and generosity..."

What is shown by generosity and wisdom? That which is clarity is the clarity of mind (pasāda). That which is the state of non-turbidity is faith (saddhā). Why? Because it has the characteristic of non-turbidity. Indeed, faith has the characteristic of non-turbidity. Other teachers say it has the characteristic of reaching the culmination of purity of qualities. Still other teachers say faith has the characteristic of acceptance by believing the words.

According to another method of teaching, if one has such conviction in oneself, saying, "I know nothing," then because of the state of being permitted in that clarity, there is the state of non-otherness. This is called faith.

Another method of teaching is the repeated contemplation of the faults of the sixty-one types of wrong views as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Through such contemplation, it becomes seen. Just as one sees water in a deep well with the eye but cannot reach it with the body, so too, for that person, a view (diṭṭhi) arises due to the acceptance of contemplation (nijjhānakkhanti) of the Noble Truths, but realization (sacchikata) has not yet occurred. This is called faith. And that faith is only mundane (lokika).

Another method of teaching is that a worldling (puthujjana) also delights in the twenty types of personality view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi). What is the lack of attention connected to the personality? This is the perception of the method (naya-saññā) knowing that this is not the only way. However, wrong view is truly abandoned according to reality through the five soft faculties and through the path of seeing (dassana-magga). The defilements that share the same ground as wrong view are also abandoned. This is called faith.

It is said that the factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyaṅga) are fulfilled in the noble plane where there is no suffering. It is said that in that very plane, the noble ones maintain the virtue of the trainee (sekkha-sīla). In that very plane, soft wisdom is called the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). In that very plane, there is the lack of desire for the aggregates; this lack of desire is called generosity (cāga). Therefore, faith should be pointed out by the basis of generosity.

If a monk, with an excessive mind, has faithlessness (assaddhā) which is perverted, he would have a perverted wrong view. Those who are negligent in the bases of guidance (nayana-upadhi) firmly grasp that wrong view. In that context, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is not the basis of generosity because of the abandoning of manifest evil, such as thinking "one will serve sense pleasures." It is the basis of wisdom through wisdom, and the basis of tranquility (upasama) through virtue.

These four qualities—faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom—cultivate virtue. Among those four, one crosses the flood (ogha) by faith. That which is virtue is called heedfulness (appamāda). That which is generosity is the action of wisdom. That which is wisdom is the faculty of wisdom. Among those starting with faith, that which is the faculty of faith occurs in the three unwavering faiths (aveccappasāda). That which is virtue occurs in the faculties of faith. That which is generosity...
281:
...occurs in the four jhānas. That which is wisdom occurs in the Truths. Mindfulness (sati) occurs in all objects. For that trainee (sekkha), there is good spiritual provision and a good destination in the future. For that person who, though having muddled mindfulness, undertakes virtue, those faculties or that root of merit do not become the result of kamma because of the muddled mindfulness in the body.

This is the explanation of the meaning of that triad. In that context, there are four qualities: faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom. That which is faith and that which is wisdom are called mental good conduct (mano-sucarita). That which is virtue is called bodily good conduct (kāya-sucarita) occurring in the body, and verbal good conduct (vācī-sucarita) occurring in speech. That which is generosity is called non-greed good conduct (alobha-sucarita) based in the mind. Thus, when the mind is taken, the five aggregates are also taken. Good conduct is formed by these qualities such as faith; this suffering of the three planes itself is the Noble Truth and is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the Path.

In that context, what is the Vicaya-hāra (The Mode of Investigation)? It is that which is faith and that which is virtue. What do that faith and virtue do? By that faith, one recollects the Blessed One even when encountering an elephant in rut. O friends, dogs... one does not practice everything through virtue, but one becomes confident in the situation through body or speech; thus, for the one who has joy, wisdom establishes the designation for him. For that person of unbroken virtue whose virtue is constant, for his delusion, an unwholesome mind accompanied by wrong view arises. This is called the Vicaya-hāra. Those who speak the Dhamma will likely perform only what is good; such is the logic.

In that context, what is the Padaṭṭhāna-hāra (The Mode of Proximate Cause)? That mind which has for a long time been cultivated by faith, virtue, generosity, wisdom, and concentration is the proximate cause of the first jhāna. That faith which becomes non-turbid thought (vitakka) is the proximate cause of the second jhāna. That virtue which exists through unwavering faith in the Triple Gem is loved by the Noble Ones; that faith is the proximate cause of the category of virtue (sīlakkhandha). That which is wisdom is the proximate cause of the category of wisdom (paññākkhandha). These qualities and this mind are the proximate cause of concentration called the state of singleness (ekodibhūta). Faith is the proximate cause of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). Generosity is the proximate cause of the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya). Wisdom is the proximate cause of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). Faith and wisdom are the proximate cause of insight (vipassanā). Virtue and generosity are the proximate cause of tranquility (samatha). Faith and wisdom are the proximate cause of liberation by wisdom (paññā-vimutti) for the fading away of ignorance. Virtue and generosity are the proximate cause of liberation of mind (ceto-vimutti) for the fading away of lust.

In that context, what is the Lakkhaṇa-hāra (The Mode of Characteristic)? When consciousness (viññāṇa) is mentioned, and when faith and mindfulness are cultivated, all five aggregates are said to be mentioned. When faith is spoken of, all seven treasures of the virtuous (satta-dhana) are said to be spoken of: the treasure of faith... etc. When the category of virtue is mentioned, the category of concentration and the category of wisdom are also said to be mentioned. That mind which has for a long time been cultivated...
282:
It is not possible that in a later time there will be no following of that mind. In that teaching, perception (saññā) also follows that mind. Those states (dhamma) that are of that nature also follow that mind. Attention to the repeated contemplation of the perception of form and the volition of form, thus following in the group of consciousness (viññāṇakāya) of the six sense bases—this is the Lakkhaṇa-hāra.

Among those, what is the Catubyūha-hāra? What is the Blessed One's intention in this sutta? Those who desire good provision (bhaddikā bhati) and a good destination in the future life will attend to faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom; this is the intention. Other beings who do not oppose the Blessed One's presence, hearing this Dhamma, will pass away without remorse; this is the intention.

Among those, what is the Āvaṭṭa-hāra? In this sutta, four states are known. Faith and wisdom destroy lack of faith and ignorance. Virtue and generosity destroy craving and hatred. That person abandons the two roots. He stills suffering. In the stage where defilements are not yet abandoned, the two roots are included in the five aggregates. Calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are called the Noble Truths. There is the abandoning of the two roots. These two truths are cessation (nirodha) and the path (magga). This is the Āvaṭṭa-hāra.

Among those, what is the Vibhatti-hāra? That mind which is developed by faith... (pe)... If that worldling (puthujjana) has good provision, he will surely believe that kamma will bear fruit in this very life, or it will be in another life. Or that past kamma which is ready for fruition, these results have that kamma as their root. As taught in the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta: "Therefore, this is a detailed explanation (vibhajja-vyākaraṇīya) for one who practices the Dhamma: that there is good provision."

Among those, what is the Parivattanā-hāra? That lack of faith, immorality, stinginess, and lack of wisdom which are abandoned by their opposites—this is the Parivattanā-hāra.

Among those, what is the Vevacana-hāra? That mind which has been developed for a long time is called mind (citta), mentality (mano), consciousness (viññāṇa)... (pe)... That which is the power of faith (saddhā-bala), the faculty of faith (saddhindriya); that which is virtue (sīla) is good conduct (sucarita), restraint (saṃyama), regulation (niyama), discipline (dama), and the nature of the aggregate (khandhatā)—these are its synonyms. That which is generosity (cāga) is relinquishment (paṭinissagga), non-greed (alobha), letting go (vossagga), the ground of sacrifice (cāga-yiṭṭhāna). That which is wisdom (paññā) is full understanding (paññattā), the light of wisdom (paññā-pabhā), the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), and the power of wisdom (paññā-bala).
283:
Among those, what is the Paññatti-hāra? That mind which is the seed is made known in designation. Development is made known in the designation of habit (vāsanā). Faith is made known in the designation of clarity (pasāda). Virtue is made known in the designation of good conduct (sucarita). Generosity is made known in the designation of merit-making (puññakiriyā). Wisdom is made known in the designation of investigation (vīmaṃsā). These three states—faith, virtue, and generosity—lead to the purification of the wise person.

Among those, what is the Otaraṇa-hāra? That which is the mind is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) among the aggregates, the element of mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇadhātu) among the elements, and the mind-base (manāyatana) among the bases. Those four states are included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) among the aggregates... (pe)... and in the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) among the elements and bases.

Among those, what is the Sodhana-hāra? In this sutta spoken by the Blessed One when asked by Mahānāma the Sakyan, all those states are applied.

Among those, what is the Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra? This mind is designated by way of diversity (vemattatā). It is said to be developed by unwholesome minds that were not developed; thus, those unwholesome minds are developed again. In that [hāra], it is designated depending on other states as well. All these four states are designated by way of unity (ekattatā). "Bhaddikā bhati" (good provision) means that those who enjoy sensual pleasures do not arise in the fine-material realm or the immaterial realm, but only among humans; thus there is all good provision of merit. That provision of merit alone is designated by the sequence of discourse. This is the Paññatti (hāra).

Among those, what is the Parikkhāra-hāra? The faculties (indriya) are the condition for the mind by way of the predominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya). Attention (manasikāra) is the condition by way of the root-condition (hetu-paccaya). For faith, mundane wisdom is the condition by way of the root-condition. Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is also a condition. For virtue, living in a suitable locality (patirūpadesavāsa) is the condition. Right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi) is the productive cause (janaka-hetu). For generosity, non-greed (alobha) is the productive cause. Freedom from remorse (avippaṭisāra) is the productive cause and the decisive-support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). For wisdom, the voice of another (paratoghosa) and wise attention within oneself (ajjhatta-yoniso-manasikāra) are the productive cause and the decisive-support condition.

Among those, what is the Samāropana-hāra? Just as it is said that the mind is developed for a long time, the mental factors (cetasika) are also developed. In this sutta, when all states are developed, there will be good provision for you, and there will be a good rebirth and destination in the future life. Thus, all various internal and external requisites that occur among humans are indeed good provision. This is the Samāropana-hāra.
284:
There is the verse: "Lust-free above, below, and everywhere" (See Udāna 61). In that verse, what is meant by "above" (uddha)? That which will occur in the future from this present is called "above." "Below" (adho) refers to the past that has been transcended; thus it is stated in the Apadāna. In that verse, regarding the past, eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) arises for those who speculate on the beginning (pubbanta). For some, the view of the future (aparanta-diṭṭhi) arises. These views—annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) and eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi)—arise for those who speculate on what has been mentioned.

Among those views, this eternalism and the fifteen modes of personality view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) resort to the eternalist view. They distress wisdom with the view stated as: "My self possesses form, in my self there is form, form is my self." Whatever annihilationism there is, that annihilationism and five hundred views resort to the view of annihilation. They see that "the soul (jīva) is the same as the body (sarīra)." Such personality view which assumes "form is my self" is of four types by way of annihilation and eternity. Thus, among the personality views with twenty bases in the five aggregates, fifteen modes resort to the past (pubbanta). In eternalism, five modes resort to the future (aparanta). In annihilationism, five modes resort to the future.

Among those wrong views, those who see "this body is I" regard form as self. Such a person is an annihilationist and sees that "the self possesses form, in the self there is form, in form there is self." In this way, one clings through annihilationism, through eternalism which clings to a self, and by way of the past (pubbanta). For one who does not see "this body is I," the outflows of views (diṭṭhāsava) reach abandonment.

Whosoever, in the three periods of time—past, future, and present—is lust-free through various indications and does not repeatedly see "I am": by this method, by this effort, and by this means, this stage of seeing (dassana-bhūmi) and the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) occur. The effort of that Noble One (ariya) reaches the state of no further rebirth in Saṃsāra. Whatever effort of a Noble One there is, whether with weak, medium, or sharp five faculties (indriya), all lead to the total abandonment of rebirth in a new existence. In the clinging to "I" (ahaṃ), there are four divisions: the flood of views (diṭṭhogha), the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha), the flood of existence (bhavogha), and the flood of ignorance (avijjāogha). Among those modes (hāra), by way of the Mode of Conveying a Teaching (desanā-hāra), it shows the four truths through the five faculties; through the fruit of stream-entry, it shows two truths: the Path and Cessation; through the origin of personality (sakkāya-samudaya), it shows two truths: Suffering and Origin. This is the Mode of Conveying a Teaching.

## Among those modes, what is the Mode of Investigation (vicaya-hāra)? One who does not see "this body is I" abandons the three fetters (saṃyojana) that are to be abandoned by the stage of seeing (dassana-bhūmi). This is the Mode of Investigation.

## Among those modes, what is the Mode of Construing (yutti-hāra)? There are three types of persons: one of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), one of diffuse understanding (vipañcitaññū), and one to be led (neyya). The person of quick understanding has sharp faculties. Below that, the person of diffuse understanding has duller faculties. Below that, the one with dull faculties is called the person to be led. Among those persons, the person of quick understanding, because of the sharpness of their faculties...
285:
Having reached the stage of seeing and attained the fruit of stream-entry, he becomes a "one-seeder" (ekabījī) stream-enterer. This is the first type of stream-enterer. The person of diffuse understanding (vipañcitaññū), having reached the stage of seeing with duller faculties and attained the fruit of stream-entry, becomes a "family-to-family" (kolaṃkola) stream-enterer. This is the second type of stream-enterer. Among those persons, the person to be led (neyya), having reached the stage of seeing and attained the fruit of stream-entry, becomes a "seven-times-at-most" (sattakkhattuparama) stream-enterer. This is the third type of stream-enterer.

There is this construing (yutti): that one should realize the weak, medium, or sharp stage with weak, medium, or sharp faculties. Also, by abandoning personality view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), one abandons wrong views. This is the Mode of Construing.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Proximate Cause (padaṭṭhāna-hāra)? In this sutta, personality view is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for all wrong views. Personality (sakkāya) is the proximate cause for mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa). Mind-and-matter is the proximate cause for personality view. The five material faculties are the proximate cause for lust for form (rūpa-rāga). The six sense bases (saḷāyatana) are the proximate cause for the conceit "I am" (ahaṃkāra). Among those modes, what is the Mode of Characteristic (lakkhaṇa-hāra)? When two views are abandoned, in that abandonment, one view and other wrong views reach abandonment. One who is lust-free above and below is lust-free in all attractive objects. In a corresponding higher stage, one sees according to reality: "This formation exists because of this cause." He investigates the entire dependent origination (paṭicca-samuppāda). This is the Mode of Characteristic.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Analysis (catubyūha-hāra)? In this sutta, what is the Blessed One's intention? Those beings who will not delight (in Saṃsāra) will strive to abandon views. This is the Blessed One's intention in this sutta. This is the Mode of Analysis.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Reversal (āvaṭṭa-hāra)? Whatever five weak faculties there are, they are the five lower-fetter faculties (or faculties pertaining to the lower realm). Covetousness (abhijjhā) and ill-will (byāpāda) are totally uprooted. Faith (saddhā) is the power in the liberation of the trainee (sekha) by way of the manner of development. Faith is the power in abandoning the higher fetters by way of view. Through the exertion of the faculty of energy (vīriya) and the upholding of the faculty of mindfulness (sati), they reach the ultimate end. In that teaching, whatever faculties there are, this is the Path Truth. The abandonment of defilements is the Cessation Truth. The nature of non-arising in the future is Suffering (as the cessation of suffering). This is the Mode of Reversal.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Classification (vibhatti-hāra)? Whosoever regards "this aggregate is I," he exists in the mundane stage with superior faculties. Even if not through the effort associated with the Noble Path, he abandons personality view. Therefore, it is called "superior (adhimatta) faculties corresponding to that stage." In that stage, one attains the state of having superior faculties through five aspects: virtue (sīla), practice (vata), great learning (bāhussacca), concentration (samādhi), and the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamma-sukha). In that teaching, regarding what has not yet been reached...
286:
One who perceives attainment in what has not been attained takes up overestimation (abhimāna). Regarding this very occurrence, the Blessed One spoke this sutta: "Just by virtue..." In that teaching, the concentration of one who perceives attainment in an unattained meditative absorption (jhāna-samāpatti) is carnal (sāmisa) and practiced by inferior persons (kāpurisa). In this context, worldlings (puthujjanas) are called inferior persons. Because the carnal nature that arises depending on the Noble Path is mundane, that concentration is ignoble and practiced by inferior persons. However, one who does not know or see according to reality in a noble manner abandons attainment. One who is led by noble concentration, which is not practiced by inferior persons and is non-carnal, is led out of the round of suffering; in this context, Noble Persons (Ariyas) are called superior persons (akāpurisa). The concentration practiced by those Ariyas is concentration practiced by superior persons. Therefore, one who does not repeatedly regard "This I am" lets fall one point to be answered by analysis (vibhajja-byākaraṇīya) in such a manner.

Among those modes (hāras), what is the Mode of Turning Round (parivattanā-hāra)? There are defilements to be abandoned by this Stage of Vision (the Path of Stream-entry); they are abandoned. Even if not explicitly indicated by the Blessed One, there is a meaning to be indicated.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Synonyms (vevacana-hāra)? Whatever view exists in the view of self-identity (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) and the view of self (atta-diṭṭhi), this is called the stage (bhūmi). Whatever defilements are to be abandoned, they are not yet abandoned. Even if not explicitly indicated by the Blessed One, there are the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) and the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). That view is also called the view of finitude (pariyanta-diṭṭhi). Whatever view of infinitude (apariyanta-diṭṭhi) exists, that is also called the view of eternalism. Whatever view of annihilationism exists, that is called the view of nihilism (natthika-diṭṭhi). Whatever view of eternalism exists, that is called the view of the inefficacy of action (akiriya-diṭṭhi). This is the Mode of Synonyms.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Description (paññatti-hāra)? Craving is described by the description of "fetter" (saṃyojana). The Path is described by the description of "attainment" (paṭilābha). The faculties (indriyas) are described by the description of "attainment." Among those modes, what is the Mode of Landing (otaraṇa-hāra)? The Truth of Suffering, called self-identity (sakkāya), is abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (vision). The Truth of Origination (samudaya), the Truth of the Path (magga), and those faculties are shown by making them enter into the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Cleansing (sodhana-hāra)? Whatever discourse the Blessed One spoke based on, it is indicated based on that discourse. Among those modes, what is the Mode of Equipment (parikkhāra-hāra)? The cause of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) is called the supporting cause (paccaya). Consciousness (viññāṇa) is called the seed-cause (hetu-bīja). Therefore, ignorance (avijjā) and volitional formations (saṅkhāra) are also called causes (paccaya). There is no other cause called the method of cessation (nivatti-naya). There is the whole of existence and whatever generative causes of the whole of existence there are, as well as the cause of external goods. Thus, for the arising of Right View, the voice of another (paratoghosa) and wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) are called causes (paccaya). Whatever wisdom it produces, that wisdom is called the generative cause (hetu) of Right View. Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa) occurs. Whatever Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi) exists, this is the Mode of Equipment.
287:
Among those modes, what is the Mode of Co-ordination (samāropana-hāra)? It is the viewing of the fifteen aspects such as suffering, disease, etc., without habitually viewing "This I am."

"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose of virtues? What is their benefit?" "Ānanda, virtues have non-remorse (gladness) as their purpose; they have benefits up to the fruit of Arahantship." In that teaching, the meaning (benefit) is of two kinds: the purpose for the person (purisattha) and the verbal meaning (vacanattha).

Among those two, what is the purpose for the person? Whatever non-remorse (avippaṭisāra) exists, this is called the benefit of non-remorse; this non-remorse is called the purpose for the person. For example, if someone develops and pursues this meaning, and that person should say, "In this matter, there is a certain dhamma connected to me; for the sake of that dhamma, I undertake this specific practice," this is called the purpose for the person.

Among those teachings, what is the verbal meaning? It is the fact that virtues are good conduct of body or speech and are the cause of non-remorse. In that sutta, there is only the appearance of virtue and practice. The dhamma that is not other than the work of the Sugata (the Well-Gone One) is called good conduct; this is called non-remorse. Thus, in each term such as "up to the fruit of Arahantship," there are two kinds of meaning: the purpose for the person and the verbal meaning. Just as there are two kinds of meaning in this sutta, so too there are two kinds of meaning in all suttas.

This is called the ultimate meaning (paramattha) and the supreme meaning (uttamattha). Whatever Nibbāna is realized, and depending on which Nibbāna one becomes a person who has realized it, that person is called "one who has achieved the goal" (katattha). Furthermore, one knows this synonym well. Because the appropriate meaning is obtained through this synonym, it is called the verbal meaning. In that sutta, whatever meaning the disciple (sāvaka) desires, the attainment of that meaning is called the purpose for the person. Knowing the meaning of the various dhammas taught by the Blessed One is called the meaning (attha). In that context, the non-remorse (gladness of heart) of virtues is called both the purpose and the benefit. That benefit is indeed not going to a miserable destination (duggati). As taught by the Blessed One, the fact that one who practices the Dhamma does not go to a miserable destination is the benefit of the well-practiced Dhamma; this is the purpose.

For whatever reason a man exerts himself in virtues at the stage of meditation (bhāvanā-bhūmi) and becomes endowed with virtue, it continues thus up to the fruit of Arahantship; likewise, it is the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). In that context, the non-remorse (gladness of heart) shown by the power of underlying tendencies (anusaya), as well as that virtue, is the aggregate of virtue. Gladness (pāmojja), joy (pīti), and tranquility (passaddhi) produced by the faculty of concentration are called the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). The knowing according to reality by one who is concentrated is called the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). These three aggregates—virtue, concentration, and wisdom—are called aggregates. Likewise, by whatever faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) one fulfills virtue, because of that energy, that person fulfills virtue. For the non-arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, for the abandoning of unwholesome states that have arisen, for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and for the wholesome states that have arisen...
288:
One exerts effort for the sake of further development; thus, the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) is pointed out. In that discourse, whatever aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha) there is, this aggregate of concentration is called the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya). The aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) is called the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya); that wisdom should be understood in the four right efforts (sammappadhāna). Likewise, when one exerts effort for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, this exertion is called the first right effort. The abandoning of arisen unwholesome states is the second right effort. The four right efforts should be seen in the four jhanas.

Likewise, through the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the element of renunciation (nekkhamma-dhātu) should also be seen. The three thoughts that arise excessively are the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka), the thought of non-ill will (abyāpāda-vitakka), and the thought of non-harming (avihiṃsā-vitakka); these arise in association. Whatever affection and state of being loved exists through joy, this is called bodily pleasure (kāyika-sukha). Bringing [something] with unregulated affection exists; this is called suffering (dukkha). In that teaching, whatever non-distraction exists, this non-distraction is called concentration (samādhi). This is the first jhana with five factors. What is the tranquility of mind? It is the opposition to the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) that occur with initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), as well as whatever defilement and feverish heat exist; that feverish heat ceases in the first jhana. In that manner, both the tranquility of defilements and the tranquility of initial and sustained thought occur in the tranquility of those states. In that discourse, the pleasure of body and mind remains in a state of happiness; this is called the tranquility of one who has rapture and pleasure (pīti-sukha). Whatever exalted state of mind exists, the clarity in the internal continuity through that exalted state is called the factor of the fourth jhana. Thus, there are internal clarity, the exalted state of mind, rapture, and pleasure; this is the second jhana with four factors.

One who has a tranquil body experiences pleasure; pervaded by that transcendent pleasure, one experiences mental pleasure; that person is dispassionate towards rapture. Thus, because of that dispassion towards rapture, one attains equanimity (upekkhā); because of dispassion towards rapture, one attains equanimity and also experiences pleasure, and attains mindfulness (sati) through right wisdom. If there is mindfulness and one-pointedness (ekaggatā), this is the third jhana with five factors. Whatever mind of a happy person is concentrated through the mental factor of one-pointedness, it has the quality of being disposed towards another state. In the first jhana, this one-pointedness of mind exists, but for the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), the feeling does not reach full completion. Just as in the fourth jhana, likewise, there are mindfulness, clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), and one-pointedness of mind which tranquilize equanimity; this is the fourth jhana.

Just as concentration should be seen, likewise the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) exists; that faculty of wisdom should be seen in the four noble truths (ariyasacca). One who is concentrated knows specifically according to reality; that knowing is fourfold: as foul (asubha), as suffering (dukkha), and as without essence (anatta). Whatever object exists, that object is called the noble truth of suffering. Because of knowing, one becomes weary and is liberated from defilements; likewise, whatever abandoning of the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) exists, such abandoning is called the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca).
289:
In the plane where they have not yet been abandoned, there is the origin (samudaya) of the taints (āsava). These four noble truths should be seen just as they are seen through the faculty of wisdom. When one who is concentrated knows in accordance with reality, this is called the plane of vision (dassanabhūmi) [the plane of the path of stream-entry]. One who knows the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) in accordance with reality becomes weary; such weariness is also the thinning [of defilements]. Because of weariness and dispassion towards sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill will (byāpāda) in the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala), this is called the first plane of development (bhāvanābhūmi); it is also the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) which is liberation of mind (cetovimutti) due to the fading away of lust. Whatever liberation one is freed by through the fruit of arahantship (arahatta-phala), this is also called the liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) which is the fruit of arahantship due to the fading away of ignorance. This freedom from remorse (avippaṭisāra) and the faculty of energy, and the four right efforts are called freedom from remorse. That freedom from remorse exists upwards until concentration. Thus, one who is concentrated through those four jhanas and the faculty of concentration knows in accordance with reality. These four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), depending on the perfection of virtue and associated with generosity, are the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), which is the state of having an undisturbed mind that is the cause of the states of penetrative knowledge. Furthermore, in this teaching, among the three instances, the faculty that enters into views and the virtue of one in training (sekha-sīla) produced by the abandoning of defilements is called the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). The four factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyaṅga) are called the fruits. The faculties of concentration should be pointed out in all discourses as states that lead upwards. For one who reflects on the attained jhana, the knowledge acquired through energy is called wisdom consisting in what is heard (sutamayī paññā). Whatever concentration has the light of preceding and succeeding signs and can be accomplished as desired because of its unerring course is called wisdom consisting in reflection (cintāmayī paññā). For one who is thus concentrated, knowing in accordance with reality is called wisdom consisting in development (bhāvanāmayī paññā). This is the exposition of the discourse (sutta-niddesa).

This discourse should be known as a discourse that leads to penetration and has a great deal of what should be understood. They will know that discourse endowed with those factors, and they will know the factors of that discourse; therefore, they are called factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). Furthermore, from the beginning up to virtue and practice, volition (cetanā) should be exercised. Why does one fulfill the virtues? The effort to prevent the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, to abandon arisen unwholesome states, to arouse unarisen wholesome states, and to further develop arisen wholesome states—this energy is the factor (cause) of each respective understood discourse. This is called the energy factor of enlightenment (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga). Because of this energy, two states—freedom from remorse and joy—arise at the beginning. Furthermore, whatever rapture arises due to the cause of freedom from remorse and joy is called the rapture factor of enlightenment (pīti-sambojjhaṅga). The body of one with a rapturous mind becomes tranquil. This is called the tranquility factor of enlightenment (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga). That tranquility brings bodily pleasure; the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This is called the concentration factor of enlightenment (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga). One who is concentrated knows in accordance with reality; this is called the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga). Depending on virtue, the conformity to the five factors of enlightenment, being the cause, and with the states that are part of rapture...
290:
This state, which is accompanied by factors leading to distinction and is characterized by non-muddiness, is called the Enlightenment Factor of Mindfulness (sati-sambojjhaṅga). Because one knows according to reality, one applies strenuous effort (vīriya). The "plane of agitation" (uddhacca-bhūmi) refers to what has been done and directs one toward aspiration. The "plane of sloth" (kosajja-bhūmi) refers to knowing the path of tranquility for the eye-sensitivity through factors free from blame; that knowing is called equanimity (upekkhā). By making that equanimity a constituent part (aṅga) of that enlightenment factor, it is called the Enlightenment Factor of Equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga). This is the Exposition of the Sutta (sutta-niddesa).

Among those hāras, what is the Desanā-hāra (Mode of Conveying a Communication)? In this Sutta, the four Noble Truths are taught. Among those hāras, what is the Vicaya-hāra (Mode of Conveying an Investigation)? In this question, from the non-remorse (avippaṭisāra) of a virtuous person up to liberation (vimutti), when it is asked "what meaning is compared?", two terms are the question (pucchā) and two terms are the answer (vissajjanā). Through two terms, the two questions are known; through two terms, the answer is known. What is asked? It asks about the "plane of the body" (kāya-bhūmi) which is not oppressed by the enemies of defilements. Therefore, the establishment of the action of cultivation (bhāvanā-kamma) gives rise to the asekha (beyond training) states.

Among those hāras, what is the Yutti-hāra (Mode of Conveying a Construing)? For a virtuous person, non-remorse occurs. For one free from desire, there is also the fading of lust (virāga). This is the Yutti-hāra.

Among those hāras, what is the Padaṭṭhāna-hāra (Mode of Conveying a Proximate Cause)? Effort (vīriya) is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the faculty of effort (vīriyindriya). Concentration (samādhi) is the proximate cause of the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya). Wisdom (paññā) is the proximate cause of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). Effort is the proximate cause of non-hatred (adosa). Concentration is the proximate cause of non-greed (alobha). Wisdom is the proximate cause of non-delusion (amoha). The faculty of effort is the proximate cause of the three path factors: right speech, right action, and right livelihood. The faculty of concentration is the proximate cause of the three path factors: right intention, right speech, and right concentration. The faculty of wisdom is the proximate cause of the two path factors: right mindfulness and right view.

Among those hāras, what is the Lakkhaṇa-hāra (Mode of Conveying a Characteristic)? When the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) is mentioned, all three aggregates are said to be mentioned. Virtue alone is like a mountain. Just as a mountain cannot be destroyed by any enemies, likewise, that mind cannot be shaken by any defilements; this is non-delusion (amoha). The absence of lust for objects of lust is non-greed (alobha). Not being angry at things that provoke anger is non-hatred (adosa). In that teaching, wisdom is the root of the wholesome called non-delusion. Non-greed is just non-greed. Non-hatred is just non-hatred. One who stands on the plane of the trainee (sekha-bhūmi) by means of these three wholesome roots gives rise to the path of the one beyond training (asekha-magga). The plane of the trainee gives rise to perfected kammic states. These ten states—namely, that right liberation (sammā-vimutti) and the knowledge and vision of the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa-ñāṇadassana)—are the states of Arahantship for those beyond training (asekha). In that teaching, by means of the Eightfold Path, the four types of cultivation are also obtained. They are: cultivation of virtue (sīla-bhāvanā), cultivation of the body (kāya-bhāvanā)...
291:
...development of the mind (citta-bhāvanā) and development of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā). Among these four developments, the body (kāya) is developed through right action and right livelihood. Virtue (sīla) is developed through right speech and right effort. The mind (citta) is developed through right intention and right concentration. Wisdom (paññā) is developed through right view and right mindfulness. Through these four developments, two things reach the fulfillment of development: the mind and wisdom. The mind in development is called tranquility (samatha); wisdom in development is called insight (vipassanā). In that teaching, wisdom, by abandoning ignorance, makes the mind unmixed with the impurities of defilements. By developing wisdom, one fulfills the development of the mind itself. Thus, for one whose mind is well-developed, from where can suffering come to him? Indeed, that venerable one has the element of non-ill-will (abyāpāda-dhātu) to which he is inclined; he enters into that element of non-ill-will. It does not give him the reckoning of being struck; in the body free from the reckoning of being struck, he does not feel suffering. This is the meaning of the sutta (suttattha).

What is the Mode of Teaching (desanā-hāra)? In this sutta, the ten beyond-trainee qualities of Arahantship, which are immeasurable and well-developed, are taught. What is the Mode of Investigation (vicaya-hāra)? Whatever things, like a mountain, reach the felt pleasure and pain—all those things reach those who see the formless; because the equipment of feeling from the body does not occur, one does not feel suffering. What is the Mode of Logic (yutti-hāra)? It is the sentence: 'For one whose mind is thus developed, from where can suffering come to him?' In these three developments—development of the mind, development of cessation (nirodha-bhāvanā), and development of immediate concentration (ānantarika-samādhi-bhāvanā)—suffering cannot enter. Thus, 'the mind of one thus developed' means that concentration is the proximate cause of the fruit (phala).

What is the Mode of Characteristic (lakkhaṇa-hāra)? In the phrase 'the mind of one thus developed', the things previously shown—wisdom, virtue, body, and mind—are developed. When virtue is well-developed, bodily pleasure and mental pleasure also do not shake because of stability; likewise, feeling, perception, and formations do not shake. 'Why would suffering reach him?' means that pleasant feeling does not follow, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling does not come.

What is the Mode of Analysis of the Fourfold Array (catubyūha-hāra)? What is the Blessed One's intention (adhippāya) in this sutta? Those who would be overcome by suffering will be deprived of such attainments. This is the Blessed One's intention here. And those who are not confident will become confident.
292:
For those who have faith, there will also be joy and gladness; this is the Blessed One's intention in this regard. Āvaṭṭa means the absence of a ground (bhūmi) for the mode of circling (āvaṭṭana-hāra).

Vibhatti (Classification) means that in the sentence, "For one whose mind is thus developed, from where will suffering come?", there are two types of description: the description of the cause of suffering and the description of its opposite. What is the cause of suffering? It is that from which suffering arises. When the opposite quality is mentioned, virtue (sīla) is both the productive cause (hetu) and the supporting condition (paccaya) for the remaining qualities; thus, all those qualities are said to be mentioned. When one factor of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) is mentioned, all qualities leading to enlightenment (bodhigamanīya-dhamma) are said to be mentioned.

Among those modes, what is the mode of plotting (catubyūha-hāra)? What is the Blessed One's intention in this sutta? Those who desire non-remorse (avippaṭisāra) possess the fulfillment of virtue. Desiring gladness, they possess the fulfillment of non-remorse. This is the Blessed One's intention in this regard... this is the catubyūha-hāra.

Among those modes, what is the mode of circling (āvaṭṭa-hāra)? This sutta is one that leads to penetration (nibbhedabhāgiya). That which is penetration is the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca). That by which one penetrates is the truth of the path (magga-sacca). That which is penetrated is the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). That which is abandoned by the path leading to penetration is called the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca).

Among those modes, what is the mode of classification (vibhatti-hāra)? "For the virtuous, there is non-remorse" is a point to be answered by classification (vibhajja-vyākaraṇīya). For one who misapprehends, there is no non-remorse as long as they undertake unwholesome actions of body or speech through anger. Even if such a person thinks, "This was well done, this was good conduct," gladness leading up to liberation (vimutti) cannot arise through that non-remorse; only for that virtuous person does non-remorse arise—this is to be answered by classification. This is the vibhatti-hāra.

Among those modes, what is the mode of conversion (parivattanā-hāra)? Through the fulfillment of these seven causes (upanisā), the eleven dependencies (upanisā) abandon those things that are to be abandoned in the classification. This is the parivattanā-hāra.

Among those modes, what is the mode of synonyms (vevecana-hāra)? These are the synonyms (pariyāya) for these Noble Dhammas, as well as for the powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), liberations (vimokkha), concentration (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti).

Among those modes, what is the mode of designation (paññatti-hāra)? In the teaching "For the virtuous, there is non-remorse," the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) is designated by the designation of renunciation (nekkhamma-paññatti), and the designation of sitting (nisajja-paññatti) is also designated. In this way, the ten factors are designated by two factors each.

Among those modes, what is the mode of entry (otaraṇa-hāra)? This sutta leading to penetration enters into the five categories. Just as it was first indicated, it should be indicated in the same way within the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana), such as the faculties (indriya).
293:
Among those modes, what is the mode of clearing (sodhana-hāra)? The undertaking "For the virtuous, there is non-remorse" is not yet pure. The undertaking "For one with non-remorse, there is gladness" is not yet pure. Only when the eleven terms are taught is the undertaking pure. This is the sodhana-hāra.

Among those modes, what is the mode of point of view (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra)? It is made known by the distinction (vemattatā) of virtue. Thus, all ten terms are the benefits of the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). Those benefits and living in a suitable locality are called the supporting condition (paccaya). Proper self-resolution is called the productive cause (hetu). Happiness is the productive cause for the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), and tranquility (passaddhi) is the supporting condition. By whatever cause the coexistence with jhāna occurs is also called a cause. Another sequence of teaching regarding the factors of jhāna is that seeing the danger in sensual pleasures is the supporting condition for concentration, and seeing the benefits in renunciation (nekkhamma) is the productive cause.

Among those modes, what is the mode of attribution (samāropanā-hāra)? That which is the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) is the aggregate of virtue. That which is virtue is established in the four dhammas. That which is practice in accordance with the Dhamma is the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara).

"Whose mind is like a rock" is a verse (see Udāna 3.4). "Like a rock" is a simile. Just as a mountain made of solid rock is not shaken by the wind, nor by heat, nor by cold. Many inanimate objects wither because of heat, dry up because of cold, and are destroyed by the wind. It is not so with a rock. Because it is said that one who is dispassionate (viratta) towards lustful objects does not hate in the face of the hateful, there is no distress (domanassa) ending in hatred towards the hateful. Such a person is not shaken by one who is hateful, nor by heat; he does not wither, nor does he dry up because of cold. Similarly, it should be known that the mind does not yearn because of lust, nor does it shake because of cold. For what reason? Because it is dispassionate towards lustful objects. It does not hate in the face of the hateful. For what reason? Because it does not hate even when it could occur towards the hateful. They will not bear ill-will toward that person who does not hate. Therefore, he does not become angry at objects that provoke anger. For one whose mind is thus developed, where would the cause of suffering be? From where would suffering come to such a person? Thus it is indicated.

Parivattanā (Conversion) means: in the mind regarding the thought "From where will suffering come to him?", that happiness (sukha) which is the Nibbāna element without residue of the results of past kamma (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) does not exist [in the sense of being felt], but it exists in the Nibbāna element with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Again, it is said: at that moment, at that instant, both were indeed experienced—the Nibbāna element with residue and the Nibbāna element without residue. At that moment, at that instant, the Nibbāna element without residue and the Nibbāna element with residue were experienced. For one who has reached happiness, there is no returning. What has been stated is the specific mode of conversion (parivattanā-hāra) in this regard.
294:
Among those modes (hāras), what is the synonym mode (vevacana-hāra)? For whom the mind is thus developed, extensively developed, well-developed, brought into being, made a foundation, and thoroughly undertaken. 'Mind' (citta) means mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa), the mind faculty (manindriya), and the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu).

Among those, what is the description mode (paññatti-hāra)? The mind is made known as the formation (saṅkhāra) called 'mind', and by the description of 'stilling' (vūpasama). Concentration (samādhi) is made known by the description of 'beyond training' (asekkha). Suffering (dukkha) is made known by the description of 'extirpation' (ucchinnapaññatti).

Among those, what is the landing mode (otaraṇa-hāra)? When the mind is shown, the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā) are shown; this is the landing into the aggregates. When the mind-consciousness element is shown, the eighteen elements (aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo) are shown; this is the landing into the elements. When the mind base (manāyatana) is pointed out, all the bases (āyatanāni) are pointed out. In that teaching, the mind base is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). With name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base (saḷāyatana) arises. The same applies to dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). This is the landing mode.

Among those, what is the clearing mode (sodhana-hāra)? The undertaking is purely pure.

Among those, what is the footing mode (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra)? It is making known the development of the six faculties in oneness. By standing in the six, the body is made known in oneness.

Among those, what is the equipment mode (parikkhāra-hāra)? It is the attention (manasikāra) to the prior cause of the mind and the inclination towards that prior cause. Because the higher states are not developed in the ground of the unconcentrated, the mind reaches constancy. If for the concentrated person, happiness (sukha) is the root cause (hetu), then non-remorse (avippaṭisāra) is the supporting condition (paccaya). This is the equipment mode consisting of the root cause (hetu) as the generator and the condition (paccaya) as the support.

Among those, what is the attribution mode (samāropana-hāra)? In the teaching 'For whom it is thus developed', the qualities of a trainee (sekkhadhamma) and one beyond training (asekkhadhamma) should be attributed to that person. The developed mental body (nāmakāya), virtue (sīla), wisdom (paññā), and the developed mind are without delight, without inclination, not diverse, not defiled, and not attached. This concentration is not the right concentration (sammā-samādhi) of that trainee for the sake of the path of Arahantship. All ten qualities of an Arahant (arahantadhamma), which are beyond training, are shown. These are the discourses (suttas) pertaining to those beyond training.

Venerable sir, if mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) is indeed not developed in someone, that person might strike against one of his fellow practitioners, collide with them, and without apologizing, depart on a tour of the countryside. That venerable one knows two things in this matter: the development of the mind and the abandoning of wrong view; he knows them distinctly and repeatedly. He knows the abandoning of view in the development of the body, and the abandoning of craving (taṇhā) in the development of the body. First, he makes an analogy: Just as the earth is not troubled, disgusted, nor does it feel joy or gladness because of either impure or pure things.
295:
Even so, with a mind like the earth, he dwells with a mind that is consistent, minimal, without enmity, and without ill-will. What does that venerable one declare? By the development of the body, he declares the abandoning of the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya). By the development of the mind, he declares the abandoning of the faculty of joy (somanassindriya). Bodily feeling (kāyikā vedanā) rejects the faculty of pleasure for those who follow the underlying tendency to lust (rāgānusaya). For that mental pleasant feeling which exists in the aggregate of feeling, pleasure and joy arise due to the condition of acquisition. He abandons that joy, but not the feeling born of mind-contact. In such feeling, among the four great elements, he speaks of the abandoning of the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). Form exists in the sensual realm, and that form also exists in the stage beyond training. Mindfulness of the body in the body (kāye kāယာnupassanā) has the benefit of dwelling happily in the present life.

For those who apply everything to the mind through power and effort, my abandoning is like the abandoning by a man who is fickle or a man who is fond of ornaments. Thus, through these applications, there is the reflection on the arising due to mother and father. That person carries two things: through the body and mindfulness of the body, and through the mind and mindfulness of the mind. He declares that he dwells in the seven attainments (samāpatti) by means of the mind regarding the basis of bodily defilements and by means of the well-developed mind regarding the support of the mind.

It should also be understood through the analogy of the guild-leader's son. A guild-leader's son might have a chest full of clothes of various colors. Whatever pair of clothes he desires in the morning, he wears in the morning. Similarly at noon and in the evening. Even so, because that venerable one's mind is well-developed, whatever way he wishes to dwell in the morning, he dwells in that way in the morning. Similarly at noon and in the evening. Therefore, by the analogy I have spoken, that venerable one has an unsurpassed development of the faculties like the earth, with a developed mind. Therefore, that venerable one declares these eight kinds of development regarding the four great elements. He declares the development of the body and the development of the mind in the cases of Upakacaṇḍāla, Purisametaka, and Bhavatalākāsa. Through these developments and by such cultivation, serenity (samatha) reaches fulfillment at the end. Through these four kinds of wisdom, they reach fulfillment at the end.

How does Upakacaṇḍāla dwell with the perception of the non-repulsive in repulsive things? Although the body is naturally not repulsive, there are nine perceptions (nava saññā) such as the perception of the bloated (uddhūmātaka-saññā) in the body. These are repulsive things. That venerable one dwells devoted to the development of mindfulness of the body, not being disgusted by the repulsive aspect. Because that disgust has been abandoned, the mind no longer finds it repulsive.
296:
How does one dwell with the perception of the repulsive in things that are not repulsive? The body is something not repulsive to the whole world; that venerable one dwells regarding that body with the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā). In this way, one dwells with the perception of the repulsive in things that are not repulsive.

How does one dwell with the perception of the unrepulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive? Indeed, in this world, when a shaven-headed person, carrying a bowl in hand, wanders among families for alms, that venerable one dwells with a mind that perceives the unrepulsive in objects of both beautiful and ugly appearance, and with a body accompanied by revulsion, yet perceiving the unrepulsive. In this way, one dwells with the perception of the unrepulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive.

How does one dwell with the perception of the unrepulsive in things that are repulsive? Among repulsive things, in the form of a woman which is perceived as beautiful, and in the repulsive and loathsome object of a bloated and festering corpse, that venerable one dwells with the perception of the repulsive.

How does one dwell avoiding both those states, remaining equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending? Regarding the form of a woman which is perceived as beautiful among unrepulsive things, and the repulsive and loathsome object of a bloated and festering corpse, he avoids both and dwells reflecting: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' In this way, avoiding both, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.

Another method: The existence of the world with its three realms is something perceived as unrepulsive by all foolish worldlings. In that regard, the venerable Sāriputta dwells with the perception of the unrepulsive. In this way, he dwells with the perception of the repulsive in things that are not repulsive.

How does one dwell with the perception of the unrepulsive in things that are repulsive? In this entire world of the three realms, all those in higher training (sekhas) have the perception of the repulsive. In that regard, who is it that has reached the plane, realized the fruit of concentration, and dwells with the perception of the unrepulsive? For what reason? Because for such a person, there is no cause to produce the perception of the repulsive for the sake of abandoning that world.

How does one dwell with the perception of the repulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive? In the existence of the world with its three realms, the state of the sense-sphere world is equal to the repulsive for those free from lust; in the fine-material and immaterial realms, it is equal to the unrepulsive. In that regard, the venerable Sāriputta dwells with the perception of the repulsive. In this way, he dwells with the perception of the repulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive.
297:
How does one dwell with the perception of the unrepulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive? Among words spoken badly and wrongly due to lust, there is some word that is not perceived [as harmful]. That word is unrepulsive. To the extent that words are improper for the people, in that manner, there is the perception of the unrepulsive. In that regard, the venerable Sāriputta, having known with higher knowledge and realized it, dwells with the perception of the unrepulsive. In this way, he dwells with the perception of the unrepulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive.

How does one dwell avoiding both those states, remaining equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending? He observes those things called misconduct (duccarita) of those people; those things are unrepulsive. In that regard, the venerable Sāriputta reflects thus: those things called misconduct have undesirable results. Those things called good conduct (sucarita) lead to the accumulation [of merit/rebirth]. Having treated good conduct as leading to accumulation and misconduct as having undesirable results, he avoids both and dwells equanimous.

Furthermore, he dwells with the perception of the repulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive. Craving (taṇhā) is called a repulsive thing. For what reason? Through the power of craving, beings are attached to two things: they are attached to the nutriment consisting of mouthfuls (kabaḷīkāra āhāra) by the craving for taste, and they are attached to contact (phassa) by the perception of pleasure. In that regard, the venerable Sāriputta dwells with the perception of the repulsive in nutriment, and he dwells with the perception of suffering in contact. In this way, he dwells with the perception of the repulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive.

How does one dwell with the perception of the unrepulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive? Foolish worldlings regard the peerless Nibbāna, which is the end of craving, as repulsive and as a perception of destruction. In that Nibbāna, the venerable Sāriputta, having seen for himself with wisdom the perception of the unrepulsive and the perception of non-ill-will, thus dwells with the perception of the unrepulsive in repulsive things.

How does one dwell with the perception of the unrepulsive in things that are both repulsive and unrepulsive? For one who still has the perception of the repulsive in the third Nibbāna, he dwells with the perception of the unrepulsive in followers and fame. In that regard, the venerable Sāriputta, knowing the gratification (assāda), the danger (ādīnava), and the escape (nissaraṇa) as they really are with right wisdom, avoids both repulsive and unrepulsive things and dwells with the perception of the unrepulsive.
298:
How does one dwell equanimous, avoiding both the repulsive and the non-repulsive? One dwells mindful and clearly comprehending. In whatever object attraction (anunaya) is a non-repulsive thing and repulsion (paṭigha) is a repulsive thing, there the Venerable Sāriputta, because of the abandonment of attraction and repulsion, dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Such repeated seeing is called the fivefold supreme development of the faculties (indriyabhāvanā). This is the exposition of the discourse (suttaniddesa).

Among those methods, what is the Method of Teaching (desanāhāra)? What is taught in this discourse? It is said that in this discourse, the dwelling in happiness in this very life is taught; likewise, the Dhamma of higher wisdom (adhipaññā), which is the reflection and the mind liberated from defilements, is taught.

Among those methods, what is the Method of Investigation (vicayahāra)? For those who dwell contemplating the body in the body, their minds do not dwell with attraction and repulsion. The power of the mind of one who delights in attraction and repulsion will not become unified (samaggata); this power is the power of development (bhāvanā). This is the Method of Investigation.

Among those methods, what is the Method of Logic (yuttihāra)? There is this logic: because of the development of the body and the development of the mind, a fellow practitioner will not despise one for any reason. This is the Method of Logic.

Among those methods, what is the Method of Proximate Cause (padaṭṭhānahāra)? The development of the body is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the first establishment of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Having a mind like the earth is the proximate cause for the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā).

Among those methods, what is the Method of Characteristic (lakkhaṇahāra)? Because of dwelling with a mind like the earth, one who contemplates the body dwells as a layperson with a mind like the earth. What is the meaning of 'like the earth'? Just as those who are unshakable like a rock mountain are not engaged [in unwholesome actions], even so, this person is like the earth because of having a sense of shame (hiri). This is the Method of Characteristic.

Among those methods, what is the Method of Fourfold Array (catubyūhahāra)? In this explanation, what is the intention of that Venerable? Whatever Arahants desire the development of the faculties, they will produce the state of having a mind like the earth. This is the intention (adhippāya).

Among those methods, what is the Method of Reversion (āvaṭṭahāra)? There is no ground for the Method of Reversion.
299:
Among those methods, what is the Method of Classification (vibhattihāra)? It is not certain that whoever dwells contemplating the body will attain a mind like the earth. Why? Because those with faults such as broken virtue cannot attain a mind like the earth. Nibbāna is the fruit of the development of a trainee (sekkhabhāvanā) who develops all mindfulness directed to the body. This is the Method of Classification.
