Among those methods, what is the Method of Transformation (parivattanahāra)? For those who will dwell contemplating the body, only for them, because of the body as a cause, the cankers (āsava) involving distress and fever might arise. This is the Method of Transformation.

Among those methods, what is the Method of Descent (otaraṇahāra)? The twenty-two faculties do not exceed the five aggregates. Likewise, whatever mind-faculty (manindriya) exists, it is called the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-base (manāyatana). Whatever concentration-faculty (samādhindriya) exists, it is called the dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) and the dhamma-base (dhammāyatana). This is the Method of Descent.

Among those methods, what is the Method of Cleansing (sodhanahāra)? When the four things to be developed by the mind are fully developed, there is that Nibbāna which is to be attained upon the abandonment of defilements; the exertion for the sake of that Nibbāna in all respects is the pure benefit. This is the Method of Cleansing.

Among those methods, what is the Method of Determination (adhiṭṭhānahāra)? This concentration is designated by way of oneness (ekatta). The six bodies are also designated by way of oneness. The five material faculties are the material body (rūpakāya). The six groups of feeling are the feeling body (vedanākāya). The six groups of perception are the perception body (saññākāya). The six groups of volition are the volition body (cetanākāya). The six groups of consciousness are the consciousness body (viññāṇakāya). All these dhammas are reckoned only as the Body of Dhamma (dhammakāya). This is the Method of Determination.

Regarding the Requisite (parikkhāra): skill in attainments (samāpatti) and skill in the process (vīthi) are called the cause (hetu). Skill in the resort (gocara) and skill in suitability (kalla) are called the condition (paccaya). Skill in purification (vodāna) is the cause, and suitability is the condition. Happiness is the cause, and freedom from anxiety (abyāpajja) is the condition. This is the Method of Requisite.

Among those methods, what is the Method of Attribution (samāropanahāra)? Just as the earth remains the same whether a clean object is placed on it or an unclean object is placed on it, even so, the body remains the same whether through pleasant touches or unpleasant touches. The mind remains the same whether through painful contact (paṭighasamphassa) or through pleasant feeling. This discourse is classified with similes for a person of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū). In this, there is no opportunity for the Method of Attribution.
300:
Among those [Hāras], what is the Sutta partaking of defilement (saṅkilesabhāgiya)? Because it does not conflict with wholesome states (kusala dhamma) and they do not increase, the Blessed One taught this danger (ādīnava). Therefore, one should uncover the roof of defilements; rain does not wet what is open. One should uncover it because of that danger. That [mind] is not destroyed by three states: lust is not able to destroy it because of the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā); hatred is not able to destroy it because of loving-kindness (mettā); and delusion is not able to destroy it because of insight (vipassanā). Thus, whatever opposing state there is for him, he will be fulfilled in that [wholesome] state. The unwholesome state which is the opposite of that wholesome state cannot overwhelm him.

Another method: These teachings are taught for those who cannot rise [from defilements] by themselves. 'Rain wets what is covered' means they [cannot succeed] through thought (vitakka); it is possible to manifest and purify the taught mind. For one who is bent, sloped, and inclined toward seclusion (viveka), there comes growth, increase, and abundance in wholesome states. For example, just as blue, white, or red lotuses in water during the waxing moon—as the moon comes throughout the night and day—only growth is to be expected for them, not decline; in the same way, such a mind cannot be destroyed. Another point here: a person who is not crooked, not deceitful, not a hypocrite, and is upright, reveals himself as he truly is. Among them, for one who conceals, unwholesome states follow the mind. 'Rain wets what is covered' means that for one who is not deceitful, not crooked, not a hypocrite, and is an upright person who reveals himself as he truly is, his mind cannot be destroyed by unwholesome states. This is the meaning of the Sutta.

Among those [Hāras], what is the Mode of Conveying a Teaching (desanā-hāra)? Here, the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusala-kammapatha) are taught because of being 'wet' [by rain], and the ten courses of wholesome action (kusala-kammapatha) are taught because of not being 'wet'. One is not purified by unwholesome states. As the Blessed One said: 'Monks, by the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled.'

Among those [Hāras], what is the Mode of Conveying an Investigation (vicaya-hāra)? For one whose mind is thus overwhelmed [by the unwholesome], whatever crookedness there might be for that person who understands—[investigating] that without interval, whether in the Teacher or by following the protection of virtues—this is the Mode of Conveying an Investigation.

Among those [Hāras], what is the Mode of Conveying a Construing (yutti-hāra)? A mind that is not thus overwhelmed rises [from defilements]. The logic (yutti) exists that the risen mind stands firm in wholesome states.
301:
The Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes (padaṭṭhāna-hāra): In the phrase 'Rain wets what is covered,' being covered is the proximate cause of non-restraint (asaṃvara). In the phrase 'Rain does not wet what is open,' being uncovered is the proximate cause of restraint (saṃvara). Therefore, 'One should uncover what is covered; rain does not wet what is open' is the proximate cause of the teaching. The Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra): In the phrase 'Rain wets what is covered,' all states that have the same characteristic as being covered in various ways reach destruction. Therefore, one should uncover what is covered. In the phrase 'Rain does not wet what is open,' all states that have the same characteristic as being uncovered are not wet by the rain of defilements. This is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics.

Among those [Hāras], what is the Mode of Conveying a Fourfold Array (catubyūha-hāra)? What is the Blessed One's intention in this Sutta? The Blessed One's intention here is that although the minds of some people are overwhelmed by unwholesome states, they will remedy them in accordance with the Dhamma. This is the Mode of Conveying a Fourfold Array.

The Mode of Conveying a Revolving (āvaṭṭa-hāra): That which is covered is of two kinds, and the agitation should be cut off by the concentration of immediate result (ānantariya-samādhi). In that Sutta, conceit arising in tranquility (passaddhi) increases the taints (āsava); through lack of faith (assaddhiya), one reaches negligence (pamāda); through negligence, one inclines toward the low and reaches a state of arrogance. This was said by the Blessed One: 'For those who are arrogant and negligent, their taints increase.' Those four kinds of clinging (upādāna) become the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā). These are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) and the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca). Therefore, in saying 'One should uncover what is covered,' by whatever cause those taints increase, by the abandoning of those causes, the taints are abandoned. In that Sutta, through heedfulness (appamāda), one abandons lack of faith; by abandoning restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), one abandons coarseness; for him, the two states of serenity (samatha) and development (bhāvanā) reach fulfillment. The destruction of those taints is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). These are the Four Noble Truths. This is the Mode of Conveying a Revolving.

Among those [Hāras], what is the Mode of Conveying a Classification (vibhatti-hāra)? The statement 'Rain wets what is covered' is not categorical (ekaṃsa). Why? Because there can be prevention, as in the case of learners (sekha). As the Blessed One said:

'Even if a learner should do evil, by body, speech, or mind,
He is incapable of concealing it;
Such is the state of one who has seen the Path [of Nibbāna].'
302:
Even if a mind possessed of hindrances arises for them, because of the absence of conditions, those dhammas are pointed out at the appropriate time; this is called the Mode of Analysis (Vibhatti-hāra).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Reversal (Parivattana-hāra)? "When it rains, it pours only upon what is covered." This means for someone, whatever dhammas [exist], the rain pours excessively upon one who is not free from the round of rebirth; it does not pour upon one who is free from the round, nor upon one who possesses hidden virtues. This is the Mode of Reversal.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Synonyms (Vevacana-hāra)? "Covered" means obstructed, blocked, hindered, overturned, well-covered, or harassed. "It does not pour upon what is open" means for one who is a monk, those dhammas are made to be without excessive rain. This is the Mode of Synonyms.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Designation (Paññatti-hāra)? "Pours upon what is covered" is designated in the category of defilements. "Does not pour upon what is open" is designated by the designation of practice (paṭipadā-paññatti) regarding one's own natural function. Therefore, "one should open what is covered" is designated by the designation of instruction (anusāsana-paññatti). "Does not pour upon what is open" is designated in the designation of selection (niddhāna-paññatti). This is the Mode of Designation.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Entry (Otaraṇa-hāra)? "Pours upon what is covered" refers to the three defilements: greed, hatred, and delusion. Among the aggregates, they are called the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). ... These defilements are shown in the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as previously explained. This is the Mode of Entry.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Clearing (Sodhana-hāra)? The undertaking by which this sutta is spoken, that undertaking is applied.

The Mode of Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra) means that the statement "it pours upon what is covered" is designated by way of unity (ekatta). Why? The statement "it pours" is designated by characteristics common to hearing, in the sense of diversity (vematta), such as "it pours upon this person" and "it pours in this way." That designation is the designation of unity.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra)? For whom those defilements pour excessively, there are two productive causes (janaka-hetu): because of being one who teaches only the practice of unwholesome states and because of excessive delight. These two, along with unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and the decline from wholesome dhammas, are the two types of decisive support conditions (upanissaya-paccaya).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Attribution (Samāropana-hāra)? In the phrase "pours upon what is covered," "seeing with doubt" means for the sake of maintaining that cover, for the sake of not teaching one with little learning, deciding that "your hatreds increase because of the doubt caused by the manifest unwholesome roots and because of craving," those formations increase due to the lack of power. With formations as condition, consciousness [arises], and so on up to aging and death. This is...
303:
...the Mode of Attribution (Samāropana-hāra). Furthermore, such a teaching exists: for that person alone, unwholesome dhammas reach growth, increase, and full abundance; for him, formations cease. This is the Mode of Attribution.

There are four types of persons: the one in darkness leading to darkness, etc. Among them, who is called "darkness" (tamo)? One who is like a person in blind darkness. As the Blessed One said: "Just as in that terrifying blind darkness, a man of trembling nature does not see, even so, the blind darkness of delusion caused by ignorance has no faith in the result of his own evil deeds." Ignorance (aññāṇa) with such a characteristic is called darkness, nescience (avijjā), or delusion (moha). Because of that delusion, beings do not know things as they really are; thus it is called darkness. That delusion is the darkness of the three eyes: the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu), the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), and the wisdom eye (paññācakkhu). In this Dispensation, the darkness of these eyes is pointed out as non-knowledge (aññāṇa). In that context, what is non-knowledge? It is simply non-seeing (adassana).

Furthermore, as a basis (nissaya), there is non-knowledge regarding the past, non-knowledge regarding the future, non-knowledge regarding both the past and the future, non-knowledge regarding the cause (hetu), and non-knowledge regarding the condition (paccaya). These exist for that person who lacks knowledge and lacks concentration. This non-knowledge is called the natural result (nissanda). Because one does not know "this person should be associated with, this dhamma should not be attended to," that person is pointed out by that delusion of non-knowledge. It is also called darkness. There is such an intention (cetanā) as "the bewildered one." Because of that delusion, that person is called "darkness." Because of that delusion which has not been abandoned or uprooted, he is one for whom that is the highest, one who is bound for that; this person is called "darkness leading to darkness" (tamo tamaparāyano).

In the afterlife, only that Dhamma should be attended to. That Dhamma burns away the darkness and establishes another mind (the mind of the fruit of Arahantship). For that person, those dhammas are worthy of contemplation. He sees with wisdom consisting of what is heard (sutamayā-paññā). Among them, who is "darkness leading to light" (tamo jotiparāyano)? That person conducts himself by the power of that wisdom. Thus, for one who conducts himself in this way, there is a destination (parāyana). This person is called "darkness leading to light."

Among them, who is the person "light leading to light" (joti jotiparāyano)? In that context, "light" (joti) refers to the dhammas that are the opposite of that darkness, at the minimum, the light of knowledge. That person who has heard the Dhamma is called "darkness leading to light." In that context, the person who is "darkness leading to light," if he obtains such a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta) who leads him away from the unwholesome...
304:
(That teacher) restrains (the pupil from unwholesome deeds); being one who has cultivated wholesome states, he engages him only in cultivation. In this way, he teaches the True Dhamma: "These states are wholesome, these states are unwholesome. These states are blameworthy, these states are blameless. These states are to be cultivated, these states are not to be cultivated. These states are to be associated with, these states are not to be associated with. These states are to be entered upon and dwelled in, these states are not to be entered upon and dwelled in. These states are to be attended to, these states are not to be attended to."

He knows the faculties of mindfulness just as they are known through perception. That person knows thus: "These states are wholesome, these states are unwholesome. These states are blameworthy, these states are blameless. These states are to be cultivated, these states are not to be cultivated. These states are to be developed, these states are not to be developed. These states are to be entered upon and dwelled in, these states are not to be entered upon and dwelled in. These states are to be attended to, these states are not to be attended to."

That person listens well to those teachings, lends an ear, and establishes another mind (the mind of the fruit of Arahatship). Those teachings are endured by him through reflection. Being endowed with wisdom derived from learning (sutamaya-paññā), he proceeds by way of that cause. To such a person who proceeds in this way, there is delight in that wisdom and that wisdom is his refuge. This person is called "Tamo Tamaparāyana" (one who goes from darkness to darkness).

Among those persons, who is the "Jyoti Tamaparāyana" (one who goes from light to darkness)? "Light" (Jyoti) refers to those states which are the opposite of that darkness, at the very least, the light of knowledge; that state itself is light. How is it said? Because of having wisdom, he is called a wise person (paṇḍita). He knows thus: "These states are wholesome, these states are unwholesome. These states are blameworthy, these states are blameless. These states are to be cultivated, these states are not to be cultivated. These states are to be developed, these states are not to be developed. These states are to be entered upon and dwelled in, these states are not to be entered upon and dwelled in. These states are to be attended to, these states are not to be attended to."

However, in this world, one who associates with evil friends, who follows the will of evil friends, increases unwholesome states and abandons wholesome states. Through that negligence, without attending to the perception that is the cause, he indulges in lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension. He increases that darkness which is the opposite (of the wholesome). Overwhelmed by darkness, he has darkness as his refuge and delights in darkness. This person is called "Jyoti Tamaparāyana" (one who goes from light to darkness).

Among those persons, who is the "Jyoti Jyotiparayana" (one who goes from light to light)? Herein, the answer is given: That person is one who relies on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), being one associated with the wholesome, he is capable of seeking and performing wholesome deeds. He approaches good friends and inquires and investigates: "What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be cultivated? What should not be cultivated? What should be developed? What should not be developed? What should be entered upon and dwelled in? What should not be entered upon and dwelled in? What should be attended to? What should not be attended to? How is there defilement? How is there purification? How is there the process of existence (pavatti)? How is there the rebirth process (upapatti)? How is there bondage? How is there liberation? How is there the origin of self-identity (sakkāya-samudaya)? How is there the cessation of self-identity (sakkāya-nirodha)?"
305:
Seeking the wholesome, he approaches a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) and inquires and investigates: "What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be cultivated? What should not be cultivated? What should be developed? What should not be developed? What should be entered upon and dwelled in? What should not be entered upon and dwelled in? What should be attended to? What should not be attended to? How is there defilement (saṅkilesa)? How is there purification (vodāna)? How is there the process of existence (pavatti)? How is there cessation (nivatti)? How is there bondage (bandha)? How is there liberation (mokkha)? How is there the origin of self-identity (sakkāya-samudaya)? How is there the cessation of self-identity (sakkāya-nirodha)?"

When he practices well according to the Dhamma taught in this matter as it appears, he knows thus: "These states are wholesome, these states are unwholesome." This should be expanded up to "How is there the origin of self-identity? How is there the cessation of self-identity?" Being one who greatly desires those teachings, he increases the light of characteristics, knowledge, and true vision (vijjā). That person delights in that wisdom and has that wisdom as his refuge. This person is called "Jyoti Jyotiparayana" (one who goes from light to light).

Among those four, what kind of person is "Tamo Tamaparāyana" (one who goes from darkness to darkness)? The person who manifests unwholesome states. Because of the development of that unwholesome, he manifests rebirth in inferior destinations (gati). He delights in that unwholesome and has that unwholesome as his refuge. This person is called "Tamo Tamaparāyana."

Among those four, who is the person "Tamo Jyotiparayana" (one who goes from darkness to light)? That person manifests the result of unwholesome kamma through darkness (delusion). With the eye (wisdom) of a good friend, he abandons unwholesome states and increases wholesome states.

Among those four, the one who manifests rebirth in excellent destinations and delights in those excellent destinations, for that reason, is called "Tamo Jyotiparayana."

Among those four, what kind of person is "Jyoti Tamaparāyana" (one who goes from light to darkness)? He manifests the result of wholesome kamma. That person who possesses the eye of wisdom, through association with evil friends and serving evil friends, follows the will of evil friends and increases unwholesome states. Because of the development of that unwholesome, he manifests rebirth in inferior destinations. He delights in those inferior destinations. For that reason, he is called "Jyoti Tamaparāyana."

Among those four, the person who is "Jyoti Jyotiparayana," through the radiant light, manifests rebirth in excellent destinations. He delights in those excellent destinations. For that reason, he is called "Jyoti Jyotiparayana."
306:
Through the person who is light but bound for darkness (joti-tamaparāyana), the arising of the ten unwholesome actions is shown. Through that 'dark' (tamo) person, the ripening (vipāka) of unwholesome actions is shown. However, the ripening of unwholesome states (dhamma) is not shown. Through that 'darkness' (delusion), the eight wrongnesses (micchatta) are shown. Through 'light' (joti), the eight rightnesses (sammatta) are shown. Through the joti-tamaparāyana, the ten unwholesome courses of action are shown. Through 'light', excellence is shown. Through the tamo-jotiparāyana (darkness but bound for light), the state that does not cause remorse is shown. Through the joti-tamaparāyana, the state that causes remorse is shown. This is the meaning of the Sutta.

Among those (modes), what is the Mode of Conveyance of a Teaching (desanā-hāra)? What is taught in this Sutta? To that question, it is said: In this Sutta, wholesome and unwholesome states are taught. The ripening of wholesome and unwholesome states is also taught. The various differences in the destinations (gati) of beings, whether low or excellent, are also taught. This is the Mode of Conveyance of a Teaching.

In that context, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Investigation (vicaya-hāra)? Whosoever experiences the ripening of unwholesome karma, and while remaining in that (state of experience), produces unwholesome states—the investigation of those unwholesome states is appropriate in the Mode of Conveyance of Investigation. Whosoever experiences the ripening of wholesome karma, and while remaining in that (state of experience), produces wholesome states—the investigation of those wholesome states is also appropriate. This is the Mode of Conveyance of Investigation and the Mode of Conveyance of Logic (yutti-hāra).

In that context, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Proximate Cause (padaṭṭhāna-hāra)? It is shown that the person who is 'light' (joti) is the proximate cause for reflection (paccavekkhaṇā). The person who is 'darkness' (tamo) is the proximate cause for the repeated contemplation of things grasped through darkness. Through the tamo-jotiparāyana, the proximate cause of heedfulness (appamāda) is shown; 'darkness' (delusion) is shown as the proximate cause of ignorance (avijjā) and wrong view (diṭṭhi). Through the joti-tamaparāyana, the proximate cause of heedlessness (pamāda) and wrong view is shown. This is the Mode of Conveyance of Proximate Cause.

In that context, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Characteristic (lakkhaṇa-hāra)? When 'darkness' as ignorance is indicated by the tamo-tamaparāyana, all states of defilement are said to be indicated. When 'light' as clear vision (vijjā) is indicated by the tamo-jotiparāyana, all states partaking of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) are said to be indicated. Through the joti-tamaparāyana, heedlessness (pamāda) is indicated. Through the tamo-jotiparāyana, heedfulness (appamāda) is indicated. This is the Mode of Conveyance of Characteristic.

In that context, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Fourfold Array (catubyūha-hāra)? What is the Blessed One's intention in this Sutta? Those beings of low birth, even upon hearing this Dhamma, will not undertake and practice wholesome states. Those beings of high birth, (upon hearing) this Dhamma teaching...
307:
...having heard (this Dhamma teaching), will undertake and practice wholesome states to an even greater extent. This is the Mode of Conveyance of Fourfold Array (catubyūha-hāra). It is an instruction (upadesa) regarding the ground (of occurrence).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Reversion (āvaṭṭa-hāra)? There is that craving (taṇhā) which arises beginning with ignorance (avijjā); this craving is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (samudaya-sacca). There is that darkness (delusion) which is directed toward darkness; this delusion is called the Noble Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). These two truths, suffering and origin, as well as 'light' (joti), are made known by the Dhamma of this Sutta; that Dhamma is called the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). Through that non-delusion (amoha), the three wholesome roots reach fulfillment; it is the proximate cause of the heavenly realm.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Classification (vibhatti-hāra)? The phrase "tamo tamaparāyana" (one in darkness bound for darkness) is not absolute. Why? Because darkness and existence (bhava) exist in the state of co-occurrence with a 'light' person who possesses wholesome karma to be experienced in some subsequent existence (aparāpariya-vedanīya). There is also the occurrence of 'light' and existence in the state of co-occurrence with a 'dark' person who possesses unwholesome karma to be experienced in some subsequent existence. Due to the reversal which is the opposite of darkness, one becomes a tamaparāyana (one bound for darkness) through 'light'.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Synonyms (vevacana-hāra)? There is that darkness (delusion); such a person practices for his own affliction. Because of lack of faith, he is a fool, unskilled, lacking proficiency, and not seeing the danger. There is that light (one who has light); he practices for his own benefit, is wise, skilled, proficient, and sees the danger. This is the Mode of Conveyance of Synonyms.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Description (paññatti-hāra)? That person is made known by the description of ripening (vipāka); he is made known by the state of being completely overcome by unwholesome states. 'Light' is made known by the description of the arising of wholesome states and by the description of the ripening of wholesome states.

The Mode of Conveyance of Landing (otaraṇa-hāra) means: there are mental formations (saṅkhāra) caused by ignorance, as well as old age and death (jarā-maraṇa) and ignorance; these states are called the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). By way of indication, there is the arising of clear vision (vijjā) and the cessation of ignorance, leading up to the cessation of old age and death; these two states are included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). In terms of the elements (dhātu), the mind-element (dhamma-dhātu) and the mind-base (dhammāyatana) are called the proximate cause by way of indication.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Clearing (sodhana-hāra)? It is the preliminary undertaking of this taught Sutta. The Mode of Conveyance of Terms of Expression (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra) means: the Blessed One says 'darkness' (tamo), but He does not teach regarding only a single person. In whatever destinations (gati) beings may go, those who arise through the state of misconduct are indicated by the collective term (bahulādhivacana) 'darkness'. Whatever arising of wholesome states there is among all beings is called 'light'. This is the description of wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) which is the cause for the state of unity for persons consisting of the four great elements.
308:
Among these modes, what is the Mode of Conveying Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra)? The condition (paccaya) for the unwholesome is having bad friends, and the root cause (hetu) is unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). The condition for the wholesome is having good friends, and the root cause is wise attention (yoniso manasikāra).

Among these modes, what is the Mode of Conveying Loading (Samāropana-hāra)? In this world, some are reborn in a low family—one reborn in a low family [experiences] sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches; he is reborn among all the human enjoyments and pleasures. The 'Joti' (shining one) is reborn in noble wholesome states and is reborn among all the human enjoyments and pleasures.

Among these modes, what is the discourse (sutta) that pertains to defilement (saṅkilesabhāgiya) and the discourse that pertains to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya)? It is the verse: "The wise do not say that bond is strong." For what reason is that bond [called] strong? [Other bonds are not strong because] they can be released by four reasons: power, wealth, other entreaties, or refuge. Whatever lustful concern there is for jeweled earrings, sons, and wives—this is his mental bond (cetasika-bandhana). That bond cannot be released through power, wealth, other entreaties, or refuge. In such a bond, there is no deva or human who can guarantee, "I will release [you] from this bond." This bond binds through the underlying tendency of lust (rāgānusaya) and in the six external sense bases. Craving for forms binds to forms, up to craving for mental objects [binding to mental objects]. Whatever bond exists in this world, that bond is carried over to the next world. He is born with the bond, he dies with the bond. With the bond, he goes from this world to the next world. Except for the Noble Path, it is not possible to be released from this bond. Knowing the state of death and the state of rebirth as a danger, one abandons desire and lust (chandarāga). Having abandoned this desire and lust, he transcends [existence]. And this world has a second [existence] after this.

In that context, the abandoning of the formations (saṅkhāra) that are bonds is called energy (viriya) in two instances. The very pure sage, surrounded by knots (gantha), is not smeared [by defilements]. Likewise, in the case of sons and wives who are possessed, the dart of greed remains unextracted; for him, the abandoning of craving is shown. Because of abandoning the root of craving, this person becomes one who is diligent in the noble [wholesome states]. One who desires liberation from the round (vaṭṭa), in order to abandon the occurrence of negligence, delights in renunciation (nekkhamma) and lives diligently. To abandon longing (āsaya), he does not long for this world nor for the next world. He does not long for the dear and pleasant forms based in this world, nor for the dear and pleasant forms based in the next world...
309:
...he does not long for pleasant forms; therefore, it is said, "He does not long for this world or the next world." The Blessed One showed that abandoning and that cutting off for him in the Aṭṭhakavagga. In this Dispensation, that opposition is the absence of longing in the Aṭṭhakavagga, and the absence of refuge in this Dispensation. Similarly, for one who grasps at the objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma) through craving, all these sensual desires are shown with a single verse. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Having cut that [craving] also, without concern, abandoning all sensual desires, they wander forth."

In this verse, there are two kinds of exposition: the exposition by connection (saṃsandana-niddesa) and the exposition by occasion (samaya-niddesa). Just as this verse pertains to defilement and penetration, so the answer given by that verse is an answer pertaining to defilement and an answer pertaining to penetration. Thus, the discourse (sutta) is pointed out in all verses or in the expositions (veyyākaraṇa).

Among those [sixteen modes], what is the Mode of Conveying Teaching (Desanā-hāra)? With what intention was this discourse taught? The intention of the Blessed One in this discourse is that beings of lustful temperament will abandon sensual desires.

Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying Investigation (Vicaya-hāra)? For whom the defilements with ten bases have been crossed over, vomited out, and understood. What are the ten kinds? They are: the defilement of sensual desires (kilesa-kāma), the lower fetters and the higher fetters [totaling ten], and the ten-based sense bases (āyatana). This is the Mode of Conveying Investigation.

Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying Construing (Yutti-hāra)? There is this logical reasoning: those who are intensely infatuated are bound by a strong bond.

Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying Proximate Cause (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra)? Intense infatuation with jeweled earrings is the proximate cause for the sense of 'mine' (mamaṅkāra). Concern (apekhā) is the proximate cause for being with lust for past objects. "Having cut that [craving] also" is the proximate cause for mental development (bhāvanā).

Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying Characteristic (Lakkhaṇa-hāra)? One whose mind is intensely infatuated with jeweled earrings clings to the sense of 'I' (ahaṅkāra) and clings to the sense of 'mine' (mamaṅkāra). There is also intense infatuation with sons and wives, and intense infatuation with fields and lands. This is the Mode of Conveying Characteristic.

Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying a Fourfold Array (Catubyūha-hāra)? What is the Blessed One's intention in this discourse? The intention of the Blessed One in this discourse is that those who desire Nibbāna will abandon craving for sons and wives. These are the Four Truths.

Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying a Reversal (Āvaṭṭa-hāra)? Craving for sons and wives is the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca). The grasping of the aggregates of clinging and the grasping of forms in external forms is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca).
310:
In the cause of that suffering, whatever cutting there is, this cutting is called the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha-sacca). By whichever path-factor the defilements are destroyed, this destruction of defilements is called the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca). Regarding 'Vibhatti', there is no ground for Vibhatti; regarding 'Parivattana-hāra', the opposite is shown.

Among those Hāras, what is Vevacana-hāra? Synonymous terms are shown. Among those Hāras, what is Otaraṇa-hāra? There is craving; because of that craving as a cause, consciousness crosses over until aging and death. In that round of suffering, whatever feeling (vedanā) there is, this feeling is called ignorance (avijjā). Because of the arising of knowledge (vijjā), ignorance ceases, and it ceases until aging and death.

Among those Hāras, what is Sodhana-hāra? The exertion in the verse is pure. Among those Hāras, what is Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra? In the verse 'Na taṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhီrā', the four types of lust (rāga) are made known by way of unity, not by way of diversity. The four types of lust called sensual lust (kāmarāga), lust for form (rūparāga), lust for existence (bhavarāga), and lust for views (diṭṭhirāga) are made known by way of unity.

Among those Hāras, what is Parikkhāra-hāra? For those who wear jeweled earrings, the lust (rāga) for wives and children, and the perception of beauty (subha-saññā) of that person, are called the generative cause (janaka-hetu). Grasping the signs of female and male and the major and minor limbs that produce defilements is called the supportive cause (upanissaya-paccaya). By whatever nature those defilements are cut, for that person, the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) is called the generative cause. Dispelling the grasping of the signs of female, etc., and the grasping of the major and minor limbs that produce defilements is called the supportive cause.

Among those Hāras, what is Samāropana-hāra? Intense lust, delusion, diversity, and malice toward the person wearing jeweled earrings—having cut these, they practice. Therefore, to fully understand and avoid such lust, etc., they are abandoned; this is called Samāropana-hāra.

Whatever action is done by the mind, for whatever reason it is intended; by way of elaboration, it is called a supportive cause. There is bodily action born of the mind, and whatever action is born of the mind. Why? Because it occurs depending on the mind, intention (cetanā) is called mental action (manokamma); that intention is called kamma. Whatever action is done by the mind, this action done by the mind is called both physical (kāyika) and vocal (vācasika). These three types of kamma are shown. Bodily action and vocal action are also called wholesome (kusala). Because one exerts and misapprehends through body and speech, this misapprehension is called 'clinging to rites and rituals' (sīlabbataparāmāsa). There are these three intended formations (saṅkhāra): those consisting of merit (puññamaya), those consisting of demerit (apuññamaya), and those consisting of imperturbability (āneñjamaya). Because of those formations as a cause, consciousness arises; that object exists for the establishment of consciousness. Whatever perception of beauty (subha-saññā), perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā), and perception of self (atta-saññā) there are, these perceptions are born of the mind. Whatever consciousness exists depending on form, whatever form-object exists depending on the great elements, being delighted by craving, it reaches growth, increase, and abundance. This is called 'intending' (saṅkappanā). Thus, whatever...
311:
The first arising that is established in the stations of consciousness (viññāṇa-ṭṭhiti) is called clinging (upādāna) by way of the object; this clinging is called 'mental' (cetasika).

For the formless states (arūpa-dhamma) established in those stations of consciousness, whatever lust and deep-seated attachment there is, all this is called 'agitation'. Whatever attention (ābhoga) there is toward pleasant forms, toward dear and agreeable forms, this attention is called 'mental' (cetasika). Because of whatever reason the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha) incites toward agreeable beings, and the bodily tie of ill-will (byāpāda-kāyagantha) incites toward underlying tendencies of aversion (paṭighānusaya), all four ties (gantha) exist. This is the initial falling of the mind into the five strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguna), which is the intention (cetanā) of the mind. For one who habitually contemplates the gratification in that object, many evil unwholesome states follow the mind. A person who is bound by the pursuit of lust is made to do as desired by those defilements of sensuality; this doing is called 'intending in sensualities' (pakappanā). In this way, all four floods (ogha) occur. Living in conjunction with those sensualities, being oppressed and deeply attached—this is intention (cetanā). For that person who is not yet free from lust and has reached a state of affection, it happens in such a way; because of the transformation and change in that [object], sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise for him. Consciousness occurs following suffering. For one who has mindfulness, the arising of the nature of decay takes possession of the mind; this is called 'that which is intended' (pakappita).

One incites and intends toward each and every object; whatever establishment of consciousness occurs, that establishment is of two kinds: establishment in an object (ārammaṇa-ṭṭhiti) and establishment in nutriment (āhāra-ṭṭhiti). Among those two, whatever establishment in an object there is, this is the cause of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Whatever establishment in nutriment there is, which has the nature of arising in a new existence, and whatever establishment is called 'leading to renewed existence' (ponobbhavika), this establishment is called 'object'. That object occurs because of the establishment of consciousness. Because of consciousness as a cause, that person incites name-and-form until aging and death. Furthermore, because of whatever reason, one aspires for the non-arising of a new existence in a future basis; this opposite is shown. If one destroys without inciting or aspiring, there are two kinds of indications. For him, previously, that mental state and that intended state were not eradicated because of that cause; this is the establishment of consciousness.

Alternatively, the underlying tendencies (anusaya) become manifest for him; because of those underlying tendencies as a cause, arising in a new existence occurs for him. Alternatively, even if he is put into a house, he is blamed; whether he is subtle or peaceful, he is not blamed in sensualities. In this way, he is born in stable houses. He brings about the welfare of that house, not for the sake of intending the welfare of [another] house. In this way, the formations (saṅkhāra) being incited and intended...
312:
Volitional formations that are intended and planned become objects and arise. Whatever there is of volition, whatever of planning, and whatever object has arisen, both of these are called objects for consciousness. Likewise, beings who come into existence through volition, planning, and longing, both intend and plan. In whatever seeking, one neither intends nor plans.

What are the beings called bhūta? Those born within a thin shell, those staying in a membrane and hatching accordingly, and those born depending on moisture but not yet broken through, these are called bhūta. What are the sambhavesino (those seeking birth)? There are beings staying in the womb, beings staying in the egg, and those wandering. These do not intend, do not long for, and do not plan. Only because of the underlying tendency (anusaya) does the arising in a new existence occur again. Whatever beings are bhūta and whatever are sambhavesino, those beings are called thāvara (stable). Or, those who, being mindful, intend and long for, they are called thāvara. They neither intend, nor long for, nor plan, but wander only through the underlying tendency.

Another way: There are noble persons who are trainees (sekha); in that noble plane, those trainees neither intend nor plan, but arise again through the underlying tendency.

Another way: There are subtle beings staying on land or in water that cannot be seen with the eye. They neither intend nor plan, but wander only through the underlying tendency.

Another way: There are all those monks outside the Dispensation who are very conceited. They neither intend nor long for, but wander only through the underlying tendency. They neither intend, nor plan, nor does [the tendency] lie latent. That object also does not serve for the stationing of consciousness.

By the words "does not intend," the total eradication of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) is shown. By the words "does not lie latent," the total eradication of the underlying tendency (anusaya) is shown. By the words "does not intend," the abandonment of gross defilements is shown. By the words "does not lie latent," the abandonment of subtle defilements is shown. By the words "does not intend," the plane of vision (dassana-bhūmi) is shown. By the words "does not long for," the Once-returner and Non-returner are shown. By the words "does not lie latent," the Arahant is shown. By the words "does not intend," the abandonment of the opposite of virtue (sīla) is shown. By the words "does not long for," the abandonment of the opposite of concentration (samādhi) is shown. By the words "does not lie latent," the abandonment of the opposite of wisdom (paññā) is shown. By the words "does not intend," the abandonment of unwholesome formations (akusala-saṅkhāra) is shown. By the words "does not long for," the abandonment of wholesome formations (kusala-saṅkhāra) is shown. By the words "does not lie latent," the abandonment of imperturbable formations (āneñja-saṅkhāra) is shown. By the words "does not intend," the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) is shown. By the words "does not long for," the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) is shown. By the words "does not lie latent," the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) is shown. By the words "does not intend," the development of the soft faculties is shown.
313:
Longing is the medium development of the faculties, and the absence of lying latent is the superior development of the faculties. This is the meaning of the Sutta.

Among those modes (hāra), what is the Mode of Conveying a Teaching (desanā-hāra)? In this Sutta, the Four Noble Truths are taught. If there is intention and planning, the mind is established in that object and investigates and associates with it. Even if it is said "does not intend, does not long for," in the underlying tendency, the object is investigated and associated with as consciousness. Due to the abandonment of the underlying tendency, they no longer seek a station for consciousness, and it is associated with investigation. This is the Investigation of Logic (yutti-vicaya).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Proximate Cause (padaṭṭhāna-hāra)? Volition is obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), and volition is the proximate cause of obsession. Planning is the proximate cause of clinging (upādāna). The underlying tendency is the proximate cause of obsession. The development for the destruction of their desire and lust is the abandonment of lust for existence (bhava-rāga).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Characteristic (lakkhaṇa-hāra)? Among feeling, planning, grasping with the view of eternalism, and cognizing, which are called mental factors (cetasika), that consciousness is both an object and a condition (paccaya).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Fourfold Array (catubyūha-hāra)? What is the Blessed One's intention in this Sutta? The intention is that those who do not desire further rebirth will no longer intend or long for it.

The Mode of Conveying a Reversal (āvaṭṭa-hāra) consists of volition, longing, the underlying tendency, and the abandonment of the station of consciousness; these are two truths. There is no scope for the Mode of Conveying an Analysis (vibhatti-hāra) here. The Mode of Conveying a Reversal (parivattanā-hāra) is the opposite Sutta itself.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (vevacana-hāra)? Volition ranges from volition regarding forms (rūpa-sañcetanā) to volition regarding mental phenomena (dhamma-sañcetanā). The underlying tendencies are the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya).

The Mode of Conveying a Designation (paññatti-hāra) makes volition known in the designation of obsession. Planning is made known in the designation of clinging. The underlying tendency is made known in the designation of cause (hetu). The station of consciousness is made known in the designation of the cause of rebirth. Volition, planning, the underlying tendency, and total eradication are made known in the designation of the discipline of desire and lust. For some initial ones, through the two cycles, dependent origination is the middle designation of "this being the condition for that" (idappaccayatā).
314:
The Mode of Entry (Otaraṇa-hāra) means the entry into the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origin by means of the two rotations (parivatta), and into the Truth of the Path and the Truth of Cessation by means of the middle way (majjhima-paṭipadā). The Mode of Clearing (Sodhana-hāra) is the beginning (ārambha) of a Sutta within a Sutta.

The Mode of Terms of Expression (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra) means that all that is intended (cetayita) is designated as a unity through determination (adhiṭṭhāna). 'Conceived' (saṅkappita) is designated as a unity in clinging (upādāna). Consciousness (viññāṇa) is designated as a unity.

The Mode of Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra) means that a beautiful object, unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), and volition (cetanā) are causes by way of root-condition (hetu-paccaya). The state which is the standing-place of consciousness is a cause by way of object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). His attention is a cause by way of root-condition.

Among these, what is the Mode of Projection (Samāropana-hāra)? This Sutta should be noted; it is indicated in that Sutta by the answer 'he intends' (ceteti). The arising from consciousness as condition for name-and-form up to aging-and-death through his view (diṭṭhi) is called this Mode of Projection. This object does not exist for the standing of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, there is cessation up to aging-and-death.

Among those Suttas, which are those partaking of defilement (saṅkilesabhāgiya), partaking of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), and partaking of the adept (asekkhabhāgiya)? It begins with 'This world is born of heat' up to 'Whatever recluses or brahmins speak of liberation from existence through existence.' 'This suffering arises dependent on the basis (upadhi)' is partaking of defilement. 'Those cravings are abandoned, he no longer delights in existence'—this refers to the monk who has broken the sequence of greed and is cooled (nibbuta), for whom there is no further rebirth without clinging; this is partaking of penetration. 'Such a one who has transcended all existences' is partaking of the adept.

In that Sutta, 'born of heat' (santāpajāta) means the heat born of lust, the heat born of hatred, and the heat born of delusion. It shows the standing-place (cause) of those beings. 'The world is born of heat' means there are three kinds of contact (phassa): contact felt as pleasant, contact felt as painful, and contact felt as neither-pleasant-nor-painful. Therein, contact felt as pleasant is the heat of lust; contact felt as painful is the heat of hatred; contact felt as neither-pleasant-nor-painful is the heat of delusion. This is as the Blessed One said in the first Valāhaka Sutta: 'Householder, those heats born of lust, hatred, and delusion by which one sleeps in suffering—those heats do not exist in me.'
315:
To speak of the disease as 'self' means that the person burning with those heats acquires the three kinds of perversion (vipallāsa): perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa), perversion of mind (citta-vipallāsa), and perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa). Among these three, perceiving the beautiful in what is foul is called perversion of perception. Thinking of the pleasant in what is painful is called perversion of mind. Holding the permanent in the impermanent, and the self in the non-self, is called perversion of view.

Just as there is perversion of mind, so too are perception and view. There are also three kinds of thought (vitakka): perversion of mind-thought, perversion of perception-thought, and perversion of view-thought. Among these three, the perversion of ignorance (avijjā-vipallāsa) has a domain and a plane of falling by taking an object; it is as one perceives, as one cognizes, as one both perceives and cognizes, and as one intends with endurance. By these four perversions, beings speak of the fourfold basis of selfhood—which is a disease-like round (vaṭṭa) and a boil-like round—as 'self'. Speaking of the disease as self is the Mode of Reversal (Āvaṭṭa-hāra). For whatever reason they imagine it, that suffering becomes otherwise. Though they imagine it as beautiful, it does not become so. Thus, imagining it as pleasant, permanent, and self, such a person desires a future existence which is otherwise than what is present. Therefore, it is called 'lust for existence' (bhava-rāga).

He delights only in existence. The five aggregates are indicated as 'that delighted existence is suffering.' Because of that delight, sorrow, lamentation, and pain will increase for him. To this extent, there is the defilement of corruption (saṅkilesa). Indeed, the holy life (brahmacariya) is lived for the sake of abandoning that. It is the discipline of desire and lust (chandarāga-vinaya) for the three heats.

'This suffering arises dependent on the basis (upadhi)'—for those who delight only in existence, that path will be developed; by developing that path, the Buddha taught the abandonment of the suffering of the round. He taught according to the clinging (upādāna) shown as the four perversions: 'When there is no clinging of any kind, there is no arising of suffering.' Among those perversions, the first is clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna), the second is clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), the third is clinging to rules and rituals (sīlabbatupādāna), and the fourth is clinging to a doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). The exhaustion of these clingings means there is no arising of suffering. He spoke of the cessation of suffering which has the basis (upadhi) as its source. Thus, for one who sees this as it really is with right wisdom, craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā) does not occur. By not delighting in non-existence, the plane of vision (dassana-bhūmi) is indicated. He spoke of the two kinds of liberation—the fading of lust (rāga-virāga) and the fading of ignorance (avijjā-virāga)—as Nibbāna, the total exhaustion of craving. 'For that monk' refers to the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). This is the explanation of the meaning of the Sutta.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Investigation (Vicaya-hāra)? For whomsoever there is burning with the fires of lust in whatever round of suffering, for that person who is so burning, there is no weariness (nibbidā) with that thing as it really is. This is the Mode of Investigation and the Mode of Construing (Yutti-hāra).
316:
Burning caused by greed is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) and the faculty of displeasure (domanassindriya). Burning caused by hatred is the proximate cause of the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of displeasure. Burning caused by delusion is the proximate cause of the faculty of equanimity (upekkhindriya) and the faculty of displeasure.

Among those modes (hāras), what is the Lakkhaṇa Hāra? One who is oppressed by contact, oppressed by feeling, oppressed by perception, or oppressed by formations, for whatever reason, cannot reflect; if they perceive the unattractive as attractive through the sign of beauty (subha-nimitta), the sign of happiness (sukha-nimitta), the sign of permanence (nicca-nimitta), or the sign of self (atta-nimitta), then when all is described as burning caused by greed, the four burnings are said to be described. One speaks of that which is caused by greed, hatred, delusion, and wrong view as 'greed' in terms of its individual essence (attato). All fifteen terms are impermanent (anicca) and suffering (dukkha).

Among those modes, what is the Catubyūha Hāra? What is the Blessed One's intention in this Sutta? Those who do not dwell with burning do not delight in existence (bhava). Those who do not delight in existence will attain Parinibbāna. This is the intention.

Among those modes, what is the Āvaṭṭa Hāra? Through things partaking in defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), it points out suffering (dukkha) and origin (samudaya). Through things partaking in penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), it points out the path (magga) and cessation (nirodha).

Among those modes, what is the Vibhatti Hāra? The burning that has arisen is caused by disease; one speaks of disease as self (attato). That disease does not exist in an absolute sense; only the burning arisen from lack of attention (amanasikāra) does not speak of disease as self.

Among those modes, what is the Parivattana Hāra? It is the ground (bhūmi) for reversal in order to show the opposite side.

Among those modes, what is the Vevacana Hāra? One speaks of disease as self; one speaks of the dart (salla) as self. All fifteen terms should be stated.

Among those modes, what is the Paññatti Hāra? 'Arisen from fever' (santāpajāta) is the proximate cause of displeasure. All are made known by the designation of terms (vacana-paññatti). The perversion (vipallāsa) of speaking of disease as self is made known by the designation of defilement (saṃkilesa-paññatti). That which is not delighted in is prescribed as suffering through the designation of the abandonment of perversion (vipallāsa-nikkhepa-paññatti). Those beings of the world who are attached are prescribed by the state of diversity (vemattatā) in the midst.

Among those modes, what is the Otaraṇa Hāra? 'Arisen from fever' refers to the three unwholesome roots (akusalamūla); those unwholesome roots are called formations (saṅkhāra) and are included in the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Among the elements (dhātu), it is the element of mental objects (dhamma-dhātu); among the bases (āyatana), it is the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana). Among the faculties (indriya), the femininity faculty (itthindriya) and the masculinity faculty (purisindriya) are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).
317:
Among those modes, what is the Sodhana Hāra? The beginning of the Sutta is the cleansing itself.

Among those modes, what is the Adhiṭṭhāna Hāra? 'Burning' (pariḷāha) refers to the beings in the world who are designated by a single designation, who are the attached worldlings designated by the state of diversity (vemattatā) in the midst.

Among those modes, what is the Parikkhāra Hāra? 'Arisen from fever' (santāpajāta) has unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) as the root cause (hetu) and perversion (vipallāsa) as the condition (paccaya). In that teaching, due to the wrong attention to mind (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) as self, it causes one to obtain both types of things. In another way, it is the removal of the perception of self (atta-saññā) and the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā) through mental factors. In another way, although it is the removal of the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) in mental factors, it is the inability to remove the perception of self. This is what is called mind (citta), or intellect (mano), or consciousness (viññāṇa). This suffering has arisen intensely for a long time as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' In that teaching, the continuous contemplation of mental factors is also the perception of phenomena (dhamma-saññā). What is the cause and what is the support for that perception of phenomena? I-making (ahaṃkāra) is the cause, and my-making (mamaṃkāra) is the support.

Among those modes, what is the Samāropana Hāra? To perceive that 'this world is arisen from fever' is to think unwholesome thoughts. The process from consciousness being the condition for name-and-form up to aging and death is the Samāropana Hāra.

Thus, one sees this matter as it really is with right wisdom, seeing the abandonment of the unwholesome roots. In that Sutta, the cessation of aging and death due to the cessation of ignorance (avijjā) is the Samāropana Hāra.

There are four types of persons: the one who goes with the stream (anusotagāmī), the one who goes against the stream (paṭisotagāmī), the one who is steady (ṭhitatto), and the Brāhmaṇa (Arahant) who has crossed over to the other shore of Nibbāna and stands on the dry land.

Among those four, the person who goes with the stream is one who indulges in sensual pleasures and performs evil deeds. As long as they indulge in sensual pleasures, the unwholesome root of greed (lobha) exists. That greed itself is craving (taṇhā), and because they are carried away by those sensual pleasures, they are called 'one who goes with the stream.' The person who is led by those cravings and, because of that reason, performs unwholesome deeds through body and speech is called 'one who performs evil deeds.' For that person, there are three streams: personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), and clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa). By these three...
318:
Through the three types of streams, it arises in the three elements: the sense-sphere element, the fine-material element, and the immaterial element. By means of the opposite of that sensuality, one does not indulge in sensual pleasures; one does not wrongly misapprehend those with virtue; one sees the danger in sensual pleasures as it really is in order to abandon the views of self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). By whatever quality one indulges in those qualities, and because of that indulgence, one who stands in the fruit of Arahantship is called a Brahmin (one who has put away evil); he is indeed an Arahant (Arahaṃ) worthy of special offerings. In that teaching, he who has reached the further shore of Nibbāna is an Arahant. That Arahant who has reached the further shore stands on the dry land of the Nibbāna element with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

'Anusotagāminī' (going with the stream) means the non-abandoning of the fetters (saṃyojana) that are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry. 'Paṭisotagāminī' (going against the stream) means the abandoning of the defilements (kilesa) that are of the same class as wrong view in the fruit. 'Ṭhitatta' (one of stable nature) means the abandoning of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) that lead to the lower sense-sphere element. In this sutta, by 'one who goes with the stream' (anusotagāmī), the nature of the path is spoken of. By 'one who goes against the stream' (paṭisotagāmī) and 'one of stable nature' (ṭhitatta), the stability in the path is spoken of. By 'one who has reached the further shore' (pāraṅgata), the disciples who are beyond training (asekha) and the Fully Enlightened Buddhas (Sammāsambuddha) are meant. By 'one who goes with the stream', the practice leading to the arising of self-identity is spoken of. By 'one who goes against the stream' and 'one of stable nature', the practice leading to the cessation of self-identity is spoken of. By 'one who has reached the further shore', the ten qualities of the Arahants who are beyond training are spoken of. This is the meaning of the sutta.

## Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Teaching (Desanā-hāra)?
In this sutta, the Four Noble Truths and the transcendence of the triple world are taught.

## Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying an Investigation (Vicaya-hāra)?
The investigation that 'if one indulges in sensual pleasures, one would commit evil,' and 'if one does not indulge in sensual pleasures, one would not commit evil,' and 'having crossed over these two stages, one has reached the further shore,' is called the Mode of Conveying an Investigation.

The Mode of Conveying a Construing (Yutti-hāra) is the investigation into whether it is consistent or inconsistent with the suttas. The Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra) speaks of the proximate cause of the seven fetters by 'one who goes with the stream.' The performance of unwholesome actions is the proximate cause of the unwholesome roots. By 'one who goes against the stream,' the proximate cause of seeing things as they really are is spoken of. By 'one of stable nature,' the proximate cause of being unleadable (asanhāriya) is spoken of. By 'one who has reached the further shore,' the proximate cause of a certain stage is spoken of.

## Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇa-hāra)?
One who goes with the stream (anusota) by the power of craving is said to go by the power of all defilements. One who strives against the stream (paṭisota) against craving is said to strive against the stream of all defilements.
319:
He who stands by himself (in that Dhamma), he stands by way of body, and he stands by way of speech and mind. This is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇa-hāra).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Fourfold Array (Catubyūha-hāra)? What is the Blessed One's intention in this sutta? 'Those who do not delight in the practice of going with the stream (the state of a blind worldling) will strive against the stream (the state of a virtuous worldling)'—up to reaching a certain stage; this is the intention. As for 'Circulation' (āvaṭṭa), four suttas are taught in this context.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Classification (Vibhatti-hāra)? In saying 'one who indulges in sensual pleasures and commits evil actions is one who goes with the stream,' it is not the case that a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) also indulges in sensual pleasures; he also performs evil actions that are part of a stream-enterer's lot. Even if a trainee (sekha) should commit an evil act as indicated in the sutta, he is not 'one who goes with the stream'; this is a point to be answered by classification. If one neither indulges in sensual pleasures nor performs evil actions, one is 'one who goes against the stream.' In fact, not all people are free from lust for external sensual objects; though they do not indulge in sensual pleasures, they commit evil actions because of them, being both 'one who goes with the stream' and 'one who goes against the stream'; this is the classification (vibhatti).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Reversal (Parivattana-hāra)? The opposite side is shown. 'Synonyms' (vevacana) refers to, among sensual pleasures, both sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) and sensual defilements (kilesa-kāma), as well as the acquisition of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, children, wives, slaves, workers, and men.

'Designation' (paññatti) means all worldlings are designated by their common state. 'One who goes with the stream' is designated by the designation of the habitual practice of defilements. Those who are trainees (sekha) are designated by the designation of Nibbāna (or the designation of the goal). Those who are non-returners (anāgāmī) are designated by the designation of being unleadable (asanhāriya). This is Designation.

'Descent' (otaraṇa) means: he who is 'one who goes with the stream' is suffering (dukkha). Whatever qualities he has are the origin of suffering (samudaya). Whatever form there is, this is the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). Thus, the five aggregates and dependent origination are present. Those defilements are included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) and are designated in the mind-base (dhammāyatana), the mind-element (dhammadhātu), and the faculties (indriya).

'Clearing' (sodhana) means purification. The initiative with which this sutta was taught, that entire initiative is pure.
320:
The Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra (Mode of Conveying a Formulation) is as follows: by means of the "one who goes against the current" (paṭisotagāmī), all Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) are shown in a collective manner. For a "one who goes against the current" who has the underlying tendency of lust (rāgānusaya), both the Truth of the Path and the person as a trainee (sekha) are established only as a trainee. An Arahant is made known in a collective manner. "One who has gone to the beyond" (pārangata) means that all Arahants, all Paccekabuddhas, and the Fully Enlightened Buddhas are made known in a collective manner.

The Parikkhāra-hāra (Mode of Conveying Requisites) is as follows: for the "one who goes with the current" (anusotagāmī), a bad friend is the support; the outburst of sensual desire (kāma-pariyuṭṭhāna) is the productive cause (janaka-hetu). For the "one who goes against the current", there are two productive causes and two supporting causes (upanissaya). Up until reaching Right View, there is the view that arises by clinging. His attained path is the productive cause; effort and the mental factors associated with the body are the supporting causes. The Samāropana-hāra (Mode of Conveying a Combined Treatment) is the analysis of this Sutta; in this Sutta, there is no ground for Samāropana.

The five benefits for those who have states that follow the stream (sotānugata) and who have well-penetrated views are to be elaborated up to the Sutta. A person who strives, exerts, and makes an effort—whether ill or at the time of death—becomes a deva and reaches the state of a Paccekabuddha. "Follower of the stream" (sotānugata) means one has practiced good conduct by hearing the True Dhamma. His mind is not terrified by the insight into the Dhamma of higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā), nor is it unable to penetrate. This Sutta is taught to five types of persons: the Saddhānusārī (follower by faith) with dull faculties and with sharp faculties, and the Dhammānusārī (follower by Dhamma) with sharp faculties and with dull faculties. Although a person of delusional temperament (moha-carita) is unable to strive, exert, or make an effort according to reality, when he is liberated through concentration, it shows the fruit in that moment, that instant, that second. Even if he declines well, another destroys that unwholesome state; it is not that there is no result of happiness. For him, it occurs in this very life (diṭṭhadhamma), as well as in kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajja-vedanīya) and in subsequent lives (aparāpariya-vedanီya).

In that Sutta, for a Dhammānusārī person with superior wisdom, if there are states that follow the stream, he reaches [attainment] while striving. A Dhammānusārī person with superior wisdom but dull faculties reaches it when ill. A Saddhānusārī person with superior faith and sharp faculties reaches it at the time of death. A person with dull faculties reaches it when he has become a deva. If he has not yet reached it when becoming a deva, he reaches the state of a Paccekabuddha through that lust for the Dhamma and delight in the Dhamma. One who strives, exerts, and makes an effort in the states that follow the stream knows the distinction through prior attainment; upon knowing, he reaches it. If a sick person has wise attention (manasikāra), he reaches it by striving at that time of illness. If he experiences terror at the time of death...
321:
...he attains by striving at that time of death. If a sense of urgency (saṃvega) does not occur at any time, while living happily as a deity, words connected to the Dhamma arise without lamentation. That young deity realizes: 'This is the Dhamma-Vinaya where we formerly lived the holy life as humans.' Then, while being a deity, he attains. Or, if he is obsessed with the five cords of divine sensual pleasure and lives heedlessly, he attains the enlightenment of a Private Buddha (paccekabodhi) due to that root of merit (kusalamūla).

Wisdom known through the voice of another or through speech well-practiced is 'wisdom consisting in what is heard' (sutamayī paññā). Those teachings which are reflected upon and examined by the mind are 'wisdom consisting in thought' (cintāmayī paññā). That which is well-penetrated by view (wisdom) is 'wisdom consisting in development' (bhāvanāmayī paññā). Those for whom the teachings follow the ear and are practiced by speech, if they attain Parinibbāna in this very life, they are Arahants. One who arises as a deity, attains there, and attains Parinibbāna there is a Non-returner (anāgāmī). One who attains the enlightenment of a Private Buddha due to that root of merit is a person arisen from the accumulation of prior application (pubbayoga-sambhāra).

'Teachings following the ear' (sotānugatā dhammā) is the first base of liberation (vimuttāyatana). 'Practiced by speech' is the second and third bases of liberation. 'Reflected upon by the mind' is the fourth base of liberation. 'Well-penetrated by view' is the fifth base of liberation.

In the liberation following the ear, speech well-penetrated by speech, having heard the sequential Dhamma with the ear, fulfills the category of virtue (sīlakkhandha). Reflection by the mind fulfills the category of concentration (samādhikkhandha). Well-penetrating by view (wisdom) fulfills the category of wisdom (paññākkhandha).

'Teachings following the ear are of great learning' should be elaborated. This is the first ground of faith (saddhāpadāna). 'Reflected upon by the mind' means living with much seclusion (paṭisallāna); this should be elaborated. This is the second ground of faith. 'Well-penetrated by view' means staying in the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) free from taints (anāsava) and knowing 'there is no more for this state of being.' This is the third ground of faith.

By the words 'teachings following the ear,' the Teacher shows the trainee (sekkha). By the words 'reflected upon by the mind,' the Teacher shows Arahantship. By the words 'well-penetrated by view,' the Teacher shows the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened Buddha.
322:
By the words "teachings followed by the ear" (sotānugatā dhammā), the escape from sensual desires (kāma) is shown. By the words "examined by the mind" (manasā anupekkhitā), the escape from the form element (rūpadhātu) is shown. By the words "well-penetrated by view" (diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā), the escape from the three realms (tedhātuka) is shown. This is the meaning of the sutta.

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Teaching (desanā-hāra)? In this sutta, three types of seeking (esanā) are taught. Through teachings followed by the ear and mastered by speech, there is the path of serenity (samatha-magga) for the seeking of sensual desires. Through teachings well-penetrated by view, there is the path of serenity for the seeking of the holy life.

The Mode of Investigation (vicaya-hāra) is as follows: One who investigates while attending to the sutta as it was heard attains wisdom based on hearing (sutamaya-paññā). As he attends to it, because of those teachings heard, he then attains wisdom based on reflection (cintāmaya-paññā). As he attends to it in the present state of the self, he then attains wisdom based on mental development (bhāvanāmaya-paññā). This is the Mode of Investigation.

Through hearing, one attains wisdom based on hearing. Through reflection, wisdom based on reflection; through mental development, wisdom based on mental development. Such is the logical reasoning (yutti).

The Mode of Proximate Cause (padaṭṭhāna-hāra) is as follows: "Teachings followed by the ear" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for hearing the Dhamma. "Mastered by speech" is the proximate cause for application (exertion). "Examined by the mind" is the proximate cause for insight (vipassanā) in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma. "Examined by view" means repeated examination by both wisdom and view (diṭṭhi).

The Mode of Analysis (catubyūha-hāra) is as follows: What is the Blessed One's intention in this sutta? Those who are endowed with these two types of wisdom, by them...

By the words "He is extinguished" (sa nibbuto), He speaks of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala) and the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). By giving (dāna), He speaks of the abandoning of coarse defilements. By virtue (sīla), He speaks of the abandoning of medium defilements, and by wisdom (paññā), the abandoning of subtle defilements. By the words "He is extinguished due to the destruction of lust, hate, and delusion," the planes (of the worldling, trainee, and non-trainee) are established.

Merit increases for one who gives;
Enmity is not accumulated for one who is restrained;
The skilled one abandons evil—
This refers to the Path.

He is extinguished due to the destruction of lust, hate, and delusion—
This refers to the Path and Fruit.
323:
By these three phrases—"Merit increases for one who gives; for one who is restrained (enmity does not increase)"—the mundane wholesome roots are stated. By the phrase "He is extinguished due to the destruction of lust, hate, and delusion," the supramundane wholesome roots are stated.

By the phrase "Merit increases for one who gives; enmity is not accumulated for one who is restrained," the plane of the worldling (puthujjana-bhūmi) is indicated. By the phrase "The skilled one abandons evil," the plane of the trainee (sekha-bhūmi) is indicated. By the phrase "He is extinguished due to the destruction of lust, hate, and delusion," the plane of the non-trainee (asekha-bhūmi) is stated.

By the phrase "Merit increases for one who gives; enmity is not accumulated for one who is restrained," the practice leading to the Path is stated. By the phrase "The skilled one abandons evil," the liberation of the trainee (sekha-vimutti) is stated. By the phrase "He is extinguished due to the destruction of lust, hate, and delusion," the liberation of the non-trainee (asekha-vimutti) is stated.

By the phrase "Merit increases for one who gives; enmity is not accumulated for one who is restrained," the teaching of mundane qualities such as the talk on giving (dāna-kathā), the talk on virtue (sīla-kathā), and the talk on the path (magga-kathā) is stated. By the phrase "The skilled one abandons evil," the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā) in the world is stated. By the phrase "He is extinguished due to the destruction of lust, hate, and delusion," penetration through the Dhamma teaching special to the Buddhas (sāmukkaṃsikā dhammadesanā) is also stated.

By the phrase "Merit increases for one who gives," one gives fearlessness to beings by refraining from taking life through the gift of fearlessness (abhaya-dāna). In this way, all training rules are to be practiced. By the phrase "Enmity is not accumulated for one who is restrained," one restrains the mind by being established in virtue; for such a restrained person, the fulfillment (of Path and Fruit) is reached. By the phrase "He is extinguished due to the destruction of lust, hate, and delusion," the two types of liberation (vimutti) are stated. This is called the Exposition of the Sutta (sutta-niddesa).

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Teaching (desanā-hāra)? What is taught in this sutta? The two happy destinations—the deva realm and the human realm—are taught, as well as the five cords of sensual pleasure pertaining to devas and those pertaining to humans. The exposition is by way of two phrases. By the phrases "Merit increases for one who gives; enmity is not accumulated for one who is restrained; the skilled one abandons evil," the Path is stated. By the phrase "He is extinguished due to the destruction of lust, hate, and delusion," the two Nibbāna elements—the Nibbāna element with residue (sopādisesa-nibbānadhātu) and the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu)—are taught. This is the Mode of Conveying a Teaching.

The Mode of Investigation (vicaya-hāra) is as follows: By this first phrase, "Merit increases for one who gives," the ground of meritorious action consisting in giving (dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu) is stated. Therefore, for that person, the wholesome states that are immediate (are taught). By the second phrase... they (lead); it is the Dispensation (sāsana) that leads out of suffering—this is the intention. By not hearing, not attending, and not penetrating, the practice leading to the origin of self-identity (sakkāya-samudaya) is stated.
324:
Through hearing, wise attention, and penetration, the practice leading to the cessation of personality (sakkāya-nirodha) is taught. This is the Āvaṭṭa-hāra (Mode of Rotation).
