Vibhatti-hāra (Mode of Classification) is a matter to be answered categorically. In this mode, there is no ground for analytical division. Parivattana-hāra (Mode of Reversal) is the experiencing of the five existing benefits in this very life through their opposites. This occurrence is another method of the teaching.

Vevacana-hāra (Mode of Synonyms) refers to the Sutta seen, the wisdom faculty (paññindriya), the communication (viññatti), the thorough penetration through wisdom, and the manifestation within the phrase 'teachings followed by the ear' (sotānugatā dhammā).

Paññatti-hāra (Mode of Designation) is making known the teaching 'teachings followed by the ear' through the designation of ignorance (avijjā), wise attention through the designation of joy (pāmojja), and present phenomena through the designation of benefits.

Otaraṇa-hāra (Mode of Entry) consists of the three kinds of wisdom: wisdom based on learning (sutamayī-paññā) in teachings mastered by speech, wisdom based on reflection (cintāmayī-paññā) in teachings repeatedly contemplated by the mind, and wisdom based on development (bhāvanāmayī-paññā) in teachings thoroughly penetrated by wisdom. These teachings are the Noble Truths and the faculties (indriya). The arising of clear vision (vijjā) is the Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) which is the cessation of ignorance. Among the faculties, they are known as the three faculties; among the bases (āyatana), as the teachings included in the mind-base (dhammāyatana); and among the elements (dhātu), as the teachings included in the mind-element (dhammadhātu). Sodhana-hāra (Mode of Clearing) is the exertion and application to enter into the Sutta.

Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra (Mode of Terms of Expression) is the presentation of the five benefits in their distinctiveness. It presents the Noble usage (ariya-vohāra) in its distinctiveness as 'the benefits follow the ear.' However, it presents the hearing of the Dhamma in its unity.

Parikkhāra-hāra (Mode of Requisites): For hearing the Dhamma, association is the condition (paccaya) and faith (saddhā) is the root cause (hetu). For repeated contemplation by the mind, understanding the meaning is the condition and understanding the Dhamma is the root cause. For thorough penetration by wisdom, hearing the True Dhamma and wise attention are the conditions, while wisdom based on learning and wisdom based on reflection are the root causes. Samāropana-hāra (Mode of Coordination) is when the analyzed Sutta is another method of teaching and does not exist in the productive power. There is no ground for attribution in that Sutta.

Among those Suttas, what is the Sutta that partakes of habit (vāsanābhāgiya) and the Sutta that partakes of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya)? It is the verse beginning with 'Merit increases for the giver' (dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati). By the word 'for the giver' (dadato), the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving (dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu) is meant. By the phrase 'for the restrained, enmity is not accumulated' (saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyati), the basis of meritorious action consisting in virtue (sīlamaya-puññakiriyavatthu) is meant. By the phrase 'the skilled one abandons evil' (kusalo ca jahāti pāpakaṃ), the abandoning of greed (lobha), delusion (moha), and ill-will (byāpāda) is spoken of. By the phrase 'with the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished' (rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbuto), [the destruction of] greed and delusion...
325:
...and ill-will, as well as the discipline of desire and lust (chandarāga-vinaya), are spoken of. In the verse 'Merit increases for the giver' (dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati), non-greed (alobha) is the root of wholesome action. In 'For the restrained, enmity is not accumulated' (saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyati), non-hatred (adosa) is the root of wholesome action. For one who is restrained, enmity is not accumulated; thus, because of non-ill-will (abyāpāda), there is always no enmity and no adversary. In 'The skilled one abandons evil' (kusalo ca jahāti pāpakaṃ), the cessation of ignorance (aññāṇa) occurs due to the arising of knowledge (ñāṇa). By the fourth line, through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, there is liberation of mind (cetovimutti) through the fading away of lust, and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) through the fading away of ignorance due to the destruction of delusion. This is the Vicaya-hāra (Mode of Investigation).

Yutti-hāra (Mode of Construing): One who is established in giving fulfills both [benefits]. He abandons stinginess (macchariya) and merit (puñña) increases. This is the Yutti-hāra.

Padaṭṭhāna-hāra (Mode of Proximate Cause): 'Merit increases for the giver' is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the foundation of generosity (cāgādhiṭṭhāna). 'For the restrained, enmity is not accumulated' is the proximate cause for the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna). 'The skilled one abandons evil' is the proximate cause for the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna). 'With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished' is the proximate cause for the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna). This is the Padaṭṭhāna-hāra.

Among those modes, what is the Lakkhaṇa-hāra (Mode of Characteristics)? Merit increases for the giver; for the restrained, enmity is not accumulated. One should not act with enmity even toward a giver; thus, the wholesome also abandons the unwholesome. Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, that person is at peace. He is at peace through the destruction of form (rūpa) and through the destruction of feeling (vedanā). With whatever form [the Tathāgata] is seen, through the destruction, fading away, and cessation of that form, the Blessed One would designate [Nibbāna]; thus [it is designated] by way of the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā).

In the Catubyūha-hāra (Mode of Fourfold Array), what is the Blessed One's intention in this Sutta? Those who desire great wealth will give gifts to abandon obstacles. Those who desire freedom from enmity will abandon the five enmities. Those who desire the wholesome will develop the Eightfold Path to abandon the eight wrongnesses (micchatta). Those who desire to be extinguished will abandon lust, hatred, and delusion. This is the Blessed One's intention (Catubyūha-hāra).

Āvaṭṭa-hāra (Mode of Rotation): There is the stinginess of the non-giver, the enmity of the unrestrained, and the non-abandoning of evil unwholesome states. All this is the description of suffering (dukkhaniddesa), not the origin (samudaya). These three—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are the roots of wholesome action. The eight rightnesses (sammattā), which are the conditions for those wholesome roots, are the Truth of the Path (maggasacca). The destruction of that lust, hatred, and delusion is the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca).

Vibhatti-hāra (Mode of Classification): 'Merit increases for the giver' is not categorical. One who gives out of fear of royal punishment, or one who gives to the virtuous so they may enjoy what is unallowable—merit does not increase for him. Thus, he gives that gift with an unwholesome mind. Only the unwholesome (apuñña) called 'giving punishment' or 'giving weapons' increases; merit does not increase. 'For the restrained, enmity is not accumulated' is also not categorical...
327: From the front of his body, a golden-hued ray emerged and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the sky. From the back of his body, from his right hand, and from his left hand, golden-hued rays emerged, and from the soles of his feet, coral-colored rays emerged and occupied a space of eighty cubits on the thick earth. Thus, all around for about eighty cubits, the six-colored Buddha-rays shone, vibrated, and radiated. All directions appeared as if scattered with golden campaka flowers, as if poured with streams of liquid gold from a golden pot, as if wrapped in spread-out golden cloth, or as if covered with the pollen of Butea, Mahālekhā, and Kaṇikāra flowers carried by the Veramba wind. His body, brilliant with the eighty minor marks and a fathom-wide aura, and shining with the thirty-two excellent marks, was like the sky filled with stars, like a blooming lotus pond, or like a Pāricchattaka tree a hundred yojanas high in full bloom. He was perfectly peaceful, endowed with the thirty-two marks, shining like the light of thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, thirty-two universal monarchs, thirty-two king of gods, and thirty-two Great Brahmas. For the Arahant, there is no further peace to be attained. The Mode of Synonyms (Vivevacana-hāra): In the sentence 'merit increases for the giver,' it should be understood that merit also increases for one who rejoices, for one who directs the mind well, and for one who performs services. The Mode of Description (Paññatti-hāra): 'Merit increases for the giver' is made known by the description of destroying the basis of non-greed (alobha). 'Enmity is not accumulated by the restrained' is made known by the description of destroying the basis of non-hatred (adosa). 'The virtuous person abandons evil' is made known by the description of destroying the basis of non-delusion (amoha). The Mode of Entry (Otaraṇa-hāra): Among the five faculties, 'merit increases for the giver' and 'enmity is not accumulated by the restrained'—through restraint, the aggregate of virtue (sīla-kkhandha) is noted. Restraint (saṃvara) in the six faculties is called the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-kkhandha). That the virtuous person abandons evil is called the aggregate of wisdom (paññā-kkhandha). 'He is at peace due to the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion' is called the aggregate of liberation (vimutti-kkhandha). Among the elements, it enters the element of phenomena (dhamma-dhātu), and among the bases, the mind-base (manāyatana). The Mode of Cleansing (Sodhana-hāra): The reason for which this sutta was taught is pure. The Mode of Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra): Giving (dāna) is made known by way of unity. The eight kinds of giving, such as generosity (cāga), relinquishment (pariccāga), the gift of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna), and the gift of material things (āmisa-dāna), should be performed in detail; this is the aspect of diversity. It is not...
328:
For one who gives, it is made known by the designation of oneness (ekatta-paññatti). Patience is made known by the designation of faultlessness. "With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this is made known by the designation of effort in restraint.

As for the Mode of Equipment (Parikkhāra-hāra): the joy of giving is the decisive support condition (paccaya), and non-greed is the productive cause (hetu). The wise reflection of one who is restrained is the productive cause (hetu), and relinquishment is the decisive support condition (paccaya). In the statement "The wholesome abandons the evil," seeing things as they really are is the decisive support condition (paccaya), and the attainment of knowledge is the productive cause (hetu). In the statement "With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the speech of others (heard from another), wise reflection within oneself, and the Path are both the productive cause (hetu) and the decisive support condition (paccaya).

As for the Mode of Induction (Samāropana-hāra): in the verse "For one who gives, merit increases," virtue also increases for him, and restraint also increases. In the statement "For one who is restrained, enmity is not accumulated," other defilements are also not accumulated; those taints and distresses that would arise for him because of those defilements also do not arise. In the statement "With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," because of the destruction of lust and hatred, because of the destruction of the underlying tendency to lust, and because of the destruction of hatred and delusion, he is said to be extinguished; this refers to both the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu) and the Nibbāna element without residue remaining (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). This is the Mode of Induction.

## In the Peṭakopadesa of the Elder Mahākaccāyana,
## the Ground of Convergence (Sampātabhūmi) of the Modes is finished.
## 8. Suttavebhaṅgiya (Analysis of Suttas)

The prior end of ignorance (avijjā) and of craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) is not apparent. In that teaching, the prior end of beings who are hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving is not apparent. Among them, those beings who are fettered by craving are mostly given to indulging in the flavor of objects and are weak in insight (vipassanā). Those beings who have abundant views are mostly given to insight and are weak in indulging.

Among those, beings of craving-nature are obsessed with the perception of a 'being' and are accustomed to seeing things with wrong knowledge as having no arising or passing away. They regard the five aggregates as the self. They regard that "the self possesses form," or "form is in the self," or "the self is in form." Thus, they regard the five aggregates as the self through designations other than the aggregates. For those beings with abundant views, when they investigate, they regard the aggregates directly as the self. They regard form as the self. Whatever form there is, that is the self. Whatever 'I' am, that is form. He sees the destruction of form, and this is...
329:
...an annihilationist (ucchedavādī). Thus, the five types of identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) that first fall into views regarding the five aggregates resort to annihilationism, thinking 'the soul is the same as the body.' Regarding each aggregate, through the latter three modes, one resorts to eternalism (sassatavāda), thinking 'the soul is one thing, the body is another.' Recluses outside this Dispensation, being of craving-nature, dwell devoted to the pursuit of sensual happiness. As a consequence of that, some who are of view-nature dwell devoted to self-mortification. With that happiness associated with wrong view, such an effort is called an effort outside the Dispensation.

Among them, beings of view-nature who enter the Dhamma-Vinaya of the Noble Ones become Dhamma-followers (dhammānusārī). Beings of craving-nature who enter the Dhamma-Vinaya of the Noble Ones become Faith-followers (saddhānusārī).

Among them, beings of view-nature see the faults in sensual pleasures, yet without having yet uprooted the underlying tendencies (anusaya) inherent in sensual pleasures, they dwell devoted to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga). To them, either the Teacher or another disciple teaches the Dhamma, saying 'there is no benefit in sensual pleasures.' Since they had no desire for sensual pleasures even in previous lives, they can relinquish sensual pleasures without difficulty. They are not attached to objects through mental suffering. Therefore, it is called 'pleasant practice' (sukhā paṭipadā). Beings of craving-nature, however, are attached to sensual pleasures; to them, either the Teacher or another monk teaches the Dhamma, saying 'there is no benefit in sensual pleasures.' They relinquish the beloved objects with pain and difficulty. Therefore, it is called 'painful practice' (dukkha paṭipadā). Thus, all these beings converge into these two types of practice: the painful and the pleasant.

Among them, beings of view-nature are of two kinds: those with dull faculties and those with sharp faculties. Among them, beings of view-nature with sharp faculties can relinquish easily and also realize quickly; therefore, it is called 'pleasant practice with quick direct-knowledge' (khippābhiññā sukhā paṭipadā). Among them, beings of view-nature with dull faculties, depending on those with sharp faculties, realize more slowly; though they can relinquish easily, they realize slowly. Therefore, it is called 'pleasant practice with slow direct-knowledge' (sukhā paṭipadā dandhāဘိညာ). Among them, beings of craving-nature are of two kinds: those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties. Among them, beings of craving-nature with sharp faculties relinquish with pain and difficulty but realize quickly. Therefore, it is called 'painful practice with quick direct-knowledge' (dukkha paṭipadā khippābhiññā). Among them, beings of craving-nature with dull faculties, depending on those with sharp faculties, realize more slowly; they relinquish with pain and difficulty and also realize slowly. Therefore, it is called 'painful practice with slow direct-knowledge' (dukkha paṭipadā dandhāဘိညာ). These practices are only four; there is no fifth or sixth practice. Those who have become extinguished...
330:
Only by these four practices will they be extinguished (from defilements), and not by any other practices. In this way, the defilements are pointed out through the four practices. This entire method, which is to be pointed out in the noble qualities (ariya-dhamma) by way of the fourfold path, is called the method of the 'Lion's Play' (Sīhavikkīḷita).

In that context, there are the four nutriments, the four perversions, the four clingings, the four yokes, the four knots, the four taints, the four floods, the four darts, the four stations of consciousness, and the four wrong courses. Thus, there are these ten sets of terms. This is called the collation (saṃsandanā) of the Sutta.

There are four nutriments. Among those four, edible food and contact are to be abandoned by one of craving-temperament. Among those four, mental volition and consciousness are to be abandoned by one of view-temperament.

The first nutriment is called the first perversion; the second nutriment is called the second perversion; the third nutriment is called the third perversion; and the fourth nutriment is called the fourth perversion. These perversions are only four; there is no fifth or sixth. This much is the extent of the four nutriments.

Among those perversions, one who stands in the first perversion clings to sensual pleasures; this clinging is called clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna). One who stands in the second perversion clings to future existence; this clinging is called clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna). One who stands in the third perversion clings to wrong views in a distorted way; this clinging is called clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna). One who stands in the fourth perversion clings to the aggregates as a self; this clinging is called clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna).

Among those clingings, one who stands in clinging to sensual pleasures ties a knot by way of coveting sensual pleasures; this tying is called the bodily knot of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha). One who stands in clinging to rules and observances ties a knot of ill-will; this tying is called the bodily knot of ill-will (byāpāda-kāyagantha). One who stands in clinging to views ties a knot of misapprehension in a wrong way; this tying is called the bodily knot of misapprehension (parāmāsa-kāyagantha). One who stands in clinging to the doctrine of self ties a knot of the body that expands the cycle of rebirth; this tying is called the bodily knot of insistence that 'this is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha).

For that person, defilements flow out by way of these knots. Specifically, remorse (vippaṭisāra) is mentioned. Whatever remorses exist, those are called underlying tendencies (anusaya). Among those defilements, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) arises because of the bodily knot of covetousness; the taint of existence (bhavāsava) arises because of the bodily knot of ill-will; the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) arises because of the bodily knot of misapprehension; and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) arises because of the bodily knot of insistence that 'this is the truth'.
331:
When those four taints reach a state of abundance, they become floods; therefore, they are called 'floods' (ogha). Among those taints, the taint of sensual desire is the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha); the taint of existence is the flood of existence (bhavogha); the taint of ignorance is the flood of ignorance (avijjogha); and the taint of views is the flood of views (diṭṭhogha).

Those four floods are said to enter the dwelling place (anusaya) and occur together with the underlying tendencies. Darts (salla) are so called because they remain after striking the heart. In that context, the flood of sensual desire is the dart of lust (rāgasalla); the flood of existence is the dart of hatred (dosasalla); the flood of ignorance is the dart of delusion (mohasalla); and the flood of views is the dart of views (diṭṭhisalla).

Consciousness, being overwhelmed by these four darts, stands in four things: in form, in feeling, in perception, and in mental formations. These four are the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). Among those darts, consciousness that is poured over with delight by the dart of lust stands by approaching form. Consciousness that approaches feeling stands by the dart of hatred; consciousness that approaches perception stands by the dart of delusion; and consciousness that is poured over with delight by the dart of views stands by approaching mental formations.

Through the four stations of consciousness, they go to the four kinds of wrong courses (agati): desire, hatred, fear, and delusion. One goes to a wrong course through desire because of lust; one goes to a wrong course through hatred because of hatred; one goes to a wrong course through delusion because of delusion; and one goes to a wrong course through fear because of views. Thus, there is this karma and there are these defilements. This is the cause of the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra).

In that context, the things that are 'directions' (disā) are these four. Edible food, the perversion of 'the beautiful in the ugly', clinging to sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual desire, the bodily knot of covetousness, the taint of sensual desire, the flood of sensual desire, the dart of lust, the station of consciousness approaching form, and going to a wrong course through desire—all this is called the first direction (paṭhamā disā).

Contact as nutriment, the perversion of 'the pleasant in the painful', clinging to rules and observances, the yoke of existence, the bodily knot of ill-will, the taint of existence, the flood of existence, the dart of hatred, the station of consciousness approaching feeling, and going to a wrong course through hatred—all this is called the second direction (dutiyā disā).

Mental volition as nutriment, the perversion of 'self in the non-self', clinging to views, the yoke of views, the bodily knot of misapprehension, the taint of views, the flood of views, the dart of views, the station of consciousness approaching perception, and going to a wrong course through fear—all this is called the third direction (tatiyā disā).

Consciousness as nutriment, the perversion of 'the permanent in the impermanent', clinging to the doctrine of self, the yoke of ignorance, the bodily knot of insistence that 'this is the truth', the taint of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the dart of delusion, the station of consciousness approaching mental formations, and going to a wrong course through delusion...
332:
This is the fourth direction (disā). Thus, by the first word of these ten suttas, there is a viewing in the first direction. This viewing is called Disālokana (Viewing of the Directions). There is a viewing of the directions (disāvilokanā) in the unwholesome side by associating defilements through the four perversions (vipallāsa). This is the Disāvilokanā in the unwholesome side. What is the meaning of the first words among the five or ten suttas that are the basis of this Disāvilokanā? The meaning is one and the same; only the phrasing (byañjana) is different. The same applies to the second, third, and fourth. This is called the first collation (saṃsandanā).

By this method of abbreviation (peyyāla), all defilements should be included in the four words. Then, on the wholesome side, the four modes of progress (paṭipadā), the four jhanas, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four abidings (vihāra: divine, brahma, noble, imperturbable), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four wonderful and marvelous qualities (acchariya-abbhutadhamma), the four determinations (adhiṭṭhāna), and the four concentrations (samādhi: concentration of intention, energy, consciousness, and investigation) should be included. There is no happiness without the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), without austerity (tapa), without restraint of the faculties (indriya-saṃvara), and without total relinquishment (sabba-nissagga). Thus, there are four qualities that lead to happiness. There are also four immeasurables (appamāṇa).

Among those four, when the mode of progress that is painful with slow realization (dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā) is developed and frequently practiced, it fulfills the first jhana. When the first jhana is fulfilled, it fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness. When the first foundation of mindfulness is fulfilled, it fulfills the first abiding. When the first abiding is fulfilled, it fulfills the first right effort. When the first right effort is fulfilled, it fulfills the first wonderful and marvelous quality. When the first wonderful and marvelous quality is fulfilled, it fulfills the first determination. When the first determination is fulfilled, it fulfills the concentration of intention (chanda-samādhi). When the concentration of intention is fulfilled, it fulfills the restraint of the faculties. When the restraint of the faculties is fulfilled, it fulfills the first immeasurable of loving-kindness (mettā-appamāṇa). In this way, up to total relinquishment (sabba-nissagga), it fulfills the fourth immeasurable.

Among those qualities, there are the first mode of progress, the first jhana, the first foundation of mindfulness, the first abiding, the first right effort, the first wonderful and marvelous quality, the determination of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna), the concentration of intention, the restraint of the faculties, and the immeasurable of loving-kindness. This entire group is called the first direction (pathama-disā). The second mode of progress which is painful with quick realization (dukkhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā), the second jhana, the second foundation of mindfulness, the second abiding, the second right effort, the second wonderful and marvelous quality...
333:
...the wonderful quality, the determination of generosity (cāgādhiṭṭhāna), the concentration of consciousness (citta-samādhi), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), and the immeasurable of compassion (karuṇā-appamāṇa). This is the second direction (dutiya-disā).

The mode of progress that is pleasant with slow realization (sukhā-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā), the third jhana, the third foundation of mindfulness, the third abiding, the third right effort, the third wonderful quality, the determination of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna), the concentration of energy (viriya-samādhi), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the immeasurable of appreciative joy (muditā-appamāṇa). This is the third direction (tatiya-disā).

The mode of progress that is pleasant with quick realization (sukhā-paṭipadā khippābhiññā), the fourth jhana, the fourth foundation of mindfulness, the fourth abiding, the fourth right effort, the fourth wonderful quality, the determination of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna), the concentration of investigation (vīmaṃsā-samādhi), total relinquishment (sabba-nissagga), and the immeasurable of equanimity (upekkhā-appamāṇa). This is the fourth direction (catuttha-disā). The viewing of these four directions is called the Method of Viewing the Directions (Disālokana-naya).

The application (yojanā) in this method is as follows: the four nutriments (āhāra), the four modes of progress (paṭipadā), the four perversions (vipallāsa), the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four clingings (upādāna), the four jhanas, the four yokes (yoga) and abidings (vihāra), the ties (gantha) and right efforts (sammappadhāna), the taints (āsava) and wonderful qualities, the floods (ogha) and determinations (adhiṭṭhāna), the darts (salla) and concentrations (samādhi), the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), the four qualities leading to happiness, the four wrong courses (agatigamana), and the four immeasurables (appamāṇa). Thus, the application of wholesome and unwholesome states by way of opposites is called the Method of Viewing the Directions.

This method culminates in the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). In the exposition of wholesome and unwholesome states, the exposition of the first direction culminates in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). The second culminates in the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala), the third in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and the fourth in the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala).

Among those methods, what is the Tipukkhala method? There are two persons who emerge [from saṃsāra] through the painful mode of progress (dukkhā paṭipadā) with slow realization and quick realization, and there are two persons who emerge through the pleasant mode of progress (sukhā paṭipadā) with slow realization and quick realization.

Among these four persons, there is the person who emerges through the pleasant mode of progress with slow realization, and the person who emerges through the painful mode of progress with quick realization. These are the two persons. Among them, the one who [emerges] through the pleasant mode of progress with quick realization...
334:
He escapes from the round of rebirths; this person is called one of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū). There is the latter person who is common to the teaching; this person is called one who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū). The person who escapes from the round of rebirths through sluggish direct knowledge and painful practice; this person is called one to be led (neyya). Having developed these four types of persons, they become three. Among those persons, for the person of quick intuition, there is insight preceded by serenity (samatha-pubbaṅgamā vipassanā). For the person to be led, there is serenity preceded by insight (vipassanā-pubbaṅgamo samatha). For the person who understands through elaboration, serenity and insight occur coupled together (yuganaddhā).

For the person of quick intuition, there is gentle teaching; for the person to be led, there is sharp teaching; for the person who understands through elaboration, there is teaching that is both sharp and gentle. For the person of quick intuition, there is the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā); for the person to be led, there is the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā); for the person who understands through elaboration, there is the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). Thus, the escape from the round of rebirths for these persons through the four practices should be understood.

In that unwholesome side, the following is defilement (saṃkilesa): there are three unwholesome roots, three contacts, three feelings, three mental explorations (upavicāra), three defilements, three thoughts (vitakka), three fevers (pariḷāha), three conditioned characteristics, and three states of suffering (dukkhatā).

The three unwholesome roots are: the unwholesome root of greed (lobha), the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa), and the unwholesome root of delusion (moha). The three contacts are: contact felt as pleasant, contact felt as painful, and contact felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant. The three feelings are: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. The three mental explorations are: exploration accompanied by joy (somanassa), exploration accompanied by grief (domanassa), and exploration accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā). The three defilements are: lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha). The three thoughts are: sensual thought (kāma-vitakka), thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka), and thought of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka). The three fevers are: fever born of lust, fever born of hatred, and fever born of delusion. The three conditioned characteristics are: arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhitī), and dissolution (vaya). The three states of suffering are: the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkhatā), the suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā), and the suffering of formations (saṃkhāra-dukkhatā).

Among those unwholesome roots, due to what cause does the unwholesome root of greed arise? It arises due to the three kinds of objects: the pleasant, the unpleasant, and the neutral. Among those three, the unwholesome root of greed arises due to a pleasant object. Thus, due to a pleasant object, contact felt as pleasant arises. Dependent on contact felt as pleasant, pleasant feeling arises. Dependent on pleasant feeling, mental exploration accompanied by joy arises. Dependent on mental exploration accompanied by joy, lust arises. Dependent on lust, sensual thought arises. Dependent on sensual thought, fever born of lust arises. Dependent on fever born of lust, the conditioned characteristic of arising (uppāda) occurs. Dependent on the conditioned characteristic of arising, the state of suffering due to change occurs.
335:
Due to what cause does the unwholesome root of hatred arise? The unwholesome root of hatred arises due to an unpleasant object. Thus, due to an unpleasant object, contact felt as painful arises; dependent on contact felt as painful, painful feeling arises; dependent on painful feeling, mental exploration accompanied by grief arises; dependent on mental exploration accompanied by grief, hatred arises; dependent on hatred, thought of ill-will arises; dependent on thought of ill-will, fever born of hatred arises; dependent on fever born of hatred, the conditioned characteristic called the alteration of what is present (ṭhitassa aññathatta) arises; dependent on the conditioned characteristic called the alteration of what is present, the feeling called the state of suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkhatā) arises.

Due to what cause does the unwholesome root of delusion arise? The unwholesome root of delusion arises due to a neutral object. Thus, due to a neutral object, contact felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant arises; dependent on contact felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises; dependent on neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, mental exploration accompanied by equanimity arises; dependent on mental exploration accompanied by equanimity, delusion arises; dependent on delusion, thought of cruelty arises; dependent on thought of cruelty, fever born of delusion arises; dependent on fever born of delusion, the conditioned characteristic called disappearance (vaya) arises; dependent on the conditioned characteristic called disappearance, the state of suffering of formations (saṃkhata-dukkhatā) arises. This is the exposition of the three defilements; this method is called the Triple-Person Method (Tipukkhala Naya) in the wholesome side.

Thus, the unwholesome roots are only three; there is no fourth or fifth. They occur from the three contacts and three feelings up to the suffering of formations. Whatever unwholesome side there is, all that unwholesome side converges only into the three unwholesome roots.

In that method, what is the wholesome side? The three wholesome roots; the three kinds of wisdom, namely, wisdom resulting from listening (sutamayī-paññā), wisdom resulting from reflection (cintāmayī-paññā), and wisdom resulting from mental development (bhāvanāmayī-paññā); the three concentrations beginning with concentration with initial and sustained thought; the three trainings beginning with the training in higher virtue; the three signs, namely, the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta), the sign of exertion (paggaha-nimitta), and the sign of equanimity (upekkhā-nimitta); the three thoughts beginning with the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka); the three faculties beginning with the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmīti-indriya) should be understood in detail. There are also the three mental explorations, namely, exploration of renunciation, exploration of non-ill-will, and exploration of non-cruelty; the three seekings, namely, seeking for sensual pleasures (kāmesanā), seeking for existence (bhavesanā), and seeking for the holy life (brahmacariyesanā); and the three aggregates, namely, the aggregate of virtue (sīla-kkhandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-kkhandha), and the aggregate of wisdom (paññā-kkhandha).
336:
In that method, there is the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha); that wholesome root fulfills wisdom based on learning (sutamaya-paññā). When wisdom based on learning is fulfilled, it fulfills concentration with initial and sustained thought (savita-kkasavicāra-samādhi). When concentration with initial and sustained thought is fulfilled, it fulfills the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā). When the training in higher mind is fulfilled, it fulfills the sign of tranquility (samatha-nimitta). When the sign of tranquility is fulfilled, it fulfills the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka). When the thought of renunciation is fulfilled, it fulfills the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya). When the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' is fulfilled, it fulfills the sustained thought of renunciation (nekkhammūpavicāra). When the sustained thought of renunciation is fulfilled, it abandons the search for sensual pleasures (kāmesanā); the abandonment of the search for sensual pleasures fulfills the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha).

The wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa) fulfills wisdom based on reflection (cintāmaya-paññā). When wisdom based on reflection is fulfilled, it fulfills concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only (avitakkavicāramatta-samādhi). When concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only is fulfilled, it fulfills the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). When the training in higher virtue is fulfilled, it fulfills the sign of equanimity (upekkhā-nimitta). When the sign of equanimity is fulfilled, it fulfills the thought of non-ill will (abyāpāda-vitakka). When the thought of non-ill will is fulfilled, it fulfills the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya). When the faculty of final knowledge is fulfilled, it fulfills the sustained thought of non-ill will (abyāpādūpavicāra). When the sustained thought of non-ill will is fulfilled, it abandons the search for existence (bhavesanā); the abandonment of the search for existence fulfills the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).

The wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha) fulfills wisdom based on mental development (bhāvanāmaya-paññā). When wisdom based on mental development is fulfilled, it fulfills concentration without initial and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra-samādhi). When concentration without initial and sustained thought is fulfilled, it fulfills the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). When the training in higher wisdom is fulfilled, it fulfills the sign of exertion (paggaha-nimitta). When the sign of exertion is fulfilled, it fulfills the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya). When the faculty of one who has known is fulfilled, it fulfills the sustained thought of non-harming (avihiṃsūpavicāra). When the sustained thought of non-harming is fulfilled, it fulfills the search for the holy life (brahmacariyasanā). When the search for the holy life is fulfilled, it fulfills the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha).

Thus, these three factors which belong to the wholesome side are indicated by all wholesome states through three types of triad expositions (tikaniddesa). The three doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha) are the conclusion of that wholesome side. Therein, by the first term, it is the desireless (appaṇihita); by the second term, it is emptiness (suññata); by the third term, it is the signless (animitta). This is called the second method named Tipukkhala.

In that method, there are these three types of persons: the one of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū), the one of expanded intuition (vipañcitaññū), and the one to be led (neyya). Among these three types of persons, those two types of persons who emerge from the round of rebirths by way of pleasant practice with quick intuition (sukhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññā) and pleasant practice with slow intuition (sukhāpaṭipadā dandhābiññā); and those two types of persons who emerge by way of painful practice with quick intuition (dukkhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññā) and painful practice with slow intuition (dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābiññā)...
337:
...who emerge from the round of rebirths, these four types of persons, by that distinction, become two: the one of view-temperament (diṭṭhicarita) and the one of craving-temperament (taṇhācarita). These four types having been, they become three; having been three, they become two. The states of defilement (saṃkilesa) of these two types of persons are: ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā), lack of shame (ahirika) and lack of fear of wrongdoing (anottappa), lack of mindfulness (asati) and lack of clear comprehension (asampajañña), the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and the fetters (saṃyojana), attachment (ajjhosāna) and dogmatic adherence (abhinivesa), I-making (ahaṃkāra) and mine-making (mamaṃkāra), lack of faith (assaddhiya) and being difficult to admonish (dovacassa), laziness (kosajja) and unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), doubt (vicikicchā) and covetousness (abhijjhā), not hearing the true Dhamma (asaddhammassavana) and lack of attainment (asamāpatti).

Among those states, ignorance, lack of shame, lack of mindfulness, the hindrances, attachment, I-making, lack of faith, laziness, doubt, and not hearing the true Dhamma constitute one direction (disā).

Craving, lack of fear of wrongdoing, lack of clear comprehension, the fetters, dogmatic adherence, mine-making, being difficult to admonish, unwise attention, covetousness, and lack of attainment constitute the second direction (disā). Among the ten dyads, the first ten terms should be made. They make the meaning known in brief. On the opposite side of the unwholesome side, among all the dyads, the second ten terms constitute the second direction.

Thus, the exposition of the suffering of unwholesome states is the Origin (samudaya). That state which takes in the flavor of the object and persists, namely mind and matter (nāma-rūpa), is Suffering (dukkha). Thus, these two truths—the Truth of Origin and the Truth of Suffering—are the first exposition (paṭhamaniddesa) of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.

In that method, what is the wholesome side? It is tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), clear knowledge (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa), mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña), shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), the abandoning of I-making and the abandoning of mine-making, right effort (sammāvāyāma) and wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), right mindfulness (sammāsati) and right concentration (sammāsamādhi), wisdom (paññā) and disenchantment (nibbidā), attainment (samāpatti) and hearing the true Dhamma, joy (somanassa) and practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapaṭipatti).

Among those states, tranquility, clear knowledge, mindfulness, shame, the abandoning of I-making, right effort, right mindfulness, wisdom, attainment, and joy constitute one direction. Insight, conduct, clear comprehension, fear of wrongdoing, the abandoning of mine-making, wise attention, right concentration, disenchantment, hearing the true Dhamma, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma constitute the second direction. Thus, there are four directions of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method in both the wholesome side and the unwholesome side.
338:
Among those methods, those unwholesome terms that arise first on the unwholesome side are abandoned by wholesome states; those unwholesome terms are abandoned by the second terms on the wholesome side. Through the abandoning of those unwholesome terms, there is liberation of mind (cetovimutti) [the fruit of Non-returning] through the fading of lust (rāga-virāga). Those unwholesome terms that arise second on the unwholesome side are abandoned; those unwholesome terms are abandoned by the first terms on the wholesome side. Through the abandoning of those unwholesome terms, there is liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) [the fruit of Arahantship] through the fading of ignorance (avijjā-virāga) as the conclusion. Among these three methods, the first method is called Sīhavikkīḷita. These eight terms, consisting of four wholesome and four unwholesome, are called the root terms (mūlapada). In terms of meaning (atthanaya), the second method is called Tipukkhala. That method is led by six states. It leads both the wholesome roots and the unwholesome roots. Thus, these six terms and the eight root terms mentioned before, these fourteen terms are included among the eighteen root terms. Among those methods, the last one, the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, is led by four states. These four states—ignorance (avijjā), craving (taṇhā), tranquility (samatha), and insight (vipassanā)—along with these eighteen root terms, are shown in the three methods.

In those methods, all wholesome states are subsumed within the nine wholesome terms. Among those nine roots, four terms are in the Sīhavikkīḷita method, three terms are in the Tipukkhala method, and two terms are in the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. These are the sides of the wholesome. All wholesome states are associated with those nine wholesome terms. Among those methods, these nine wholesome terms are shown as four terms in the Sīhavikkīḷita method, three in the Tipukkhala method, and two in the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.

In the four terms of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, the eighteen root terms are subsumed. How are they subsumed? These five terms on the wholesome side—tranquility (samatha), non-greed (alobha), non-hate (adosa), the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā), and the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā)—resort to tranquility. These four terms—insight (vipassanā), non-delusion (amoha), the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), and the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā)—resort to insight. These nine wholesome terms are associated with the two terms. Similarly, on the unwholesome side, among the nine unwholesome root terms, these five terms—craving (taṇhā), greed (lobha), hate (dosa), the perception of beauty (subha-saññā), and the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā)—resort to craving. These four terms—ignorance (avijjā), delusion (moha), the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā), and the perception of self (atta-saññā)—resort to ignorance. These nine unwholesome terms are well summarized. Thus, the three methods do not enter into a single method. In this way, the eighteen root terms should be pointed out in the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.
339:
How do the eighteen root terms associate in the Tipukkhala method? Among the nine wholesome terms, these four terms—insight (vipassanā), non-delusion (amoha), the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), and the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā); and these four terms—non-delusion (amoha), tranquility (samatha), non-greed (alobha), and the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā); and greed and hate—thus, these nine terms should be associated with the three wholesome [roots]. Among those methods, in the nine unwholesome terms, these four terms—craving (taṇhā), greed (lobha), the perception of beauty (subha-saññā), and the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā)—are the unwholesome root of greed. These four terms—ignorance (avijjā), delusion (moha), the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā), and the perception of self (atta-saññā)—along with delusion and hate, are those nine terms; those nine terms should be associated with the three unwholesome [roots]. In this way, the eighteen root terms are associated with the wholesome roots and pointed out by the Tipukkhala method.

How do the eighteen root terms associate in the Sīhavikkīḷita method? Craving and the perception of beauty are called the first perversion (vipallāsa). Greed and the perception of pleasure are called the second perversion. Ignorance and the perception of permanence are called the third perversion. Delusion and the perception of self are called the fourth perversion. Thus, the nine unwholesome roots are associated with the four terms. Among those methods, in the nine wholesome root terms, tranquility and the perception of foulness are called the first foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Non-greed and the perception of suffering are called the second foundation of mindfulness. Insight and the perception of impermanence are called the third foundation of mindfulness. Non-delusion and the perception of non-self are called the fourth foundation of mindfulness.

These eighteen root terms enter into the Sīhavikkīḷita method. The ground (bhūmi), the lust (rāga), and the hate (dosa) of these three methods enter into a single method. When the unwholesome states or wholesome states of one method are known, the opposite states should be sought. Having sought the opposite, that method should be pointed out. It has been pointed out in that method. Just as all methods enter into one method, so they should be pointed out. The eighteen root terms also enter into one method. When that state is known, all states become known.

Among these three methods, the conclusion of the Sīhavikkīḷita method is the four fruits. By the first face (disā), the first fruit; by the second face, the second fruit; by the third face, the third fruit; and by the fourth face, the fourth fruit. The conclusion of the Tipukkhala method is the three doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha). By the first face, the desireless (appaṇihita); by the second face, the void (suññata); and by the third face, the signless (animitta). The conclusion of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method is liberation of mind (cetovimutti) [the fruit of Non-returning] through the fading of lust and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) [the fruit of Arahantship] through the fading of ignorance.
340:
The conclusion (of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method) is: by the first aspect (disā), there is deliverance of mind through the fading of lust (the fruit of Non-returning); by the second aspect, there is deliverance through wisdom through the fading of ignorance (the fruit of Arahantship).

These three methods involve the surveying of the eighteen root-terms of these three methods; this is called the Disālocana (Directional Survey) method. Having surveyed, one knows that "this dhamma resorts to that dhamma," and thus there is right application in both the wholesome side and the unwholesome side; this method is called Aṅkusa (The Hook). These are the five methods.

## Here are the summary verses (Uddānagāthā)
Craving and ignorance, greed, hatred, and likewise delusion,
And the four perversions (vipallāsa)—these are the nine terms in the plane of defilements (kilesabhūmi).

Those foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), tranquility (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the wholesome roots,
All these wholesome things are the nine terms in the plane of faculties (indriyabhūmi).

All that is wholesome is associated with nine terms, and the unwholesome likewise with nine;
These are the root-terms, which together make eighteen terms.

Craving and ignorance, tranquility and insight,
That method which leads by being associated with all these is the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.

That which leads by the wholesome roots, or by both wholesome and unwholesome roots,
To the meaning that is real, true, and unerring—that method they call Tipukkhala (The Three-Pronged).

That which leads the dhammas by means of the perversions,
And by the defilements and faculties—that method they call the guidance named Sīhavikkīḷita (The Lion's Play).

In the explained discourse, by means of wholesomeness and unwholesomeness,
It surveys the three aspects (disā)—this method is named Disālocana.

That method which, having surveyed with Disālocana, takes up and brings together
All wholesome and unwholesome things—this is the Aṅkusa method.

## Origin of the Methods.
## In the Peṭakopadesa, the exposition of the Suttavibhaṅga by the Elder Mahākaccāyana is completed.
341:
Those tetrads (groups of four) which are unwholesome and wholesome are shown in the Sīhavikkīḷita method. The triads (groups of three) which are wholesome and unwholesome are shown in the Tipukkhala method. The dyads (groups of two) which are wholesome and unwholesome are shown in the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.

Among those two pure wholesome dhammas, the analysis of that meaning in the triads is called the plane of existence (bhavabhūmi). Furthermore, the entire meaning is indicated by three phrasings (byañjana). Those meanings are called the 'Tattaka' (the 'so-many'). When one proceeds to indicate the plane of non-existence (natthibhūmi) for a meaning by four terms and twenty-eight parts, it is indicated by only four terms. Thus, the non-distortion (invariability) of what is indicated is called the Measure (pamāṇa).

Just as all concentrations (samādhi) are to be sought within the three concentrations—namely, concentration with initial and sustained thought, concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only, and concentration without initial or sustained thought—this is the Measure; there is no fourth concentration. Likewise, the three kinds of wisdom—wisdom based on reflection (cintāmayā-paññā), wisdom based on learning (sutamayā-paññā), and wisdom based on mental development (bhāvanāmayā-paññā)—are indicated in all wisdoms. There is no fourth wisdom. If it is not wisdom based on reflection, nor learning, nor development, then that person has no wisdom. The unwaveringness (non-distraction) of these dhammas is called the Measure (pamāṇa).

The Peṭakopadesa by the Elder Mahākaccāyana, a dweller of the Jambu Grove (Jambuvana), is completed.

## The Treatise of Peṭakopadesa is finished.
